title: Ground Truth

modules.title: Thinking in ML
modules.blurb: What a model is, which kind of problem you are looking at, how to frame it, and how to work with an assistant without being fooled.
modules.mission: Take one question you were asked this month. Write five lines: the decision it feeds, what kind of problem it is, what one row would be, the target with its time window, and who is not eligible.

modules.title: The scoreboard
modules.blurb: How to judge a prediction before you know how any model works: hold-outs, baselines, the right measures, and whether a difference is real.
modules.mission: Find one accuracy-style number in a recent report or deck. Work out what doing nothing would score, and ask for the precision and recall behind it.

modules.title: Core models, and reading the work
modules.blurb: The three models everything else is built from, what goes wrong before a model is even fitted, and how to audit a script you could not have written.
modules.mission: Ask your assistant for a baseline and a simple model on a table you know well, in stages. Make it print row counts after every step. Find one count that surprises you.

modules.title: Stronger models, honestly validated
modules.blurb: Memorising versus learning, validation that cannot cheat, when complexity earns its keep, and who the model is quietly wrong about.
modules.mission: For a model your team uses or is building, ask for training and test scores side by side, how the settings were chosen, and the result for your two most important client segments.

modules.title: From drivers to decisions
modules.blurb: The gap between what predicts and what causes, how to close it with experiments or careful comparisons, and how a score becomes an action you can measure.
modules.mission: Find one 'X drives Y' claim in a recent deck. Write down a hidden common cause that could produce it, and which evidence tier the claim really stands on: observed, adjusted or tested.

modules.title: Time
modules.blurb: Forecasts and their honest ranges, alerts that do not cry wolf, and how long customers last.
modules.mission: Pick one alert or weekly report your team watches. Count how often it fired last quarter and how many were real. Then find out what 'expected' it is comparing against.

modules.title: No labels, text, and the playbook
modules.blurb: Segments without an answer column, text as numbers, language models as tools you can score, and the whole course on one page.
modules.mission: Take the next new question you are asked through the ten-minute path before you open your assistant.

path: What decision does this feed, and who will act on it?
What kind of problem is it: a category, a number, groups, something unusual, a series, a cause, text?
What is one row, what is the target, and what is the timeline (snapshot, what is known before, what happens after)?
What is the baseline: the rule or the naive answer you would use today?
How will we know it worked, on which rows, with which measure, and how wide is the noise?
Simplest model first. Add complexity only if it beats the simple one by more than the noise.
Who is it wrong about? Cut the result by the segments the business cares about.
Is this a prediction, or a claim about cause? If cause: observed, adjusted or tested?
How will it be used, measured and watched once it ships?

p: A course in machine-learning fundamentals built for one working analyst: someone fluent in SQL and dashboards whose analysis is now largely written by an AI assistant. The skill it trains is directing and auditing that work: framing a problem, choosing an approach, briefing in stages, and knowing what the output must show before it can be believed.

It is deliberately not a churn course. Churn, spend, video adoption, hitting a CPA goal, forecasting, alerts and support tickets are examples; each lesson says its idea in general form, and the questions that come back in review are set in other domains on purpose.

Every table in the course was generated from equations written for it. That makes two things possible that real data cannot offer. Nothing confidential is involved, so the files are safe to hand to any assistant. And the true answer is known: a practice can be switched on for every advertiser and off again and the difference counted, which is the only reason a lesson can say how far a naive comparison lands from the truth.
The cost is that simulated worlds are tidier than real ones. Where a result is a property of the simulation rather than of machine learning, the lesson says so.
No number in a lesson was typed from memory. One pipeline generates the data, fits every model with scikit-learn and writes every result to a single file; lessons may quote only what is in that file.

A script also compares every figure in every lesson with that file. It is a weak check, and it is better to say so: when 206 figures were deliberately corrupted to test it, it flagged about 34 percent of them. A wrong number usually still matches some other number in the file. So it is kept as a tripwire, and the real checking was done by readers.

about.h: Who checked it, and how good the checkers were
p: Before any lesson was written, the syllabus went to a council of five independent seats: two Gemini models (a curriculum expert and an adtech practitioner), a Gemini Deep Research comparison with established curricula, and two fresh Claude agents, one playing the learner and one a sceptical expert who re-ran the code. It found a bug in a true-effect calculation, results that were artefacts of how test cases had been planted, an unfair comparison, a missing gap month between training and test data, and a syllabus still built around one problem. The evidence was rebuilt and the course re-planned from 30 lessons to 37 before writing began.

After writing, seven independent readers went through the lessons: a Gemini model holding the results file, four Claude agents acting as hard-to-please ML experts, and two acting as the learner. A review that finds nothing proves nothing unless you know what it would have found, so 58 errors were first planted in the copies they read: 48 wrong figures and 10 false statements. The four experts caught 58 of the 58 planted in their lessons. The Gemini reader caught 30 of 30 in the 20 lessons it finished in that round.

The same readers raised 186 genuine findings, from wrong keyed logic in a question to lessons that tried to teach five ideas at once. A separate editor agent, which had written none of the lessons, ruled on each one against the results file: 134 accepted, 41 accepted in part, 3 rejected with reasons, 3 set aside as belonging to a different course, 5 no longer applicable. Some findings were about the results file itself, such as a noise estimate that understated the truth by about a fifth; those were corrected in the evidence first and the lessons second.

Every corrected lesson was then fact-checked again by Gemini against the results file. Of 35 lessons, 11 came back clean on that pass; the points raised on the others were fixed or answered before publishing.

about.h: How the audio was made and checked
p: The narration is synthetic speech generated with Gemini, one clip per screen, in a voice chosen by audition: five voices read the same passage and a separate model scored them for clarity of numbers and ease over long listening. Every one of the 319 clips was then transcribed back to text by a different model and compared with its script. On average 1.5 percent of words differed, almost all of it spelling of numbers and contractions; clips with a real difference were re-recorded.

Every slide of every lesson is measured by a script at four screen sizes, from a phone to a desktop, for anything that overflows its frame or falls below a readable size. The pages were reviewed from screenshots by a Gemini model acting as art director (its first verdict was blunt: 6.5, 6.5 and 5.5 out of 10 for pretty, engaging and not confusing), reworked, and reviewed again. A Claude agent used the site as the learner would, and another read the code for security holes and ways to lose your progress.

Deep learning beyond one honest comparison, recommender systems, problems where the row is an impression, a click or an auction, fairness and stand-in columns as a topic of their own, and everything about running models in production. None of it is hard to add once the fundamentals here are in place, and the tutor button will take you into any of them.

This site sits behind a login. It stores only your progress: which lessons you finished and your review schedule. It makes no requests to any third party. The tutor is Claude on your own subscription. When the tutor relay is running on your computer, a question and the part of the lesson you asked from travel to Claude Code there and the answer comes back to the page; the site itself never holds a Claude credential. When the relay is not running, the question opens Claude in a new tab instead. Nothing is sent until you ask, and the conversation is kept only in your browser.

triage.q: Finance asks: 'How many dollars will each advertiser spend next quarter?' Which kind of problem is this?
options: Predicting a category (classification)
Predicting a number (regression)
Finding groups without an answer column (clustering)
Judging what is unusual (anomaly detection)
triage.why: The thing to predict is an amount, and past advertisers show what the amount turned out to be. A category question would be 'will they spend at all?'.

triage.q: Product asks: 'What kinds of advertisers do we actually have?' There is no column that says which kind each one is. Which kind of problem?
options: Classification
Forecasting
Clustering
A causal question
triage.why: No answer column exists for past cases, so nothing can be predicted. The task is to look for groups, and then to check they mean something.

triage.q: Leadership asks: 'If we turned auto-bidding on by default, would advertisers do better?' Which kind of problem?
options: Classification: predict who does well
Regression: predict performance
A causal question: what happens if we change something
Clustering: group similar advertisers
triage.why: They want to know the effect of an action, not who is likely to do well. A model that predicts well can still be useless as advice; this needs an experiment or a careful comparison.

triage.q: Operations asks: 'Is today's drop in conversions something to worry about?' Which kind of problem?
options: Anomaly detection: is this far from what was expected?
Classification: will conversions fall?
Clustering: which days are alike?
A causal question: what caused the drop?
triage.why: The question is whether today is unusual, which first needs a statement of what was expected. Why it happened is a separate question that comes after.

triage.q: Sales asks: 'Which of these 5,000 leads should we call first?' Past leads are marked won or lost. Which framing fits best?
options: Cluster the leads and call the biggest cluster
Predict won or lost, then rank leads by the score
Forecast the total number of wins next month
Flag leads that look unusual
triage.why: There is an answer column for past cases and the output needed is an order to work in. A score for each lead, sorted, is a ranked list. A forecast of the total would not say whom to call.

triage.q: Support asks: 'Sort incoming tickets into billing, tracking, policy and other.' You have 200 tickets a human already sorted. Which kind of problem?
options: Clustering, because it is text
Classification, with text as the input
Regression
Forecasting
triage.why: The categories are given and past tickets carry the right answer, so it is prediction of a category. That the input is text changes how it is turned into numbers, not what kind of problem it is.

triage.q: Planning asks: 'How much platform spend should we expect each day in December?' Which kind of problem?
options: Classification
Forecasting: project a dated series forward
Clustering
A causal question
triage.why: Time is the main axis: the task is to carry a dated series forward, with its trend, weekly rhythm and holidays. It is still predicting a number, but it must be tested from a past date forward, never on shuffled days.

triage.q: Retention asks: 'Which at-risk advertisers should our team phone?' You already have a churn score for everyone. What is still missing?
options: Nothing: phone the highest scores
A clustering of the at-risk advertisers
Evidence of who changes because of a call, which a churn score does not give
A longer list
triage.why: A churn score says who is likely to leave, not who can be persuaded. Many of the highest scores will leave whatever anyone does. Knowing who responds to a call needs data where calls were assigned at random.

triage.q: A manager says: 'Advertisers who use our new report builder renew more. Let's push everyone to use it.' What kind of claim is this, and what is it resting on?
options: A prediction, well supported
A causal claim resting on an observed association
A forecast
A tested result
triage.why: Recommending the action assumes the report builder causes renewals. All that was seen is that the two go together; engaged advertisers may both use more features and renew more anyway.

triage.q: Success asks: 'How long does a typical advertiser stay with us?' A third of advertisers joined this year and are still active. What must the method handle?
options: Nothing special: average the lifetimes of those who left
Advertisers who have not left yet, about whom we only know they lasted at least this long
The weekly rhythm in sign-ups
Missing values in spend
triage.why: Averaging only those who left counts the quick leavers and ignores everyone still here. A time-to-event method uses the still-active advertisers for as long as they have been watched.

triage.q: You are asked to 'build an ML model' that flags advertisers whose spend fell more than 50 percent week on week. What is the right first reaction?
options: Start with gradient boosting
Ask whether a rule or a report already answers it
Collect more data
Cluster the advertisers first
triage.why: The request describes a rule with a known column and a known cut-off. A model earns its place when the pattern involves many columns and the cut-offs are not known in advance; here a query does the job.

triage.q: Quality asks: 'Find publishers sending us suspicious traffic.' There are almost no confirmed cases to learn from. Which framing fits where you are today?
options: Classification: train on the confirmed cases
Anomaly detection: define normal traffic and look for what is far from it
Forecasting
Regression on click volume
triage.why: With hardly any confirmed cases there is too little to learn a category from. You can still describe normal and rank what is far from it, then have people check the top of the list, which also starts building the labelled cases a classifier would need later.

lessons.title: From rules to learned models
lessons.subtitle: What does a model do that your CASE WHEN does not?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can explain a model as a rule whose columns, cut-offs and weights were chosen by data, and point to the row, the features, the label and the score or prediction in any modelling task.

predict.q: You flag advertisers with a hand-written rule: spend trend below 0.7. How is a machine-learning model different from that rule?
options: It is not a rule at all: it reasons about each advertiser one by one
It is the same kind of thing, but past outcomes choose the columns, cut-offs and weights
It works from information that is not in your table
It explains why advertisers leave, where a rule can only flag them
predict.reveal: The same kind of thing: a model is a rule whose columns, cut-offs and weights were chosen by checking against known outcomes. The lesson shows what that changes, and what it leaves to you.

segments.narration: Monday morning. An account director wants to know which advertisers are about to walk away. You know what you would do: flag every advertiser whose spend trend is below 0.7. Spend trend compares the last four weeks of spend with the four weeks before. Below 0.7 means spend is down thirty percent or more. A sensible rule. Hold on to it. That rule is already most of what a model is. So is any hand rule: block a traffic source as invalid when its click-through rate passes a line you picked, and you have built a small model too.

visual.title: From rules to learned models
visual.sub: Your CASE WHEN is already most of a model

segments.narration: Look at what you decided when you wrote it. You chose the column: spend trend, out of everything in the table. You chose the cut-off: 0.7, because it felt about right. And you chose that nothing else counts. Two advertisers with the same spend trend get the same flag, even if one logged in this morning and the other has been gone for two weeks. Three decisions, all yours. That is already a model, a small one, with one column and one hand-picked cut-off. Machine learning starts from a plain question. What if those decisions were checked against what actually happened?

visual.title: The rule you would write today
visual.code:
SELECT advertiser_id,
       CASE WHEN spend_trend < 0.7
            THEN 'at risk'
            ELSE 'ok'
       END AS flag
FROM advertisers;
visual.note: Three choices, all yours: the column, the cut-off, and that nothing else counts.

segments.narration: Checking needs past cases where the ending is known. The practice table for this course has 12,000 advertisers, one row each. It is simulated, so that the truth is knowable, but it is shaped like a table you could pull yourself. Each row has 17 columns describing one advertiser on one date: who they are, how they are set up, and what they did in the eight weeks before. Those input columns are called features. Then one more column. Did this advertiser stop spending in the 60 days after that date? That answer column is called the label. Features are what you knew at the time. The label is what happened next.

visual.title: 12,000 advertisers, one row each
visual.note: Features: 17 columns, all known on one date. Label: what happened in the 60 days after it. Simulated data.

segments.narration: Take one advertiser out of those 12,000. [[1]] Their spend trend is about 0.89, comfortably above your cut-off, so the rule says they are fine. [[2]] But they were active on only five of the last 28 days. [[3]] And over the next 60 days they did not spend a dollar. Your rule was never going to catch that one. It took a second column, and somebody had to know to look there. And that is one row out of thousands, each with its own mix of signals.

stats.label: spend trend: the rule says ok
days active
no spend in the next 60 days

segments.narration: So let the table do the checking. [[1]] Your rule is one column and one cut-off, picked by you. [[2]] A learned model can lean on many columns at once, each with its own cut-off or its own weight, which means how much that column counts. Is active days a better signal than spend trend? Is 0.7 really the best cut-off? Nobody tries every possible rule. The computer tries cut-offs and weights, measures how far its outputs are from what really happened to thousands of past advertisers, keeps the changes that shrink that miss, and repeats. That adjusting is called training. What comes out is still a rule. The data chose it, instead of you.

right.label: A learned model
right.sub: chosen by checking against known outcomes

segments.narration: The order matters. [[1]] First, learn. Training runs on past rows where the label is known. [[2]] Then freeze. The rule stops changing. [[3]] Then score. The frozen rule is applied to new rows, today's advertisers, whose ending nobody knows yet. For each one it returns a score, a number between 0 and 1. Higher means this advertiser looks more like the ones who left. It is not a yes or a no. Nor is it a percentage yet: whether 0.3 means a 30 percent chance is checked in a later lesson. How high is high enough to act on is a business decision, not something the model settles for you.

steps.label: Score
steps.sub: new rows get a number from 0 to 1

segments.narration: Here is the catch, and most of this course lives inside it. Matching the past is easy. Give the computer enough freedom and it can reproduce almost every known outcome in its table, the way you could memorise last year's exam answers. That proves nothing. What counts is whether the frozen rule holds up on rows it has never seen. And know what a model is not. It knows only the columns it was given. If an advertiser leaves because their marketing budget was cut, and no column records that, the model cannot see it. It finds patterns in your table. It does not understand your advertisers.

visual.text: Matching the past is easy. Holding up on new rows is the whole game.
visual.sub: And a model knows only the columns it was given.

segments.narration: Which leaves your part. Your assistant can write training code in minutes. It cannot know what churn should mean for your business, or when each column was actually recorded. You are the director and the auditor. So at this first stage, ask for a description of the table, not a model, and look for four things in it. [[1]] What one row is, in a sentence, with the row count. [[2]] Which column is the label, and exactly how it is defined. [[3]] The list of features, with the label nowhere in it. [[4]] And a few example rows you can hold up against accounts you know. Meanwhile, keep your hand rule: it is the bar any model has to beat.

visual.title: Brief and audit: describe the table first
items: What one row is, and how many rows there are
The label column, and its exact definition
The feature list, with the label not in it
Example rows you can check against accounts you know

segments.narration: So the next time a model lands on your desk, treat it as what it is, a rule, and ask what went in, what it was trained to match, and how it does on rows it never saw. Next, before anything gets built: which kind of problem is this?

visual.title: From rules to learned models
items: Your CASE WHEN is a model: one column, one cut-off, chosen by you
Learning: known outcomes choose the columns, cut-offs and weights; then freeze and score
It counts only on rows it has not seen, and it knows only its columns

takeaways: A model is a rule whose columns, cut-offs and weights were chosen by data instead of by you.
Training matches past rows with known labels; the frozen model then scores each new row, from 0 to 1 for a yes-or-no outcome.
Matching the past proves nothing: what counts is new rows, and a model knows only the columns it was given.

quiz.concept: a model is a learned rule
quiz.q: Your assistant trains a model on past advertisers and reports: 'It leans most on spend trend and active days, each with its own cut-off.' The account director asks who decided all that. Which reply is accurate?
options: The assistant did: it picked those columns and cut-offs from what it knows about advertisers in general
Past outcomes did, among the columns we supplied. What churn means, and which columns exist, we chose
Nobody did: a model weighs up each advertiser individually and has no fixed columns or cut-offs at all
The data did, all of it, including what counts as churned, so nobody's opinion is in the model at all
quiz.why: Training chooses among the columns it was given, and sets their cut-offs and weights, by checking against known outcomes. It does not choose what the outcome means or which columns were put in the table: those stay your decisions, so 'the data decided everything' goes too far. And the assistant only ran the training; the cut-offs did not come from its general knowledge.

quiz.concept: matching the past is not the test
quiz.q: The assistant reports: 'I trained a model on all 12,000 advertisers. It reproduces the known outcome for almost every one of them, so it is ready to use.' What is the right read?
options: Good news: reproducing the known outcomes is exactly what training a model is supposed to achieve
The code must be broken: no honest model matches its known outcomes that closely
Fine, provided all 17 feature columns were used and not just a convenient handful of them
No evidence yet: those are the rows it was adjusted to match. Ask about advertisers it never saw
quiz.why: Matching the rows a model was trained on is the easy part and says nothing about new advertisers, which is the only place the model will be used. It is not proof of a bug either: the result is simply untested, so the next request is for results on rows the model never saw.

quiz.q: Sales wants inbound leads ranked by how likely each is to become a paying customer. You have last year's leads with company size, source channel, pages viewed, and whether each one eventually paid. Which description gets the vocabulary right?
options: Each lead is a row; size, channel and pages viewed are features; 'eventually paid' is the label
Each lead is a row; all four columns are features, so that the model can use everything available
Each lead is a row; 'eventually paid' is a feature; the ranking the model produces is the label
Each column is a row of the model; the label is the list of leads that sales should call first
quiz.why: Features are what you know about a lead at the time; the label is the known outcome the model is trained to match. Feeding 'eventually paid' in as a feature hands the model the answer, and the ranking it produces is built from scores, not labels.

quiz.concept: a model knows only its columns
quiz.q: A frozen churn model gives a large gaming advertiser a low score. Their account manager knows the client's marketing lead resigned last week and all budgets are on hold. What is the right read?
options: Trust the score: it was learned from thousands of advertisers, and one anecdote should not outweigh that
The model has been shown to be wrong, so it should be switched off until it has been retrained
The score reflects only the model's columns. This news is in none of them, so it should override the score here
Type the resignation into the account notes and score the advertiser again, so the model can take it into account
quiz.why: A model sees only the columns it was trained on, and none of them records a resignation, so the account manager holds information the score cannot contain. Scoring again does not help, because a frozen model cannot use a column it never learned from; and one blind spot is no reason to discard the model for every other account.

review.concept: features, label and score

variants.q: A colleague wants to predict which new creatives will lose half their click-through rate within two weeks of launch. She has 9,000 past creatives with format, headline length, launch-day CTR, and whether each one did lose half its CTR. What is the label?
options: Launch-day CTR, because CTR is the metric the team cares about
The number between 0 and 1 the model gives each new creative
Whether the creative lost half its CTR within two weeks
Format, because it separates the two groups most clearly
variants.why: The label is the known outcome for past cases that the model is trained to match: here, whether CTR halved. Launch-day CTR is known at the start, so it is a feature, and the number the model returns for a new creative is a score.

variants.q: A model built to flag invalid traffic, trained on sources that were later confirmed valid or invalid, returns 0.83 for a new source. What is that number?
options: A score: it resembles past invalid sources; where to draw the line is still your call
A verdict: the model has established that the traffic from this source is in fact invalid
A measurement: about 83 percent of the clicks from this source are invalid
A label: the source can now be added to the training table as a confirmed case
variants.why: A model returns a score between 0 and 1, where higher means the row looks more like past positive cases. It is not a yes or no, not a share of clicks, and not a confirmed outcome: labels come from what actually happened, never from the model's own output.

variants.q: Finance wants a model that predicts each client's revenue for the coming quarter. You have three years of quarterly history per client. Which rows can the model be trained on?
options: Only the latest quarter, since it is closest to the one being predicted
Client-quarters for which the following quarter's revenue is already known
Every client-quarter, with the unknown revenue after the latest one set to zero
Only the largest clients, whose revenue is recorded most carefully
variants.why: Training adjusts a model until its outputs match known outcomes, so it needs rows whose label already exists. The latest quarter has no outcome yet: those are the rows you score, and writing zero where the answer is unknown would teach the model something false.

review.concept: matching the past is not the test

variants.q: An assistant trains a lead-scoring model on last year's leads and says it 'correctly reproduces the outcome of 98 percent of them'. What does that tell you about next month's leads?
options: It should be right about roughly 98 percent of them as well
Very little: last year's leads are the cases it was adjusted to match
It will do a bit worse, so take about ten points off to be safe
Nothing can be known about any model until it is running in production
variants.why: A model can match the cases it was trained on without having learned anything that carries over, so the 98 is not a forecast, and there is no standard discount to apply to it. You do not have to wait for production either: check it on leads the model never saw.

variants.q: Two analysts each tuned a rule on last quarter's 40 confirmed invalid traffic sources. Analyst A's rule flags all 40; analyst B's flags 31. Which rule will catch more invalid sources next quarter?
options: A's rule: it caught every one of the confirmed cases
B's rule: a looser fit to the past always holds up better
A's rule, provided that it does not also flag too many valid sources
Unknown: both counts come from the cases the rules were tuned on
variants.why: Both numbers measure how well each rule matches the cases it was built around, which is the easy part. Catching all 40 may mean A's rule is better or merely more tailored to those 40, and a looser fit is not automatically better either. Only sources neither rule has seen can settle it.

variants.q: A model trained on last year's 8,000 advertisers matches their known churn outcomes almost perfectly. The success team wants to start calling from its list tomorrow. What do you ask for first?
options: Its results on advertisers that were not used to train it
The full training code, so you can read it line by line
More feature columns, to push the match closer still
The same check run again on those 8,000, to confirm the match is stable
variants.why: A match on training rows shows the model can reproduce the past, not that it holds up on new advertisers, which is where the list will be used. More columns would only tighten the fit to the past, repeating the check on the same 8,000 repeats the easy part, and reading code does not answer the question. Results on unseen rows do.

drill.q: In one sentence, what is the difference between a rule you write by hand and a machine learning model?
drill.a: They are the same kind of thing. In a model, the columns, the cut-offs and the weights are chosen by checking against past cases with known outcomes, instead of being chosen by you.

drill.q: A model reproduces almost every known outcome in the table it was trained on. Why is that not good news yet?
drill.a: Because matching the past is easy. The test that counts is how the frozen model does on rows it has never seen.

recall.prompt: Explain to a colleague, in about thirty seconds, what training a model does. Use the words feature, label and score.
recall.model_answer: You start with past rows where the outcome is known: the input columns are the features and the known outcome is the label. Training tries out which columns, cut-offs and weights make the output match those labels best, then freezes the result. Applied to a new row, the frozen model returns a score, between 0 and 1 for a yes-or-no outcome. It deserves trust only if it holds up on rows it never saw, and it knows nothing that is not in its columns.

lessons.ask_assistant: Before building anything, describe the table you would train on to answer this: [the question, in one sentence]. In one sentence, say what one row is, and give the row count and the number of distinct [units, such as advertisers, leads or creatives]. Name the label column, the outcome to be predicted, and write its exact definition in plain words. List every feature column with a one-line description; the label must not be in that list. Show five example rows including the label, with at least one row for [each outcome]. Do not train a model yet: stop and wait for my go-ahead.
audit_checklist: A one-sentence statement of what one row is, with the row count and the number of distinct units
The label column, named, with its definition in plain words
The full feature list, one line each, and the label is not in it
Example rows, label included, that you can check against accounts you know
transfer: Lead scoring: 'call anyone from a company with more than 200 staff' is a one-column rule; past won and lost leads could choose the columns and cut-offs instead.
Invalid traffic: a hand-set threshold on clicks per source, versus cut-offs learned from sources already confirmed valid or invalid.
Creative fatigue: 'refresh every 30 days' is a hand-picked cut-off; past creatives whose decline is already known could set it.

other_ways.approach: Keep the hand rule
other_ways.when: When it is cheap, people trust it, and nobody has yet shown that anything better is needed. It also becomes the bar any model has to beat.

other_ways.approach: A report cut by segment
other_ways.when: When the question is what is happening, not who is next: no prediction is required.

other_ways.approach: Ask the people who know the accounts
other_ways.when: When the reason sits in no column: account managers know things a table cannot hold.

glossary.def: A rule that turns a row's columns into an output, with its columns, cut-offs and weights chosen by data.
An input column: something known about the row at the time of the prediction.
The answer column: the known outcome of past rows, which the model is trained to match.
Adjusting a model until its outputs line up with the known labels of past rows.
The number a model returns for a row; for a yes-or-no outcome it runs from 0 to 1, and higher means more like past positive cases.

lessons.title: Which kind of problem is this?
lessons.subtitle: Five requests in one week: are they all the same job?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can sort a business question into its kind of problem with four triage questions, and choose between framings by the decision the answer feeds.

predict.q: An account director asks: 'Does auto-bidding actually help our advertisers?' What kind of problem is that?
options: A prediction: which advertisers will hit their goal
A prediction: what each advertiser's CPA will be
A grouping: sort advertisers by how they bid
A what-if: what would change if they switched it on
predict.reveal: A what-if, which is called a causal question: it asks about changing something, not predicting it. The lesson gives four questions that sort any request this way.

segments.narration: Here is one week of requests. Monday: which advertisers are going to leave? Tuesday: how much will each of them spend over the next eight weeks? Wednesday: what kinds of advertisers do we actually have? Thursday: spend dropped yesterday, is that unusual? Friday: does auto-bidding actually help? It is tempting to pass all five to your assistant with the same four words: build me a model. But these are five different kinds of problem, with different data, different methods and different ways of being wrong. Choosing the kind comes first. Get it wrong, and clean code will not rescue you.

visual.title: Which kind of problem is this?
visual.sub: Five requests, five different jobs

segments.narration: So here is the map. [[1]] Who will leave is a yes or a no for each advertiser. Predicting a category is called classification. Which leads will convert is the same kind, on a different topic. [[2]] How much will they spend is predicting a number. That is regression. [[3]] What kinds of advertisers do we have? Nobody has an answer column for that. Finding groups without one is clustering. [[4]] Is yesterday's drop unusual? Judging what is far from normal is anomaly detection. [[5]] Does auto-bidding help is not a prediction at all. It asks what would happen if you changed something, which makes it a causal question. [[6]] [[7]] Two more rows come later in the course: projecting a daily series forward, and reading or writing text.

visual.title: The map
rows: What kinds of advertisers do we have?
Clustering: find groups, no answer column
Causal: what if we change it?
What will platform spend be next month?
What is this support ticket about?
Language models: read or write text

segments.narration: You do not need to memorise seven names. You need four questions. [[1]] First: is there an answer column for past cases? Last lesson called that the label. If there is, you can learn to predict it: that is supervised learning. If not, decide which you are after: the groups, or the odd ones out. That is unsupervised learning. A third family, reinforcement learning, is not in this course. [[2]] Second: is the answer a category or a number? [[3]] Third: is time the main axis? Projecting one series forward is forecasting. Asking whether yesterday was strange is still about the unusual. [[4]] Fourth, and the one people skip: do I want to predict it, or change it? Knowing who will leave is prediction. Knowing what would make them stay is a causal question, and a model that predicts does not answer it.

visual.title: Four triage questions
items: Is there an answer column for past cases? If not: groups, or the unusual?
Is the answer a category or a number?
Is time the main axis? Projecting forward, or judging one day?
Do I want to predict it, or change it?

segments.narration: Now the awkward part. One business question can sit in several boxes. Take retention. [[1]] Frame it as a yes or no: will this advertiser stop spending in the next 60 days? [[2]] Frame it as a number: how many dollars will they spend in the next eight weeks? [[3]] Frame it as a length of time: how long do advertisers last? [[4]] Or frame it around action: which advertisers would stay because we called them? Same word in the meeting. Four different pieces of work, and four different things you would hand back.

visual.title: One question, four framings: retention
rows: Will they stop spending within 60 days?
How many dollars in the next 8 weeks?
How long: its own kind, in module 6
Who would stay because we called?

segments.narration: So which is right? None of them, in the abstract. The decision the answer feeds picks the framing. [[1]] Say the success team can call two hundred accounts a month. They need a ranked list, so a yes or no with a score is the fit. [[2]] Finance is building a revenue plan. A list of names is no use to them. They need dollars. [[3]] And if the real question is whether the calls are worth making at all, you need to know how many advertisers stay because of the call. A list of likely leavers does not tell you that. So before you choose a kind of problem, ask one thing. What will somebody do differently once they have the answer?

visual.title: The decision picks the framing
rows: Whom should the success team call?
Yes or no, with a score: a ranked list
What goes into the revenue plan?
Are the calls worth making at all?
How many stay because of the call
visual.note: A risk score ranks who may leave, not whom a call would save: a later lesson weighs that.

segments.narration: One more choice, and it is about ambition. Think of a ladder. [[1]] The bottom rung is a report: churn by vertical, by month. Sometimes that settles it and you are finished. [[2]] Next comes a rule, like spend trend below 0.7. [[3]] Then a simple model, where the data picks the columns and the weights. [[4]] Then a complex model, which can capture patterns a simple one misses, and is harder to explain and to check. Every rung up costs something. So climb only when the step pays, meaning the rung you are standing on has been tried and is not good enough for the decision. Start at the top, and you can spend a month modelling what a GROUP BY had already answered.

visual.title: The ladder: climb only when the step pays

steps.label: A simple model
steps.sub: data weighs the columns you supply

segments.narration: Which brings us to the brief. At this stage, do not ask your assistant for a model. Ask it to restate the problem before it writes any code. [[1]] What kind of problem it thinks this is, and why. [[2]] Which column is the answer column, or a plain statement that there is none. [[3]] What decision the output is supposed to feed. [[4]] And the lowest rung of the ladder that could answer it. If you asked whether a practice helps, and it describes a prediction of who will churn, stop right there. It has swapped your question for an easier one, and nothing built afterwards will repair that. And when the room cannot agree on a framing, ask for two mock outputs side by side, and let people choose.

visual.title: Brief and audit: restate before you build
items: What kind of problem, and why
The answer column, or "there is none"
The decision the output feeds
The lowest rung that could answer it

segments.narration: So when the next request lands, hold the code until you can name the kind of problem, the decision it feeds, and the lowest rung that could settle it. Next: once you have decided to predict something, you have to say exactly what, for whom, and by when.

visual.title: Which kind of problem is this?
items: Name the kind first: four triage questions
One question, several framings: the decision picks
Report, rule, simple model, complex model: climb only when it pays

takeaways: Name the kind of problem first: answer column or not, category or number, time or not, predict or change.
One business question has several framings; the decision it feeds picks the one to build.
Report, rule, simple model, complex model: climb a rung only when the one below is not good enough.

quiz.q: A stakeholder says: 'Build a churn model so we finally know what makes advertisers stay.' What is the best first response?
options: Agree: the columns the model leans on most heavily will show what makes advertisers stay
Two questions are tangled here: who will leave, and what would change it. Ask which one they need
Decline: nothing useful can be said about churn until a properly designed experiment has been run
Suggest clustering instead, because the goal is understanding advertisers, not predicting them
quiz.why: Who will leave is a prediction; what makes them stay asks what happens if something is changed, and a model that predicts does not answer that. Reading the model's strongest columns as levers is the tempting mistake: they show what goes along with churn, not what would alter it.

quiz.q: You ask the assistant: 'What kinds of advertisers do we have?' It comes back with a model that predicts churn in the next 60 days from 17 columns, plus a ranked list of risky accounts. What went wrong?
options: It stopped short: cut the ranked list into three risk tiers and those are the kinds
It should have predicted spend instead of churn, because spend is a number
It chose an answer column you never asked about; your question has none
Seventeen columns are too few to describe the different kinds of advertiser
quiz.why: 'What kinds do we have' has no answer column: it is a question about finding groups. The assistant quietly swapped it for a prediction of churn, which is a different kind of problem. Predicting spend instead would repeat the same swap with a different column, and cutting the risk list into tiers would still describe advertisers by an answer nobody asked about.

quiz.q: The traffic-quality team wants to 'use ML to find bad sources'. They have click logs for every source, but no source has ever been confirmed as invalid. A colleague proposes training a classifier. What is the right read?
options: A classifier needs past cases with a known answer; without them, look for the unusual or collect labels
Go ahead: given enough click logs, a classifier will work out for itself what invalid traffic looks like
Use regression instead: click counts are numbers, so the model should be predicting a number, not a category
Forecast each source's clicks: the sources that turn out hardest to forecast will be the invalid ones
quiz.why: The first triage question is whether past cases have an answer column. Here they do not, so there is nothing for a classifier to be trained to match, however many logs there are. The honest options are to judge which sources are far from normal, or to get some sources reviewed first.

quiz.q: The head of sales must decide which vertical gets an extra account manager, and asks which vertical loses the most advertisers. The assistant proposes a complex model on all 17 columns. What is your call?
options: Accept: the more columns a model uses, the more reliable its answer about verticals will be
Ask for a simple model first, and the complex one only if the simple model is not good enough
Reframe it as clustering, so that the natural groupings among the verticals can emerge
Start with a report: churn rate by vertical, with group sizes, answers the question asked
quiz.why: The question asked is about groups, not individual advertisers, so the bottom rung, a report of churn by vertical, already answers it; a simple model is a rung too high until the report has been shown not to be enough. Whether an extra account manager would reduce churn in that vertical is a separate question, about changing something, and no report of who left settles it.

review.concept: which kind of problem

variants.q: Pricing asks: 'If we raise the minimum daily budget, how many small advertisers will we lose?' Which kind of problem is this?
options: Classification: predict which small advertisers will churn
A causal question: it asks what happens if we change something
Regression: predict the daily budget of each small advertiser
Forecasting: project the number of small advertisers forward
variants.why: The question is about the effect of a change you would make. A classifier trained under today's pricing predicts who leaves as things are; it has never seen the higher minimum, so it cannot say what that change would do.

variants.q: Product asks: 'What types of publishers are in our network?' You have 30 columns per publisher, and nobody has ever assigned a type. Which kind of problem is this?
options: Clustering: finding groups, because there is no answer column
Classification: predict each publisher's type from its columns
Regression: predict a single quality number for each publisher
Anomaly detection: find the publishers that do not fit in
variants.why: No past publisher has a known type, so there is nothing to train a classifier to match; with no answer column, looking for groups is clustering. Anomaly detection also works without an answer column, but it asks who is unusual, not what the groups are.

variants.q: An ops lead asks: 'Did conversions from this traffic source look strange last night?' You have the source's hourly conversions for the past six months. Which kind of problem is this?
options: Forecasting: the data is a series over time, so project it forward
Classification: label each past hour as normal or strange
Anomaly detection: is last night far from this source's normal?
A causal question: work out what made conversions change
variants.why: The question is whether something is unusual, which is anomaly detection. Time being the main axis tempts you towards forecasting, and a forecast may well supply the expected value, but nobody asked what next month looks like. And no hour was ever labelled strange, so there is nothing to classify.

review.concept: the decision picks the framing

variants.q: The video team asks for 'a model for video adoption'. Sales can make 300 calls this quarter and is measured on how many advertisers adopt. Which framing fits?
options: A yes or no with a score: who is likely to adopt in the next 60 days
A number: the dollars of video spend each advertiser would bring in
A score and a dollar figure together, so sales can pick between them later
Groups: cluster the advertisers and describe the habits of each cluster
variants.why: The decision is whom to call with a fixed number of calls, and success is counted in adoptions, so a ranked yes or no score is the fit. Dollars sound richer, but nobody here is deciding on dollars; building two outputs to pick between later skips the question that should come first.

variants.q: Finance is building next quarter's revenue plan and asks to 'plug in the churn model', which gives each advertiser a score between 0 and 1. What is the mismatch?
options: Only the scale: multiplied by 100, each score becomes a share of the revenue
The plan should be built from clusters of advertisers, not from scores
A plan needs dollars; a score for leaving does not say how much is at stake
Only the cut-off: count every advertiser above one half as lost revenue
variants.why: A revenue plan is a decision about dollars, so the framing that fits predicts a number: how much each advertiser will spend. A score for leaving says nothing about whether the account is worth fifty dollars or fifty thousand, and rescaling it or cutting it at one half does not change that.

variants.q: The creative team plans production a month ahead and asks: 'When do our creatives wear out?' Analyst A proposes predicting, yes or no, whether each creative drops below a CTR floor next week. Analyst B proposes estimating how many days a creative lasts. Which framing serves the decision?
options: A's: a yes or no is the simplest framing and should always come first
B's: a production schedule needs to know how long creatives last
A's, run every week: the yes or no answers add up to what B gives
A third one: flag unusual drops in CTR, since wearing out is an anomaly
variants.why: The team is deciding how many replacements to produce and when, a month ahead, so it needs a length of time. A next-week yes or no would suit a different decision, such as which creatives to pause on Monday. The two framings are not interchangeable: a weekly yes or no says what is failing now, not how many replacements to schedule a month ahead.

drill.q: What are the four triage questions for working out which kind of problem you are facing?
drill.a: Is there an answer column for past cases. Is the answer a category or a number. Is time the main axis. And do I want to predict it, or change it.

drill.q: There is a ladder of four ways to answer a business question, from simplest to most complex. Name the rungs, and the rule for climbing.
drill.a: A report, a rule, a simple model, a complex model. Climb a rung only when the one below has been tried and is not good enough for the decision.

recall.prompt: A stakeholder says: 'We need machine learning for retention.' Talk through how you would work out what kind of problem that is.
recall.model_answer: First I would ask what decision the answer feeds, because retention can be framed as a yes or no within 60 days, as dollars, as how long advertisers last, or as who would stay because we acted. Then the four triage questions: is there an answer column, is it a category or a number, is time the main axis, and do we want to predict or to change. And I would start on the lowest rung, a report or a rule, and climb only if that is not enough.

lessons.ask_assistant: My request: [the question, in the stakeholder's words]. It feeds this decision: [who will do what differently with the answer]. Before writing any code, restate it. Say what kind of problem you think it is and why, and whether I am asking to predict something or to change it. Name the answer column and how many past rows have it filled in, or say plainly that there is none. Propose the simplest approach that could answer it (a report, a rule or a simple model) and describe what it would hand back. List any other reasonable framings, then stop and wait for my go-ahead.
audit_checklist: The kind of problem in plain words, with a reason; a question about changing something is not restated as a prediction
The answer column by name, with how many past rows have it filled in, or an explicit statement that there is none
The decision the output feeds, in one sentence that matches the one you gave
The lowest rung of the ladder that could answer it, proposed first, with what it would hand back
transfer: Creative fatigue: predicting which creatives will fade, and finding what would slow the fade, are two different kinds of problem.
Invalid traffic: with confirmed cases it is classification; with none, it is a question about what is unusual.
A forecast for finance: one daily series projected forward, not a score for each advertiser.

other_ways.approach: Start from the data instead of the question
other_ways.when: As a sanity check: if no answer column exists yet, some framings are simply not available today.

other_ways.approach: Sketch the same question in two framings
other_ways.when: When stakeholders cannot agree on what they need: two mock outputs side by side make the choice concrete.

other_ways.approach: Stay on the bottom rung with a report by segment
other_ways.when: When the decision is about groups (which vertical, which month) and not about individual advertisers.

glossary.def: Predicting a category, such as will churn or will not.
Predicting a number, such as dollars of spend.
Finding groups in rows that have no answer column.
Judging whether something is far from what is normal.
Learning from past rows that have an answer column, the label: classification and regression are both supervised.
Finding structure in rows with no answer column, such as clustering and anomaly detection. Reinforcement learning, learning by trial and reward, is a third family this course does not cover.
A question about what would happen if you changed something, as opposed to predicting what will happen anyway.

lessons.title: Framing: target, unit and time
lessons.subtitle: What exactly are you predicting, for whom, and by when?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can pin a label to a timeline (what counts, for which unit, in which window) and spot the rows that are not eligible, not yet observed, or invisible to a proxy.

predict.q: Churn is defined as 'no spend at all in the 60 days after the snapshot date'. A table is built from a snapshot taken 20 days ago. Which of its advertisers already have a definite label?
options: Only those who have spent since the snapshot: they stayed
Only those who have not spent since the snapshot: they churned
All of them: 20 days is long enough to see who has gone quiet
No row yet: every label needs the full 60 days
predict.reveal: Only the ones who have spent: a single day of spend inside the window makes them stayers. Everyone else could be pausing or gone, and the lesson shows how that quietly bends a churn rate in either direction.

segments.narration: Picture the meeting. Someone asks for a churn model, and you ask the obvious question back: what counts as churned? Take an advertiser who stopped spending for three weeks and then came back. One account manager says yes, churned, they went dark. Another says no, that client always pauses in spring. Finance says churn is when the contract ends. Nobody in the room agrees. A model will not settle it. It learns whatever definition you write down, faithfully, including a bad one. So the label, which you will also hear called the target, is a business decision. The same goes for any outcome a model predicts: whether an advertiser adopted the video format is just as arguable. Every label needs three things pinned down: what, who and when.

visual.title: Framing: target, unit and time
visual.sub: Is a three-week pause churn?

segments.narration: [[1]] Start with what. In the practice table, churned means no spend at all in the 60 days after a snapshot date. Not paused, not slowing down: nothing. Under that definition the three-week pauser stayed: they spent again inside the window. Shorten the window to two weeks and the same advertiser could count as churned, and you would be training a different model. [[2]] Then who. What is one row, the grain of the table? Here it is one advertiser at one snapshot date. Not one campaign, and not one advertiser per day. Settle that early, because every count and every rate that follows depends on it. [[3]] Then when, which is the part that goes wrong quietly.

visual.title: A label needs three things pinned down
items: What: no spend at all in the 60 days after the snapshot
Who: one row is one advertiser at one snapshot date
When: a timeline, with the snapshot date in the middle

segments.narration: Put it on a timeline. The snapshot date is the day you would actually make the prediction. [[1]] Everything the model is allowed to know comes from before it. In the practice table that is the eight weeks leading up to the snapshot, called the observation window. The features are built from it. [[2]] Everything you are trying to predict happens after it: the 60 days that follow, called the outcome window. The label is read from there. Features on one side, label on the other, and the snapshot date standing between them like a wall. If you cannot draw that picture for a table, you do not yet know what it predicts.

visual.title: Features before the snapshot, label after it
visual.note: The snapshot date is the day the prediction would be made.

segments.narration: Two groups of rows distort a label without any error message. [[1]] The first is the not eligible. An account that had already stopped spending before the snapshot is not a prediction. It is history. Leave those rows in, and any model looks clever for spotting advertisers who were already gone. So write down who is in. [[2]] The second is the not yet observed. Take a snapshot from 20 days ago. Anyone who has spent since is settled: they stayed. Anyone who has not is undecided. They may be gone for good, or three weeks into a pause. Count them as churned and the rate is too high. Default them to stayed and it is too low. So a snapshot enters the table only when its whole outcome window has passed.

visual.title: Two kinds of row that quietly distort a label
rows: Stopped before the snapshot: history, not a prediction
Snapshot 20 days ago: no spend yet may be a pause or a churn
No snapshot in the table until its window closes

segments.narration: Sometimes the thing you care about has no column at all. Take the other question you keep getting: which advertisers are happy? There is no happiness column, so you reach for a proxy, a measurable stand-in. Say happy means the advertiser hit their own CPA goal. Reasonable. [[1]] But a CPA exists only for advertisers with conversion tracking, about 58 percent of the total. [[2]] The rest drop out silently, and they are not a random sample. Advertisers with tracking churn at about 7 percent. Those without, about 18. So anything you conclude about happy advertisers is really about tracked advertisers. The size of that gap belongs to this simulated data. The habit of asking who a proxy cannot see belongs everywhere.

visual.title: "Happy" = hit their CPA goal. Who can that see?

right.label: Without tracking
right.sub: 4,984 advertisers · goal cannot be measured

segments.narration: Before a model ever sees a label, check it. First, the rate by month. Here, churn sits near 11 percent from January through April. Then it is about 13 in May and 14 in June. A drift like that deserves a question, and a later lesson comes back to it. A sudden jump or a sudden drop in the newest months means asking whether the definition changed, or whether those months' outcome windows have closed. Second, read examples. Pull twenty advertisers labelled churned and twenty labelled stayed, and look at them as accounts you know. If several of the churned ones turn out to be seasonal clients who always pause, the definition is wrong, and you found out before any model was built.

visual.title: Churn rate by snapshot month
visual.note: 2,000 advertisers in each month. Simulated data.

segments.narration: So, the brief. Before any modelling, ask your assistant to write the definition down and then prove it with output. [[1]] The label in one sentence, including the number of days. [[2]] What one row is, who is eligible, and how many rows were left out. [[3]] The snapshot dates, and the most recent one whose outcome window has fully closed. [[4]] The label rate and row count by month. [[5]] And twenty example rows, churned and stayed. What you are checking is dates and counts, not code. If the newest snapshot is less than 60 days old, its labels are not finished. And if the room still cannot agree on a definition, have two built side by side, and read the accounts that change sides.

visual.title: Brief and audit: define it, then prove it
items: The label in one sentence, with its days
One row is…; who is eligible; rows left out
Snapshot dates; the latest with a closed window
Label rate and row count by month
Twenty example rows: churned and stayed

segments.narration: So before anyone models a label, you can make it prove itself: one sentence, a timeline, and a count of who was left out. Next: what happens when a feature slips onto the wrong side of the snapshot date, and already knows the answer.

visual.title: Framing: target, unit and time
items: A label is a business decision: what, who, when
Features before the snapshot, outcome after; label only when the window has closed
Ask who is missing: not eligible, not yet observed, not measurable

takeaways: A label is a business decision: what counts, for which unit, and in which window.
Features come from before the snapshot, the outcome from after it, and only a closed window gives a real label.
Ask who is missing: rows that are not eligible, not yet observed, or invisible to your proxy.

quiz.concept: the outcome window must have closed
quiz.q: Today, on your own platform's data, the assistant builds a churn table with one snapshot per month for the last six months. Churn means no spend in the 60 days after the snapshot, and the flag is computed as 'no spend since the snapshot'. It reports: 'Churn by snapshot month: 11, 12, 11, 12, 19 and 38 percent. Churn is accelerating.' What is the right read?
options: Churn really is accelerating, and the account teams should be warned about it this week
The newest snapshots' 60 days are not over, so advertisers on a pause count as churned
The recent months contain fewer advertisers, so their rates are simply noisier
The definition is too strict and should be loosened until recent months look normal
quiz.why: A snapshot from this month or last has not had its 60 days, so everyone with no spend yet is counted as churned, including advertisers who are only pausing and will spend again inside the window. Had unfinished rows been defaulted to stayed, the same months would have come out too low instead. Noise would scatter the rates up and down, not push exactly the two open months the same way.

quiz.q: A churn table includes every account that has ever existed. Many rows show no spend at all during the 8-week observation window, and the model gives nearly all of those rows a very high score. What is the problem?
options: The scores are too confident and should be scaled down before the list is shared
Those rows should have their missing spend filled in with the average before training
The model leans too heavily on spend and should be given some other columns to use
Those accounts had already stopped before the snapshot, so they are not predictions
quiz.why: An account with no spend before the snapshot has already left: flagging it is history, not prediction, and it flatters any model. The fix is an eligibility rule that states who is in, such as advertisers with spend during the observation window, not patching the rows or the feature list.

quiz.concept: a proxy has a blind spot
quiz.q: To study 'satisfied customers', an analyst uses the rating from the survey sent after each support ticket. About a quarter of customers ever answer it. The report concludes that satisfied customers use the reporting API more. What should the report say up front?
options: That the finding describes survey responders, who may differ from everyone else
That a quarter of all customers answered, which is a large enough sample to rely on
That missing ratings were filled in with the average, so every customer is covered
That ratings are subjective, so no conclusion at all can be drawn from them
quiz.why: The proxy can only see customers who answered, and they may differ from those who did not, so the conclusion is about responders. Sample size is not the issue: a large group that selected itself is still not everyone. Filling the gaps with an average hides the blind spot instead of stating it.

quiz.q: Stakeholders want to know which advertisers will leave. The assistant's training table has one row per campaign, each labelled with whether its advertiser churned. What is the issue?
options: The label: churn should be redefined for each campaign on its own
A campaign-level table is simply not able to carry an advertiser-level label
The unit is wrong: an advertiser with ten campaigns is counted ten times
It should go finer still, with one row per advertiser for every day
quiz.why: The decision is about advertisers, so one row should be one advertiser at one snapshot. At campaign grain, advertisers with many campaigns dominate every count and rate, and the extra rows repeat the same outcome instead of adding evidence. Going finer still makes that worse, and a campaign-level label would answer a question nobody asked.

review.concept: a label needs a closed outcome window

variants.q: A lead counts as 'converted' if it becomes a paying customer within 90 days of sign-up. A table built today labels every lead from the last 30 days that has not paid yet as 'not converted'. What is wrong?
options: Those rows are right but uncertain, so they should get a lower weight
Recent leads behave differently, so they need a separate model
Those leads have had 30 days at most, not 90: they have no label yet
The 90-day window is too long and should be cut to 30 days for all leads
variants.why: The definition gives every lead 90 days and these have had 30 at most, so some will still convert; calling them 'not converted' writes in an answer that does not exist yet, at any weight. Shortening the window for everyone would be a different label: a business decision to make on purpose, not to fit this month's table.

variants.q: Video adoption is defined as starting video ads within 60 days of a snapshot. The adoption rate is steady at about 20 percent for older snapshots, but 7 percent for the snapshot taken three weeks ago. What should you check before explaining the drop?
options: Whether the newest snapshot has had its 60 days: it has had three weeks
Whether interest in video ads is fading among the newest advertisers
Whether the newest snapshot is smaller, which would make its rate noisier
Whether the newest advertisers were offered video ads at all by sales
variants.why: Adoption is counted over 60 days and the newest snapshot has had three weeks, so many of its eventual adopters have not been counted yet. Fading interest is a story the data cannot support until the window has closed: check the dates before explaining a drop.

variants.q: A creative is called 'durable' if its CTR holds for 30 days after launch. An analyst labels a creative launched 10 days ago, with CTR still holding, as durable. What is the right label?
options: Durable: its CTR has held on every day observed so far
Not durable: it has not yet reached the 30 days required
Durable, but with a lower weight than the older creatives
None yet: it has been observed for 10 of the 30 days
variants.why: The label is defined over 30 days and only 10 have been seen, so neither answer exists yet. Calling it durable assumes the next 20 days; calling it not durable punishes it for being new. It gets a label when its window closes.

review.concept: who the label cannot see

variants.q: The 'invalid' label for traffic sources comes from manual reviews, and a source is reviewed only after an advertiser complains about it. A model trained on the reviewed sources is then used to score every source. What should you say about it?
options: It can be trusted everywhere, because the reviewed labels are accurate
It learned from sources that drew complaints; the rest are a blind spot
It cannot be used at all, because the labels were assigned by people
It will work once the unreviewed sources have been labelled as valid
variants.why: Labels exist only for sources that drew a complaint, and those may differ from sources nobody complained about, so the model's behaviour on the rest is unknown. Accurate labels do not fix who was left out, and assuming every unreviewed source is valid writes in answers nobody checked.

variants.q: An analyst defines 'price-sensitive' advertisers as those who redeemed a discount code. The codes were emailed only to self-serve accounts. The report says managed accounts are almost never price-sensitive. What is the right read?
options: Managed accounts are less price-sensitive, as you would expect
The sample of managed accounts is too small to be sure of it
The discount-code data is unreliable and should be discarded
Managed accounts could not qualify: the proxy cannot see them
variants.why: An advertiser who was never sent a code cannot redeem one, so for managed accounts the proxy measures who got the email, not price sensitivity. The finding sounds plausible, which is exactly why it slips through. The data is fine for self-serve accounts; it is silent on the rest.

variants.q: A slide says: 'Happy advertisers, the ones who hit their CPA goal, refresh creatives more often.' A CPA exists only for advertisers with conversion tracking. What belongs in the first line of that slide?
options: That it covers tracked advertisers only, and how the untracked differ
That untracked advertisers were counted as unhappy, to keep every row
That it holds for all advertisers, since most of them have tracking
That CPA goals are set by advertisers, so the proxy is too subjective
variants.why: The proxy is blind to every advertiser without tracking, and that group differs from the tracked one, so the claim has to be scoped to tracked advertisers. 'Most have tracking' does not make the rest similar, and counting the invisible ones as unhappy invents an answer.

drill.q: What three things does a label definition have to pin down before anyone builds a model?
drill.a: What exactly counts as the outcome. Who, meaning what one row is and which rows are eligible. And when, meaning a snapshot date, with features from before it and the outcome from a fixed window after it.

drill.q: Churn means no spend at all in the sixty days after a snapshot. An advertiser has not spent in the three weeks since theirs. Why can you not label them yet?
drill.a: Because their outcome window has not closed. They may be gone for good or only pausing, and nobody can tell which until the sixty days are up. Call them churned and the rate runs too high. Call them stayed and it runs too low.

recall.prompt: Someone hands you a table and says the churned column is the label. What do you ask before you trust it?
recall.model_answer: I would ask for the definition in one sentence, with its window in days, and what one row is. Then where the snapshot date sits, so that features come from before it and the outcome from after. Then who was left out: rows that were not eligible, rows whose outcome window had not closed, and anyone a proxy cannot see. Finally I would look at the label rate by month and read twenty examples of each class.

lessons.ask_assistant: Before any modelling, write the label definition in one sentence: [outcome] within [number of days] of [reference date]. Say what one row is, [unit] at [snapshot date], and which rows are eligible. List the snapshot dates beside the date the data was pulled, and keep only snapshots whose [outcome window] had fully closed by then; say which you dropped. Show the row count and [outcome] rate by snapshot [period], how many rows were excluded and why, and how you treated rows whose outcome was not yet decided. Then show twenty example rows with the outcome and twenty without.
audit_checklist: The label in one sentence, with its window in days
Snapshot dates beside the data pull date: every snapshot kept is at least one full outcome window older than the pull
Label rate and row count by month, with no unexplained jump or drop in the newest months
Rows excluded as not eligible or not measurable: how many, and how they differ
transfer: Lead scoring: 'converted' within how many days of which date, and are last month's leads old enough to judge?
Creative fatigue: 'fatigued' against which baseline, counted from launch, and for creatives that have run how long?
Invalid traffic: 'confirmed invalid' exists only for the sources somebody reviewed.

other_ways.approach: Ask how long advertisers last, instead of yes or no in a fixed window
other_ways.when: When timing matters and many accounts are too recent to judge; a later module covers it.

other_ways.approach: Predict a number instead: spend in the next 8 weeks
other_ways.when: When nobody can agree on one definition of churned and the decision is about revenue anyway.

other_ways.approach: Build two label definitions side by side
other_ways.when: When stakeholders disagree: count how many advertisers change class, and read those cases together.

glossary.def: The day the prediction would be made: features come from before it, the outcome from after it.
The period before the snapshot that the features describe: here, 8 weeks.
The period after the snapshot in which the label is decided: here, 60 days.
The rule for which rows belong in the table at all, such as advertisers still spending at the snapshot.
A measurable stand-in for something that has no column, blind wherever it cannot be measured.

lessons.title: Leakage: features that know the future
lessons.subtitle: Why does a model that looks perfect on past data fail on the day you use it?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can test any feature for leakage by asking whether its value could have been computed on the snapshot date, and say what the assistant's output must show to prove it.

predict.q: An honest churn model picks its 200 highest-risk advertisers, and 136 of them really churn. The assistant adds one more column and the count becomes 200 out of 200. Which column is most likely to have done that?
options: Support tickets in the last 8 weeks
Days since last login
Days since last spend
Payment failures in the last 8 weeks
predict.reveal: Days since last spend. The name is innocent; the trouble is when it was read: months after the snapshot, when the churners had already stopped. The lesson shows why that is fatal and how to catch it.

segments.narration: You ask your assistant for a churn model on the advertiser table. Four minutes later it is back, and the result is spectacular. Of the 200 advertisers it rated most at risk, all 200 really churned. Not most of them. All of them. Your first instinct is to forward it to the head of account management. Hold that thought for five minutes. A result this clean is not a reason to celebrate. It is a reason to ask one specific question, and this lesson is that question. It is the same question for any model, whether it predicts churn or which creatives will fatigue: was one of its columns recorded after the outcome?

visual.title: Leakage
visual.sub: Features that know the future

segments.narration: First, how the result was measured. The model scored 4,000 advertisers it had not seen while learning. Sort them by score, take the top 200, and count how many really churned. [[1]] With every column the assistant found, the count is 200. [[2]] Take out one single column and repeat, on the same advertisers, and it falls to 136. That is the honest number, and it is still a strong list: among those 4,000 advertisers only about 13 percent churned. So one column accounts for the whole gap between very good and perfect. Be suspicious of any single column that powerful.

visual.title: Of the 200 highest-risk advertisers, how many really churned?

right.label: Without it
right.sub: same advertisers, the honest result

segments.narration: The column is called days since last spend. It sounds like exactly the behaviour signal you would want. [[1]] For advertisers who churned, the typical value is 86 days. [[2]] For everyone else it is 3. Now remember how the label was defined: no spend at all in the 60 days after the snapshot. [[3]] And the assistant read the column from the accounts table on the day of the export, months after the snapshot. So it is counting the empty days of the outcome window itself. That is not a hint about who will churn. It is the answer, written in different units.

visual.title: The extra column: days since last spend

stats.label: typical value, advertisers who churned
typical value, advertisers who stayed
after the snapshot: when the column was read

segments.narration: Put it on the timeline from the last lesson. [[1]] Features describe the 8 weeks before the snapshot. [[2]] The label describes the 60 days after it. [[3]] This column was measured later still, once the outcome had already happened. That is leakage: a feature that carries information from after the moment of prediction. And it is useless, not just suspicious. On the day you score live advertisers, that future value does not exist. The value you can compute that day is small for nearly everyone, because anyone who had already stopped spending would not be on your list. The model learned to read tomorrow's newspaper. In production there is no newspaper.

visual.title: When was each thing measured?
visual.note: A feature may only use what lies before the snapshot. This one was read from the live accounts table, 60–120 days after it.

segments.narration: Leaks come from four places. [[1]] First, current-state tables. An accounts table holds each advertiser as they are today, so anything read from it is today's truth, not the snapshot's. [[2]] Second, fields somebody fills in after the event, like a closure reason or a note from a win-back call. [[3]] Third, totals whose window runs past the snapshot. Lifetime spend sounds harmless, but read today it includes the weeks after the snapshot, when churners added nothing. [[4]] Fourth, the label itself in another form, which is what we just caught. Each one looks like an ordinary, helpful column.

visual.title: Where leaks come from
rows: Account status or tier, as stored today
Field filled in after the event
Window that runs past the snapshot
Days since last spend, read at export
