segments.narration: So here is the question to ask of every column. Could I have computed this exact value on the snapshot date, using only data up to that date? Call it the time-travel test. If the answer is no, or not sure, the column is out. The test is about when a value was recorded, not about its name. Days since last spend, counted up to the snapshot, is an honest feature. The same name, read months later, is the outcome. And do not wait for a perfect score. This data is simulated and its leak is deliberately blatant. A quieter leak just makes a model look somewhat better than it is.

visual.text: Could I have computed this exact value on the snapshot date, using only data up to that date?
visual.sub: The time-travel test: ask it of every column

segments.narration: The fix is one you could write yourself, because it is SQL. Features are built from dated events, like the daily spend log or the ticket log, and every one is filtered to dates on or before the snapshot. With that one condition in the join, nothing from the future can get in. Days since last spend becomes the snapshot date minus the last spend date before it. Same name, honest value. For fields that live only in the accounts table, ask whether they could have changed after the snapshot, whatever the reason. Vertical and sign-up date cannot, so they are fine, with a note. Status, tier and last-activity dates can, so they need a copy dated at the snapshot.

visual.title: The fix: dated events, filtered to the snapshot
visual.code:
SELECT a.advertiser_id,
       a.snapshot_date - MAX(s.spend_date)
         AS days_since_last_spend
FROM   snapshots a
LEFT JOIN daily_spend s
  ON   s.advertiser_id = a.advertiser_id
 AND   s.spend > 0
 AND   s.spend_date <= a.snapshot_date  -- the date filter
GROUP  BY a.advertiser_id, a.snapshot_date;
visual.note: Same column name, honest value: no row dated after the snapshot can get in. Accounts-table fields: fine if they cannot change after the snapshot (vertical, sign-up date); otherwise use a copy dated at the snapshot.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Put the rule in the brief: every feature built from dated events on or before each advertiser's snapshot date, and from the accounts table only fields that cannot change after the snapshot, each one flagged. [[2]] Then make the output prove it, with a list of every feature, its source table and the latest date of data it used. [[3]] When a result arrives, ask which columns the model leans on most, and when each is recorded. [[4]] And when a number looks too good, ask for the same run without the suspect column, on the same advertisers. [[5]] If you want status or tier as features one day, start saving a dated copy of the accounts table now.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Brief: dated events up to the snapshot; from accounts, only fields that cannot change after it
Show: each feature, its source table, the latest date it used
Show: the columns the model leans on, and when each is recorded
Too good? Rerun without the suspect column, same advertisers
Want status or tier? Start saving dated copies of the accounts table

segments.narration: So when a result looks too good, ask which columns the model leans on and when each was recorded, before anyone else sees the number. Next we make that a routine: briefing the assistant in stages, so every output arrives with its own proof.

visual.title: Leakage in three lines
items: Recorded after the prediction moment: brilliant on the past, useless live
The check: the time-travel test, on every column
The fix: dated events with a date filter

takeaways: A column recorded after the prediction moment hands the model the answer: brilliant on past data, useless live.
Time-travel test for every column: could I have computed this exact value on the snapshot date, from data up to then?
Build features from dated events with a date filter, and make the output list each feature's source and latest date.

quiz.concept: a result that is too good
quiz.q: The assistant reports: 'Checked on 4,000 advertisers the model had not seen. Nearly all of the 200 highest-risk churned. Strongest columns: account status, spend trend, active days.' It adds that account status comes from the accounts table. What is the right read?
options: It was checked on unseen advertisers, so the result is safe to share
The model has probably memorised its data; ask for a simpler one
Ask when account status is recorded: today's value may already show who left
Ask for the top 400 as well, to see whether the result holds on a longer list
quiz.why: A current-state column such as today's account status is written after the outcome, so it can carry the answer. Checking on unseen advertisers does not protect you, because the leaked column sits in their rows too.

quiz.q: You are building the churn table with a snapshot date of 1 March; the data is exported in July. Which of these proposed columns fails the time-travel test?
options: Average daily spend over the advertiser's whole history in the warehouse
Support tickets opened in the 8 weeks before 1 March, from the ticket log
Weeks between the advertiser's sign-up date and 1 March
Spend in the 4 weeks before 1 March divided by the 4 weeks before that
quiz.why: The whole-history average includes the months after 1 March, when churners spent nothing, so the outcome leaks in through the window. The ticket count sounds riskier, but it is dated and stops at the snapshot.

quiz.concept: fix the column, do not just drop it
quiz.q: A lead-scoring model predicts which new leads will become paying advertisers. Its strongest column is 'calls with the sales team', taken from the CRM as it stands today. Sales calls a lead most in the weeks around signing. What should you ask for?
options: Keep it as it is: sales contact is a genuine driver of conversion
The calls counted only up to the day each lead was scored
Every sales-activity column dropped, since they will always leak
More leads, so the model can learn the pattern properly
quiz.why: Today's count includes calls made after the scoring day, some of them because the deal was already closing, so it knows the outcome. Counted up to the scoring day it is honest and may still be useful, which is why dropping all sales activity overshoots.

quiz.concept: why a leak fails in production
quiz.q: Against your advice, a churn model that leans on days since last spend, as exported months after the snapshot, goes live. On Monday it scores advertisers who are all currently active. What will most likely happen?
options: It performs as in the report, since the column still exists
It crashes, because the column cannot be computed for advertisers who are live
It flags far too many advertisers, because the column is so strong
It flags almost nobody, because the live value is small for nearly everyone
quiz.why: The model learned that a large value means churn, and on scoring day active advertisers all have small values, so nearly everyone looks safe. The column can still be computed, which is exactly why nothing crashes and nobody notices.

review.concept: the time-travel test

variants.q: A model should flag invalid clicks at the moment a click arrives. Which of these columns fails the time-travel test?
options: Clicks from the same IP address in the previous hour
Whether the advertiser was later refunded for the click
Seconds between the page loading and the click
The publisher's share of flagged clicks in the previous month
variants.why: A refund is issued after the click has been investigated and judged invalid, so it is the label arriving late. The other three are known at or before the moment of the click, however suspicious they may sound.

variants.q: You want to predict, on the day an invoice is issued, whether it will be paid late. The assistant's table includes 'payment reminders sent for this invoice'. What is the right read?
options: Useful: reminders are a strong sign of a customer who pays slowly
Fine, as long as the invoice ID is left out
Leak: reminders go out only after an invoice is overdue
Harmless: a model learns to ignore weak columns
variants.why: On the day of issue the reminder count is always zero; the exported value was written after the invoice went overdue, so it encodes the outcome. It will look like the strongest column precisely because it is the answer.

variants.q: For a model predicting who will upgrade to a managed account in the next 60 days, the assistant reads 'has an account manager' from today's accounts table. What do you ask for?
options: The flag as it stood on each advertiser's snapshot date
The flag as stored today: account type is a stable profile field
That flag removed, along with every other yes or no column
A longer outcome window, so more upgrades are captured
variants.why: Anyone who upgraded since the snapshot now shows an account manager, so today's flag is the label in another form. A field that can change after the snapshot needs its value as of the snapshot date; only fields fixed since then, such as vertical, are safe to read from today's table.

review.concept: a leak passes the check on past data and fails live

variants.q: A stakeholder says: 'The model was checked on advertisers it had never seen, so a suspiciously good result must be real.' What is the best reply?
options: Agreed: unseen advertisers rule out a model that is fooling itself
Unseen rows catch memorising, not a column carrying the answer
Only if the unseen group was large enough
Only if the check is repeated on a second unseen group
variants.why: A leaked column is present in the unseen advertisers' rows too, so the check passes for the wrong reason. A bigger group or a repeat does not help when the answer is sitting among the features.

variants.q: A model predicts which support tickets will escalate. On past tickets it is nearly perfect, and its top column is ticket priority. Agents raise priority to urgent when a ticket escalates. What happens when it scores brand-new tickets?
options: It misses most escalations: new tickets all start at normal priority
It works as it did on past tickets: every ticket still has a priority
It flags nearly every ticket: priority is always filled in
It fails to run: priority is empty when a ticket is created
variants.why: The model learned that urgent means escalated, but at creation no ticket is urgent yet, so the signal it relies on is absent. The column exists and is filled in, which is why nothing crashes and the failure is silent.

variants.q: A model that predicts which creatives will fatigue next week comes back nearly perfect on creatives it had not seen. What is the most useful first request to the assistant?
options: A longer report with more charts of the result
The same model retrained on twice as many creatives
A more complex model, to confirm the finding
The columns it leans on most and when each is recorded
variants.why: A near-perfect result is the classic sign of a column recorded after the outcome, and the top columns with their recording times expose it in one step. More data or a fancier model would simply reproduce the leak.

drill.q: What is leakage, and why does a model with a leak fail once it goes live?
drill.a: Leakage is a feature recorded after the moment of prediction, so it carries the answer. The model looks brilliant on past data, but on scoring day that future value does not exist yet.

drill.q: What is the time-travel test for a feature?
drill.a: Ask whether you could have computed that exact value on the snapshot date, using only data up to that date. If not, or if you are not sure, the column stays out.

recall.prompt: Your assistant's model looks too good to be true. Explain what leakage is and how you would check for it without reading the code.
recall.model_answer: Leakage is when a feature was recorded after the moment the prediction is supposed to be made, so it carries the outcome in disguise; the model scores brilliantly on past data and fails live, because on scoring day that value does not exist yet. I would ask which columns the model leans on most and when each is recorded, and apply the time-travel test: could this exact value have been computed on the snapshot date from data up to then? Any column that fails comes out, or is rebuilt from dated events filtered to the snapshot, and the result is rerun on the same advertisers.

lessons.ask_assistant: Build every feature from dated event tables, such as [event tables], filtered to dates on or before each row's [prediction date]. From a table that only shows the present, such as [current-state table], use only fields that cannot change after the [prediction date], such as [stable fields], and flag each one; any other field needs a copy dated at the [prediction date]. In the output, list each feature with its source table and the latest date of data it used, next to the [prediction date]. After fitting, list the five columns the model relies on most and when each value is recorded. If a column cannot be computed as of that date, leave it out and tell me which.
audit_checklist: A list of every feature with its source table and the latest date of data it used: none later than the snapshot date
Every field taken from a current-state table, each marked 'cannot change after the snapshot' (vertical, sign-up date) or 'copy dated at the snapshot' (status, tier, last-activity dates)
The columns the model relies on most, each with when its value is recorded
For any suspect column: the result with and without it, on the same advertisers
transfer: Which leads will convert? Check whether 'number of sales calls' was counted up to the scoring day, or includes calls made once the deal was already closing.
Which clicks are invalid? Check whether a 'refunded' or 'blocked' flag was set before the click was judged, or as a result of the judgement.
How much will each advertiser spend next month? Check that no input total includes days from the month being forecast.

other_ways.approach: Dated snapshots of current-state tables: keep a copy of the accounts table as it stood on each date
other_ways.when: When the columns you want (status, tier, account manager) live only in a table that shows the present, and you need them as honest features.

other_ways.approach: Drop-one check: retrain without the suspect column and compare on the same advertisers
other_ways.when: When nobody can tell you when a field is written and you need a quick read on how much of the result depends on it.

other_ways.approach: Scoring-day rehearsal: rebuild the features for a past date using only data loaded by that date, and compare with the training table
other_ways.when: Before a model goes live, when a silent leak would be expensive.

glossary.def: A feature that carries information from after the moment of prediction, so the model is quietly handed the answer.
The check for every column: could this exact value have been computed on the snapshot date, using only data up to then?
A table that holds each record as it is today, with no history, such as an accounts table.
Rows that each carry the date something happened, such as daily spend, so they can be filtered to before the snapshot.

lessons.title: Brief in stages, audit by evidence
lessons.subtitle: How do you get work from an AI assistant that you can actually check?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can brief an assistant in four gated stages and name what each output must show before you let the next stage start.

predict.q: Your assistant can turn one long prompt into a finished churn report. What is the main thing you lose, compared with asking in steps and checking each one?
options: Accuracy: a model built in one pass is weaker than one built step by step
Detail: a one-pass report has to leave out the row counts and the charts
Control of the wording: the report's text cannot be edited afterwards
The chance to catch a wrong assumption before everything is built on it
predict.reveal: The chance to catch an early mistake. Everything arrives at once, so a wrong table or a wrong label is buried under the model and the report. The lesson shows where to put the checks and what each one must show.

segments.narration: It is Thursday afternoon and the head of account management wants a churn model. You type one long, careful prompt: build a model from the advertiser table and write me a report. Ten minutes later you have a beautiful HTML page. Charts, a headline number, confident paragraphs. Now the uncomfortable question. Which of those numbers do you trust? You cannot tell. Everything arrived at once, and anything that went wrong in the first step is buried under everything built on top of it. Last lesson's leak looked exactly like this: a polished result with the flaw four layers down. It would be the same with a spend forecast for finance: whatever the question, work that arrives in one piece cannot be checked piece by piece.

visual.title: Brief in stages, audit by evidence
visual.sub: Getting work from an assistant that you can check

segments.narration: [[1]] The one-shot prompt asks you to inspect a finished building. [[2]] The alternative is to inspect it floor by floor. You ask for one small piece of work, you look at what came back, and only then do you ask for the next. Each of those checkpoints is a gate. The reason is not that the assistant is careless. It is that it cannot know what one row should be in your business, or when a column was recorded, and nothing in a one-shot prompt makes it stop and ask. A wrong assumption in the first step flows silently into every later one. Gates are where your knowledge gets in.

right.label: Four stages
right.sub: one small output to check before the next begins

segments.narration: There are four stages. [[1]] Stage one is the table. Before any model: what one row is, how many rows there are, what dates they cover, whether any advertiser appears twice, and which columns have gaps. [[2]] Stage two is the target and the split: the exact definition of the label, its rate month by month, and which rows the model will learn from and which are held back to check it. [[3]] Stage three is a baseline, then the model. A baseline is the simple answer you would give with no model at all, like your spend trend rule. Both are judged on the same held-back rows. [[4]] Stage four, and only then, is the report, built from numbers you have already checked.

visual.title: Four stages, each with a gate

steps.label: 1 · The table
steps.sub: one row is…, counts, dates, duplicates, gaps

steps.label: 2 · Target and split
steps.sub: definition, rate by month, learn rows vs held-back rows

steps.label: 3 · Baseline, then model
steps.sub: both on the same held-back rows

segments.narration: To make a gate something you can check, every output the assistant sends ends with a short section. Call it the audit block. It grows with the work. [[1]] From stage one: row counts after every step, so you can see where rows appeared or vanished. [[2]] And the date range the data covers. [[3]] From stage two: the label rate, overall and by month. [[4]] From stage three: the list of features, each with the table it came from and the latest date of data it used. [[5]] And the baseline right next to the model. Notice what kind of things these are. Counts, dates and rates. You have been sanity-checking counts, dates and rates on dashboards for years.

visual.title: The audit block: it grows by stage
items: From stage 1: row counts after every step
From stage 1: date range of the data
From stage 2: label rate, overall and by month
From stage 3: each feature, its source table, the latest date it used
From stage 3: the baseline next to the model

segments.narration: Here is the audit block for the advertiser table after stage two. Twelve thousand rows, one per advertiser, nobody appearing twice. CPA versus goal is empty for nearly five thousand of them, and you know why: those advertisers have no conversion tracking. The assistant does not know that. The label runs at about 11 percent in the rows the model learns from, and about 13 percent in the rows held back. And 2,000 April rows are set aside altogether, which should make you ask why. Good. The next lesson answers it. Every line is something you can compare with a dashboard, or question out loud. None of it required reading Python.

visual.title: An audit block, after stage two
visual.code:
AUDIT BLOCK - stage 2
one row     = one advertiser, seen once
rows        = 12,000    duplicates = 0
snapshots   = Jan to Jun, 2,000 a month
missing     = cpa_vs_goal, hit_cpa_goal: 4,984 rows
label       = churned_next_60d: 11.8% overall
by month    = 11.25 10.90 11.25 11.25 12.65 13.70 %
learn from  = Jan-Mar   6,000 rows   churn 11.1%
left out    = Apr       2,000 rows
held back   = May-Jun   4,000 rows   churn 13.2%
features, baseline = not yet: they join at stage 3
visual.note: Counts, dates and rates: all checkable without reading code. The block grows: features and the baseline join at stage 3.

segments.narration: A gate is also where you push back. Suppose stage three arrives and the model looks far too good, like 200 out of 200. You send one line: show me the top five columns and when each was recorded. That turns a suspicion into evidence you can read. And if the honest reply is that nothing in the table says when, that is evidence too: you now know which column to go and ask about. If a gate fails, the rule is simple. You do not carry on with a caveat. The assistant fixes that stage, reruns it, and shows the audit block again. At the gate, a problem costs you minutes. In the finished report, it costs you credibility.

visual.text: Show me the top five columns and when each was recorded.
visual.sub: What to send back when a number looks too good. "The table does not say" is an answer too.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Open every project with a standing instruction: work one stage at a time, and after each stage stop and wait for my go-ahead. [[2]] End every output with the audit block. [[3]] If the block is missing, or a count in it does not match what you know, the next stage does not start. [[4]] When the report arrives, read its sentences against the numbers. After a re-run, the prose can still describe the old result. For work you repeat every month, save the checked pipeline as a template with the audit block built in. [[5]] And one rule sits above all of this. Advertiser data goes only into tools your company has approved for it. If you are not sure, treat the answer as no.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: One stage per request, then stop and wait
Every output ends with the audit block
No audit block, no next stage
Read the report's prose against its numbers
Client data only in approved tools

segments.narration: So your next request to an assistant is not a model and a report: it is stage one, ending in an audit block you can hold against a dashboard. Next, module two and the scoreboard: which rows a model is judged on, and what it has to beat.

visual.text: Four stages, four gates. Check evidence in the output, not Python.
visual.sub: Next: which rows a model is judged on, and what it has to beat

takeaways: Never ask for a model and a report in one go: four stages, each with a gate you check before the next.
Every output ends with an audit block that grows by stage: row counts and dates, then the label rate, then each feature's source and latest date and the baseline beside the model.
Check evidence in the output, not Python, and the report's prose against its numbers; when a number looks too good, ask for the top five columns and when each was recorded.

quiz.q: Stage one comes back with this audit block: 'Rows loaded: 12,000. Rows after cleaning: 7,016. Duplicate advertisers: 0. Snapshots: January to June.' The assistant asks whether to continue to stage two. What is the right response?
options: Continue: cleaning is meant to remove bad rows, and there are no duplicates
Continue, and note the smaller sample as a limitation in the final report
Stop: ask which rows the cleaning step removed, and why
Ask the assistant to rerun stage one and see whether the count changes
quiz.why: Nearly five thousand advertisers vanished in a step called cleaning, and whatever removed them will shape every later number, so the gate stays shut until it is explained. Carrying on with a caveat is the tempting mistake: a line in the report does not repair a table that no longer represents your advertisers.

quiz.q: A one-shot prompt has already produced a polished churn report, and it is due in an hour. Which next step gives you the most reason to trust its numbers?
options: Ask the assistant whether it is confident that the analysis is correct
Ask it to add the audit block: counts per step, dates, label rate
Read through the Python script it wrote, line by line
Forward it marked as preliminary and check it properly afterwards
quiz.why: Counts, dates and rates in the output are evidence you can compare with what you already know, in minutes. Asking the assistant whether it is confident only produces reassurance, and reading the script is slower and not where your strength lies.

quiz.concept: the first gate is the table
quiz.q: Finance asks for a forecast of next quarter's platform spend. Working in stages, what is your first request to the assistant?
options: A description of the data: what one row is, counts, dates, gaps
A quick first forecast, to see whether the approach looks promising
An outline of the final report, so that the work has a clear target
A comparison of the three most accurate forecasting methods available
quiz.why: Every later number inherits the table, so the first gate is always what one row is, how many there are and which dates they cover. A quick first forecast feels efficient, but if days are missing or doubled you have no way to know whether to believe it.

quiz.concept: the baseline next to the model
quiz.q: For a lead-scoring model, the assistant's stage three output reads: 'The model picked 500 leads from the held-back group; 210 of them converted.' The audit block lists row counts, dates and feature sources. What is still missing before you can judge the result?
options: The Python code that produced the number
A chart of the 500 leads and their scores
A second, more complex model to compare the first against
What the current simple rule finds on the same leads
quiz.why: Without a baseline beside it, 210 out of 500 could be excellent or no better than what the sales team already does. A more complex model is the tempting request, but it answers a different question from whether a model is worth having at all.

review.concept: work in gated stages

variants.q: You need an upsell model: which advertisers are likely to adopt a new ad format. The assistant offers to 'build the whole thing and write it up in one pass, it is faster'. What is the best reply?
options: Yes, but add a request to double-check the work at the end
Yes, but ask for the code to be thoroughly commented
No: the table first, then stop and show its counts and dates
No: the report outline first, so the result has a clear shape
variants.why: A check after each stage catches a wrong table or target before anything is built on it; a self-check at the end is made by the same assistant on the same assumptions. Starting from the report outline puts the least checkable step first.

variants.q: In stage two of an invalid-traffic project, the audit block shows the share of clicks labelled invalid at about 2 percent for five months and 9 percent in the sixth. The assistant asks whether to go on to modelling. What do you do?
options: Go on: a model can learn something from the unusual month too
Hold the gate until someone explains why the rate moved
Go on, but drop the sixth month to be on the safe side
Go on, and mention the jump in the final report
variants.why: A label rate that jumps may mean the definition or the logging changed, and every later stage would inherit it, so the gate stays shut until it is understood. Dropping the month sounds careful, but it is a decision made without knowing what happened.

variants.q: The assistant returns stage two for the churn table and, to save time, has also trained a model and drafted the report. Its audit block shows the label defined as 'no spend in the next 30 days', not the 60 you agreed. What now?
options: Keep the model and report, with the 30-day definition as a caveat
Have the report text corrected to say 30 days throughout
Look at the model results first, since they already exist
Fix the label, rerun and check stage two, then redo what follows
variants.why: Everything after stage two was built on the wrong target, so it has to be redone once the gate is passed. Keeping finished work with a caveat is tempting because it already exists, but its numbers answer a different question.

review.concept: audit by evidence in the output

variants.q: A lead-scoring output ends with: 'Data was validated and cleaned; no issues found.' What is the right read?
options: Not evidence: ask for row counts, dates and the label rate
Good: the assistant has already checked the data on your behalf
Good, provided the model's result also looks reasonable
Not enough: ask the assistant to confirm it a second time
variants.why: A statement that all is well cannot be checked; counts, dates and rates can be compared with what you already know. Asking for a second confirmation only repeats the reassurance.

variants.q: Four outputs describe the same creative-fatigue analysis. Which one can you actually verify?
options: 'The analysis follows best practice throughout and the results are robust.'
'18,400 creatives loaded; 17,950 left after dropping those live under 7 days.'
'The model is highly accurate on unseen creatives and is ready for production.'
'All six steps of the pipeline completed successfully, with no errors.'
variants.why: Only the second states counts you can compare with your own dashboards, and it shows where rows were removed. The others are verdicts: they may be true, but nothing in them can be checked.

variants.q: A spend forecast for finance comes back with an error far lower than anyone expected. Before reacting, what do you send back?
options: 'Great result. Please go ahead and write the report.'
'Are you sure this is right? Please check everything once more.'
'Please try a more advanced method to confirm it.'
'Show me the top five inputs and when each was recorded.'
variants.why: A result that looks too good is a cue to ask for evidence, and the inputs with their recording times show whether something from the forecast period slipped in. Asking whether it is sure invites reassurance, not proof.

drill.q: Why not ask an AI assistant for the model and the report in a single prompt?
drill.a: Because everything arrives at once, and an early mistake is buried under everything built on it. Working in stages gives you one small output to check before the next step starts.

drill.q: What goes into the audit block that every output should end with?
drill.a: Row counts after every step and the date range. From stage two, the label rate. From stage three, the list of features with where each came from and the latest date it used, and the baseline next to the model.

recall.prompt: A colleague is about to ask an AI assistant for 'a churn model and a report' in one prompt. Talk them out of it: what would you do instead, and why?
recall.model_answer: Ask in four stages with a gate after each: the table, then the target and the split, then a baseline and the model on the same held-back rows, then the report. Every output ends with an audit block: row counts after each step, the date range, the label rate, each feature with its source and latest date, and the baseline beside the model. That way you check evidence you understand, counts, dates and rates, instead of Python, and a wrong assumption is caught before anything is built on it. If a number looks too good, ask for the top five columns and when each was recorded.

lessons.ask_assistant: Work in four stages: (1) the table, (2) the [outcome] definition and the held-back rows, (3) a baseline, then the model, on those rows, (4) the report. One stage per reply, then stop and wait for my go-ahead. End every reply with an audit block that grows by stage: from stage one, row counts after every step and the date range; from stage two, the [outcome] rate overall and by [period]; from stage three, each feature's source table and latest date, and the baseline beside the model. In stage four, quote every number from those blocks. Start with stage one for [table]: what one row is, rows and distinct [units], dates covered, duplicates, missing values.
audit_checklist: From stage one: row counts after every step and the date range, with any drop or growth explained
From stage two: the label rate, overall and by month
From stage three: every feature with its source table and the latest date of data it used, and the baseline beside the model on the same held-back rows
In the report: every number in a sentence matches the audit block of the latest run, and both carry the same run date
transfer: How much will the platform spend next quarter? Check the daily series for missing or doubled days before any forecasting method is tried.
Did the new bidding option work? Confirm who was in each group, and over which dates, before reading the difference.
What are customers writing to support about? Agree the categories and check a sample of labels before the whole inbox is sorted.

other_ways.approach: A written plan agreed up front, then a single run
other_ways.when: When the pipeline is routine, has passed its gates before, and only the month of data changes.

other_ways.approach: An independent second pass: a colleague, or a fresh assistant session, re-derives the key numbers from the raw table
other_ways.when: When the result feeds a decision big enough that one unnoticed error would be costly.

other_ways.approach: A reusable template script with the audit block built in
other_ways.when: When the same analysis is repeated regularly and you want the evidence produced without asking each time.

glossary.def: A check you make on one stage's output before you allow the next stage to start.
A short section at the end of every output that grows by stage: row counts and dates, then the label rate, then feature sources with their latest dates and the baseline.
The simple answer you would have without a model, such as a hand rule, used as the yardstick for the model.
Asking for the work one stage at a time, each checked before the next, instead of in a single prompt.

lessons.title: Hold-out, the gap, and baselines
lessons.subtitle: When does a model's result actually count?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can say which rows a model must be judged on, why a month is left out between training and test, and which baseline belongs next to any result.

predict.q: A lazy 'model' predicts that every advertiser stays, whoever they are. On the 4,000 advertisers from May and June, how often is it right?
options: Close to 0 percent
About 13 percent
About 50 percent
About 87 percent
predict.reveal: About 87 percent, because only about 13 percent of them churn, and it finds none of the churners. The lesson shows why a result only counts next to a baseline like this, on rows the model never saw.

segments.narration: A vendor is pitching an invalid-traffic filter, and the first slide says 99 percent accurate. Accurate means the share of cases where the yes or no call turned out right. Heads nod. But that number is missing two things. Measured on which rows? And compared with what? Both apply to any yes-or-no model, whether it flags invalid clicks or picks leads that will convert, and to any model that predicts a number. You cannot open the vendor's data, so we will answer on a table you can check: the 12,000 advertisers, where a teammate's churn model was reported at stand-up as 88 percent accurate.

visual.title: Hold-out, the gap, and baselines
visual.sub: Measured on what? Compared with what?

segments.narration: Start with measured on what. In the first lesson we said that matching the past is easy, and holding up on new rows is the whole game. A model graded on the rows it learned from is a student marking the exam with the answer key open. [[1]] So before any training, the rows with known outcomes are divided. [[2]] One part is the training set, which the model learns from. [[3]] The other part is held out, and it is called the test set. The model never sees it while learning, and only the result on the test set counts. The textbook name for holding up on rows it never saw is generalisation. The interesting question is which rows to hold out.

steps.label: Test set
steps.sub: never seen while learning; the result that counts

segments.narration: The obvious way is to shuffle all the rows and hold out a random slice. But think about how the model will be used. You train it on advertisers whose outcome is already known, then score advertisers whose outcome has not happened yet. Past to future. So the split should rehearse exactly that. [[1]] Train on the January to March snapshots, 6,000 advertisers. [[2]] Test on May and June, 4,000 advertisers from a later period. [[3]] And April, 2,000 advertisers, is used for neither. That looks wasteful. It is the most honest part of the design.

visual.title: Split by time: learn on the past, judge on later months
visual.note: Snapshot months, 2,000 advertisers in each.

segments.narration: Here is why. Churn means no spend in the 60 days after a snapshot. [[1]] So the label for an April advertiser is not finished until 60 days after the April snapshot. [[2]] Now stand on the day you score the May advertisers, about a month later. April's window is only about half over, and you cannot yet say who from April churned. A model trained on April would be using answers that did not exist on scoring day. You know this pattern. It is the time-travel test from the leakage lesson, applied to rows instead of columns. Whenever a label takes time to appear, the most recent period cannot be used for training.

visual.title: Why April is left out

spans.label: Not yet happened on scoring day

visual.note: On the day you score May, nobody yet knows who from April churned.

segments.narration: Treat the test set as a sealed envelope. Each time you look at a test result and then change the model, a little of the answer leaks into your choices. So make every choice on the training months. A later lesson shows how. Open the envelope for the final answer, not for every experiment. This course keeps showing you test results so you can watch each idea on the same advertisers: teaching, not a habit to copy. One note on this simulated data: a shuffled split happens to score almost the same. That is a property of this data, not a rule. Only a later period can show you that the world has moved.

visual.text: The test set is a sealed envelope. Open it for the final answer, not for every experiment.
visual.sub: Make every choice on the training months. Split by time even when a shuffle happens to score the same.

segments.narration: Now the second question: compared with what. Take the laziest model imaginable. It predicts that every advertiser stays. [[1]] On the test months it is right about 87 percent of the time, because only about 13 percent of advertisers churn. [[2]] It also finds exactly none of the 527 advertisers who left. [[3]] So the 88 percent from the stand-up is less than two points better than doing nothing at all. A simple reference result like this is called a baseline. It does not have to be clever. Its job is to tell you what a number means.

visual.title: Baseline one: predict that everyone stays

stats.label: accuracy of predicting 'stays' for all 4,000
churners it finds
accuracy of the model

segments.narration: A better baseline is what you would do today with no model. Your rule from the first lesson: flag every advertiser whose spend trend is below 0.7. [[1]] On the test months it flags 711 advertisers. [[2]] Of those, 246 really churned, about one in three. [[3]] It misses the other 281. That is the bar. A model earns its place only by beating the rule on the same advertisers, with the same number of flags. [[4]] This one does: its top 711 contain 321 churners. When the target is a number, like next month's spend, the idea is identical. The baselines are the plain average, or the same as last period.

visual.title: Baseline two: the rule you would write today

stats.label: flagged: spend trend below 0.7
of those really churned
churners the rule missed
churners in the model's top 711

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Tell the assistant to split by date, not by shuffling: train only on periods whose outcome window had closed before the first test date, and name the period left out. [[2]] Ask for the dates, the row count and the outcome rate of each part. [[3]] Make test scoring a final stage that you trigger, with every evaluation run listed. [[4]] Ask for both baselines beside the model on the same test rows, with the model shown at the same number of flags as your rule. [[5]] When rows have no time order that matters, a random hold-out is fine. A result without these is not wrong. It is just not yet evidence.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Split by date; train only where the outcome window had closed
Dates, rows and outcome rate for each part, and the period left out
Test scoring: a final stage you trigger, every run listed with its rows
Both baselines beside the model: same rows, same number of flags
No time order that matters (a fixed pile of tickets): a random hold-out is fine

segments.narration: So when the vendor says 99 percent accurate, you have your reply: measured on which clicks, and what does flagging nothing score on those clicks? Next lesson takes accuracy apart, because it could barely tell a working model from one that does nothing.

visual.title: A result counts only when it is
items: On rows the model never saw
Split the way it will be used, with a gap for late labels
Next to a baseline, on the same rows

takeaways: A result counts only on a test set the model never saw, split by time when the question is about the future.
Leave a gap wherever labels arrive late: April is out because its 60 days are not over when May is scored.
No number without a baseline on the same rows: 'everyone stays' is about 87 percent accurate and finds no churners.

quiz.q: A stakeholder says: 'The churn model is 88 percent accurate. That is a solid B plus, let us ship it.' What is the right first response?
options: Agree: anything well above 50 percent clearly beats a coin flip
Ask what predicting 'everyone stays' scores on the same rows
Ask for the accuracy to one more decimal place before deciding
Ask for a larger group of test advertisers before deciding
quiz.why: On these test months, predicting that everyone stays is about 87 percent accurate, so 88 is barely above doing nothing. Comparing with a coin flip is the tempting mistake: when the outcome is rare, the real floor is the do-nothing baseline, not 50 percent.

quiz.q: The assistant's audit block reads: 'Label: no spend in the 60 days after the snapshot. Train: January to April, 8,000 rows. Test: May and June, 4,000 rows. Test months untouched during training.' What is the flaw?
options: The test set is too small next to the training set
The split should be random, so that both parts have the same churn rate
The label looks 60 days past the snapshot, so it leaks the future into training
April is in training, yet its labels do not exist when May is scored
quiz.why: Churn takes 60 days to show, so on the day you score May you cannot yet know who from April churned; training on April uses answers from the future. It looks like a clean past-to-future split, which is exactly why the missing gap is easy to wave through. A label is meant to look ahead; what must not happen is training on a row whose label is unfinished on scoring day.

quiz.q: A model predicts which creatives will fatigue. The assistant reports that it 'correctly identifies 94 percent of the fatigued creatives in the dataset'. What do you ask first?
options: Did it learn from those creatives? Show it on later ones it never saw
Could the remaining 6 percent be caught by adding a few more columns to it?
Which algorithm was used, and would a stronger one push the number higher?
Is 94 percent above the level the creative team said they would need?
quiz.why: A result on the rows a model learned from only shows that it can match the past; it counts when measured on creatives it never saw, from a later period. Chasing the last 6 percent assumes the 94 is real.

quiz.concept: a baseline for a predicted number
quiz.q: A model predicts each advertiser's spend for next month and is 'off by 400 dollars on average' on held-out advertisers. Finance asks whether that is good. What do you need in order to answer?
options: The model's average error on the advertisers it was trained on
The error as a share of average spend: under 10 percent is good
The error of 'same as last month' on the same advertisers
The error after a few more columns have been added to the model
quiz.why: A number is judged against the simplest alternative: if 'same as last month' is off by 420 dollars the model adds little, and if it is off by 900 the model is earning its keep. A fixed rule of thumb like 10 percent is tempting, but it says nothing about what you could get for free.

review.concept: judge on unseen rows, split the way the model will be used

variants.q: A lead counts as converted if it starts spending within 30 days. Today you want to score this week's new leads. Which past leads can the model learn from?
options: All past leads, including last week's, to keep the model current
Only leads from the past 30 days, as the most relevant ones
Leads whose 30-day window has fully passed, and no newer ones
A random half of all the leads ever created
variants.why: A lead created ten days ago has no finished label yet, so counting it as 'not converted' teaches the model something false. Using the freshest leads feels right, but their answers do not exist yet.

variants.q: Twelve weeks of creatives are labelled fatigued or not. The model will be used every Monday to score new creatives. The assistant shuffles all the rows and holds out a random fifth. What do you ask for instead?
options: A larger random hold-out, such as a third of the rows
Train on the earlier weeks, test on the latest weeks
The same random shuffle, repeated several times and averaged
No hold-out at all, so the model can learn from every row
variants.why: The model will be trained on the past and used on the future, so the test should rehearse that with a later period it never saw. A bigger or repeated shuffle still mixes later weeks into the training rows.

variants.q: An upsell model predicts who will adopt a new ad format within 60 days of a monthly snapshot. The audit block says: 'Train: July to October snapshots. Test: November.' Scoring happens on the November snapshot date. What is wrong?
options: October's 60-day outcomes are not known on the November date
July is too old to learn from: train on September and October only
The test month should have been picked at random from the five
Four training months are too few for a model of this kind
variants.why: On the November snapshot date only about a month of October's 60-day window has passed, so October's labels do not exist yet and cannot be trained on. The months are in the correct order, which is what hides the missing gap. Dropping July would not help: age is not the problem, unfinished labels are.

review.concept: no number without a baseline on the same rows

variants.q: An invalid-traffic model is reported as 99.2 percent accurate on held-out clicks. About 0.5 percent of clicks are invalid. What is the right read?
options: Excellent: almost every single click is classified correctly
Good, but it should be confirmed on a larger sample of clicks
Unclear until we know which algorithm produced the number
Calling every click valid scores 99.5, so this says little
variants.why: When only 0.5 percent of clicks are invalid, the do-nothing baseline is right 99.5 percent of the time, so 99.2 is no evidence of skill. The number sounds excellent only because nobody put the baseline beside it.

variants.q: A model forecasts next month's spend per advertiser and misses by 350 dollars on average. On the same advertisers, 'same as last month' misses by 340. What do you conclude?
options: The model is good: 350 dollars is small next to typical monthly spend
The model does not yet beat a baseline that costs nothing to run
The baseline must be miscalculated: nothing that simple matches a model
The two cannot be compared, because one of them is not a model
variants.why: The baseline is free and misses by slightly less, so the model has not earned its complexity. Judging 350 dollars against typical spend is the tempting mistake: the question is what it beats, not whether it sounds small.

variants.q: A support team escalates any ticket containing the word 'refund': 300 tickets last month, of which 120 were real escalations. A new model is 'right about escalation 80 percent of the time'. Which comparison settles whether to switch?
options: The model's 80 percent against the 50 percent of a coin flip
The model's 80 percent against the rule's 120 out of 300, or 40 percent
Both on the same new tickets, 300 flags each: escalations found by each
The model's result on the tickets it learned from against the rule's
variants.why: The bar is what the team already does, compared on the same unseen tickets with the same number flagged. Setting 80 percent against 40 percent compares two different kinds of number: a share of all tickets against a share of the flagged ones.

drill.q: Someone tells you a model is ninety percent accurate. Which two questions do you ask before reacting?
drill.a: Measured on which rows: ones the model never saw, from a later period? And compared with what: what does the simplest baseline score on those same rows?

drill.q: Why leave a gap month between the training months and the test months?
drill.a: Because the label takes sixty days to appear. On the day you score a new month, the month just before it has no finished answers yet, so training on it would use information you would not have.

recall.prompt: Someone says 'our model is 88 percent accurate'. Explain what you would need to know before that number means anything.
recall.model_answer: First, which rows it was measured on: it only counts on a test set the model never saw, split by time if the model will be used on the future, with a gap wherever labels take time to appear. Second, compared with what: on our test months, predicting that everyone stays is already about 87 percent accurate and finds no churners, so 88 is barely above doing nothing. The real bar is the simple rule we would use today, compared on the same advertisers with the same number flagged.

lessons.ask_assistant: Split by [date column], not at random. Train only on periods whose [outcome window] had closed before the first test date, test on [the latest periods], and say which period you left out and why. Make every modelling choice on the training periods. Score the test rows once, as a final stage I trigger, and list every evaluation run with the rows it used. On the test rows, put two baselines beside the model: predicting [the most common outcome] for everyone, and my rule [rule]. For each, show rows flagged and how many of those really had [outcome], with the model also shown at my rule's number of flags. Print rows and [outcome] rate for train, left-out and test.
audit_checklist: A split table: which periods train, which are left out and which test, with first and last date, rows and outcome rate for each
The gap, in dates: the last training period's outcome window ends before the first test date
Test scoring is its own final stage that you trigger, and the output lists every evaluation run with the rows it used
Both baselines beside the model on the same test rows: how many flagged and how many of those really had the outcome, with the model also shown at the rule's number of flags
transfer: Which leads will convert? Train on leads whose conversion window has closed, test on a later month, and compare with the sales team's current priority rule.
Which creatives are about to fatigue? Judge the model on creatives launched after its training period, next to the rule 'flag anything older than three weeks'.
How much will each advertiser spend next month? Test on months after the training period, with 'same as last month' beside the model.

other_ways.approach: A random hold-out
other_ways.when: When the rows have no time order that matters and the model will be used on rows like the ones it learned from, such as sorting a fixed pile of tickets.

other_ways.approach: Several time splits: repeat train-then-test from more than one starting month
other_ways.when: When a single test period is small or might be unusual, and you want to see how much the result moves.

other_ways.approach: A silent live trial: run the model next to the current rule for a period without acting on it, then compare
other_ways.when: When you can afford to wait for the outcomes and want the most honest test before anyone relies on the model.

glossary.def: Rows held back from training and used only to judge the model; also called a hold-out.
How well a model holds up on rows it never saw while learning; the test set is where you measure it.
Training on earlier periods and testing on later ones, to rehearse how the model will be used.
A period left out between training and test because its labels would not yet exist on scoring day.
A simple reference result, such as predicting that everyone stays or a hand rule, that a model must beat on the same rows.
The share of all cases where the yes or no prediction turned out right.

lessons.title: Accuracy lies: precision and recall
lessons.subtitle: If predicting 'nobody churns' is 87 percent accurate, what should you ask of a model instead?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can read a classifier's four counts and say in plain words how often its flags are right and how many of the real cases it catches.

predict.q: A churn model flags 141 of 4,000 test advertisers, of whom 527 churned, and is 88.5 percent accurate. Roughly how many of those churners did it catch?
options: Nearly nine in ten
About two in three
About half
About one in five
predict.reveal: About one in five: 104 of 527. Accuracy alone could not have told you; it is the 141 flags that pin it down. The lesson shows how a model can be 88.5 percent accurate and still miss four churners in five.

segments.narration: The churn report from the stand-up has reached the account team, and one lead has already replied: 88 and a half percent accurate, great, ship it. You know the catch from last lesson. Predict that every advertiser stays, and you are right about 87 percent of the time, having found nobody. So a working model and a useless one sit less than two points apart. Either this model is nearly worthless, or accuracy is the wrong ruler. It is the ruler.

visual.title: Accuracy lies
visual.sub: 88.5% accurate, and four churners in five get no call

segments.narration: Here is why. The test months hold 4,000 advertisers, and 527 of them churned, about one in eight. Accuracy is the share of rows you got right, and every row counts the same. In SQL terms it is an average over a table that is mostly stayers. [[1]] Call every advertiser a stayer, and the stayers alone hand you 87 percent. [[2]] The model's edge of under two points is all that its work on churners added. The rarer the outcome, the better doing nothing scores. If only five advertisers in a hundred churned, predicting that nobody churns would be 95 percent accurate, and just as useless. That holds for any yes-or-no model: when almost every click is valid, last lesson's invalid-traffic filter could flag nothing and score almost perfectly.

right.label: The model, cut-off 0.5
right.sub: 104 of 527 churners found

segments.narration: So open the result up. The model gives every advertiser a score between zero and one, and in this report anyone above 0.5 is flagged. Flagged or not, churned or not: four boxes. The model flagged 141 advertisers. Of those, 104 really churned: those it caught. The rest stayed: those are false alarms. Among the advertisers it did not flag, 423 churned anyway: those are the misses. Everyone else was left alone and stayed. The assistant will call these four boxes a confusion matrix. Accuracy counts the two correct boxes, and almost all of that count is the last one: stayers nobody was worried about.

visual.title: The model at cut-off 0.5: four boxes

segments.narration: Two questions do the work that accuracy cannot. The first: of the advertisers the model flagged, how many really churned? [[1]] That is precision. [[2]] Here it is 104 out of 141. [[3]] About 74 percent, so roughly three flags in four are right. Precision tells you the cost of acting. Every false alarm is a call to someone who was never leaving, or a retention offer handed to an advertiser who would have stayed. When the action is expensive, this is the number to watch.

visual.title: Question one: precision
lines: precision = flagged who churned ÷ everyone flagged
visual.note: What false alarms cost: wasted calls, wasted offers

segments.narration: The second question starts from the other side. Of all the advertisers who really churned, how many did the model catch? [[1]] That is recall. [[2]] Here it is 104 out of 527. [[3]] About 20 percent: one churner in five. Recall tells you the cost of silence: 423 advertisers left and nobody picked up the phone. Same numerator as precision, different denominator. So here is the 88 and a half percent model in plain words. When it speaks, it is right three times in four. And it says nothing about four churners in five. Neither figure is exact: with a different set of test advertisers, precision could land anywhere from about 67 to 81 percent. A later lesson shows how we know.

visual.title: Question two: recall
lines: recall = flagged who churned ÷ everyone who churned
visual.note: What misses cost: 423 churners nobody called

segments.narration: [[1]] Now put last lesson's hand rule beside it: spend trend below 0.7. [[2]] It flags 711 advertisers, and 246 of them churn. Its precision is about 35 percent, far below the model's, and its recall about 47, far above. At this cut-off the model is a cautious caller, the rule a loud one. Flag more, catch more, raise more false alarms: precision and recall pull against each other. Blend them into one number, the F1 score, and you hide which one is weak. Which matters more is a business call. A cheap check-in forgives false alarms, so favour recall. An expensive credit does not, so favour precision. [[3]] And notice the rule's accuracy: about 81 percent, below doing nothing. Accuracy puts a rule that finds nearly half the churners behind one that finds none.

visual.title: Same 4,000 advertisers, three ways to flag
visual.note: By accuracy, the rule ranks below doing nothing

segments.narration: One more thing the assistant may offer. Churn is rare, which it will call class imbalance, so it proposes to rebalance: copy churners, or drop stayers, until the table is half and half. Your default answer is no. Rarity is a fact about your business, not a defect in your data. A model trained on a half and half table learns that churn is common, and its scores come out too high. On the test rows, never: a rebalanced test set no longer looks like the advertisers you will score, so its precision is inflated. On the training rows it is a last resort for very rare outcomes, and the scores must then be corrected and checked against what happened. Keep the data. Change the measures.

visual.text: Rarity is a fact about the business, not a defect in the table.
visual.sub: Keep the data. Change the measures.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask the assistant for the four counts on the test months, at a cut-off it states. [[2]] Ask for precision and recall, with the same numbers for both baselines beside them: everyone stays, and your hand rule. Then the evidence. [[3]] The four counts must add up to the test row count, 4,000 here. [[4]] Churners caught plus churners missed must equal the churner total in your audit block, 527. [[5]] And the test rows should still churn at about 13 percent, which shows nothing was rebalanced. If the output leads with accuracy alone, send it back.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Ask: the four counts on the test months, cut-off stated
Ask: precision and recall, beside both baselines
Check: the four counts add up to 4,000
Check: caught + missed = 527 churners
Check: test churn rate still about 13% (nothing rebalanced)

segments.narration: From now on, when a report or a vendor leads with accuracy on a rare outcome, ask for the four counts and read precision and recall yourself. This model only looked timid because of where the line was drawn. Next lesson: nobody said it had to be 0.5.

visual.title: Keep this
items: Rare outcome: accuracy mostly counts the easy majority
Precision: of those flagged, how many were right
Recall: of those who churned, how many were caught

takeaways: When the outcome is rare, accuracy mostly measures the easy majority: compare it with 'predict nobody' before reacting.
Precision: of those flagged, how many were right. Recall: of the real cases, how many were caught.
The two trade off, and which matters more is a business decision about the cost of a false alarm against the cost of a miss.

quiz.q: The assistant tries a second churn model on the same 4,000 test advertisers. Its accuracy is 88.2 percent against the first model's 88.5, and the note says the two are 'effectively identical'. The second model flagged 99 advertisers, of whom 77 churned; the first flagged 141, of whom 104 churned. What is the right read?
options: They are interchangeable: a 0.3-point accuracy gap on 4,000 advertisers is too small to matter.
The second is the better model: 77 of its 99 flags were right, against 104 of the first's 141.
They differ: the second's flags are right more often, but it catches 77 churners, not 104.
The first is the better model: 88.5 beats 88.2 on exactly the same 4,000 rows.
quiz.why: Accuracy barely moves because both models agree on thousands of easy stayers. The counts show a real difference: precision 77.8 against 73.8 percent, but recall 14.6 against 19.7 percent, and which is preferable depends on what a miss and a false alarm cost. Calling them identical, or crowning one on accuracy or on precision alone, ignores half the picture.

quiz.q: The assistant's summary reads: 'Test months: 104 flagged and churned, 37 flagged and stayed, 423 churned but not flagged, 3,436 not flagged and stayed. Accuracy 88.5 percent: the model correctly identifies 88.5 percent of churners.' What is wrong with it?
options: The four counts are inconsistent: they do not add up to the 4,000 advertisers in the test months.
The sentence confuses accuracy with recall: by its own counts it caught 104 of 527 churners.
Only a baseline is missing: beside 'everyone stays' at 86.8 percent, the sentence would be fine.
The accuracy is miscalculated: 104 right out of 141 flagged gives about 74 percent, not 88.5.
quiz.why: Accuracy is the share of all 4,000 rows that were right, and most of those are stayers. The share of churners caught is recall: 104 of the 527 who churned, about 20 percent. The counts do add up, and 74 percent is the precision, not the accuracy. A baseline beside it would be welcome, but it would not make the sentence true.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches an invalid-traffic filter as '99 percent accurate'. Suppose about 1 click in 100 on your platform is invalid. What is the most useful reply?
options: Of the clicks it flags, how many are truly invalid, and of the invalid clicks, how many does it flag?
Run it on our own clicks first: if it is still 99 percent accurate there, we can trust the claim.
Was the test data rebalanced to half invalid clicks, so that the accuracy really means something?
Can you repeat the test on ten times as many clicks, to make the 99 percent more certain?
quiz.why: With 1 invalid click in 100, a filter that flags nothing at all is already 99 percent accurate, so the figure says nothing about the filter. Precision and recall are the questions that look at the rare group directly. Testing on your own clicks is the right instinct, but 99 percent accuracy there is still what flagging nothing scores. More clicks only make a meaningless number more exact, and a rebalanced test set would no longer resemble your traffic.

quiz.q: Finance will approve a costly retention credit for every advertiser the model flags at the 0.5 cut-off. The finance lead asks: 'How much of that credit goes to advertisers who were never going to leave?' Which figure answers her?
options: Recall: 104 of the 527 churners were flagged, so one credit in five is well spent.
Accuracy: 88.5 percent were classified correctly, so about 11.5 percent of the credit is wasted.
The misses: 423 of the 527 churners were not flagged, so four fifths of the credit is wasted.
Precision: 104 of the 141 flagged really churned, so the other 37 credits are wasted.
quiz.why: Her question is about the flagged group, so the denominator is everyone flagged: that is precision, and what is left over is the false alarms, 37 of 141. Recall and the 423 misses answer a different question, how many churners got no credit, and accuracy mixes in thousands of stayers nobody flagged. None of those three is a share of the credit.

review.concept: accuracy with a rare outcome

variants.q: A lead-scoring model is reported as 96 percent accurate. In the test data, 40 of 1,000 leads converted. What does the 96 percent tell you?
options: That it finds 96 percent of the leads that convert: about 38 of the 40.
Very little yet: predicting 'no lead converts' would also score 96 percent.
That 96 percent of the leads it flags will convert, so sales can trust the list.
That it is strong: rare outcomes are hard to predict, so 96 percent is impressive.
variants.why: 960 of the 1,000 leads do not convert, so the do-nothing guess is already 96 percent accurate. Accuracy is neither the share of converters found, which is recall, nor the share of flags that are right, which is precision. Ask for those two.

variants.q: A model that marks support tickets as urgent is 93 percent accurate on 2,000 test tickets, 100 of which were urgent. Its four counts: 10 urgent tickets flagged, 50 non-urgent flagged, 90 urgent missed, 1,850 correctly left alone. What is the right read?
options: Good: 93 percent is high, and 50 false alarms are few next to 2,000 tickets.
Usable: it is right about 1,860 of the 2,000 tickets and rarely raises a false alarm.
Poor: it catches 10 of 100 urgent tickets, and flagging nothing would score 95 percent.
Unclear: with only 100 urgent tickets in the test set, nothing can be concluded yet.
variants.why: Only 100 of 2,000 tickets are urgent, so flagging nothing scores 95 percent: the model is below the do-nothing baseline. Its recall is 10 of 100 and its precision 10 of 60. Being right about 1,860 tickets sounds solid only because 1,850 of them were never in question, and a hundred urgent tickets is plenty to see that nine in ten are missed.

variants.q: A colleague reports two churn models. On product line A, 8 percent of advertisers churn and the model is 92 percent accurate. On line B, 30 percent churn and the model is 80 percent accurate. Which model adds more over doing nothing?
options: Line B's: it beats 'everyone stays' by ten points, while line A's only matches it.
Line A's: 92 percent against 80 means twelve more advertisers in a hundred are right.
Line A's: churn is rarer there and harder to predict, so 92 percent is worth more.
It cannot be said: with different churn rates, the two accuracies are not comparable.
variants.why: Accuracy only means something next to the do-nothing rate: 'everyone stays' scores 92 percent on line A and 70 percent on line B. So A's model adds nothing and B's adds ten points. The higher headline is the tempting answer, and it belongs to the model that may be finding no churners at all. Different churn rates do not block the comparison: they are the reason to make it against each line's own baseline.

review.concept: precision versus recall

variants.q: A model flags creatives that are about to fatigue. Last month it flagged 200, and 150 of those did fatigue. In total 600 creatives fatigued. The design lead asks: 'What share of the creatives that fatigued were we warned about?'
options: 75 percent: 150 of the 200 flagged.
25 percent: 150 of the 600 that fatigued.
33 percent: 200 flagged against 600 fatigued.
It cannot be answered without the model's accuracy.
variants.why: She is asking about all the creatives that fatigued, so they are the denominator: that is recall, 150 of 600. The 75 percent is precision, the share of warnings that were right. It is a true number that answers a different question.

variants.q: An upsell model picks accounts for a half-day workshop with a solutions engineer, and engineers are scarce. An account that is missed simply gets the usual sales email. Which measure should the team push up first?
options: Recall, so that no interested account is missed.
Accuracy, because it balances both kinds of error.
Precision, because each false alarm burns a scarce half-day.
Neither: with a rare outcome both are unreliable.
variants.why: The action is expensive and a miss is cheap, so the cost sits in the false alarms: that is precision. Recall would come first if the action were cheap and a miss costly. Accuracy does not balance the two errors, it hides which one you are making.

variants.q: Account managers can send a two-line check-in email to any flagged advertiser at almost no cost, while a churned advertiser is a lost account. The current setting has precision of about 74 percent and recall of about 20 percent. What is its main weakness for this use?
options: Precision: one flag in four is a false alarm, and every one of them wastes an email.
Neither figure: both must pass 50 percent before the setting is usable.
Its balance: precision and recall should be about equal, and here they are far apart.
Recall: four churners in five never get the email, and each is a lost account.
variants.why: When acting is cheap and missing is costly, the misses are what hurt, and this setting misses about four churners in five. One false alarm in four costs only a few unneeded emails. The high precision is the tempting number, but here it prices the wrong mistake. Nothing says the two must be equal or pass a fixed mark: the costs decide.

drill.q: Why can a model that is ninety-five percent accurate be useless?
drill.a: Because accuracy counts every row the same. If only five cases in a hundred are positive, answering no to everything is already ninety-five percent accurate and finds nothing. Always compare accuracy with the do-nothing guess.

drill.q: What is the difference between precision and recall?
drill.a: Precision starts from the flagged list: of those flagged, how many were right. Recall starts from the real cases: of all the real ones, how many were flagged. Same numerator, different denominator.

recall.prompt: A stakeholder says: 'The model is 88.5 percent accurate, so it must be catching most churners.' Explain why that does not follow, and what you would report instead.
recall.model_answer: About 87 percent of advertisers stay, so predicting that everyone stays is already about 87 percent accurate while finding no churners: accuracy is dominated by the easy stayers. The useful numbers are precision, the share of flagged advertisers who really churned, about 74 percent, and recall, the share of churners who were flagged, about 20 percent. So this model is usually right when it flags and misses four churners in five. Which of the two matters more depends on what a false alarm costs against what a miss costs.

lessons.ask_assistant: For [model], report results on [the test period] only, at a stated cut-off of [cut-off]. Show the four counts (flagged and had [outcome], flagged and did not, had [outcome] but not flagged, neither) with precision and recall, and put the same figures for 'predict [the common outcome] for everyone' and for my rule [rule] in the same table. Print the test row count and the [outcome] rate beside them, so I can check that the counts add up. Do not rebalance or resample the test rows. If you reweighted or resampled the training rows, say so and show the average predicted rate beside the actual rate. Do not lead with accuracy.
audit_checklist: The four counts are shown and add up to the test row count (4,000 here).
Churners caught plus churners missed equals the churner total from the audit block (527 here).
Precision and recall are stated with their cut-off, beside the same figures for both baselines.
The churn rate in the test rows matches the real rate (about 13 percent): nothing was rebalanced.
transfer: Which clicks are invalid traffic? Almost every click is valid, so 'flag nothing' is almost perfectly accurate.
Which leads will convert? Ask what share of flagged leads convert, and what share of converters were flagged.
Which support tickets are urgent? A missed urgent ticket and a false alarm cost very different amounts.

other_ways.approach: Put a cost on each of the four boxes and compare models by total cost
other_ways.when: When you can price a false alarm and a miss in dollars; a later lesson does exactly this.

other_ways.approach: One blended number from precision and recall (the F1 score)
other_ways.when: When you must screen many candidate models quickly and have no costs; it hides which of the two is weak.

other_ways.approach: Class weights or resampling applied to the training rows only
other_ways.when: When positives are so few the model learns nothing from them; the scores then need correcting, and the test rows stay untouched.

glossary.def: The four counts behind any yes-or-no prediction: flagged and real, flagged and not real, missed, and correctly left alone.
A row the model flagged that did not have the outcome.
A row that had the outcome and was not flagged.
Of the rows the model flagged, the share that really had the outcome.
Of the rows that really had the outcome, the share the model flagged.
When one outcome is rare, like churn at about one row in eight: accuracy then mostly counts the common outcome.
One number blended from precision and recall; handy for screening models, but it hides which of the two is weak.

lessons.title: Scores, cut-offs and ranked lists
lessons.subtitle: The model gives a score. Who decides where to cut, and how do you judge the ranking?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can turn a model's scores into a list sized for the team, compare it fairly with a baseline, and say in one sentence what an AUC means.

predict.q: At the default cut-off of 0.5 the model flags 141 advertisers and catches about 20 percent of the churners. Lower the cut-off to 0.2 and it flags 690. What share of the churners does it catch now?
options: About 25 percent
About 40 percent
About 60 percent
About 90 percent
predict.reveal: About 60 percent, three times as many, while precision falls from about 74 to about 46 percent. The lesson shows how to choose that trade.

segments.narration: Last lesson's model caught one churner in five, and the account lead is back with a fair question: can it be less timid? It can, without retraining anything. The model never said yes or no. It gave each of the 4,000 test advertisers a score between zero and one, and a line at 0.5 turned those scores into flags. That line was a default in the code. Nobody in your business chose it. So the question is not what the model flags. It is where you want the line. That holds for any yes-or-no model, whether it scores churn risk or who will adopt the video format.

visual.title: Scores, cut-offs and ranked lists
visual.sub: Nobody said the cut-off had to be 0.5

segments.narration: [[1]] At 0.5 the model flagged 141 advertisers. Precision was about 74 percent and recall about 20. [[2]] Now slide the line down to 0.2. The model flags 690 advertisers. Recall triples, to about 60 percent: three churners in five now get a call. Precision drops to about 46 percent, so more than half the calls are false alarms. Nothing about the model changed: same scores, same order. You moved a line, and traded precision for recall. The assistant's code will call that line a threshold.

visual.title: Same model, same scores, two cut-offs

right.label: Cut-off 0.2
right.sub: precision 45.7% · recall 59.8%

segments.narration: Every test advertiser's real score is loaded, and the cut-off is yours to drag. Start at 0.5, then pull it down and watch the four counts change. Three things to find. The cut-off that catches nine churners in ten, and how many advertisers it flags. The cut-off where nine flags in ten are right, and how many flags are left. And the cut-off that flags about as many advertisers as the hand rule did. You will not find one that makes precision and recall both high. That is the trade you are choosing. Try it now.

visual.name: threshold
visual.title: Drag the cut-off over the real test scores
visual.note: Find the cut-off that catches 9 churners in 10, the one where 9 flags in 10 are right, and the one that flags about 711, the size of the hand rule's list.

segments.narration: Here is what the slider shows. Nine churners in ten: a cut-off of 0.05, with nearly half of all advertisers flagged. Nine right flags in ten: 0.7, with only 43 flagged. The hand rule's list size: just under 0.2. [[4]] In practice a list length is easier to pick than a cut-off. If account managers can call 200 advertisers, sort by score and take the top 200. In SQL terms: order by score descending, limit 200. The assistant will call it a top K list. It holds 136 churners, 68 percent: that share is called precision at K. A random list would hold about 26, so this one is about five times richer. That ratio is called lift. The churner count wobbles too: on other test advertisers it could be anywhere from 123 to 150.

visual.title: Sort by score, take the top K
visual.note: ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 200

segments.narration: Earlier the bar was set: beat the hand rule with the same number of flags. Here is why. The rule flagged 711 advertisers and the default cut-off 141, so comparing their precision compares a long list with a short one, and a short list usually looks more precise. Give both the same length. [[1]] The rule's 711 advertisers hold 246 churners. [[2]] The model's top 711 hold 321. Same effort for the team, more churners reached, and the model is ahead on precision and recall at once. Here the model wins; elsewhere a rule might. Either way, the only fair comparison is at the same list size.

right.label: Model: top 711 by score
right.sub: precision 45.1% · recall 60.9%

segments.narration: What you are judging, then, is the ranking. Sort all 4,000 test advertisers by score and cut the list into ten equal slices. [[1]] In the top slice, 55 percent churned. [[2]] In the second, about 30 percent. [[3]] In the third, about 14. [[4]] In the fourth, 12, already below the overall average of about 13.
