A good ranking looks like that: churners piled at the top, almost none at the bottom. The top two slices, a fifth of all advertisers, hold about 64 percent of the churners.

visual.title: Churn rate by slice of the ranked list (400 advertisers each)
visual.note: Test-month average: 13.2%. Six more slices follow, down to 0.5%.

segments.narration: One number sums up a ranking with no cut-off involved: AUC, short for area under the curve. Pick one advertiser who churned and one who stayed, at random. AUC is how often the churner has the higher score. A coin flip gives 0.5. A perfect ranking gives 1. This model gets about 0.85: in 85 pairs out of a hundred, the churner comes out on top. If a report draws the curve, hugging the top left corner is good and the diagonal is the coin flip. Now what AUC hides. It averages over the whole list, so it says little about the top 200, the only part your team will touch. And it only checks order, so it cannot tell you whether a score of 0.3 really means 30 percent.

visual.text: AUC: pick one churner and one stayer at random. How often does the churner have the higher score?
visual.sub: 0.5 = a coin · 1 = perfect · this model: 0.845 · reports draw it as the ROC curve

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask the assistant for a score for every test advertiser, never just a yes or no. [[2]] Ask for precision and recall at several cut-offs, not one. [[3]] Ask for the top of the list at sizes your team could handle, with the count a random list would hold beside it. Then the evidence. [[4]] Every precision or recall figure must name the cut-off or list size behind it. [[5]] Any claim that the model beats a baseline must be made at the same list size. And AUC goes in the report on the test months, beside the top of the list, never instead of it.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Ask: a score per advertiser, not a yes or no
Ask: precision and recall at several cut-offs
Ask: top 100, 200, 400, 800 with the random-list count
Check: every figure names its cut-off or list size
Check: model and baseline at the same list size

segments.narration: So when someone needs a list, ask how many the team can handle, take that many from the top, and judge any rival at the same size. So far the score has only been an order. Next lesson: can it be read as a percentage?

visual.title: Keep this
items: The model ranks; you choose where to cut
Compare lists at the same size
AUC: how often a churner outscores a stayer

takeaways: A model outputs scores; where to cut is your decision, usually set by capacity or cost.
Compare a model and a rule at the same list size, never at different ones.
AUC is how often a random churner outscores a random stayer: it judges the ranking, not the top of the list and not the percentages.

quiz.q: The retention team can call 400 advertisers this month. The assistant's report uses the default cut-off of 0.5 and lists 141. The team lead says: 'The model only gives us 141 names, so we will fill the other 259 from the old rule.' What do you tell her?
options: Good plan: the model has no view on anyone below 0.5, so the rule should fill the gap.
Take the model's top 400 by score: the 0.5 line was a default, not part of the model.
Ask the assistant to retrain until at least 400 advertisers score above the 0.5 line.
Call only the 141: everyone else is predicted to stay, so more calls would be wasted.
quiz.why: Every advertiser has a score, so the list can be any length: the top 400 by score hold 220 churners. Scoring below 0.5 does not mean 'predicted safe', only lower on the same ranking, so the model has an opinion about all 4,000. Retraining to push scores over an arbitrary line fixes nothing.

quiz.concept: compare at the same list size
quiz.q: The assistant's summary says: 'The model clearly beats the hand rule: precision 73.8 percent against 34.6 percent.' The same output shows that the model flagged 141 advertisers and the rule 711. What is the flaw?
options: It should have compared false alarms: 37 for the model against 465 for the rule.
It should have compared recall: 19.7 against 46.7 percent shows the rule is better.
It should have compared accuracy, 88.5 against 81.4 percent, which uses all four boxes.
The lists differ in length: compare the rule with the model's top 711 instead.
quiz.why: A list of 141 and a list of 711 are different jobs for the team, and a short list from a ranking usually looks more precise than a long one. At the same size the model holds 321 churners against the rule's 246, and that is the claim the evidence supports. Switching to recall, to false alarms or to accuracy still sets a short list against a long one.

quiz.q: A lead-scoring model is reported with an AUC of 0.80. The sales manager says: 'So 80 percent of the leads it flags will convert.' What is the right read?
options: No: a random converter outscores a random non-converter 80 percent of the time.
Yes, roughly: AUC is the model's precision averaged over every possible cut-off.
No: it means the model puts 80 percent of all leads on the right side of the cut-off.
No: it means the model catches 80 percent of the leads that go on to convert.
quiz.why: AUC describes the ranking: how often a converter is placed above a non-converter. It is not precision, accuracy or recall, each of which needs a cut-off, so the share of a flagged list that converts has to be read from a top-K table. When few leads convert, that share can sit far below 80 percent even with a good AUC.

quiz.concept: moving the cut-off is a trade
quiz.q: A stakeholder asks for a cut-off that 'catches 90 percent of churners and is right at least 70 percent of the time'. The assistant's table shows recall reaches 90 percent only at a cut-off of 0.05, where precision is 24 percent, and precision passes 70 percent only at 0.5, where recall is 20 percent. What do you reply?
options: Use a cut-off halfway between the two, which should land close to both targets.
Flag only advertisers who clear both cut-offs, 0.05 and 0.5, so both targets are met.
No cut-off on these scores does both: pick the trade by cost and by team capacity.
Rebalance the training data to half churners, so precision and recall rise together.
quiz.why: Moving the cut-off slides along one trade-off: recall is bought with precision, and on these scores the two targets never meet. A halfway cut-off gives roughly half of each, not both, and clearing both cut-offs is just the 0.5 cut-off again. Only a model that ranks better would shift the whole trade, and rebalancing does not do that, so the reply is a choice driven by what a miss and a false alarm cost.

review.concept: the cut-off is your decision

variants.q: A traffic-quality model scores every publisher from 0 to 1 for likely invalid traffic. At the default cut-off of 0.5 it flags 30 publishers. The review team can audit 150 publishers a week. What should the weekly list be?
options: The 30 flagged publishers: the rest are predicted clean.
The 150 highest-scoring publishers: capacity sets the length.
The 30 flagged, plus 120 picked at random for fairness.
Whatever a cut-off of 0.25 produces, since that is half the default.
variants.why: The score ranks every publisher, so the team's capacity sets the list length: sort and take the top 150. The 0.5 line is a default, not a verdict, and publishers below it are simply lower on the same ranking. Random picks or an arbitrary new cut-off throw that ranking away.

variants.q: An upsell model's list has 300 accounts, and 40 percent of them bought. The sales team's own rule produced a list of 1,200 accounts, and 25 percent bought. A manager concludes that the model is better. What is missing?
options: The buyers as counts: 120 on the model's list against 300 on the rule's.
The accuracy of each list, which also counts the accounts left off it.
A comparison at one size: the model's top 1,200 against the rule's 1,200.
A second month of results: one month of lists is too few to compare.
variants.why: A list of 300 and a list of 1,200 are different jobs, and a short list from a ranking usually has the higher hit rate. The rule found 300 buyers; the question is how many buyers sit in the model's top 1,200. Only at equal size do you learn which finds more for the same effort. Setting 120 buyers against 300 is the same unequal comparison written as counts.

variants.q: After a staffing cut, the retention team can call 100 advertisers a month instead of 400. The model is unchanged. What should you expect when the list shrinks from the top 400 to the top 100?
options: Precision rises and recall falls: a shorter list is purer and reaches fewer churners.
Precision and recall both fall, because the model is now applied to fewer advertisers.
Both stay where they were: precision and recall belong to the model, not to the list.
Recall rises and precision falls: the calls are now focused on the likeliest churners.
variants.why: The scores and their order stay the same; only the cut moves up the list. On the course data the top 400 are 55 percent churners and reach about 42 percent of all churners, while the top 100 are 76 percent churners and reach about 14 percent. Precision and recall describe a model plus a cut-off, never the model alone.

review.concept: what AUC means and what it hides

variants.q: A model that scores support tickets for urgency has an AUC of 0.90. Which statement is true?
options: Of the tickets it flags as urgent, 90 percent really are urgent when a person checks.
It finds 90 percent of all the urgent tickets in the inbox and misses one in ten.
It gives the correct label, urgent or not, to 90 percent of all the tickets.
A random urgent ticket outscores a random non-urgent one 90 percent of the time.
variants.why: AUC is about pairs: take one urgent and one non-urgent ticket at random, and it is the chance the urgent one scores higher. The other three statements are precision, recall and accuracy, and each of those needs a cut-off that AUC never uses.

variants.q: Two models rank creatives by risk of fatigue. Model X has an AUC of 0.88 and model Y 0.86. The design team can refresh only the 200 highest-ranked creatives. In the top 200, X has 80 that really fatigued and Y has 124. Which do you use?
options: X: the higher AUC means the better ranking everywhere.
Y: the team only uses the top 200, and Y is better there.
Either: a gap of 0.02 in AUC means the two lists are the same.
Neither, until one of them reaches an AUC of 0.90 or more.
variants.why: AUC averages ranking quality over the whole list, including the many creatives nobody will act on. The decision uses only the top 200, so judge the top 200: 124 against 80. A slightly higher AUC promises nothing about any one part of the list.

variants.q: By mistake, the assistant's script divides every churn score by two before reporting. What happens to the AUC and to the top-200 list?
options: Both get worse, because the scores are now wrong.
The AUC halves; the top-200 list is unchanged.
Neither changes: both depend only on the order of the scores.
The AUC is unchanged, but the list shrinks to a top 100.
variants.why: Halving every score keeps every advertiser in the same order, and AUC and a top-K list use nothing but the order. That is exactly why AUC cannot tell you whether scores are right as percentages: they have all just been cut in half, and AUC did not notice.

drill.q: A model gives every customer a score between zero and one. Who decides where the cut-off goes, and how?
drill.a: You do, not the model. Usually by capacity: sort by score and take as many as the team can handle. The halfway line is only a default in the code.

drill.q: What does an AUC of zero point eight five mean in plain words, and what does it not tell you?
drill.a: Pick one churner and one stayer at random: eighty-five times in a hundred, the churner has the higher score. It measures ranking only. It does not tell you how good the top of the list is, or whether the scores are right as percentages.

recall.prompt: The report says the model's precision is 74 percent and the hand rule's is 35 percent. Explain why that comparison is unfair, how to make it fair, and what single number sums up the ranking.
recall.model_answer: The model's figure is for 141 flagged advertisers and the rule's for 711, and a short list from a ranking usually looks more precise, so the two are not comparable. Sort by score and take the model's top 711: it holds 321 churners against the rule's 246, which is the fair comparison. To sum up the ranking in one number use AUC, the chance that a random churner outscores a random stayer, about 0.85 here. Read the top of the list as well, because AUC averages over everyone.

lessons.ask_assistant: Output a score for every test row, not a yes or no. Show a table of number flagged, precision and recall at [several cut-offs across the range]. Show the top [list sizes my team could handle] by score, with the number of real [outcome] cases on each list and the number a random list of that size would hold. Compare the model with my rule [rule] at the rule's own list size, on the same test rows. Report AUC on [the test period] beside these tables, not instead of them, and print the test row count and [outcome] rate.
audit_checklist: Every precision or recall figure names the cut-off or list size it belongs to.
The model and the baseline are compared at the same number flagged.
Each top-K row shows what a random list of that size would hold.
AUC is stated for the test months and sits beside the top-of-list numbers, not in place of them.
transfer: Which leads should sales call first, when the team can make 50 calls a day?
Which publishers should the traffic-quality team audit this week?
Which creatives should be refreshed first, before they fatigue?

other_ways.approach: Set the cut-off from costs: the value of a catch against the cost of a false alarm
other_ways.when: When you can put dollars on both and the percentages can be trusted; a later lesson does this.

other_ways.approach: Two cut-offs and three bands: act now, watch, leave alone
other_ways.when: When you have a cheap action and an expensive one for the same list.

other_ways.approach: A precision-recall summary in place of AUC
other_ways.when: When the outcome is very rare and only the top of the list matters; it weights the top more heavily.

glossary.def: The score above which a row is flagged; a decision you make, not something the model learns.
The K highest-scoring rows: a list sized by what the team can handle, judged against what a random list of that size would hold.
The share of the top K rows that really have the outcome: 136 churners in the top 200 is 68 percent.
How many times richer a list is in the outcome than a random list of the same size: about five times for the top 200 here.
The chance that a randomly chosen positive case scores higher than a randomly chosen negative one; 0.5 is a coin, 1 is perfect.
The chart behind AUC: the closer the line hugs the top-left corner the better the ranking, and the diagonal is a coin flip.

lessons.title: Can you trust the percentage?
lessons.subtitle: When the model says 30 percent, do 30 in a hundred leave?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can ask for and read a predicted-versus-actual table, and say whether a model's scores are safe to multiply by money.

predict.q: The model gave 291 test advertisers a churn score between 20 and 30 percent, about 25 percent on average. What share of those 291 actually churned?
options: About 15 percent
About 25 percent
About 33 percent
About 50 percent
predict.reveal: About 33 percent. The model ranks well, but its percentages run low here; the lesson shows why, and when that matters.

segments.narration: The sales lead shows you next quarter's forecast. Every open deal carries a win probability, and the forecast multiplies each one by the deal's value and adds it up. That assumes deals scored at 30 percent close three times in ten, and nobody has checked. Any yes-or-no model, whether it scores deals, video-format adoption or churn, makes two separate claims: that it ranks cases in the right order, and that its percentages are right. AUC tested only the first, and a model can pass one and fail the other. Finance wants the same sum from your churn model, score times spend, called revenue at risk, and on the churn table the second claim can be checked. Of the advertisers the model scored at around 30 percent, how many actually left?

visual.title: Can you trust the percentage?
visual.sub: The model says 30 percent. How many left?

segments.narration: The check is a GROUP BY. Put the test advertisers into buckets by score, and in each bucket compare two numbers: the average score, and the share who really churned. [[1]] Take the bucket scored between 20 and 30 percent. The model said about 25 percent on average, and about 33 percent left. One in four promised, one in three delivered. [[2]] The next bucket up, the thirties, was promised about 35 percent and delivered about 40. When predicted and actual agree in every bucket, a model is called calibrated: its 30 percent means 30 in a hundred. This one runs low on both sides of 30.

visual.title: Around a score of 30%: what the model said, what happened
visual.note: Test months. Calibrated would mean the last two columns match.

segments.narration: Now every bucket at once. For a calibrated model, each bucket's prediction and its actual rate would match. Here the actual rate is above the prediction in all eight buckets, from the safest advertisers to the riskiest. The gap is small at the bottom, where the model says 2 percent and about two and a half percent churn. It is widest from the twenties upward. Watch the bucket sizes as well: the top bucket holds only 43 advertisers, so its gap is the least certain. Explore it now, one bucket at a time: what the model said, what happened, and how many advertisers stand behind it.

visual.name: calibration
visual.title: Predicted against actual, bucket by bucket
visual.note: For each bucket: what the model said, what happened, and how many advertisers stand behind it.

segments.narration: Read those buckets two ways. First, compare each bucket with the next one up. The actual churn rate climbs every time, from under 3 percent in the lowest bucket to about 90 percent in the highest. So the ranking is intact: a higher score really does mean a riskier advertiser. That is what AUC measured. Second, compare prediction with outcome inside each bucket. The model's number is below the truth every time. The order is right and the level is wrong. A top 200 list built from these scores is exactly as good as it was last lesson. A sum of money built from them is not.

visual.title: The same buckets, read two ways

left.label: Bucket to bucket: the order
left.sub: actual churn climbs at every step, so the ranking is intact

right.label: Inside each bucket: the level
right.sub: the model said less than happened, every time

segments.narration: Why low? [[1]] The model learned from January to March, when about 11 percent of advertisers churned. On those months its average prediction and the actual rate match exactly. That is no achievement: training tunes the scores to agree with the outcomes it was shown. [[2]] Then it was tested on May and June, when about 13 percent churned. It still expects about 11. That is about two points too low overall, and away from the safest advertisers the gap opens to several points per bucket. A model carries the churn rate of its training months forward, and when the real rate moves, the percentages go stale even if the order holds. That every bucket runs low is how this simulated world was built: churn creeps up month by month. Do not expect that pattern elsewhere. Measure it.

right.label: Test months (May–Jun)
right.sub: predicted → actual: runs low

segments.narration: When does this matter? [[1]] If you only sort and take the top of the list, it does not. Order is all a list uses. [[2]] It matters the moment a score is multiplied by money. Finance's revenue at risk adds up thousands of scores that run low, so the total comes out low too. [[3]] And it matters when someone states a cut-off in percent. Say the policy is to call everyone above 30 percent risk. The advertisers the model scores at about 25 are really churning at about 33, and the policy walks straight past them. So use the score as a rank freely. Use it as a number only after checking.

visual.title: When the percentage has to be right
items: Sort and take the top K: order is enough
Score × dollars: every term inherits the error
A cut-off stated in percent: the line is not where you think

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask the assistant for a predicted versus actual table on the test months: score buckets, the number of advertisers in each, the average prediction and the actual rate. [[2]] Ask for the same table by the segments the business cares about, because a model can be right overall and wrong for one group of clients. Then the evidence. [[3]] The bucket counts must add up to the test rows, 4,000 here. A table built on the training months will match beautifully and prove nothing. [[4]] The overall average prediction must sit beside the overall actual rate. [[5]] And every bucket needs its count, so you can discount the thin ones. If the scores are off, the repair is called recalibration. Ask for it, then ask for the same table, on rows the adjustment never saw.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Ask: predicted versus actual by score bucket, test months
Ask: the same table by segment
Check: bucket counts add up to the 4,000 test rows
Check: overall predicted beside overall actual
Check: a count in every bucket

segments.narration: The next time someone multiplies a probability by money, in a sales forecast or a revenue at risk figure, you know which table to ask for first. So far every prediction was a yes or a no; next lesson, it is a number, like dollars of spend.

visual.title: Keep this
items: Ranking and percentages are separate claims
Check predicted versus actual, on test rows
Rank freely; multiply by money only after checking

takeaways: Ranking well and stating honest percentages are separate claims; AUC only checks the first.
Check the percentages with a predicted-versus-actual table on test rows, overall and by segment.
A score works as a rank straight away; multiply it by money or set a cut-off in percent only after that check.

quiz.q: The churn model has an AUC of about 0.85. The finance lead says: 'That is a strong model, so we can treat each score as that advertiser's probability of leaving and add up the expected lost revenue.' What is the right read?
options: Agreed: an AUC above 0.8 is the usual bar for treating scores as probabilities.
Not usable at all: an AUC of 0.85 means about 15 percent of the scores are wrong.
Not yet: AUC only shows that churners outrank stayers, so check predicted against actual first.
Agreed for the total: single scores may be off, but the errors cancel when thousands are added up.
quiz.why: AUC uses only the order of the scores, so it is silent on whether 0.3 means 30 percent. On the test months the scores run low: the model expected about 11 percent to churn and about 13 percent did, so the revenue total would be understated. Errors that all lean the same way do not cancel in a sum, AUC is not an error rate, and no AUC level certifies the percentages.

quiz.q: The assistant reports: 'Calibration check on the 6,000 advertisers the model was fitted on: average predicted churn 11.1 percent, actual churn 11.1 percent. The model is perfectly calibrated and its scores can be used as probabilities.' What do you send back?
options: Approved for totals: with the two averages equal, a sum over all advertisers will come out right.
A match on the fitted rows is automatic: show the same check on the test rows, by bucket.
An average can hide the buckets: show the bucket table for those same 6,000 advertisers.
Show the AUC on those 6,000 rows as well: if it is above 0.8, the calibration claim holds.
quiz.why: The check was run on the rows the model was fitted on, January to March, where the average prediction matches the actual rate because training made it so. On the 4,000 test advertisers the model said 10.9 percent and 13.2 percent churned. Asking for buckets is a good instinct, but buckets on the fitted rows would flatter the model too, and AUC says nothing about the level of the scores.

quiz.q: An upsell model scores accounts on how likely they are to buy an add-on. It ranks well, but a check shows its percentages run high: of the accounts it scored around 40 percent, about 25 percent bought. The scores feed two uses. One: sales calls the 50 highest-scoring accounts each week. Two: finance forecasts add-on revenue as score times price, summed. What is the right read of the two uses?
options: The call list and the forecast are both off: scores that are wrong as percentages are wrong as an order too.
The call list and the forecast both stand: a model that ranks well gives a sound total when its scores are summed.
The call list is off and the forecast stands: over-scored accounts crowd the top 50, but the errors cancel in a sum.
The call list stands and the forecast is overstated: the order is untouched, but every term in the sum is too high.
quiz.why: The call list uses only the order of the scores, and the order is good. The forecast uses the scores as numbers, so every term is inflated and the total is too high; errors that all lean high do not cancel. Wrong percentages do not mean a wrong ranking: they are separate properties, checked separately.

quiz.q: An account lead sets a policy: 'Call every advertiser the model puts above 30 percent churn risk.' The predicted-versus-actual table shows that advertisers scored between 20 and 30 percent churned at about 33 percent. What does that mean for her policy?
options: It skips advertisers whose real risk is above her line: those scored about 25 percent are leaving at about 33.
It works as she intends: the ranking is correct, so the riskiest advertisers are still the ones called.
It should be dropped: a model whose 25 percent means 33 percent cannot rank advertisers either.
Her line should move up, to about 40 percent, because the model flags more advertisers than she meant.
quiz.why: She means a real risk above 30 percent, but the line is drawn on the model's scores, and a score of about 25 here goes with a real rate of about 33. So a whole group above her intended line is left out. The ranking is fine, which is why this is easy to miss and why the model need not be dropped; to reach the advertisers she means, her line on the scores has to come down, not up.

review.concept: ranking and calibration are separate

variants.q: A lead-scoring model ranks leads well, but its percentages run high: leads it scores around 20 percent convert about 8 percent of the time. Sales uses the scores only to order the daily call queue. What is the impact?
options: The queue is in the wrong order: a lead scored at 20 percent belongs lower down.
None on the queue, which uses order only; just keep the percentages out of quotes and forecasts.
The model must be retrained before the next queue goes out, because inflated scores inflate the ranking too.
The queue should be cut to less than half its length, since fewer than half the promised conversions arrive.
variants.why: A call queue needs only the order of the scores, and the order is good. The inflated percentages would do harm only where they are used as numbers: quoted to a rep, or multiplied into a forecast. A model can rank well and still state the wrong percentages, so neither the order nor the length of the queue has to change.

variants.q: A click model orders ads from best to worst correctly, but its predicted click rates are about twice the real ones for every ad. Which task will it get wrong?
options: Picking the ten ads most likely to be clicked.
Ordering a client's creatives from strongest to weakest.
Forecasting next week's clicks as predicted rate times impressions.
Flagging the weakest tenth of a client's ads for a refresh.
variants.why: Picking the top ten, ordering creatives and flagging the weakest tenth all use only the ranking, which is right. The forecast multiplies the predicted rate by a volume, so it uses the rate as a number and comes out about double. Doubling every rate changes the level and leaves the order alone.

variants.q: A check shows the churn model's scores run low in every bucket, while the actual churn rate still rises steadily from the lowest-scored bucket to the highest. What can you still rely on?
options: Only the bottom buckets, where the gap is small; the top of the list is no longer trustworthy.
The percentages but not the order: a steady rise shows each bucket's number is about right.
The order and the percentages: a rate that rises bucket by bucket shows the scores are right as numbers too.
The order: top-K lists and AUC stand, but the scores are not yet percentages.
variants.why: A churn rate that rises bucket by bucket shows the ranking is intact, so anything that uses order alone still stands, at the top of the list as much as the bottom. Running low in every bucket shows the level is off, so the scores are not yet percentages. A steady rise says nothing about the level: the scores could all be half the truth and still rise.

review.concept: check percentages on unseen rows before using them as numbers

variants.q: A model that estimates the chance a support ticket is urgent was trained in a quarter when 5 percent of tickets were urgent. After a product launch, 10 percent are. The model has not been touched. What should you expect of its percentages now?
options: They run low on average, because the model still carries the old 5 percent rate; the ordering may still hold.
They run high, because with twice as many urgent tickets the model finds more to flag.
They are unchanged and still right: a model that was not retrained gives the same numbers.
They and the ordering are both unusable, since the inbox no longer resembles the training data.
variants.why: A model carries forward the rate it was trained on, so when urgent tickets become twice as common its percentages come out too low on average. 'Its numbers are the same' is exactly the problem: the inbox changed and the model did not. Ordering is a separate property and can survive, so check both on recent tickets.

variants.q: A colleague wants to forecast renewal revenue as each customer's predicted renewal probability times contract value. Which piece of evidence should come first?
options: The model's AUC on the test rows, to confirm that it ranks well.
The model's accuracy at a 0.5 cut-off on the test rows, beside an always-renews baseline.
A predicted-versus-actual table by score bucket, on rows the model did not train on.
A predicted-versus-actual table on the training rows, where there are more customers per bucket.
variants.why: Multiplying by money uses the probability as a number, so the question is whether 70 percent means 70 in a hundred. The bucket table answers that, and only on unseen rows. AUC and accuracy say nothing about the level of the scores, and a table on training rows flatters a model that was fitted to those very outcomes.

variants.q: Two checks of the churn model arrive. Check A, on the 6,000 advertisers it was trained on: predicted 11.1 percent, actual 11.1 percent. Check B, on 4,000 advertisers from later months: predicted 10.9 percent, actual 13.2 percent. Which one tells you what to expect when the model is used next month?
options: Check A: it rests on more advertisers, so its numbers wobble less.
Neither alone: average them, weighted by rows, for about 12 percent actual.
Check A: an exact match is the strongest evidence that the scores are calibrated.
Check B: those advertisers come from months the model never saw.
variants.why: Check A is the training months, where predicted and actual agree because the model was fitted to those outcomes. Check B is the test months, later advertisers the model never saw, and it is the only one that resembles how the model will be used. More rows do not help when they are the rows the model already learned from, and averaging the two only dilutes the honest check.

drill.q: A model ranks customers well. Does that mean you can trust its percentages?
drill.a: No. Ranking only needs the order to be right. Every score could be too low or too high and the order would be the same. Check the percentages separately, by comparing predicted with actual in score buckets on rows the model never saw.

drill.q: When does it matter that a model's percentages are right, and when does it not?
drill.a: It matters whenever the score is used as a number: multiplied by money, or compared with a cut-off stated in percent. It does not matter when you only sort and take the top of the list.

recall.prompt: Finance wants revenue at risk computed as churn score times spend. Explain what you would check first, what that check showed on the course data, and why a good AUC did not settle it.
recall.model_answer: AUC only says churners tend to score above stayers: it uses the order of the scores, not their size. Before multiplying by money I would ask for a predicted-versus-actual table on the test months. Here every bucket ran low: advertisers scored about 25 percent churned at about 33 percent, and overall the model said 10.9 percent where 13.2 percent churned, because it learned from months with about 11 percent churn. So the ranked list is fine as it is, but the dollar total would be understated until the scores are recalibrated and checked again.

lessons.ask_assistant: On [the test rows: a period or holdout the model never trained on] only, group rows by predicted probability into [8 to 10] score buckets. For each bucket print the number of rows, the average prediction and the actual [outcome] rate, and add one line with the overall average prediction beside the overall actual rate. State how many rows the table covers and which [period] they come from. Repeat the table for [the two or three segments the business cares about]. Do not adjust the scores yet. If I later ask for recalibration, say which rows it was fitted on and show this table again on rows it did not use.
audit_checklist: The table is built on test rows: the bucket counts add up to the test row count (4,000 here), not the training count (6,000).
Every bucket shows its row count, and the overall average prediction sits beside the overall actual rate (10.9% against 13.2% here).
The same table appears for each segment the business cares about.
After any recalibration: the output names the rows the adjustment was fitted on, and the table is shown again on rows it did not use.
transfer: Can an upsell score be multiplied by price to forecast add-on revenue?
Can a predicted click rate be multiplied by impressions to forecast a client's clicks?
Can sales be told that a lead scored 0.4 has a 40 percent chance of closing?

other_ways.approach: Recalibration: adjust the scores so that predicted matches actual on recent outcomes
other_ways.when: When the ranking is good but the percentages are off; check the table again on rows not used for the adjustment.

other_ways.approach: Use the score as a rank only: a top-K list, with no percentage quoted
other_ways.when: When the decision is a fixed-capacity list and nobody multiplies by money.

other_ways.approach: One summary number for probability error (the Brier score)
other_ways.when: When comparing many models at once; it will not show where, or in which direction, the percentages are off.

glossary.def: Whether predicted percentages match what happens: of the rows scored about 30 percent, about 30 in a hundred have the outcome.
Rows grouped into score buckets, with the average prediction beside the actual rate in each.
A group of rows whose scores fall in the same range, such as 20 to 30 percent.
Adjusting a model's scores after training so that they match observed rates.

lessons.title: Judging number predictions
lessons.subtitle: Two spend models, two error measures, two different winners. Which one do you believe?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can choose the error measure for a predicted number (MAE, RMSE or total error) from what a miss costs, and explain why two measures can rank the same models differently.

predict.q: Two made-up spend models, 100 advertisers. Model 1 is off by $1,000 on every one of them. Model 2 is exactly right on 99 and off by $100,000 on the last. Which has the larger average miss?
options: Model 1
Model 2
Neither: the two are equal
It cannot be worked out from this
predict.reveal: Neither: both miss by $1,000 on average. The lesson shows the measure that tells them apart, and when it should decide between two real models.

segments.narration: Finance wants a number for every advertiser: how much will they spend over the next eight weeks. You ask your assistant for two candidate models. Call them model A and model B. How they work inside comes later. The assistant's note says B has the lower error, so ship B. You ask for a second error measure, on the same test advertisers, and now A is ahead. Neither number is wrong. Until now the prediction was a yes or a no. For a number, there are several honest ways to score a miss, and they do not always agree. The same holds for any model that predicts a number, such as the CPA a new campaign will reach.

visual.title: Judging number predictions
visual.sub: When each model wins on a different measure

segments.narration: Start with one advertiser. The model predicted one amount, they spent another, and the gap between the two is the miss. [[1]] Do that for every test advertiser, ignore whether each miss was high or low, and average. That is the mean absolute error, MAE: the average miss, in dollars. [[2]] As always, it needs a bar to beat. The laziest forecast says each advertiser will spend what they spent in the last eight weeks. It misses by about 2,400 dollars. [[3]] A sharper one doubles the most recent four weeks. Call it the run-rate. It misses by about 2,000 dollars, and that is the bar.

visual.title: MAE: the average miss, in dollars
lines: MAE = average of |predicted − actual|
Same as last 8 weeks: MAE $2,404
Run-rate (2 × last 4 weeks): MAE $2,022
visual.note: Scored on the 4,000 test advertisers (May–June)

segments.narration: Both candidates clear the bar. [[3]] [[4]] Model A and model B each miss by about 1,700 dollars on average, and B is ahead by 58 dollars. Before you believe that, ask how much of that gap is luck. Score the same two models on a different draw of advertisers and the gap moves. Here it could plausibly sit anywhere from about 180 dollars in B's favour to about 70 in A's. That range crosses zero. On average miss, then, this is a tie. More on that check in the next lesson.

visual.title: Average miss (MAE), 4,000 test advertisers
visual.note: B minus A: −$58, plausible range −$177 to +$73. A tie. Inside the models: A in lesson 3-1, B in lesson 4-3.

segments.narration: Now a second way to keep score. Picture two made-up models and 100 advertisers. [[1]] The first is off by 1,000 dollars on every single one. [[2]] The second is exactly right on 99 of them and off by 100,000 dollars on the last. Same MAE: 1,000 dollars each. Would finance call them equally good? The second measure says no. Square every miss, average the squares, then take the square root to get back to dollars. That is root mean squared error, RMSE. Squaring means a miss ten times bigger counts a hundred times more. The steady model scores 1,000. The model with one disaster scores 10,000.

visual.title: Toy example: 100 advertisers, same MAE
visual.note: RMSE: square each miss, average, take the square root.

segments.narration: Back to the real candidates. [[1]] Model A has an RMSE of about 4,900 dollars. [[2]] Model B, about 5,800. Same average miss, but when B is badly wrong, it is wrong by more. So which model wins depends on what a miss costs. If one huge surprise on a big account hurts more than a hundred small errors, judge by RMSE and take A. If every dollar of error costs the same, judge by MAE, call it a tie, and take whichever is simpler to run. Make that choice before you see the scoreboard, not after. That ordering comes from one simulated test set, and RMSE leans on a few accounts. On your data it may flip.

visual.title: Same average miss, different big misses

segments.narration: Finance will also add your predictions up into a revenue number. MAE and RMSE both ignore direction, so neither says whether that sum comes out right. R-squared, which assistants like to print, does not either: it is the share of the variation explained, a fraction, not dollars. For that, compare the predicted total with the actual total. [[1]] The same-as-last forecast comes out about 23 percent low. [[2]] The run-rate, about 20 percent low. In this simulated world total spend grows from one period to the next, and a forecast that repeats the past cannot see growth. [[3]] [[4]] Models A and B both come out about 6 percent high. Misses that lean one way are called bias, and bias does not average out. It adds up.

visual.title: The full scoreboard
visual.note: Actual total: $21.0M across 4,000 test advertisers

segments.narration: One more habit. An average miss describes nobody in particular. Leave A and B for a moment and take the stronger spend model you will meet in module five. Cut its test advertisers into thirds by past spend. [[1]] On small accounts it misses by about 170 dollars. [[2]] [[3]] On large accounts, by over 3,300. A small group of advertisers carries nearly half of all its error, and the worst single miss was a large account forecast at about 133,000 dollars that left and spent nothing. So ask for error by size tier, and for the biggest misses by name.

visual.title: One overall MAE of $1,416, three different stories
visual.note: A stronger spend model, from lesson 5-5. 46% of its total error comes from 5% of advertisers.

segments.narration: So, the brief. Ask your assistant to predict spend for the next eight weeks and to score it on the test advertisers only. The output must show four things. [[1]] Both baselines beside every model, on the same rows. [[2]] Three measures side by side: MAE, RMSE, and predicted total against actual total. [[3]] Error by size tier, with the ten largest misses listed. [[4]] And one trap. If it quotes an average percentage error, ask what happened to the zeros. About one test advertiser in eight spent nothing, and you cannot divide by zero. Those rows were dropped or patched, and the output has to say which. [[5]] Need a percentage? Ask for total absolute error divided by total actual spend, which a zero cannot break.

visual.title: Brief and audit: what the output must show
items: Both baselines beside every model, same test rows
MAE, RMSE and predicted total vs actual total
Error by size tier, plus the ten largest misses
Zero-spend rows (13.2% here): how did a percentage error treat them?
Need a percentage? Total absolute error ÷ total actual spend

segments.narration: The next time someone asks which forecast is better, answer with a question: what does a big miss cost you, and what does a small one? One thread is still loose, that 58 dollar gap that might be luck, and telling real from noise is the next lesson.

visual.text: Pick the error measure from what a miss costs. Then look at the scoreboard.
visual.sub: MAE: every dollar counts the same · RMSE: big misses count most · Total: do the misses cancel?

takeaways: MAE is the average miss in dollars; RMSE makes large misses count far more.
The two can rank models differently, so choose the measure from what a miss costs before you compare.
Then look past the average: the total, the size tiers, the largest misses and the zeros.

quiz.q: Two spend models are scored on the same 4,000 test advertisers. Model A: MAE $1,733, RMSE $4,878. Model B: MAE $1,675, RMSE $5,824. Finance says one large surprise on a big account costs them far more than many small misses. Which model do you put forward?
options: B: its MAE is lower, and MAE is the measure that is stated in dollars
A: RMSE weights large misses most, and those are what finance fears
Either: a $58 gap in MAE is a tie, and a tie on MAE makes the two models interchangeable
B: a lower MAE means its RMSE will also come out lower on new data
quiz.why: Finance has said a large miss costs disproportionately more, which is what RMSE measures, and A's RMSE is lower ($4,878 against $5,824). B's $58 edge on MAE is tiny, but a tie on one measure does not make two models interchangeable when their large misses differ. Both measures are in dollars, so 'MAE is the dollar one' is not a reason to prefer it.

quiz.q: The assistant writes: 'Baseline: same as last 8 weeks, MAE $2,404 per advertiser. Good enough for a first revenue plan, so I summed the predictions for finance.' The output hides a flaw. What do you check before finance uses that sum?
options: The RMSE: if it is lower than the MAE, the large misses are under control and the sum is safe
The row count: across 4,000 advertisers the misses cancel, so the sum only needs enough rows
The MAE as a share of average spend: if it is under half, the summed plan is within tolerance
The direction of the misses: predicted total against actual total, which runs about 23% low here
quiz.why: MAE averages the size of the misses and throws away their direction, so it cannot say whether a sum is right. This baseline's misses lean low, and the summed plan undershoots actual spend by about 23%. More rows do not cancel misses that lean one way, and RMSE is never lower than MAE, so that check cannot pass.

quiz.q: Lead scoring. A model predicts each new lead's first-month revenue. About 30% of leads never buy, so their actual revenue is zero. The assistant reports: 'Average percentage error: 22%.' What is the right read?
options: It can only describe the leads that bought: ask for the dollar error on all leads
It is sound as long as it beats the baseline's percentage error
The model gets about 22% of the leads wrong, which is better than the 30% who never buy
It should be converted to RMSE, which handles zero-revenue leads correctly, before anyone judges it
quiz.why: A percentage error divides by the actual value, and you cannot divide by zero, so the leads that never bought were dropped or patched before that 22% was computed. Beating a baseline on the same crippled measure does not repair it, 22% is the size of a miss, not the share of leads the model got wrong, and converting to RMSE does not bring the dropped leads back.

quiz.concept: averages hide where the error falls
quiz.q: A spend model's overall MAE is $1,416. An account manager whose book is all small accounts, averaging about $500 of spend, says: 'Off by $1,400 on a $500 account? Useless to me.' What do you tell her?
options: She is right: an error nearly three times the size of the account makes the model unusable for her book
She should judge it by RMSE instead, because RMSE is the fairer measure for small accounts
The overall figure is driven by large accounts: look at the miss in her own size tier, about $170
The model misses every account by about $1,416, so it only suits books of large accounts
quiz.why: An overall MAE mixes tiers: for this model the miss is about $170 on small accounts and over $3,300 on large ones, and nearly half of all error comes from 5% of advertisers. Applying the overall average to one small account is the mistake, and RMSE would be dominated by large accounts even more.

review.concept: MAE or RMSE: choose by what a miss costs

variants.q: Two daily revenue forecasts for the treasury team. Forecast X: MAE $9,000, RMSE $11,000. Forecast Y: MAE $8,000, RMSE $25,000. A day that is badly off forces an expensive overnight loan; small daily errors cost almost nothing. Which forecast suits them?
options: Y, because its average miss is $1,000 smaller on an ordinary day
X, because its much lower RMSE shows it avoids the badly wrong days
Y, because RMSE is larger than MAE for every forecast, so the gap between them means little
Neither yet: first find out what share of days each forecast got exactly right
variants.why: The cost here comes from rare large misses, and RMSE is the measure that weights them: Y's RMSE is more than twice X's, so Y has days that are far off. Y's slightly lower MAE only says its ordinary days are a little closer, which is not what treasury pays for.

variants.q: A model predicts how many minutes each support ticket will take, to estimate each agent's daily workload. Every minute of error matters equally. Model P: MAE 6 minutes, RMSE 9. Model Q: MAE 4.5 minutes, RMSE 14. Which do you choose?
options: P, because a lower RMSE is the safer choice whatever the errors cost
Q, because its average miss is lower; note its few large misses
P, because Q's RMSE is about three times its MAE, the sign of a broken model
Q, because a higher RMSE shows that it captures more of the variation in tickets
variants.why: When each minute of error costs the same, the average miss is the cost, so the lower MAE wins. Q's high RMSE tells you a few tickets are badly misjudged, which is worth knowing, but 'lower RMSE is always safer' ignores what a miss costs in this use.

variants.q: The assistant compares two models that predict next-8-week spend and reports one line: 'Both have an MAE of about $1,700, so they are equivalent.' Which follow-up tests that claim best?
options: Ask for the accuracy of each model at a sensible cut-off
Ask for the MAE again, this time on the training rows
Ask for the MAE to more decimal places, to break the tie
Ask for the RMSE of each, and for each model's ten largest misses
variants.why: Equal average misses can hide very different large misses; RMSE and a list of the biggest misses expose them. Accuracy does not apply to a predicted number, error on the training rows says nothing about new advertisers, and more decimals of the same average still hide the large misses.

review.concept: Bias: small misses that lean one way add up in a total

variants.q: An upsell model predicts the extra monthly spend of each account after an upgrade. The per-account MAE is small, $40. Finance sums the predictions and the total is 18% above what actually came in. What explains both facts?
options: The misses lean one way: most predictions are a little high, and across every account that adds up
The MAE must have been computed on the training rows, where every model looks better
Misses of $40 are too small to move a total, so the sum itself was computed wrongly
An 18% gap in the total is what a $40 MAE normally produces once it is summed
variants.why: MAE ignores direction, so small misses that all lean high look harmless per account and still pile up in a sum. Small per-account errors only protect a total when they point both ways and cancel.

variants.q: A model predicts how many days each creative will last before its CTR fades. Its average miss is 2 days. The refresh calendar built from it keeps replacing creatives after they have already faded. What should you ask the assistant for?
options: The RMSE, to see whether a few creatives have very large misses
A larger training set of creatives, since 2 days is already a small miss
The average signed miss: are predictions mostly too long?
The same MAE broken down by vertical, to find where it is worst
variants.why: Refreshes that are consistently late point to predictions that lean one way, and MAE cannot show direction; the average of predicted minus actual can. RMSE would reveal a few large misses, not a consistent tilt.

variants.q: Per-advertiser spend predictions have an MAE of $300 across 5,000 advertisers. The CFO asks: 'So the total will be off by about $1.5 million?' What is the accurate answer?
options: Yes: the error of the total is the MAE times the number of advertisers
No: with 5,000 advertisers the misses always cancel, so the total is nearly exact
No: the error of the total is the RMSE times the number of advertisers
It depends on direction: compare the predicted total with the actual total
variants.why: MAE counts every miss as positive, so $1.5 million is the sum of the miss sizes, not the error of the sum. If the misses lean one way the total can be off by nearly that much; if they balance it can be almost exact. Only predicted total against actual total tells you.

drill.q: Two models have the same average miss, but one has a much higher root mean squared error. What does that tell you about it?
drill.a: It makes a few very large misses. Squaring makes big misses count far more, so its root mean squared error climbs while its average miss stays the same.

drill.q: Per-customer predictions are going to be added up into a revenue forecast. Besides the average miss, which number do you ask for, and why?
drill.a: Predicted total against actual total. The average miss ignores direction, so misses that all lean low can look small for each customer and still leave the total far short.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: 'Model B has the lower MAE, so B is the better spend model.' In 30 seconds, what else would you want to know before agreeing?
recall.model_answer: MAE is the average miss and treats every dollar of error alike, so first ask what a miss costs: if rare huge misses hurt most, compare RMSE, where the order can reverse. Then check whether the gap is bigger than chance, whether the predicted total matches the actual total, and where the error sits: by size tier and in the largest misses. Any percentage error needs a second look wherever the actual is zero.

lessons.ask_assistant: Predict [the number] for each [unit], training on [training period] and scoring only on [test rows the model never saw]. In one table, on the same rows, show [the simplest baseline, such as same as last period], [a sharper baseline if there is one] and each model, with MAE, RMSE and predicted total versus actual total, and state the row count. Add MAE by [size tier or segment] and list the [10] largest misses with predicted and actual values. State how many test rows have an actual value of zero and how many rows any percentage error was computed on; if I need a percentage, use total absolute error divided by total actual.
audit_checklist: Both baselines and every model scored on the same test rows, with the row count stated
MAE, RMSE and predicted total versus actual total side by side
Error by size tier and a list of the largest individual misses
The count of rows with zero actual spend, and the row count behind any percentage error: if it is smaller than the test set, rows were dropped
transfer: Forecasting daily platform spend for finance: is one badly wrong day worse than many slightly wrong days?
Predicting how long support tickets take, to plan staffing: does each ticket matter, or the day's total?
Estimating the CPA a new campaign will reach before an account manager promises it to a client: what does a large miss cost?

other_ways.approach: Median absolute error
other_ways.when: When you want the miss for the advertiser in the middle and a few giant accounts should not move the number.

other_ways.approach: Total absolute error divided by total actual spend
other_ways.when: When stakeholders want a percentage: it weights by dollars and does not break on advertisers who spent zero.

other_ways.approach: Share of predictions within a stated tolerance
other_ways.when: When the business has a clear 'close enough', such as within $200, and wants a hit rate it can track.

glossary.def: Mean absolute error: the average size of a miss, ignoring direction, in the units of the prediction.
Root mean squared error: square the misses, average them, take the square root; large misses count far more.
Misses that lean one way on average, so the predicted total lands above or below the actual total.
Predicted total divided by actual total, minus one: the measure that matters when predictions are summed.
A baseline that doubles the most recent four weeks of spend to predict the next eight.

The share of the variation in actual values that the predictions explain: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than the average. Built from squared misses, it ranks models like RMSE, but it is a fraction, not dollars.

lessons.title: Real or noise?
lessons.subtitle: Gaming churn jumped five points in a month. Is that a finding, or a coin flip?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can ask of any gap, between groups, months or models, how big it would be by chance, and read an interval to tell a real difference from one the data cannot settle.

predict.q: Draw two random groups of 250 advertisers. Nothing is different between them. How often will their churn rates differ by more than 2 points?
options: Almost never
About 1 time in 20
About 1 time in 6
About half the time
predict.reveal: About half the time, with nothing going on at all. The lesson shows where that comes from and what it means for every gap on your dashboard.

segments.narration: Monday morning. The retention dashboard shows gaming churn at 14 percent in March and 19 percent in April. Five points in a month. The head of the gaming vertical wants a meeting and a root cause. You could spend the week slicing April by country, by device, by account manager. You would find something, because you always do. Or you could ask one question first. If nothing at all had changed for gaming advertisers, how big a jump could show up anyway? That question comes first for any gap between two measured numbers, whether churn in two months or the click rates of two creatives: how big would it be by chance?

visual.title: Real or noise?
visual.sub: How big would this gap be by chance?

segments.narration: Every rate on a dashboard comes from a limited group of advertisers, and a different draw would have given a slightly different rate. The margin of error says how different: nineteen draws in twenty land within it. That is the 95 percent you will see quoted. Take a churn rate of around 12 percent. [[1]] Measured on 100 advertisers, the margin is about 6 points either way. [[2]] On 250 advertisers, about 4 points. [[3]] On 1,000, about 2. [[4]] On all 12,000, under 1. Look at the middle two. Four times the advertisers, and the margin only halves. It shrinks with the square root of the group size, which makes certainty expensive. So the first question about any percentage is how many advertisers stand behind it.

visual.title: Margin of error (±) around a churn rate near 12%
visual.note: 95% margin. Four times the advertisers, half the margin.

segments.narration: Here is that wobble at work. Draw two random groups of 250 advertisers from the advertiser table. Random, so there is no real difference between them. Compare their churn rates anyway, and repeat that 2,000 times. [[1]] The typical gap between the two groups is 2 points. [[2]] In other words, half the time the gap is bigger than that. [[3]] One time in twenty, it is bigger than 5.6 points. With nothing going on. This is an A-A test: both sides are the same, so whatever gap you see is noise. [[4]] Now make each group 4,000 advertisers. A gap above 2 points turns up about once in 200 draws.

visual.title: A/A test: two random groups, no real difference

stats.label: typical gap, groups of 250
of draws: gap over 2 points
gap exceeded 1 time in 20
of draws: gap over 2 points, groups of 4,000

segments.narration: Now back to gaming. Each monthly cohort holds only about 250 gaming advertisers. [[3]] So March is 14 percent, give or take about 4 points. [[4]] April is 19 percent, give or take about 5. Those ranges overlap. And look at the two months before: 15 percent, then 17. This number has been bouncing all year.

visual.title: Gaming churn by month
visual.note: 95% margins. About 250 gaming advertisers in each month.

segments.narration: The cleaner check puts an interval on the gap itself: the range of true differences this much data cannot rule out. [[1]] The gap is about 5 points. [[2]] Its interval runs from roughly minus 2 to plus 11. [[3]] Zero is inside. So no change fits the data, and so does a rise of 10 points. That is not proof that nothing happened. It means 250 advertisers a month cannot tell you. Reports often quote a p-value: how often noise alone would produce a gap at least this large. Under 5 percent, the gap is called statistically significant, roughly the same verdict as an interval clear of zero. The interval also shows the size.

visual.title: An interval on the gap itself

stats.label: gaming churn, April minus March
95% interval for that gap
no change fits the data, and so does a rise of 10 points

segments.narration: Put three gaps through the same check. [[1]] April against March you have just seen: the data cannot tell. [[2]] Health against education, with more than a thousand advertisers on each side: about half a point apart, and the interval straddles zero. Big groups do not make a tiny gap real. [[3]] Then June. May was already up, at about 23 percent on about 220 advertisers: a warning, no more. In June, gaming churn reached about 30 percent, against 16 percent across January to April. That is a gap of 14 points. Its interval runs from about 8 to 20, nowhere near zero. That one earns the meeting. Because this world is simulated, we can look up the truth: something did change for gaming, in June only. On real data you cannot look it up. The interval is what you have.

visual.title: Three gaps, three intervals
visual.note: May: 22.6% on 217 advertisers (±5.6 pts). June is set against the four months before the rise, pooled.

segments.narration: Models are no different. A model's score is measured on a sample too. [[1]] The churn model's AUC of about 0.85 comes from 4,000 test advertisers. [[2]] Draw a different set and it could land anywhere from about 0.83 to 0.86. So when the assistant says a new model is better by a hair, ask for an interval on the gap between the two, measured on the same test rows. [[3]] Last lesson's 58 dollar gap between model A and model B is the example. [[4]] Its interval runs from 177 dollars one way to 73 the other. Zero is inside. Call it a tie, and keep the simpler model.

stats.label: churn model AUC, 4,000 test advertisers
95% interval for that AUC
MAE gap, model B minus model A
95% interval for the gap: a tie

segments.narration: So, the brief. Whenever your assistant compares anything, two groups, two months or two models, the output must carry the evidence. [[1]] The number of advertisers behind every rate. [[2]] The gap, with a 95 percent interval beside it. [[3]] One line on how the interval was made. The usual way is to redraw the rows at random, repeats allowed, a thousand times, and watch how far the number moves. The assistant calls that a bootstrap. [[4]] Then check the words against the numbers. If the text says churn rose, the interval must sit clear of zero. [[5]] And if the assistant scanned thirty segments and reports the biggest mover, be suspicious. The biggest of thirty wobbles always looks like news. No interval to hand? Look at the metric's own history: has it moved this much before with no cause?

visual.title: Brief and audit: evidence beside every comparison
items: Group size beside every rate
The gap with a 95% interval, not two bare percentages
How the interval was computed
Words match numbers: “rose” needs an interval clear of zero
Biggest mover out of many cuts? Expect one by chance

segments.narration: So when a tile jumps and someone wants a root cause, your first reply is two requests: how many advertisers, and what is the interval on the gap. That completes your scoreboard, and module three opens up the models themselves, starting with the simplest way to predict a number.

visual.text: Before reacting to a gap, ask how big it would be by chance.
visual.sub: Group size and an interval beside every comparison

takeaways: Every number from a sample wobbles, and it takes four times the data to halve the wobble.
A gap is a finding only when its interval excludes zero; otherwise the data cannot tell.
Ask for the group size and an interval beside every comparison, for models as well as rates.

quiz.concept: margin of error and group size
quiz.q: An account manager writes: 'My book of 100 advertisers churned at 16% this quarter. The platform is at 12%. What am I doing wrong?' What is the best first reply?
options: A 4-point gap is a third above the platform rate, so something in the book is clearly wrong
On 100 advertisers a rate swings about 6 points by chance: this gap shows nothing yet
A hundred advertisers is a solid sample, so the gap is real, though it may be small
A book can never be compared with the platform, because its mix of advertisers differs
quiz.why: A churn rate measured on 100 advertisers carries a margin of roughly ±6 points, so 16% against 12% is well inside what chance produces. Restating the gap as 'a third higher' makes it sound bigger without making it more certain, 100 is a small group for a rate, and a different mix is a reason to look closer later, not to refuse the comparison.

quiz.concept: a gap needs an interval, even with large groups
quiz.q: The assistant's summary: 'Churn by vertical: health 11.8%, education 11.2%. Education retains better, so I recommend copying its onboarding for health advertisers.' The group sizes, 1,868 and 1,159, sit in a footnote. No interval is given. What is the flaw?
options: Education has fewer advertisers, so its rate has to be weighted up before the two are compared
The group sizes belong in the main text: with over a thousand a side, the gap itself is reliable
The gap is real but only 0.6 points, which is too small to justify copying an onboarding flow
A 0.6-point gap between groups this size is inside the wobble: ask for the interval first
quiz.why: Even with more than a thousand advertisers on each side, each rate still wobbles by a point or two, so a gap of 0.6 points can easily be chance; here its interval runs from about −1.7 to +2.9 points, straddling zero. Large groups make an interval narrow, not automatically narrower than the gap, and 'real but small' accepts a difference the data has not shown.

quiz.concept: cannot tell is not the same as no difference
quiz.q: Two versions of a landing page get 250 visitors each. Version A converts at 12%, version B at 14%. The product manager wants to ship B as the winner. What is the right read?
options: Two random groups of 250 differ by more than 2 points about half the time: no verdict yet
B wins: 14% is higher than 12%, and equal group sizes make the comparison fair
The test shows the two pages convert equally well, so keep the one already live
B wins by about 17%, because 2 points on a base of 12 is a sixth more conversions
quiz.why: Two random groups of 250 with no real difference show a gap over 2 points about half the time, so this result is what noise alone looks like. That makes it inconclusive: not a win for B, and equally not proof that the pages are the same, because a real difference of a few points would look just like this.

quiz.q: Gaming churn was 30.5% in June (272 advertisers) against 16.3% for January to April (992). The gap is 14.2 points with a 95% interval of 8.2 to 20.1. A colleague says: 'Only 272 advertisers. It is noise, like April was.' What do you answer?
options: Agreed: with under 1,000 advertisers in the June group nothing can be concluded
The rise is 14.2 points, so plan retention capacity around exactly that figure
The interval is wide, but all of it is far above zero: a real rise of uncertain size
It is real because June is the most recent month, and recent data always outweighs old data
quiz.why: A small group makes the interval wide, not the conclusion wrong: the whole range sits well above zero, so chance is not a reasonable explanation, unlike April's gap, whose interval included zero. What stays uncertain is the size, somewhere between about 8 and 20 points, which is why 'exactly 14.2' overstates it.

review.concept: Small groups wobble: the margin of error shrinks with the square root of group size

variants.q: A satisfaction survey of 400 advertisers reports 62% satisfied, with a margin of error of about 5 points. Marketing wants the margin down to about 2.5 points. Roughly how many responses does that take?
options: Twice as many: about 800
Two and a half times as many: about 1,000
Four times as many: about 1,600
Sixteen times as many: about 6,400
variants.why: The margin shrinks with the square root of the group, so halving it takes four times the responses: 400 becomes 1,600. Doubling to 800 is the tempting answer, but it trims the margin by less than a third, and sixteen times as many would cut it to a quarter, more than was asked.

variants.q: A new publisher is audited: 9 of 100 sampled sessions are flagged as invalid traffic, against a network rate of 5%. Sales wants the publisher suspended today. What is the sound call?
options: Suspend today: 9% is nearly double the network rate, and invalid traffic costs advertisers money
Sample more sessions first: 100 sessions cannot separate 9% from 5%
Clear the publisher: a gap this small on 100 sessions has been shown to be noise
Average the two rates to 7% and compare that figure with other new publishers
variants.why: A rate measured on 100 sessions carries a margin of several points either way, so 9% and 5% are not yet distinguishable. 'Nearly double' is the same thin evidence in bigger words, and declaring it noise is just as unsupported: a larger sample settles it.

variants.q: Four tiles on a churn dashboard moved this month. Each group's churn rate is around 12%. Which move is hardest to explain by chance alone?
options: 8 points, in a group of 50 advertisers
4 points, in a group of 250 advertisers
0.5 points, in a group of 12,000 advertisers
3 points, in a group of 4,000 advertisers
variants.why: A single month's rate wobbles by about ±9 points for 50 advertisers, ±4 for 250, ±1 for 4,000 and ±0.6 for 12,000, and a move between two months wobbles about 1.4 times as much: roughly ±13, ±5.6, ±1.4 and ±0.8. Only the 3-point move is about twice its wobble. The 8-point move is the largest on the screen and the least reliable, and half a point is still inside the wobble of even the biggest group.

review.concept: A gap is a finding only if its interval excludes zero; otherwise it is 'cannot tell', not 'no difference'

variants.q: A new invalid-traffic model scores an AUC of 0.912 against the current model's 0.905 on the same test set. The interval for the difference runs from −0.004 to +0.018. The assistant recommends switching. What is the right read?
options: Switch: 0.912 is higher than 0.905 on the very same test set
Switch: most of the interval is above zero, so the new model is probably better
A tie on this evidence: zero is inside the interval for the difference between the two models
Keep the current model: an interval that dips below zero shows the new one is worse
variants.why: The interval for the difference includes zero, so this test set cannot tell the two models apart. 'Most of the interval is above zero' is tempting, but it is not the bar, and dipping below zero does not show the new model is worse either; with a tie, the usual choice is whichever model is simpler or already running.

variants.q: Accounts with a dedicated rep adopted a new ad format at 21%, other accounts at 18%. The gap is 3 points, with a 95% interval of 0.5 to 5.5. Which statement is supported?
options: Adoption is higher among accounts with a rep, by somewhere between 0.5 and 5.5 points
Assigning a rep raises an account's adoption by about 3 points
There is no real difference, because an interval this wide settles nothing
Adoption is exactly 3 points higher among accounts with a rep
variants.why: The interval excludes zero, so the difference is real, but its size is only pinned down to a range. It describes a difference between two groups, not what assigning a rep would do, and a wide interval that stays clear of zero is still a finding.

variants.q: A new creative's CTR is compared with the old one's. The difference is +0.35 points, with an interval from −0.2 to +0.9. The product manager concludes: 'So the new creative makes no difference.' What is wrong with that?
options: The bar is wrong: most of the interval is above zero, so the new creative is the winner
The interval also allows a gain of 0.9 points: the result is inconclusive, not negative
The difference is +0.35 points, so the new creative is simply better and should ship
A CTR difference this small cannot be given an interval, so the figure itself is suspect
variants.why: An interval that includes zero means the data cannot tell, and this one is just as consistent with a useful gain. Treating 'not shown' as 'shown to be zero' is as much an over-read as declaring +0.35 a win, and 'most of the interval is above zero' is not the bar either.

drill.q: Two random groups of advertisers, treated exactly the same, show different churn rates. Why, and what does group size have to do with it?
drill.a: Every rate measured on a sample wobbles by chance, and small groups wobble most. To halve the wobble you need about four times as many advertisers.

drill.q: Someone shows you a jump in a metric for one small segment. What two things do you ask for before looking for a cause?
drill.a: How many advertisers are in the segment, and an interval around the jump. If zero is inside the interval, the data cannot tell the jump from chance.

recall.prompt: A stakeholder points at a 5-point jump in one segment's churn and asks for a root cause. Explain what you check first and how you read the answer.
recall.model_answer: First I ask how many advertisers stand behind each rate, because a rate on a few hundred advertisers swings several points by chance. Then I get an interval for the gap itself. If zero is inside it, the data cannot tell the jump from noise, which is not the same as proving nothing happened. If the whole interval is clear of zero, the change is real, and the interval says how big it might be.

lessons.ask_assistant: For every comparison in this analysis, between [groups, periods or models], show the number of [units] behind each figure and the difference with a 95% interval, and say in one line how the interval was computed. For model comparisons, bootstrap the difference on the same [test rows]. List every cut you examined with its group size and interval, not only the one you report. Do not call a change a rise or a fall unless its interval excludes zero; when zero is inside, write 'cannot tell'. Beside each headline gap, show the same metric for [the last 6 to 12 periods] so I can see how much it normally moves.
audit_checklist: The number of advertisers beside every rate
A 95% interval beside every difference, with the method named
Wording that matches the interval: no 'rose' or 'beats' while zero is inside it
Every cut that was examined is listed with its group size and interval, not only the biggest mover
transfer: Creative A has a higher CTR than creative B after two days: is the gap bigger than two identical creatives would show?
A publisher's invalid-traffic rate looks twice the network's on a small audit sample: suspend, clear, or sample more?
A new model scores slightly higher than the current one on the same test set: is that a win or a tie?

other_ways.approach: Collect more data before deciding
other_ways.when: When the interval includes zero but also includes a difference large enough to matter.

other_ways.approach: Run an A/A check on your own metric
other_ways.when: When a stakeholder needs to see, in numbers they know, how large a gap pure chance produces.

other_ways.approach: Compare the move with the metric's own history
other_ways.when: When you have many past periods: if the number has moved this much before with no cause, it is ordinary.

glossary.def: How far a rate measured on a sample is likely to sit from the true rate; it shrinks with the square root of the group size.
The range of values the data cannot rule out; a 95% interval is built to contain the truth 19 times in 20.
Comparing two groups that were treated identically, to see how big a gap chance alone produces.
The part of a number that comes from which cases happened to be in the sample, not from any real change.
Estimating an interval by redrawing a same-sized sample of the rows at random, repeats allowed, many times and seeing how far the number moves.
How often noise alone would produce a gap at least as large as the one observed; this lesson reads the interval instead, because it also shows the size.
The usual label for a p-value under 5%; it gives roughly the same verdict as a 95% interval that excludes zero, and says nothing about how big or useful the gap is.

lessons.title: Linear regression: predicting a number
lessons.subtitle: Can a model that reads every column beat the run-rate, and why does the first attempt lose?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can read a linear regression as a weighted sum, say what one weight means, and check which scale it was fitted on and how its predictions were turned back into dollars.

predict.q: The run-rate baseline misses next-8-week spend by about $2,000 per advertiser. You fit a linear regression in dollars on every column in the table. What happens to the average miss?
options: It drops a lot: more columns means more information
It drops a little
It gets worse than the baseline
It cannot be compared with a baseline
predict.reveal: It gets worse: about $2,360. The lesson shows why, and the two changes, neither of them a cleverer algorithm, that bring it down to about $1,430.

segments.narration: Finance still wants a spend forecast for every advertiser. The bar to beat is the run-rate: twice the last four weeks, which misses by about 2,000 dollars on average. Surely a model that reads all seventeen columns can beat one multiplication. So you ask the assistant for the standard first model for a number, a linear regression. It comes back with an average miss of about 2,360 dollars. Worse than the baseline. That is not a bug. It is the lesson for any model that predicts a number, whether spend or what a new lead will be worth: the columns you feed it and the scale you fit it on matter more than a cleverer algorithm.

visual.title: Linear regression
visual.sub: A weighted sum, and the scale you fit it on

segments.narration: A linear regression is a weighted sum. [[1]] Start from a base amount. Then multiply each column by its own weight and add everything up. If you have written a sum-product formula in a spreadsheet, you have written this model. [[2]] The weights are not typed in. They are learned: the fit picks the set of weights that makes the squared misses on the training advertisers as small as possible. [[3]] And each weight has a precise reading: how much the prediction moves for one more unit of that column, with the other columns held fixed.

visual.title: Linear regression = a weighted sum
lines: predicted spend = base + weight 1 × column 1 + weight 2 × column 2 + …
weights are learned: the set with the smallest squared misses on the training rows
one weight = change in the prediction per unit of its column, others held fixed
visual.note: In a spreadsheet: base + SUMPRODUCT(weights, columns)

segments.narration: So why did it lose? [[1]] The baseline sits at about 2,000 dollars. [[2]] The regression, fed every raw column, at about 2,360. The interval on that gap is nowhere near zero: worse, not tied. One reason sits in the columns. The table has eight-week spend and the trend ratio, but not the last four weeks alone.
