Getting them back takes a multiply and a divide, and a weighted sum can only add. [[3]] So hand it the run-rate as a column. Now it misses by about 1,730 dollars, clearly ahead of the baseline. That is model A from the last module. The gain came from a column you built, not from the algorithm.

visual.title: Average miss (MAE), 4,000 test advertisers

data.label: Same, plus run-rate as a column (model A of lesson 2-5)

visual.note: Gap to baseline: +$339 (interval +$205 to +$479), then −$288 (−$407 to −$171)

segments.narration: The second reason is the shape of money. [[1]] The advertiser in the middle spends about 1,700 dollars. The average is about 5,300. [[2]] The largest account spends about 174,000. The weights were chosen to make squared misses small, and squaring makes big misses count most. [[3]] So the fit bends its weights to suit a handful of giant accounts, and thousands of ordinary ones get worse predictions. The fix is a change of scale, not a cleverer model. [[4]] Put spend on a log scale, the kind you pick for a chart axis when one bar dwarfs the rest. There, one thousand dollars to ten thousand is the same step as ten thousand to a hundred thousand. Equal steps are equal percentage changes, so the giants no longer dominate.

visual.title: The shape of money: next-8-week spend, 4,000 test advertisers

stats.label: advertiser in the middle (median) vs the average
the largest account
middle miss (median): raw-dollar regression vs run-rate

segments.narration: One thing to settle first. A log cannot take a zero, and about one test advertiser in eight spends nothing in the next eight weeks: the ones who leave. [[1]] So the log version is fitted only on training advertisers who kept spending. [[2]] It is still scored like every other model, on all 4,000 test advertisers, zeros included.

left.label: Log model fitted on
left.sub: training advertisers who kept spending: a log cannot take $0

right.label: Every model scored on
right.sub: test advertisers, including the 13.2% who spend $0

segments.narration: [[3]] Fit the same weighted sum to the log of spend, with the past-spend columns on the same scale. [[4]] The average miss falls to about 1,430 dollars, the best on the ladder. [[5]] It even edges out a more flexible model, the kind model B was in the last module, fitted in dollars and tuned for the average miss: about 1,500, a gap that only just clears zero. On a log scale a weight converts to a percentage: a managed account is predicted to spend about 13 percent more, the rest held fixed. An association, not a lever. One caution: this simulated world was built so that effects on spend multiply, which suits a log fit. On your data, fit both ways and compare.

visual.title: The ladder: average miss (MAE), same 4,000 test advertisers

data.label: Model B's kind, aimed at the average miss, in dollars

visual.note: Log regression vs that flexible model: −$72, interval −$155 to −$5. Model B itself, fitted to squared misses: $1,675. Managed account, log weight converted to a percentage: +12.8%.

segments.narration: Now the catch. Turn a log prediction back into dollars and you get the typical advertiser: the one in the middle, with half spending more and half less. Not the average: a few accounts spend far more than the middle and pull it up. That is fine for one account and wrong for a total. [[1]] Add up the typical values for the advertisers who kept spending, and the total comes out about 4 percent low. [[2]] Scale every prediction up by a correction factor of about 1.04, and the total lands within a fraction of a percent. That total leaves out the advertisers who left and spent nothing. This model cannot see them coming; a later lesson adds that piece.

visual.title: Log model, summed over the 3,473 test advertisers who kept spending

right.label: Corrected to averages (× 1.039)
right.sub: predicted total vs actual total, same 3,473 advertisers

segments.narration: The brief: four plain asks. [[1]] Fit the regression in dollars and on a log scale, and score both beside the baseline on the same test advertisers. [[2]] Say which rows were fitted and which were scored, and what happened to the zeros. [[3]] Say how log predictions were turned back into dollars, and show predicted total against actual. [[4]] Put an interval on every gap between one model and the next. If a rough forecast is enough, or the interval on the model's gain over the run-rate includes zero, keep the run-rate. Nobody has to maintain a multiplication.

visual.title: Brief and audit: four asks
items: Two fits, dollars and log, beside the baseline, on the same test rows
Rows fitted, rows scored, and what happened to zero-spend rows
Back to dollars: typical or corrected? Predicted total vs actual total
An interval on each gap between one model and the next

segments.narration: So when a number model disappoints, look at the columns it was given and the scale it was fitted on before you ask for a cleverer algorithm. Next, the same weighted sum is bent to answer a yes or no question.

visual.text: What moved the result was the column you built and the scale you chose, not the algorithm.
visual.sub: Run-rate $2,022 · raw dollars $2,361 · plus run-rate column $1,733 · log scale $1,428

takeaways: A linear regression is a weighted sum; each weight is read with the other columns held fixed, and is an association.
With a skewed target like money, the column you build and the scale you fit on can matter more than the algorithm.
A log model turned back into dollars gives typical values: correct to averages before you add predictions up.

quiz.q: A linear regression for next-8-week spend, fitted in dollars, shows the weight 'managed: +598'. An account director reads it as: 'Give an account a manager and it spends about $600 more.' What does the weight actually say?
options: Across the whole table, managed accounts spend $598 more on average than unmanaged ones
Assigning a manager to an account will add about $598 to its spend over the next 8 weeks
With the other columns equal, a managed account is predicted $598 higher
The weight is smaller than the model's average miss of $1,733, so it carries no meaning
quiz.why: A weight is the change in the prediction with the other columns held fixed, so it compares otherwise similar advertisers; it is not the raw gap between the two groups. It is also an association learned from past data, not a promise about what happens if you assign a manager.

quiz.q: The assistant fits spend on a log scale, converts the predictions back to dollars and reports: 'Lowest MAE of all models. Per-advertiser forecasts summed into a revenue total for finance.' The output does not say how the conversion was done or which advertisers the total covers. What do you ask for before that total goes out?
options: How the predictions became dollars, typical or corrected, and predicted total beside actual, with its row count
Whether MAE in dollars is a valid measure at all for a model that was fitted on a log scale rather than in dollars
Whether the same model also had the lowest RMSE, since a summed total is driven mostly by the largest accounts
Whether the log model used fewer columns than the dollar model, since every extra column inflates a summed total
quiz.why: A log model turned straight back into dollars gives typical values, and summed they run low: 3.6% low here among the 3,473 test advertisers who kept spending, until the correction to averages. Which rows the total covers matters as much: over all 4,000, the same model runs 6.1% high after the correction, because it also predicts spend for advertisers who then leave. MAE in dollars is a fair way to score the model; the risk is in how the predictions are used, not in the measure.

quiz.q: A linear regression predicts how many minutes a support ticket will take. Most tickets take 5 to 10 minutes; a few escalations take days. Fitted on raw minutes, it does worse than always predicting the median. What is the most promising first change?
options: Switch to a more complex kind of model, still fitted on raw minutes
Fit the same model on the log of handling time
Remove the multi-day escalations from the test set before scoring
Add several more months of tickets to the training set and refit
quiz.why: With a few enormous values, a squared-error fit spends its weights on the escalations and gets ordinary tickets wrong; a log scale turns the giants into ordinary-sized steps. A more complex model changes the algorithm but leaves the same scale problem, and removing escalations from the test only hides the error.

quiz.concept: what a weighted sum cannot build
quiz.q: Fitted in dollars on all 17 raw columns, the regression misses by $2,361 on average. The run-rate baseline misses by $2,022, and the interval on the gap excludes zero. A colleague concludes that linear regression is too weak for this problem. What is the better next step?
options: Agree, and report that no model can beat the run-rate on this table
Move straight to a more complex kind of model on the same raw columns
Drop the baseline from the report, since it already uses recent spend
Add the run-rate as a column: a weighted sum cannot multiply columns itself
quiz.why: The run-rate is a combination of two columns that a weighted sum cannot construct, so the model was missing its best input; given that column it misses by $1,733 and clearly beats the baseline. One losing configuration is not evidence about the whole method, and removing the baseline removes the only honest yardstick.

review.concept: A regression weight: the change per unit with other columns held fixed, an association and not a lever

variants.q: A linear regression predicts deal size for inbound leads. Its weight for 'attended a webinar' is +$1,200. Which reading is correct?
options: Across all leads, those who attended a webinar close deals $1,200 larger on average
Among leads alike on the other columns, attendees are predicted $1,200 higher
Inviting any lead to a webinar will add about $1,200 to the size of their deal
Webinar attendance accounts for $1,200 of the value of every deal that closes
variants.why: The weight compares leads that match on every other column, which is not the raw average gap between attendees and everyone else. And it describes a pattern in past deals, not the effect of inviting someone.

variants.q: A regression predicts ticket handling time in minutes. Its weight for 'customer is on the enterprise plan' is +4. The support lead says: 'So enterprise tickets take 4 minutes longer than the rest.' What needs correcting?
options: The unit: in a model like this a weight is a percentage, so it means 4 percent longer
The direction: a positive weight means enterprise tickets are handled 4 minutes faster
It is 4 minutes longer than otherwise similar tickets, not than all the rest
The size: a weight as small as 4 is inside the noise and should not be read at all
variants.why: The weight holds the other columns fixed, so it compares enterprise tickets with otherwise similar ones. The raw gap between enterprise tickets and all others can be larger or smaller, because enterprise tickets differ on the other columns too. The unit is minutes, the target's own unit, and a positive weight means longer.

variants.q: A regression of campaign CTR on creative features gives 'headline contains a number: +0.08 points'. A creative strategist wants numbers added to every headline. What is the honest position?
options: Do it: the weight shows that a number in the headline raises CTR
Do it, but only for campaigns whose CTR is currently below average
The weight cannot be used at all, because CTR is itself a percentage
It is an association among similar campaigns, not yet a proven lever
variants.why: The weight says that, among otherwise similar campaigns, those with a number in the headline had a slightly higher CTR. Whether adding a number would change CTR is a different question, which a pattern in past data cannot settle by itself.

review.concept: Skewed targets: fit on a log scale, and remember that log predictions are typical values, not averages

variants.q: A model fitted on the log of annual contract value predicts each customer's renewal amount. The CFO adds the predictions up, and the total is consistently a few percent below what comes in. What is the most likely reason?
options: Back from a log scale, predictions are typical values, which sum too low
The model was fitted on too few customers for a total to come out right
Log models always underestimate the smallest customers, and those add up in a total
Per-customer predictions carry too much noise to be added up into a total
variants.why: A log model turned back into dollars predicts the middle customer of each kind, and because a few customers spend far more than the middle, the average sits above it. Summing typical values therefore runs low until they are corrected to averages.

variants.q: A regression predicts monthly revenue per publisher in raw dollars. Three giant publishers earn more than the other 2,000 combined, and the model is poor for almost everyone else. Why, and what do you try first?
options: There are too few publishers; collect more months of data before refitting
The squared-error fit is dominated by the giants; fit on log revenue
Raw dollars are fine; the model simply needs more columns about each publisher
The giants are outliers; delete them from the data and report on the rest
variants.why: Squared misses on the giants dwarf everything else, so the weights are tuned to them; on a log scale equal percentage errors count equally. Deleting the giants hides exactly the accounts finance cares about most.

variants.q: A log-scale model predicts next month's spend per campaign. An account manager wants a forecast for one typical campaign; finance wants the sum over all campaigns. Which version of the prediction does each need?
options: Both need the corrected version, so that the two figures agree
Both need the typical version, since it has the lower average miss
The manager the typical value; finance the corrected one
The manager the corrected value; finance the typical one
variants.why: Converted straight back, a log prediction is the middle outcome for a campaign of that kind, which is the right answer for one campaign. A sum needs averages, so finance gets the corrected version; typical values would make the total run low, however good their average miss looks.

drill.q: What is a linear regression, and how are its weights chosen?
drill.a: A weighted sum: a base amount, plus each column multiplied by its own weight. The weights are the ones that make the squared misses on the training rows as small as possible.

drill.q: A model fitted on the log of spend is turned back into dollars and added up into a revenue total. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
drill.a: A log model predicts the typical account, and a few very large accounts pull the average above the typical, so the total runs low. Correct the predictions to averages before adding them up, and check the predicted total against the actual one.

recall.prompt: Your first linear regression lost to the run-rate baseline. Explain what a linear regression is, why it lost, and the two changes that fixed it.
recall.model_answer: A linear regression is a weighted sum of the columns, with weights chosen to make the squared misses on the training rows as small as possible; each weight is the change per unit with the other columns held fixed. It lost because a weighted sum cannot build the run-rate out of two columns by itself, and because spend is so skewed that a few giant accounts dominate a squared-error fit. Adding the run-rate as a column and fitting on a log scale fixed both. The catch: log predictions are typical values, so correct them to averages before summing.

lessons.ask_assistant: Predict [numeric outcome] with a linear regression fitted two ways: on the raw values, and on the log of [outcome] with [skewed size columns] logged too. Give both models [my baseline rule] as a column. Train on [training period], score on [test period], and show [baseline] beside both: MAE, RMSE, predicted total versus actual total, and a bootstrap interval on each MAE gap. State the rows fitted and the rows scored for each model, and what happened to rows where [outcome] is zero. For the log model, say how you converted back to [units], and show the total with and without the correction to averages. Print the weights with their units, converting log-fit weights to percentage effects.
audit_checklist: The weights table shows its units: dollars per unit for the raw fit; for the log fit, weights converted from log units to percent change per unit, or per 1% change for a column that was logged too
Row counts for every model: rows fitted, rows scored, and how many zero-outcome rows there were and what was done with them
Predicted total beside actual total, with and without the correction to averages, and the row count each total covers
The baseline in the same table on the same test rows, with an interval on each gap
transfer: Predicting the value of an inbound lead when a few enterprise deals dwarf the rest: which scale do you fit on?
Estimating how many minutes a support ticket will take, when most are short and a few run for days.
Forecasting revenue per publisher and adding it up for finance: typical value or average?

other_ways.approach: A more flexible model fitted in dollars
other_ways.when: When effects bend or depend on each other and you have plenty of rows: a weighted sum gives each column one steady rate and simply extends its line past the largest account it has seen. Here a flexible model fitted in dollars missed by $1,500 against the log regression's $1,428.

other_ways.approach: Predict the ratio of next period's spend to the last period's
other_ways.when: When account sizes differ enormously and the real question is growth or decline, not the level.

other_ways.approach: Keep the run-rate rule
other_ways.when: When a rough forecast is enough and nobody will maintain or monitor a model.

glossary.def: A model that predicts a number as a base amount plus each column multiplied by a learned weight.
How much the prediction changes per unit of a column, with the other columns held fixed; also called a coefficient.
A scale on which equal steps are equal percentage changes, so a few very large values no longer dominate.
The typical value is the middle one, half above and half below; with a few very large values, the average sits above it.
A factor (about 1.04 here) that scales a log model's typical-value predictions up to averages, so that a sum over the kind of rows it was fitted on comes out right.

lessons.title: Logistic regression: predicting yes or no
lessons.subtitle: How does a table of columns become a probability, and what do the weights really tell you?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can read a logistic regression's weights as shifts in predicted probability, and say why a weight is not a cause.

predict.q: About 12 percent of advertisers churn. A churn model reports that one step up in spend trend 'cuts the odds of churn by more than half'. On average, how much does that take off an advertiser's predicted probability of churning?
options: More than 50 percentage points
About 25 percentage points
About 5 percentage points
Less than 1 percentage point
predict.reveal: About 5 points. With churn near 12 percent there are not 25 or 50 points to take off: 'odds cut by more than half' sounds far bigger than it is, and the lesson shows how to translate one into the other.

segments.narration: Ask an account manager which advertisers worry her, and she runs a scorecard in her head. Spend is sliding: bad. Hardly active this month: bad. Has conversion tracking: good. She adds it up and gets a feeling. It works well enough, but the weights are hers, and nobody ever checked them. Logistic regression is that scorecard, with the weights learned from 6,000 past advertisers whose outcome is already known. The same learned scorecard works for any yes or no question, such as which clicks are invalid traffic. It is also the churn model you were judging all through module two.

visual.title: Logistic regression
visual.sub: A scorecard with learned weights

segments.narration: Start from last lesson's idea: one weight per column, multiplied and added up. [[1]] Here the total is a number of points. Everyone starts from a negative number, because most advertisers stay. A sliding spend trend adds points. Conversion tracking takes some away. But a sum can come out as anything, and you want a probability. [[2]] So the total is pushed through an S-shaped curve that squeezes any number into the range between zero and one. [[3]] Zero points lands on 50 percent. Minus three lands near 5 percent, plus three near 95. That is the whole model: a weighted sum, then a squeeze.

visual.title: From points to a probability
lines: points = −2.76 − 0.85 × spend trend − 0.59 × tracking + 0.65 × gaming + …
probability of churn = the points, squeezed through an S-shaped curve into 0–100%
−3 points → 5%      0 points → 50%      +3 points → 95%
visual.note: Spend trend is counted in standard deviations from the average; tracking and gaming are 1 or 0. 22 learned numbers in all.

segments.narration: Here is what it learned. Spend trend carries the heaviest weight. The assistant's output may report it as an odds ratio of about 0.43. Odds are the chance that something happens divided by the chance that it does not, and the ratio is a multiplier. So one typical step up in spend trend, about 0.4 and explained in a moment, cuts the odds of churn by more than half. That sounds enormous. In plain terms, it takes about 5 points off the predicted probability of churn, on average. An average, because of the curve: the same push moves an advertiser near 50 percent a long way, and one near 2 percent hardly at all. When you are handed odds, ask for probability points.

visual.title: What each weight does to predicted churn
visual.note: Average shift in predicted churn probability, in points. Spend trend as an odds ratio: 0.43.

segments.narration: What is a typical step? Before fitting, each continuous column is put on a common scale, so that one unit means one standard deviation of that column: about 0.4 for spend trend, about 5 days for active days. The reason is comparison. Left in their own units, a weight per dollar would be tiny and a weight per unit of spend trend large, and their sizes would say nothing about which matters more. Yes or no flags are left as they are, because yes versus no is already a natural step. So a weight always comes with a unit.

visual.title: What one step means
visual.note: Continuous columns: one standard deviation. Flags stay as 0 or 1.

segments.narration: Does it hold up? [[1]] On the rows it learned from, its AUC is about 0.85. [[2]] On the test months, which it never saw, also about 0.85. That near match tells you it learned a pattern and did not simply memorise its training rows. [[3]] No surprise: the whole model is 22 numbers, which leaves no room to remember 6,000 advertisers one by one. [[4]] And it earns its place. At the same list size as your hand rule, the rule found 246 churners and the model found 321.

visual.title: Does it hold up on advertisers it never saw?

stats.label: AUC on training rows (Jan–Mar)
AUC on test rows (May–Jun)
learned numbers in the whole model
churners among 711 flagged: model vs hand rule

segments.narration: The simplicity has a price. [[1]] Each column pushes one way, at a steady rate. If trouble only started once active days fell below ten, or if both very low and very high values were bad news, a single weight could not say so. [[2]] A column also adds the same points whatever the other columns say. The model cannot learn that a high click rate is good news in one vertical and bad news in another, unless somebody builds a column for it. [[3]] And columns that overlap share the credit. Days since login gets almost no weight here. Maybe logins do not matter. Maybe active days already said the same thing. The weight cannot tell you which.

visual.title: What a weighted sum cannot say
items: One direction, one steady rate per column: no thresholds, no U-shapes
The same points whatever the other columns say
Overlapping columns share the credit

segments.narration: Which brings us to the misreading that matters most. Conversion tracking has one of the heaviest weights: about 4 points off predicted churn. It is tempting to write, install tracking and churn falls by 4 points. The model never said that. Because this world is simulated, the real effect of switching tracking on is known: about 2 points, half of what the weight suggests. A later lesson takes that apart. Until then, here is what you may write. Advertisers with conversion tracking churned about 4 points less than otherwise similar advertisers without it. We have not tested whether switching it on helps. A weight is an association. Say goes with, never drives.

visual.text: A weight says what goes with churn in this table. It does not say what happens if you change it.
visual.sub: Tracking's weight: −4.4 points. True effect of switching it on, known only because the data is simulated: −2.3.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask for a logistic regression first, before anything fancier, and say what the output must show. [[1]] A table of weights in which every row states its unit and its average shift in predicted probability, in points. Odds ratios alone are not enough. [[2]] The score on training rows next to the score on test rows. [[3]] The hand rule at the same list size, so the model is compared with something. [[4]] And read the wording of the summary. If it says a column drives churn, or that a practice reduces it, send it back. The evidence supports the words is associated with, and nothing stronger.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Ask: a weights table with each unit and the shift in probability points
Check: AUC on training rows beside AUC on test rows
Check: the hand rule at the same list size
Check: 'is associated with', never 'drives' or 'reduces'

segments.narration: So when a stakeholder asks what separates happy advertisers from unhappy ones, you can answer with a weights table in probability points and one careful sentence. Next, a model built the opposite way: no sum, just a flowchart of yes or no questions the data chooses for itself.

visual.title: Keep this
items: A weighted sum, squeezed into a probability
Read a weight with its unit, in probability points
A weight is an association, not a lever

takeaways: Logistic regression is a weighted sum of the columns, squeezed by an S-curve into a probability between 0 and 1.
Read each weight with its unit, and translate odds into a shift in probability points.
A weight is an association in this table, not the effect of changing that column.

quiz.q: The weights table shows spend trend with an odds ratio of 0.43 per standard deviation and an average probability shift of −5.1 points. An account manager asks what that means for her advertisers. Which summary is accurate?
options: Advertisers whose spend trend is rising have a 43 percent chance of churning.
Every advertiser's churn probability drops by exactly 5.1 points for each step up in spend trend.
Among similar advertisers, a spend trend one step higher goes with predicted churn about 5 points lower, on average.
If she persuades an advertiser to raise their spend trend by one step, that advertiser's churn risk will fall by about 5 points.
quiz.why: The weight compares otherwise similar advertisers, and the 5 points is an average. Reading 0.43 as a chance of churning confuses an odds ratio with a probability. The shift is not the same for everyone, because the S-curve moves mid-risk advertisers more than very safe ones. And nothing in a weight says what happens if you push an advertiser's spend up.

quiz.q: The assistant returns weights with no units: spend in the last 8 weeks −0.00004, active days −0.09, spend trend −2.1. Its summary says: 'Spend trend is by far the strongest factor; spend barely matters.' What is the flaw?
options: The columns are in their own units, so the weights cannot be compared; ask for a common scale.
The summary undersells it: −2.1 against −0.00004 means spend trend matters about fifty thousand times more.
Negative weights are a sign that the model is broken; in a sound model every weight is positive.
Spend should be dropped from the model, since a weight that close to zero adds nothing.
quiz.why: A weight is per unit of its column. One dollar is a tiny step and one whole unit of spend trend is a huge one, so these sizes say nothing about which column matters more. Put continuous columns on a common scale, one standard deviation each, and then compare. A near-zero weight per dollar is no reason to drop a column.

quiz.concept: a weight is not a cause
quiz.q: A lead-scoring model for a sales team gives 'attended a webinar' its largest positive weight. Marketing proposes enrolling every new lead in a webinar to lift conversion. What does the weight support?
options: The plan: the largest weight marks the strongest lever the team can pull to raise conversion.
Nothing at all: the weights of a logistic regression are arbitrary numbers and carry no meaning.
The plan, but only if the model's AUC on the test rows is above 0.8, which makes its weights reliable.
That webinar attendees convert more than similar leads; whether enrolling leads helps needs a test.
quiz.why: The weight describes who converts: leads who chose to attend a webinar were probably keener to begin with. It says nothing about what happens to a lead who is pushed into one. A high AUC makes the ranking trustworthy, not the weights causal. The weight is still useful for scoring; it is just not evidence for the plan.

quiz.q: An account manager believes creative refresh is risky at both extremes: advertisers who never refresh churn, and so do those who swap creatives frantically every day. The model has one weight for days since the last refresh. What will it do with that pattern?
options: Capture it: the S-curve bends, so it can rise at one end of the column and fall at the other.
Fit one steady push in one direction and miss the U-shape, unless it is given a reshaped column.
Learn two weights for the column automatically, one for low values and one for high values.
Refuse to fit, and raise an error saying that the column is not suitable.
quiz.why: One weight means one direction at a steady rate, so a risk that is high at both ends averages out to a weak push or none. The S-curve only squeezes the total into a probability; it never reverses a column's direction. To capture the pattern, someone has to build a column for it, or use a different kind of model.

review.concept: a weight is an association, not a lever

variants.q: In the churn model, having an account manager carries a weight worth about 3 points less predicted churn. A director wants to give every small account a manager 'to cut their churn by 3 points'. What is the right reading?
options: Managed accounts churn less than similar unmanaged ones; what assigning a manager would do needs a test.
The plan is sound: with the other columns held fixed, the weight is exactly the effect of adding a manager.
The plan is sound only if the manager weight is larger than the weight for conversion tracking.
Weights below 5 points are within the noise, so the director should ignore this one altogether.
variants.why: A weight compares accounts that already differ in who got a manager, and nothing says managers were handed out at random. Holding the other columns fixed removes only the differences the table records. The weight is a fair description of the pattern, and no evidence about the result of changing it.

variants.q: An upsell model gives 'opened the pricing page in the last 30 days' a large positive weight. A product manager suggests redirecting every customer to the pricing page after login, to raise upgrades. What does the model actually tell you?
options: That the redirect will raise upgrades by roughly the size of the weight, measured in probability points.
That the pricing page is hard to find, which is the real reason so few customers upgrade.
That customers who chose to look at pricing upgrade more often; forcing the visit may change nothing.
That the model must be leaking the outcome, since no honest column could carry so much weight.
variants.why: Customers who open the pricing page on their own are already considering an upgrade, and the weight picks that up. Sending everyone there does not give them that intent. The column is a fine signal for ranking who to contact, and a poor argument for the redirect.

variants.q: A model predicting which support tickets get escalated gives 'customer used live chat' a negative weight: fewer escalations. The support lead proposes routing every ticket through chat. What is the catch?
options: The weight proves that chat prevents escalations; the only catch is finding enough agents to staff it.
The weight must first be converted to an odds ratio; after that the plan can go ahead as proposed.
Negative weights cannot be trusted in a logistic regression, so the column should be removed.
Customers with simpler problems may be the ones who choose chat; the weight may describe them, not the channel.
variants.why: The weight says chat tickets escalate less, other recorded columns being equal. It cannot say whether chat calms tickets down or simply attracts easy ones. Only changing the routing for a random share of tickets would separate the two. Converting the weight to another unit changes nothing about that.

review.concept: odds are not probabilities

variants.q: About 60 percent of trial accounts convert to paid. A model reports 'invited a teammate: odds ratio 3'. A colleague writes in the summary: 'inviting a teammate makes conversion three times as likely.' What is wrong?
options: Only the wording: the probability does triple, but the summary should say 'goes with', not 'makes'.
The odds tripled, not the probability, which cannot reach 180 percent; ask for the shift in points.
An odds ratio above 1 means that inviting a teammate makes conversion less likely, not more.
Odds ratios only apply to rare outcomes, so for an outcome as common as 60 percent this one is meaningless.
variants.why: Odds are the chance it happens divided by the chance it does not, so tripling the odds from a 60 percent start lands somewhere above 80 percent, not at 180. The plain-language figure is the shift in probability points. The odds ratio is valid for common outcomes too; it just must not be read as a multiple of the probability.

variants.q: About 2 percent of clicks on a network are invalid. A traffic-quality model reports 'data-centre IP: odds ratio 4'. A manager concludes that most clicks from data-centre IPs are invalid. What is the right read?
options: Correct: an odds ratio of 4 means that four clicks in five from those addresses are invalid.
Correct: any column with an odds ratio above 2 marks traffic that is mostly invalid.
Four times very small odds is still a small probability; ask for the predicted probability first.
The odds ratio cannot be read at all without first knowing the model's AUC on the test rows.
variants.why: Multiplying very small odds by four leaves a probability still under 10 percent: a real signal worth ranking on, and nowhere near 'most'. An odds ratio is a multiplier on odds, not a share of cases. Asking for the predicted probability, in points, settles what the number means for the decision.

variants.q: A churn model has one weight for payment failures: an odds ratio of about 1.3 per step, the same for every advertiser. An analyst assumes each extra step adds the same number of points to everyone's churn probability. Is that right?
options: No: the odds change by one factor, but the shift in points is larger for mid-risk advertisers.
Yes: one weight for the column means one fixed number of points for every advertiser.
Yes, as long as the column was put on a common scale before the model was fitted.
No: the shift in points is always largest for the advertisers who start out with the lowest risk of all.
variants.why: The weight is constant on the points scale, before the S-curve. After the curve, the same push moves an advertiser in the middle of the range a lot and one near zero or one very little. That is why the plain-language figure is quoted as an average shift across advertisers.

drill.q: A logistic regression gives one column a large weight. What do you need to know before you can say what that weight means?
drill.a: Its unit, meaning one standard deviation or yes versus no, and what it does to the predicted probability in points. Even then it describes an association, not what happens if you change the column.

drill.q: Someone tells you a column has an odds ratio of one half, so it halves the chance of churn. What is wrong with that?
drill.a: Odds are not probabilities. Halving the odds moves the probability by an amount that depends on where the advertiser started, so ask for the shift in probability points.

recall.prompt: Explain to a colleague how logistic regression turns an advertiser's columns into a churn probability, and what one of its weights does and does not tell you.
recall.model_answer: Each column gets a learned weight; the weighted columns are added into a total, and an S-shaped curve squeezes that total into a probability between 0 and 1. A weight is read with its unit, one standard deviation or yes versus no, and is best translated from odds into an average shift in probability points: about 5 points for spend trend here. It describes what goes with churn among otherwise similar advertisers in this table. It does not say what would happen if you changed that column.

lessons.ask_assistant: Fit a logistic regression for [yes/no outcome] on [training period] only, with continuous columns standardised and yes/no flags left as 0 or 1, and score [test period]. Show a weights table with each column's unit (per standard deviation, or yes versus no), its odds ratio, and the average shift in predicted probability in points. Report AUC on the training rows and on the test rows side by side, with row counts, and how many [positives] the model finds at the same list size as [my current rule or baseline]. Describe weights as associations; do not write that any column drives or reduces [outcome].
audit_checklist: Every weight states its unit (per standard deviation, or yes versus no) and its average shift in probability points, not only an odds ratio.
AUC on training rows and on test rows sit side by side with their row counts, and are close.
The current rule or baseline is scored on the same test rows at the same list size, beside the model.
The summary says 'is associated with', never 'drives', 'causes' or 'reduces'.
transfer: Lead scoring: which form fields and behaviours go with a lead converting, and by how many points each?
Invalid traffic: how likely is a click source to be invalid, given its traffic pattern?
Upsell: which accounts are likely to take up a new ad format this quarter?

other_ways.approach: A hand-built points scorecard
other_ways.when: When there are too few past cases to learn weights from, or the rule has to be explained in one sentence.

other_ways.approach: A decision tree
other_ways.when: When you expect thresholds or 'it depends' patterns and want rules a person can read; the next lesson.

other_ways.approach: A more flexible model
other_ways.when: When a measured gap on the test rows, larger than the noise, shows the weighted sum is missing something.

glossary.def: A model that adds up weighted columns and squeezes the total through an S-curve into a probability.
How many points one step of a column adds to or takes off the total, with the other columns held fixed.
The chance that something happens divided by the chance that it does not.
The factor by which the odds are multiplied for one step of a column; not a change in probability.
Rescale a continuous column so that one unit equals one standard deviation, which makes weights comparable.

lessons.title: Decision trees
lessons.subtitle: What does a model look like when it asks questions instead of adding up points?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can read a fitted decision tree path by path, and say when its coarseness matters.

predict.q: Your hand rule flags advertisers whose spend trend is below 0.7. An algorithm now builds its own flowchart of yes/no questions from all 17 columns, with no hints. What does it do with spend trend?
options: Ignores it and picks columns you would never think of
Uses it, with a cut-off very close to your 0.7
Uses it, but with a very different cut-off, around 0.3
Asks about nothing else, at every step
predict.reveal: It asks about active days first, then cuts spend trend at 0.74 on one branch and 0.69 on the other: your rule, rediscovered. The lesson shows what else it found, and what the approach costs.

segments.narration: In lesson one you wrote a rule: flag any advertiser whose spend trend is below 0.7. Now hand the same table to an algorithm that builds its own flowchart of yes or no questions, and give it no hints. Its first question is about active days. Its second, on both branches, is whether spend trend is below about 0.7. It rediscovered your rule on its own, and then it kept asking. That flowchart is called a decision tree. The data can design one for any outcome you have past answers for, which advertisers will hit their CPA goal, for instance. And you already know how to read one: it is a CASE WHEN with learned cut-offs.

visual.title: Decision trees
visual.sub: A flowchart the data designed

segments.narration: Here is how one gets built. [[1]] Take the 6,000 training advertisers and try every possible split: each column, each cut-off. Active days above or below ten. Spend trend above or below one. A great many candidates. [[2]] For each, look at the two groups it creates and ask how cleanly they separate churners from stayers. Keep the best. Here that was active days: 14 or fewer against 15 or more. [[3]] Then do the same again inside each group, separately. [[4]] And stop at a depth you choose: here three questions deep, which gives at most eight end points. Nobody told it which columns matter. It tried them all, and kept what separated best on the training rows.

steps.label: Keep the best
steps.sub: the one that separates churners from stayers most cleanly

steps.label: Repeat
steps.sub: inside each of the two groups

steps.label: Stop
steps.sub: here: three questions deep, at least 100 advertisers per leaf

segments.narration: Read it from the top, one path at a time. Everyone starts together, at about 11 percent churn. Take the advertisers with 14 active days or fewer. Among those, the ones whose spend trend is below 0.74. Among those, the small accounts, under about 1,000 dollars of spend in eight weeks. That leaves about 200 advertisers, and about two in three of them churned. Now the opposite path. More than 14 active days. Spend trend above 0.69, and then above 0.9 as well. That is about 3,400 advertisers, more than half the training rows, and under 4 percent of them churned. Now follow a few paths yourself, and see where an advertiser your hand rule would have flagged ends up.

visual.name: tree
visual.title: The fitted churn tree, three questions deep
visual.note: Follow a path from the top to an end point. Each box shows how many training advertisers reached it and what share of them churned.

segments.narration: Each end point is called a leaf, and a leaf is nothing more exotic than a segment with a churn rate. Written out, the whole model is one CASE WHEN: eight branches, each returning the churn rate of the training advertisers who landed there. You could paste it into your warehouse. Think of it as a GROUP BY that the data designed. Normally you choose the grouping columns and the cut-offs. Here they were chosen for you, by whichever split separated churners best. The same machinery predicts numbers too. Asked for spend, a leaf would simply return the average spend of its advertisers.

visual.title: The same tree, written as SQL
visual.code:
SELECT advertiser_id,
  CASE
    WHEN active_days_28 <= 14 AND spend_trend <= 0.74
     AND spend_8w <= 1020 THEN 0.633   -- small, quiet, shrinking
    WHEN active_days_28 <= 14 AND spend_trend <= 0.74
                          THEN 0.436
    -- ... five more branches ...
    ELSE 0.036   -- active, spend trend above 0.9
  END AS churn_score
FROM advertisers;
visual.note: Eight leaves, eight possible scores: each is one segment's churn rate. Cut-offs are rounded, as the tree prints them.

segments.narration: Read the first two questions as a table. [[1]] Among advertisers with few active days, shrinking spend takes churn from 18 percent to 54. [[2]] Among active ones, from 5 percent to 21. [[3]] So low activity costs 13 points when spend is holding and 33 when it is shrinking. Say points when you report it: as a ratio, low activity roughly triples churn either way. What a tree does differently: every branch chooses its own next question and cut-off. Quiet accounts with shrinking spend get asked about their size, those with steady spend about click rate. Last lesson's weighted sum gave each column one weight for everyone. A tree can ask something different in every corner of the table, so an answer that depends on something else costs nothing extra.

visual.title: Churn rate after the first two questions
rows: Gap between the rows, in points
visual.note: Shrinking means a spend trend below 0.74 in the first row and below 0.69 in the second: the tree picked each cut-off separately.

segments.narration: The price is coarseness. Eight leaves means eight possible scores. The 3,363 advertisers in the safest leaf all get exactly the same number, so the tree cannot say which of them is riskier. Ask for the 200 most at-risk accounts and it has to cut through the middle of a leaf, where everyone ties. [[1]] So it ranks worse: an AUC of about 0.76 on the test months. [[2]] The weighted sum scored about 0.85, a gap far bigger than the noise. The coarseness comes with any small tree. The size of the gap does not. It belongs to this simulated data, where churn is built from many small pushes that add up. On another question the order can change, so you measure.

right.label: Weighted sum (logistic regression)
right.sub: a score for every advertiser · top 200 hold 136 churners

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask for a tree as a reading aid beside the weighted sum. [[1]] The brief: a shallow tree on the training months, printed as rules, with a minimum number of advertisers per leaf. [[2]] Each leaf must show its count beside its rate, because a rate from a handful of accounts is noise. [[3]] Check the first question: a tree puts its best separating column on top, so a column recorded after the snapshot would likely sit right there. And send back any tree that asks about an ID: an ID says nothing about behaviour. [[4]] Ask for the score on training and on test rows, both models on the same test rows. [[5]] If you know which columns define your segments, skip the tree: a plain GROUP BY gives the rates.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Ask: a shallow tree as rules, beside the weighted sum (here: depth 3, 100+ advertisers per leaf)
Check: every leaf shows its count and its rate
Check: first question passes the time-travel test; no ID anywhere
Check: AUC on training and test rows (tree: 0.786, 0.761), same test rows for both models
Or: a plain GROUP BY, when you know the segment columns

segments.narration: So when someone needs rules they can read, or you want to see which segments the data would pick, ask for a shallow tree, and check its ranking before anyone builds a list from it. Next: what goes wrong in the table itself, before any model is fitted.

visual.title: Keep this
items: A flowchart of yes/no questions, found by trying every split
Each leaf is a segment with a rate: a CASE WHEN with learned cut-offs
Readable, but coarse: few leaves, few scores

takeaways: A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions, grown by trying every column and cut-off and keeping the split that separates the outcome best.
Each leaf is a segment with a rate, so a tree reads like a CASE WHEN with learned cut-offs.
A small tree is readable but coarse: one score per leaf, so check its ranking against a finer-grained model on the same test rows.

quiz.q: Reading the fitted churn tree, an account manager notices that click rate appears on only one branch: quiet accounts whose spend is holding. She concludes that click rate is irrelevant for every other advertiser. What is the right read?
options: Correct: a tree asks about a column only where it matters, so its absence elsewhere shows it is irrelevant there.
The tree is faulty: every column should appear somewhere on every branch.
Click rate was the best next split on that branch; elsewhere another column won, with no room left to ask more.
Click rate causes churn, but only among quiet accounts with steady spend.
quiz.why: Each branch keeps only the single best split at each step, and this tree stops after three questions. A column that is absent from a branch lost that contest; it has not been shown to be irrelevant there. And a split is chosen because it separates churners in the training rows, which is a description, not a cause.

quiz.concept: a leak shows up at the top
quiz.q: The assistant returns a churn tree, three questions deep, with a test AUC far above the weighted sum's 0.85. The first question is about 'days since last spend', and it separates churners from stayers almost perfectly. What do you do?
options: Send it back: the first question is the outcome in disguise, a column recorded after the snapshot.
Ship it: a tree this accurate and this easy to read is the ideal model for the team.
Ask for a much deeper tree, since three questions cannot be trusted with a result this strong.
Accept it, provided the AUC on the training rows comes out just as high, which rules out memorising.
quiz.why: A tree puts its best separating column first, so a leaked column surfaces as the first question, splitting churners from stayers almost perfectly. Days since last spend, read after the outcome window, fails the time-travel test. Matching training and test scores do not help: the leak is in both. A deeper tree would only build on the same column.

quiz.q: A tree predicts which creatives will fatigue within a week. The media team can refresh 50 creatives, and the tree's riskiest leaf holds 400, all with the same score. What does that tell you?
options: The scoring is broken: every creative should come out with a different score.
The 400 creatives have been shown to be exactly equally likely to fatigue.
Adding the creative ID as a column would fix it, since every creative would then get a score of its own.
A small tree gives one score per leaf, so it cannot order the 400; a top-50 list needs finer scores.
quiz.why: Everything in a leaf gets the leaf's rate, so a tree with few leaves cannot rank inside one. That is how the method works, not a bug, and it does not prove the 400 are equally risky: the tree simply stopped asking. An ID column describes nothing about a creative and would only let a model memorise rows.

quiz.concept: one result is not a rule
quiz.q: On the simulated churn table the tree scored an AUC of 0.76 and the weighted sum 0.85. A colleague says: 'So trees are simply worse. Skip them on the upsell project.' What is the best response?
options: Agreed: the gap is a general property of the two methods and will carry over.
Any small tree is coarse, but which model ranks better depends on the data; fit both and compare on test rows.
Disagree: trees are always the better choice, because people can read them.
The comparison was unfair from the start, because the tree and the weighted sum were scored on different test rows.
quiz.why: Coarseness is a property of any small tree. The size of the gap is a property of this simulated churn data, where many small effects add up, which suits a weighted sum. A different question can favour the tree, so the only safe move is to measure both on the new table's test rows. Both models here were scored on the same test rows.

review.concept: a leaf is a segment with one rate

variants.q: A tree for lead conversion has this leaf: 'company size above 200 and requested a demo: 310 leads, 42 percent converted'. A new lead matching both conditions arrives. What score does the tree give it?
options: A score between 0 and 100 percent that depends on the lead's other columns.
42 percent: the conversion rate of the training leads that landed in that leaf.
100 percent, because the lead matched every condition on the path.
No score until more leads like it have been collected.
variants.why: A tree's prediction is the rate of the training cases in the leaf where the new case lands. Columns the path never asked about play no part. Matching the conditions puts the lead in the segment; it does not make conversion certain.

variants.q: Two traffic sources land in the same leaf of a tree that predicts invalid traffic. One sends 5,000 clicks a day, the other 50,000, and click volume was not asked about on that path. How do their scores compare?
options: The larger source gets the higher score, since it carries more risk.
The smaller source gets the higher score, since small sources are less well known.
The scores are identical: everything in a leaf gets the leaf's rate.
They cannot be compared until the tree is retrained with volume as the first question.
variants.why: A leaf is a segment, and every case in it receives the same rate. Differences in columns the path did not ask about are invisible to the tree. If volume matters for the decision, that is a reason to look at a deeper tree or a different model, measured on test rows.

variants.q: An account manager is puzzled: a tiny advertiser that joined last month and a large one with two years of history have exactly the same churn score from the tree. What explains it?
options: They gave the same answers to the tree's three questions, so they share a leaf; nothing else was asked.
The tree weighs tenure against account size, and for these two advertisers the two effects cancelled out exactly.
It must be a scoring bug: two such different advertisers cannot have the same risk.
The tree gives every advertiser the overall churn rate until it has seen them twice.
variants.why: A tree does not add anything up. It routes each advertiser by a few yes/no answers and returns the rate of the leaf they reach. Two very different advertisers who give the same answers get the same score. That is the coarseness you accept in exchange for readable rules.

review.concept: readable but coarse: match the model to the use

variants.q: A support team wants four or five plain rules that agents can follow to route tickets to the right queue. Which starting point fits?
options: A model that gives every ticket its own score, since finer-grained output is always the better starting point.
A shallow tree: a few questions, a handful of segments, rules that can be read aloud.
No model at all: rules can only ever be written by hand.
Whichever model has the highest AUC, whatever it looks like.
variants.why: The use is a small set of readable rules, which is exactly what a shallow tree produces, with cut-offs learned from past tickets. Fine-grained scores add nothing when the output is a handful of queues. The tree's rules still have to be checked on tickets it has not seen.

variants.q: Sales wants the 100 best upsell prospects out of 20,000 accounts. The assistant's tree has four leaves, and the best leaf holds 3,000 accounts. What is the problem?
options: The leaf is too large to trust: a rate measured on 3,000 accounts is noisier than one measured on 100.
The tree needs the account ID added as a column, so that it can tell the 3,000 accounts in the leaf apart.
Four leaves is too many; a tree with two leaves would give a cleaner list.
The tree cannot rank inside a leaf, so it cannot pick 100 out of 3,000; the list needs finer scores.
variants.why: All 3,000 accounts share one score, so the tree has no opinion about which 100 are best. A ranked list that short needs a score that differs from account to account. An ID column would not help: it describes nothing about an account's behaviour. And a large leaf makes its rate steadier, not noisier.

variants.q: On the same test rows, a shallow tree scores an AUC of 0.71 and a logistic regression 0.72, and the interval around the difference comfortably includes zero. The client insists on rules they can read. Which do you recommend?
options: The tree: the two are tied within the noise, and readable rules are what the client needs.
The logistic regression: 0.72 is higher than 0.71, and the higher score should always win.
Neither: a gap this small between two models means that both of them are broken.
A much deeper tree, grown until it beats the logistic regression outright on the test rows.
variants.why: When the interval around a difference includes zero, the two are tied, so the score does not decide this one. The use does: the client needs readable rules, and the tree gives them at no measured cost. Chasing a tiny, noisy gap would be reacting to chance.

drill.q: Someone shows you a decision tree. How do you read what it predicts for one advertiser?
drill.a: Start at the top and answer each yes or no question for that advertiser until you reach a leaf. The leaf's rate, the share of training advertisers there who churned, is the prediction.

drill.q: What does a small decision tree give up in exchange for being readable?
drill.a: Fine-grained scores. Everyone in a leaf gets the same score, so a tree with a few leaves cannot order the advertisers inside a leaf, and that can cost it on ranking.

recall.prompt: Explain how a decision tree is built, how you read one, and what it trades away for being readable.
recall.model_answer: A tree is grown by trying every column and cut-off, keeping the split that best separates the outcome, and repeating inside each group down to a chosen depth. You read it from the top, answering yes or no until you reach a leaf, and the leaf's rate is the prediction, so the whole model is a CASE WHEN with learned cut-offs. Different branches can ask different questions, which is how it handles 'it depends'. The cost is coarseness: one score per leaf, so on the churn table it ranked worse than the weighted sum, about 0.76 against 0.85, a gap that belongs to this simulated data.

lessons.ask_assistant: Fit a decision tree for [yes/no outcome] on [training period] only, with a maximum depth of [small depth, such as 3] and at least [minimum rows] rows in every leaf, and print it as rules. For every leaf show the rule, the number of training rows and their [outcome] rate. Report AUC on the training rows and on [test period], with row counts, next to [my simpler model or rule] scored on the same test rows. List every column used and when each is recorded; use no ID column and nothing recorded after [prediction date].
audit_checklist: Every leaf shows its row count and its rate, and no leaf is smaller than the minimum you set.
The printed rules name each question's column, and the column list shows when each is recorded: nothing after the prediction date, and no ID.
AUC on training rows and on test rows with their row counts, and the simpler model scored on the same test rows beside it.
transfer: Which support tickets get escalated: can the triage team have a few readable rules?
Which creatives fatigue fastest: what combination of age, format and frequency goes with a falling click rate?
How much will an advertiser spend next quarter: segments with an average spend in each leaf?

other_ways.approach: A plain GROUP BY on columns you choose
other_ways.when: When you already know which two or three columns define the segments and only need the rates.

other_ways.approach: Logistic regression
other_ways.when: When you need a ranked list with a distinct score for every advertiser.

other_ways.approach: Many trees combined
other_ways.when: When one tree is too coarse and a measured gain justifies giving up readability; a later module covers it.

glossary.def: A model that routes each row through a few yes/no questions to a segment and returns that segment's rate or average.
One yes/no question on one column with one cut-off, chosen because it separates the outcome best.
An end point of the tree: a segment of rows, with the outcome rate the tree predicts for them.
The number of questions on the longest path from the top of the tree to a leaf.

lessons.title: Dirty tables
lessons.subtitle: What can go wrong before any model is fitted, without a single error message?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can catch dropped, multiplied and deleted rows by reading row counts, distinct advertisers and the label rate after every step.

predict.q: A script drops every row that has a missing value before modelling churn. In the advertiser table, CPA versus goal is empty for advertisers without conversion tracking. What share of all the churners disappears with those rows?
options: Almost none: churners are rarely the ones with missing data
About 40 percent, the same as the share of rows dropped
Nearly two thirds
All of them
predict.reveal: Nearly two thirds: 1,420 churners become 505. The rows that vanish are not a random sample, and the lesson shows the one check that catches it.

segments.narration: The assistant's report says churn is 7 percent. Your dashboard has said 12 for as long as you can remember. Nothing crashed. There is no warning in the output, and the charts are lovely. Somewhere between the raw table and the model, about four in ten of your advertisers went missing, and the script never mentioned it. This kind of damage is easy to do and hard to see, and it has nothing to do with machine learning. It happens in the clean-up and the joins, which is your home turf. The same holds whatever the model is for: a table of leads you want to score can lose rows to a clean-up line or a join just as quietly. So this lesson builds one habit: count the rows.

visual.title: Dirty tables
visual.sub: What breaks before the model

segments.narration: Here is what happened. Somewhere in the script sits one tidy-looking line that drops every row with a missing value. In the advertiser table, CPA versus goal is empty for everyone without conversion tracking. [[1]] So 42 percent of the rows vanished. 12,000 advertisers became about 7,000. [[2]] And they were not a random 42 percent. Untracked advertisers churn far more, so nearly two thirds of all the churners went with them. [[3]] What remains is a calmer population, churning at 7 percent instead of 12. The line did exactly what it says. It just answers a question about a different set of advertisers.

stats.label: rows
churners
churn rate

segments.narration: It gets worse once a model is trained on the survivors. That model has never met an advertiser without tracking. But in production it will be asked to score them, because they are still your customers. [[1]] For the untracked advertisers in the test months, it predicts an average churn risk of about 9 percent. [[2]] Their actual churn was about 20. And here is the trap. It still ranks those advertisers almost as well as a model trained on everyone, so the ranking score would not have warned you. The percentages are simply less than half the truth, for two fifths of your book. You met that kind of error in the calibration lesson. This is one way it gets made.

visual.title: Trained on the survivors, then asked about the untracked

left.label: What the model says
left.sub: average predicted churn · ranking barely hurt: AUC 0.809, against 0.824 when trained on everyone

right.label: What happened
right.sub: actual churn of untracked advertisers, test months

segments.narration: The deeper mistake was treating an empty cell as a hole. It is information. Advertisers whose CPA cell is empty churn at about 18 percent, against 7 for the rest. So do not drop the rows, and do not quietly fill the gap either. Fill it with zero, and you have told the model these advertisers are beating their goal spectacularly. The honest pattern is to keep every row, fill the cell with a typical value, and add a yes or no column saying it was empty. Filling empty cells is called imputation. Here that flag already exists: has conversion tracking. On this data the ranking score barely notices: about 0.845 with the flag against 0.84 without. Keep it anyway. It costs one column, and you cannot know in advance what a blank is worth.

visual.title: An empty cell is a signal

data.label: CPA versus goal is filled in

visual.note: Churn rate. Test AUC with a was-empty flag: 0.845. Filled silently with no flag: 0.840.

segments.narration: Joins fail in the other direction too. The assistant wants campaign details, so it joins advertisers to the campaigns table. That table has one row per campaign, so an advertiser with three campaigns now appears three times. That is called a fan-out. 12,000 advertisers become about 31,000 rows. Add up spend over those rows and the total is overstated by about 160 percent. Now the nasty part. The churn rate barely moves, because churners and stayers are duplicated alike. So the one sanity check you would think to run passes. What gives it away is the row count, set against the number of distinct advertisers.

visual.title: A join that multiplies rows
visual.code:
SELECT a.advertiser_id, a.spend_8w,
       a.churned_next_60d, c.campaign_id
FROM advertisers a
JOIN campaigns c          -- one row per campaign
  ON c.advertiser_id = a.advertiser_id;

-- rows:            12,000  ->  31,197
-- advertisers:     12,000  ->  12,000
-- SUM(spend_8w):   48.0M   ->  124.1M
-- churn rate:      11.83%  ->  11.55%
visual.note: Rows grew, distinct advertisers did not. Total spend is overstated by 158%.

segments.narration: A join can also quietly delete. Suppose the script picks up the account manager's name by joining to the account managers table, with an inner join. An inner join keeps only the rows that find a match, and most advertisers have no account manager. [[1]] You start with 12,000 advertisers. [[2]] After the join, 69 percent of them are gone. The ones left are the managed accounts, and they churn at about 6 percent. In SQL you would spot the missing LEFT. In Python it is easier to miss, because a merge with no join type stated is an inner join. Dropped rows, multiplied rows, deleted rows. Three different lines, and one check catches all of them.

visual.title: An inner join keeps only the matched

right.label: After df.merge(account_managers)
right.sub: churn 6.2% · 69% of advertisers gone

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask the assistant to print one small table and keep it in every output: after each step, the number of rows, the number of distinct advertisers, and the churn rate. [[1]] The raw table sets the reference. [[2]] If rows fall, something was dropped, and you ask who. [[3]] If rows exceed advertisers, a join fanned out: roll that table up to one row per advertiser first. [[4]] If advertisers fall after a join, it was an inner join: ask for a left join. Then three more things the output must state. How many values were missing in each column, and what was done about them. The feature list, with no ID column in it: a flexible model can memorise rows by their ID. And the churn rate, checked against a number you already trust, like your dashboard.

visual.title: Ask for this after every step
rows: Drop rows with a missing value
visual.note: Each step is shown on its own, applied to the raw table. Rows should equal advertisers, and neither should change unless you asked for it.

segments.narration: From now on, when a report disagrees with a number you trust, ask where the rows went before you question the model. Next, the script itself: eighty lines of Python you could not have written, and the six parts that let you audit it anyway.

visual.title: Keep this
items: Rows get dropped, multiplied or deleted with no error message
An empty cell is information: keep the row, add a flag
Count rows, distinct advertisers and the label rate after every step

takeaways: A dropped row or a join can change who the table is about before any model is fitted, and nothing crashes.
A missing value is information: keep the row, fill the cell, and add a flag that says it was empty.
Count rows, distinct advertisers and the label rate before and after every step, and compare with a number you already trust.

quiz.q: The assistant's audit block reads: 'Rows loaded: 12,000. Rows after cleaning: 7,016. Churn rate: 7.2 percent.' Your dashboard shows churn near 12 percent. What is the right read?
options: The dashboard must be using a different definition of churn, so the cleaned table is the one to trust.
A gap of 5 points between two churn rates is ordinary sampling noise at this scale.
Cleaning removed outliers and bad records, which makes the remaining table more reliable.
Four rows in ten were dropped, and not at random; ask which step removed them and who they were.
quiz.why: Four rows in ten are gone and the churn rate moved by five points, so the lost rows were a particular kind of advertiser: the untracked, who churn far more. With thousands of rows, noise is about a point at most. 'Cleaning' that changes the label rate has changed the question, and the dashboard number is the one you already trust.

quiz.q: After joining advertisers to the campaigns table, the report shows total 8-week spend of 124 million dollars. Finance has 48 million. The churn rate in the report matches your dashboard. What happened?
options: The join repeated each advertiser once per campaign, so spend was counted several times; totals inflate, rates barely move.
Finance leaves churned advertisers out of its total, which explains the whole difference.
The matching churn rate proves the table is sound, so the finance figure is the one to question.
The campaigns table must be recorded in a different currency from the advertiser table.
quiz.why: A table with several rows per advertiser multiplies the advertiser's row, and with it any advertiser-level column you sum. The churn rate hardly moves because churners and stayers are duplicated alike, so a matching rate proves nothing here. Rows against distinct advertisers is the check that shows it.

quiz.q: In a lead-scoring table, company size is blank for 35 percent of leads: people who skipped an optional form field. The assistant filled the blanks with the average company size and reports that everything ran cleanly. What is the concern?
options: The blanks should have been filled with zero instead, so that the model can tell those leads apart.
The assistant should have dropped those leads instead of filling them in.
Leads who skip the field may convert differently; keep a 'was blank' flag and compare the groups.
An average cannot be computed on a column that contains blanks, so the numbers are invalid.
quiz.why: Skipping a field is behaviour, and it may go with a different conversion rate. Filling with the average makes those leads look like ordinary mid-sized companies and erases the signal; filling with zero would claim they are the smallest companies of all. Dropping them would be worse: a third of the leads gone, and not at random. The fill itself is fine once a flag records that it happened.

quiz.concept: an inner join deletes the unmatched
quiz.q: An upsell analysis joins customers to the table of account-manager call notes and reports that 31 percent bought the add-on. Sales knows the overall rate is about 12 percent. The report shows no row counts. What is the most likely cause?
options: Call notes cause customers to buy the add-on, which is the real finding of the analysis.
The join kept only customers who have call notes, a smaller and more engaged group.
A difference of that size between two rates is normal sampling variation and needs no explanation.
The add-on rate has probably risen sharply since sales last looked at its own figures.
quiz.why: An inner join keeps only rows with a match, so customers without call notes vanished, and those who get calls are not typical. The rate describes that subgroup, not the customer base. A count of distinct customers before and after the join would have shown it at once; no causal story is needed.

review.concept: rows that vanish change who the answer is about

variants.q: A creative-performance script drops every row with a missing value. Video completion rate is empty for all image creatives. The report says average click rate is 0.9 percent; your dashboard says 0.4. What happened?
options: Click rates improved since the dashboard was last refreshed.
Only the video creatives survived, so the average describes a different set of creatives.
The gap is ordinary noise between two ways of averaging.
The dashboard is wrong, because it still includes creatives whose data is incomplete and should be ignored.
variants.why: A column that is empty for a whole category turns 'drop rows with missing values' into 'drop that category'. The report's average is true for video creatives and says nothing about the rest. Comparing row counts and the headline rate before and after the drop would have exposed it.

variants.q: Support tickets are inner-joined to the satisfaction survey table. The report gives a median resolution time of 3 hours; the operations dashboard says 9. Which explanation should you check first?
options: The survey itself makes agents resolve tickets faster, because they know they will be rated.
Medians cannot be compared between two different tools.
Operations measures resolution time in a different time zone.
Only tickets whose customer answered the survey were kept, and those are not typical tickets at all.
variants.why: An inner join keeps only tickets with a survey response, and customers who respond tend to be a particular group. The 3 hours describes them. Ask for the number of tickets before and after the join; a large drop means the result is about a subgroup, with no need for a story about the survey changing behaviour.

variants.q: A churn script loads 9,000 advertisers and reports results on 5,200 'after cleaning', with a churn rate well below the one on your dashboard. What do you ask for first?
options: Which step removed the rows, and the churn rate of the removed rows beside the kept ones.
A more flexible model, to make up for the smaller table.
The same analysis with the cut-off lowered, so that the model can find the churners that went missing.
The same model refitted with churners given extra weight, to restore the dashboard's rate.
variants.why: A fall in rows together with a shift in the label rate means the removed rows were different from the kept ones. Until you know who was removed and how they behave, every later number describes an unknown subgroup. No model, cut-off or weighting can recover advertisers who are no longer in the table.

review.concept: a one-to-many join multiplies rows

variants.q: Orders are joined to their line items, and revenue is then summed from the order-level column 'order total'. The result is 2.4 times the figure finance reports. What is the cause?
options: Finance reports its revenue net of tax and refunds, which accounts for the whole of the difference.
Line items include discounts that the order total leaves out.
Each order's total is repeated once for every line item, so it is counted several times.
The join dropped the orders that had no line items.
variants.why: Joining to a table with several rows per order copies every order-level value onto each of those rows. Summing the copies inflates the total by roughly the average number of line items. A dropped order would make revenue too low, not too high. Count rows against distinct orders after the join.

variants.q: Leads are joined to their marketing touchpoints, and a conversion model is trained on the result. The table has 90,000 rows; the CRM holds 30,000 leads. What is wrong with treating each row as a lead?
options: The CRM must be missing 60,000 leads, so its count of 30,000 is the figure to correct.
Each lead now appears once per touchpoint, so busy leads are counted many times over.
The model will refuse to train on a table that contains repeated lead IDs, so the result cannot exist.
Only the first 30,000 rows are real leads; the remaining rows are empty.
variants.why: The unit of the table silently changed from one lead to one touchpoint. A lead with nine touchpoints now weighs nine times as much as a lead with one, in every count, every rate and the model's training. Nothing raises an error. Either aggregate touchpoints to one row per lead before joining, or be explicit that a row is a touchpoint.

variants.q: To add billing data, 8,000 advertisers are joined to an invoices table. The result has exactly 8,000 rows, and a colleague concludes the join was clean. The output also shows 6,500 distinct advertisers. What does that tell you?
options: About 1,500 rows are exact duplicates, but every advertiser is still in the table.
The invoices table has exactly one row for every advertiser.
Distinct counts are unreliable after a join, so the row count is the only number worth checking.
Some advertisers were dropped while others were duplicated, so the matching row count is a coincidence.
variants.why: Rows and distinct advertisers must both match the starting table. Here 1,500 advertisers disappeared, those with no invoice, while others with several invoices were repeated, and the two effects happened to cancel in the row count. That is why the check is always both numbers, never the row count alone.

drill.q: A report's headline rate is far from the number on your dashboard, and nothing crashed. What do you ask the assistant for first?
drill.a: A table of row counts, distinct advertisers and the label rate after every step, to see where rows were dropped, multiplied or deleted.

drill.q: Why is it dangerous to drop every row that has a missing value?
drill.a: Because a value is usually missing for a reason. The rows you lose can be one particular kind of customer, so the result describes a different population, and a model trained on it has never seen the people you dropped.

recall.prompt: Name the three ways a table gets damaged before modelling, and the one check that catches all of them.
recall.model_answer: Rows are dropped because a column has missing values, rows are multiplied by a join to a table with several rows per advertiser, and rows are deleted by an inner join that keeps only the matched. None of them raises an error, and each changes who the table is about or how often they are counted. Counting rows, distinct advertisers and the label rate before and after every step exposes all three. Missing values themselves are information, so the row is kept and a flag records that the cell was empty.

lessons.ask_assistant: Before any modelling, build the table step by step. After each step print the number of rows, the number of distinct [unit ID] and the [outcome] rate, and flag any step where a count changes. Do not drop rows because a feature is missing, and do not fill anything yet: report missing values per column and add a yes/no flag column for each feature that has any. Fill values come later, computed from the training rows only. Never fill a missing [outcome]: list those rows separately.
