Start from [main table], join with left joins, and aggregate any table with several rows per [unit] to one row per [unit] before joining. Leave ID columns out of the feature list.
audit_checklist: A step table: rows, distinct advertisers and churn rate after every step, with rows equal to advertisers throughout and neither count changing except at a step you asked to filter.
Missing values per column, and what was done with each: no row dropped for a missing feature, a flag column for each, no outcome value filled in.
The final churn rate matches a number you already trust, such as the dashboard.
The feature list contains no ID column.
transfer: Revenue per customer after joining orders to line items: is each order counted once?
A satisfaction analysis built only on customers who answered the survey: who is missing?
Creative performance after dropping rows with empty video metrics: which formats disappeared?

other_ways.approach: Aggregate before you join
other_ways.when: When the other table has several rows per advertiser: roll it up to one row per advertiser first, then join.

other_ways.approach: A left join plus a 'matched' flag
other_ways.when: When the other table covers only some advertisers and you need to keep everyone.

other_ways.approach: A model that accepts empty cells as they are
other_ways.when: When the model type handles blanks itself; you still report how many were missing, and for whom.

glossary.def: A join to a table with several rows per advertiser, which repeats each advertiser's row and inflates counts and totals.
A join that keeps only rows with a match in both tables, silently deleting the rest.
A yes/no column recording that a cell was empty before it was filled.
The number of different advertisers in a table, as opposed to the number of rows.
Filling empty cells with a stand-in value, such as a typical value learned from the training rows; pair it with a flag that says the cell was empty.

lessons.title: Reading the assistant's script
lessons.subtitle: How do you audit eighty lines of Python you could not have written?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can find the six parts of a modelling script and check, in each, the one line where a classic bug lives.

predict.q: The assistant's script reports an AUC of 0.98 for a churn model. It turns out the score was computed on the same rows the model learned from. Scored on advertisers it has never seen, what does the same model get?
options: About 0.95: a strong model stays strong
About 0.90: a little is always lost on new rows
About 0.83: useful, but a long way from 0.98
About 0.70: most of the 0.98 was memory
predict.reveal: About 0.83: still useful, and nowhere near 0.98. The lesson shows the one line in a script that tells you which rows were scored.

segments.narration: The assistant hands back eighty lines of Python and one proud sentence: AUC 0.98. You still check the output first. But one score, with no rows named, is something the output cannot settle, and a handful of lines can. You could not have written those eighty lines, and you do not need to read them. You search them. Every modelling script has the same six parts in the same order, whether it predicts churn or flags invalid traffic. Each classic bug lives in one of those parts and shows up as one recognisable line. By the end of this lesson you will know which line produced that 0.98, and what the honest number was.

visual.title: Reading the assistant's script
visual.sub: Six parts, and the line to check in each

segments.narration: Here are the six. [[1]] Load: read the table. [[2]] Choose: say which columns are features and which one is the label. [[3]] Split: decide which rows the model learns from and which are held back to test it. [[4]] Prepare: fill empty cells, put columns on a common scale, turn categories such as vertical into numbers: one yes or no column per value, called one-hot encoding. [[5]] Fit: the model learns, from the training rows only. [[6]] Score: predictions for the test rows, compared with what really happened. None of this is new to you. Choosing the label was module one, the split was the hold-out lesson, and loading and filling was last lesson. A script just writes those decisions down in order.

visual.title: Every modelling script has six parts

segments.narration: Here is a clean one, cut down to fourteen lines, each part numbered. Fit is where learning happens, so what is handed to fit should be the training rows and nothing else. Predict proba, short for predict probability, returns scores between zero and one. And pipeline: a wrapper that ties the preparation steps to the model. Fit the pipeline, and the values used to fill gaps and to rescale are learned from the training rows too. The split names its months, with April left out. Now look at what it prints. Two scores, training and test, each labelled with its rows and how many. Beside them the baseline: spend trend alone, on the same test rows. The scoring call, roc AUC score, is the AUC you already know.

visual.title: A clean script: the six parts in fourteen lines
visual.code:
df = pd.read_csv("advertisers.csv")                      # 1 load
X, y = df[FEATURES], df["churned_next_60d"]              # 2 choose
train = df["snapshot_month"].isin(["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]) # 3 split
test = df["snapshot_month"].isin(["May", "Jun"])
num = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(), StandardScaler())   # 4 fill, scale
prep = make_column_transformer((num, NUMERIC),           #   encode
    (OneHotEncoder(), ["vertical"]), remainder="passthrough")
model = make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression())
model.fit(X[train], y[train])                            # 5 fit
for name, rows in [("train", train), ("test", test)]:    # 6 score
    scores = model.predict_proba(X[rows])[:, 1]
    print(name, rows.sum(), "rows, AUC", roc_auc_score(y[rows], scores))
rule = -X[test]["spend_trend"]                           # baseline
print("baseline, test rows, AUC", roc_auc_score(y[test], rule))
visual.note: Imports and the two column lists sit above. SimpleImputer fills empty cells, StandardScaler puts columns on one scale, OneHotEncoder turns vertical into yes/no columns, roc_auc_score is AUC. The baseline ranks by spend trend alone, falling spend first. The was-empty flag is already a named feature: has_conversion_tracking.

segments.narration: Now the 0.98. That script used a more flexible model, built from 300 trees instead of one. A later lesson covers how it works. To audit it, you go to part six and read which rows were scored. The script fitted on the training rows, and then asked for scores on those same rows. A flexible model can score almost perfectly on rows it has already seen, and that says nothing about new advertisers. Scored on the test months, the very same model gets 0.83. Still useful, and nowhere near 0.98. The output gave it away too: one score, with no word on which rows it came from.

visual.title: The line behind 0.98
visual.code:
forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5)
model = make_pipeline(prep, forest)            # same preparation
model.fit(X[train], y[train])

scores = model.predict_proba(X[train])[:, 1]   # the SAME rows
print(roc_auc_score(y[train], scores))         # prints 0.98

scores = model.predict_proba(X[test])[:, 1]    # unseen rows
print(roc_auc_score(y[test], scores))          # prints 0.83
visual.note: Same model, two sets of rows. Only the second number is about advertisers it has not seen.

segments.narration: Three more places, same idea. [[1]] Part two, choose. If the features are every column except the label, nobody chose them. The advertiser ID is in there. So is spend in the next eight weeks, which is zero for every churner: the label in disguise. A sound script names its features one by one. [[2]] Part three, split. A call to train test split deals the rows out at random. For a question about the future you want to see months named, as in the clean script. [[3]] Part four, prepare. If a fill or a rescale is fitted on the whole table, above the split, the test rows have already shaped those values. They are no longer unseen. How much each of these flatters the score varies, and the score itself will not tell you.

visual.title: Three more lines to find
rows: every other column is a feature: the ID, and next period's spend
rows dealt out at random, no months named
preparation has already seen the test rows
visual.note: None of these raises an error. Sizes on this table: a column that knew the outcome put 200 churners in the top 200 instead of 136 (lesson 1-4); a random split scored 0.851 against the time split's 0.845. No figure was computed for row 3.

segments.narration: And two quiet ones, which flatter nothing but still wreck the result. [[1]] The first is a try and except block. It says: attempt this step, and if it fails, carry on anyway. It is there so that the script always finishes. So a join can fail, a column can come back empty, and the report still renders. Ran without errors is not evidence. [[2]] The second is predict without the proba. Plain predict returns hard yes or no answers, cut at one half, and you saw in module two how few advertisers that default flags. Feed yes or no answers into a ranking score, or build a top 200 list from them, and the scores have been thrown away.

visual.title: Two quiet ones
items: try: … except: pass  →  a failed step is skipped in silence
model.predict(…) where predict_proba was needed  →  yes/no answers, not scores

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask the assistant to open every script with a header comment that states, in plain words, what each part does. What one row is, and how many rows there are. What the label is. The named features, each known on the snapshot date. Which months train and which test. That preparation sits inside the pipeline. That scores are probabilities, reported on training and test rows, beside the baseline. When a script is long, also ask it to say which lines belong to which of the six parts. Then you audit in two passes. First the header: is this the analysis you asked for? Then the six lines: does the code do what the header says? A header that promises a time split, above a line that shuffles, is a finding in itself.

visual.title: The header to ask for
visual.code:
# ONE ROW:  one advertiser at one snapshot (12,000 rows)
# LABEL:    churned_next_60d = no spend in the next 60 days
# FEATURES: 17 named columns, each known at the snapshot; no IDs
# SPLIT:    train Jan-Mar (6,000), Apr left out, test May-Jun (4,000)
# PREPARE:  inside the pipeline, fitted on training rows only
# SCORES:   predict_proba; AUC on train AND test; baseline beside
# ERRORS:   no try/except around data steps
visual.note: Read the header first, then check that the six lines agree with it.

segments.narration: So when the script runs to three hundred lines, you do not read it. You search it for a handful of strings, and check each against what it should look like. Next, module four: what happens when a model is flexible enough to memorise its training rows.

visual.title: Seven strings to search a long script for
rows: not how features are picked: they are named one by one, no ID
absent when the question is about the future: periods are named
on training rows only, never on the whole table above the split
handed the training rows and nothing else
the score you rely on comes from the test rows, and its printout says so
on a yes-or-no model, only where a hard answer is wanted, never for a ranking score
not around a data step: an error should stop the script
visual.note: A string that is missing is a finding too: on a yes-or-no model with no predict_proba, ask where the scores come from. A model that predicts a number uses predict.

takeaways: Every modelling script has six parts: load, choose features and label, split, prepare, fit on training rows, score on test rows.
Each classic bug lives in one part and shows as one line: unchosen features, a shuffled split, preparation before the split, scoring on training rows.
A script that ran without errors proves nothing; ask for a header that states the six parts, then check the code agrees.

quiz.q: The assistant's summary reads: 'Trained a new model on 6,000 advertisers. AUC: 0.98.' One score, and no mention of test rows. The simpler model scored about 0.85 last week. What do you ask first?
options: Which settings produced it, so that the same model can be rebuilt next month.
For the cut-off to be lowered, so that the model catches more churners.
Which rows that score was computed on, with the training-row and test-row scores side by side.
For a larger version of the model, to see whether the score can go higher still.
quiz.why: A single score with no rows named is the tell. A flexible model can score 0.98 on the rows it trained on and 0.83 on new ones, so the number may say nothing about new advertisers. Until both scores are on the page, 0.98 cannot be compared with 0.85, which was measured on test rows.

quiz.q: In a script, the lines that fill empty cells with column averages and rescale the columns sit above the line that separates training rows from test rows. Why does that matter?
options: In that order the test rows never get filled or rescaled, so scoring them will fail.
The averages and scales were computed with the test rows included, so those rows are no longer unseen.
Rescaling must always be done after the model has been fitted, never before, or the weights come out wrong.
Empty cells must be filled with zero, because filling with an average distorts the whole column.
quiz.why: An average or a scale is learned from data just as a weight is. Computed on the whole table, it carries information from the test rows into training. Inside a pipeline, the same steps are fitted on the training rows only and then applied to the test rows. Nothing fails as written, which is why it goes unnoticed: every row was filled and rescaled. Filling with zero would be a different mistake, not a fix.

quiz.concept: a shuffled split for a question about the future
quiz.q: A script that predicts which leads will convert next quarter calls train_test_split with its default settings on three years of leads. Its header says: 'validated on 25 percent held-out leads'. What is the flaw?
options: The held-out leads are a random mix of all three years; test on the most recent period instead.
A quarter of the leads is too small a share to hold out; a fair test needs at least half of them.
The split was not stratified, so the held-out leads may convert at a different rate.
Leads should never be held out at all, since a model always improves with more training data.
quiz.why: The default split shuffles rows, so the model is tested on leads from the same period it learned from. The real use runs from past to future, and only a later period can show whether the pattern still holds. Neither the size of the hold-out nor its conversion rate is the issue; which period its rows come from is.

quiz.concept: hard answers where scores were needed
quiz.q: An invalid-traffic report shows an AUC of 0.61, and its 'score' column contains only 0 and 1. The script has the line: scores = model.predict(X_test). What is the right read?
options: The model is weak at ranking, so the next step is to ask for a more complex one.
Scores of exactly 0 and 1 show that the model is completely sure of itself on every single click.
AUC is the wrong kind of measure to use for an invalid-traffic problem like this one.
predict returns yes/no answers, so the ranking was never measured; ask for predict_proba scores.
quiz.why: AUC judges a ranking, and a column of zeros and ones has almost no ranking in it. The model may rank well; this number cannot say. The one-word fix is predict_proba, which returns a score for every row. A score column with only two values is the visible sign, with no need to read the code.

review.concept: a score means nothing until you know which rows it was computed on

variants.q: An upsell model's report says: 'accuracy 97 percent on 40,000 accounts'. Elsewhere it says the model was trained on 40,000 accounts. What is the first question?
options: Whether 97 percent is high enough to justify launching the campaign this quarter.
Whether those are the same 40,000 accounts; if so, it says nothing about accounts the model has not seen.
Whether the cut-off behind the 97 percent could be raised to make the list shorter.
Whether more accounts could be added to the table to push the figure higher still.
variants.why: A model graded on the rows it learned from is marking its own exam with the answers open. The figure that counts is measured on held-out accounts, ideally from a later period. Nothing else in the report can be judged until that is known.

variants.q: A ticket classifier is reported as 'right on 99 percent of tickets'. The last two lines of the script are: model.fit(X, y) and then model.score(X, y). What does the 99 percent measure?
options: How well the classifier will sort next month's tickets, since 99 percent leaves little room for error.
How many tickets were labelled correctly by the support agents.
How well the model reproduces the tickets it was fitted on, and nothing about new tickets.
How confident the model is in its own answers.
variants.why: The same X and y go into fit and into score, so the model is scored on its own training rows. A flexible model can reproduce those almost perfectly. The honest figure needs tickets held out before fitting, and here there are none.

variants.q: A spend forecast is described as 'matching history within 1 percent'. The model was fitted on three years of daily spend, and the chart compares it with those same three years. What is that 1 percent worth?
options: It shows how closely the model traces data it has already seen; ask for a test on an unseen period.
It shows that the forecast for next month will also land within about 1 percent of the actual figure.
It shows the model is too simple for the job and should be replaced by a richer one.
It shows that the last three years happened to be unusually easy to predict.
variants.why: Matching the past the model was fitted on is easy and proves little. A forecast is judged by standing at a past date, predicting forward, and comparing with what then happened. Until that exists, 1 percent describes the fit, not the forecast.

review.concept: anything fitted before the split has seen the test rows

variants.q: A churn script fills every empty cell with its column's average, computed over all 12,000 rows, and only afterwards separates training months from test months. What has gone wrong?
options: Rows with empty cells should have been dropped, so that no value needed filling in at all.
The fill should have used the largest value in each column, which is safer than using the average.
Empty cells should have been left empty until after the model was fitted.
The averages include the test months, so the test rows helped shape the training data.
variants.why: A fill value is learned from data. Learned from every row, it lets the test months leak into what the model trains on. The amount of damage varies and cannot be read from the score, which is why the rule is structural: preparation goes inside the pipeline and is fitted on training rows. Dropping the rows instead would lose every advertiser with an empty cell, as the dirty-tables lesson showed.

variants.q: A ticket-classification script picks the 20 columns most strongly related to the label, using all tickets, and then splits into training and test tickets. The test accuracy looks excellent. Why should you doubt it?
options: Twenty columns is far too few for any problem that involves free text.
The columns were chosen with the test tickets' labels in view, so the test is no longer unseen.
Choosing columns is a manual job for the analyst and is never allowed inside a modelling script.
Accuracy cannot be used as a measure when there are more than two categories.
variants.why: Choosing columns by their relation to the label is learning, and here it was done on every ticket, test tickets included. The chosen columns are already tuned to the test labels. The selection has to happen after the split, on training tickets only, like any other fitted step.

variants.q: A lead-scoring script splits correctly by date, with the last quarter as the test set. But one line above the split reads: X = scaler.fit_transform(X). The header says 'time split, test = last quarter'. Is the header's promise kept?
options: Not at all: with a scaler above it, the date split no longer keeps the quarters apart.
Only partly: the scaler is fine where it is, but a single quarter is too short a test period to trust.
Only partly: the split is right, but the scaler was fitted on all quarters, test quarter included.
No: a time split and a scaler cannot be combined in the same script at all.
variants.why: The split itself is sound, but fit_transform on the whole table learned its averages and spreads from the test quarter as well. The fix is to put the scaler inside the pipeline, so it is fitted on the training quarters and only applied to the last one. The scaler moves no lead from one quarter to another, so the split still holds; but a correct split does not excuse a fitted step above it.

drill.q: Name the six parts of a modelling script, in order.
drill.a: Load the table, choose the features and the label, split into training and test rows, prepare the columns, fit on the training rows, and score on the test rows.

drill.q: A script reports a single, very high score. What is the first thing you check, and where?
drill.a: Which rows the score was computed on. Go to the scoring line near the end and see whether it uses the test rows or the same rows the model was fitted on.

recall.prompt: Without looking, explain where in a modelling script the four classic bugs live, and how you would spot each one.
recall.model_answer: In the choose part: features defined as everything except the label, which lets IDs and columns recorded after the snapshot in. In the split: a shuffled split, with no months named, for a question about the future. In prepare: a fill or a rescale fitted on the whole table above the split, so the test rows are no longer unseen. In score: predictions made on the training rows, which is how a flexible model shows 0.98 when it gets 0.83 on new advertisers. A header comment that states each part makes all four quick to check.

lessons.ask_assistant: Write the modelling script in six labelled parts: load, choose, split, prepare, fit, score. Open it with a header comment stating what one row is and the row count, the definition of [outcome], the named feature list with confirmation that each column is known at [prediction date], which [periods] train and which test, and that all preparation is inside the pipeline. Print the row counts for training and test, then the score from predict_proba on each (from predict if [outcome] is a number), labelled with its rows, beside [baseline] on the same test rows. Do not wrap data steps in try/except: let errors stop the script. Finally, list which line numbers belong to each of the six parts.
audit_checklist: Printed row counts for training and test, and two scores, each labelled with its rows, beside a baseline on the same test rows.
Training and test rows defined by named periods in the split line, not by a random split.
For a yes-or-no outcome, scores with many distinct values between 0 and 1, not a column of zeros and ones.
A header that states one row, the label, the named features, the split and where preparation happens, and a line in the script that matches each statement.
transfer: A lead-scoring script that reports one accuracy figure: which leads was it measured on?
A spend forecast that 'fits history': was it tested on days it had not seen?
A ticket classifier whose preparation step read every ticket before the split.

other_ways.approach: Ask the assistant to map the script to the six parts
other_ways.when: When a block is unfamiliar: have it say which part each block belongs to, then check that map against the code.

other_ways.approach: Ask for a rerun with one change
other_ways.when: When a number looks too good: score on the test months, remove a suspect column, or switch to a time split, and compare.

other_ways.approach: A second reviewer, human or model
other_ways.when: When the decision is expensive: hand over the script and its header, not your own conclusion.

glossary.def: The call where a model, or a preparation step, learns from the rows it is given.
On a yes-or-no model, the call that returns a probability score for each row; plain predict returns only the hard answer. A model that predicts a number has no predict_proba and uses predict.
A wrapper that chains preparation steps and a model so they are all fitted on the same training rows.
A scikit-learn helper that divides rows into training and test sets, at random unless told otherwise.
A Python block that catches an error and lets the script carry on, which can hide a failed step.
Turning a category column such as vertical into one yes-or-no column per value, so a model can use it; OneHotEncoder does it in scikit-learn.

lessons.title: Overfitting: memorising versus learning
lessons.subtitle: How can a model be perfect on its training rows and poor on new ones?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can read a training score and a test score side by side and say whether a model has learned a pattern, memorised its rows, or is too simple to do either.

predict.q: A decision tree is allowed to grow 25 levels deep instead of 3. On the 6,000 advertisers it was trained on, it now scores a perfect AUC of 1.0. What does it score on 4,000 advertisers it has never seen?
options: About 0.95: a little lower, as you would expect
About 0.76: the same as the 3-level tree
About 0.61: lower than a tree that asks one question
Exactly 0.5: no better than a coin
predict.reveal: About 0.61, below the 0.66 of a tree that asks a single question. The lesson shows how the perfect score and the poor one come from the same cause.

segments.narration: The assistant has good news. You asked whether a deeper tree would beat the three-level one, so it let the tree grow to 25 levels. Training AUC: 1.0. A perfect score. Every churner in the training months is ranked above every advertiser who stayed. It suggests putting the new tree in the report. Before you agree, ask the scoreboard question. Perfect on which rows? Because the same tree, on advertisers it has never met, tells a different story. The same is true of any flexible model, whether it predicts churn or creative fatigue: a perfect score on rows it has seen proves nothing.

visual.title: Overfitting: memorising versus learning
visual.sub: Training AUC 1.0. Perfect on which rows?

segments.narration: Take that tree at twelve depths between 1 and 25, and score it twice. Once on the 6,000 advertisers it trained on, once on the 4,000 test advertisers it has never seen. At depth 1, a single question, both scores sit near 0.66. Add levels and they climb together, as far as depth 3 or 4. Then they part. The training score climbs on to a perfect 1. The test score peaks at about 0.77 and turns down. By depth 25 it is about 0.61, lower than the single question. One caution. The test months are shown to demonstrate the effect, not to choose a depth. Next lesson says why. Drag the depth yourself, and watch where the two scores stop moving together.

visual.name: depth
visual.title: Tree depth: training rows against new advertisers
visual.note: Twelve depths, from 1 to 25. Find where the two scores part, then watch the test score from depth 10 on. The test months are here to show the effect, not to choose a depth.

segments.narration: [[1]] Consider what a 25-level tree is. The three-level tree had eight leaves, each a segment big enough for a believable churn rate. This one has more than 600, many holding only a handful of advertisers. Split until every leaf is all churners or all stayers, and the training rows are described perfectly. [[2]] On new advertisers, though, a handful is not a segment. It is an anecdote. Say three gaming accounts with eleven weeks of tenure all happened to leave. The tree records that as a rule. You would never put a GROUP BY with three rows per group into a deck. And with every leaf pure, the tree stops scoring. It answers a flat yes or no, and you cannot sort a call list on that.

right.label: 4,000 advertisers it has never seen
right.sub: accuracy 82.4% · predicting 'nobody churns' gets 86.8% · it gives only 2 different scores

segments.narration: That is overfitting. The model has fitted the accidents of its training rows along with the pattern. Memorising, where you wanted learning. And a training score cannot tell the two apart, because a memorised answer and a learned one look identical on rows the model has already seen. Only new rows separate them. So the tell is the gap: the distance between the score on training rows and the score on rows the model has never met.

visual.text: A training score cannot tell memorising from learning. Only new rows can.
visual.sub: Overfitting: fitting the accidents of the training rows along with the pattern

segments.narration: There is an opposite failure, and it is quieter. [[1]] The one-question tree scores about 0.66 on training rows and about 0.66 on test. No gap, and not much of a model. It is too simple to hold the pattern. That is underfitting. [[2]] Depth 4 has a visible gap, and the best test score of any depth. [[3]] Depth 25 is flawless in training and worse than one question outside it. So a small gap is not the goal. The best score on new rows is. The textbook name for this pull between too simple and too flexible is the bias-variance trade-off. Where the peak falls is a fact about this simulated data. That training scores keep rising after test scores stop is true of flexible models in general.

visual.title: Too simple, about right, memorised
visual.note: Where the peak falls is specific to this data. Depth 3 scores 0.767 here, with no minimum leaf size; lesson 3-3's tree required at least 100 training advertisers in every leaf and scored 0.761.

segments.narration: So a report shows both numbers, side by side. [[1]] The weighted sum from the last module scores about 0.85 on training rows and about 0.85 on test. Nothing memorised. [[2]] The deep tree: a perfect 1 against 0.61. [[3]] Then the model from last lesson's script, an average of 300 trees. It scores about 0.98 in training and 0.83 on test. A wide gap, and a tempting reason to throw it out. Don't. Its test score beats every single tree you just tried. The gap says its training number is worthless as evidence. It is a warning to look, not a verdict. The verdict is the test number.

visual.title: Both numbers, every model
visual.note: The gap says where to look. The test column decides.

segments.narration: The cure has one shape, whatever the model: make it pay for complexity. [[1]] For a tree, cap the depth, or insist that every leaf holds a minimum number of advertisers, so no rule can rest on three accounts. [[2]] For a weighted sum, charge a penalty for large weights, so it needs real evidence before leaning hard on one column. [[3]] For any model, fewer columns means fewer places for an accident to hide. [[4]] The umbrella word is regularisation. How much of it to apply is a setting somebody has to choose, and choosing it without fooling yourself is the next lesson.

visual.title: The cure: make the model pay for complexity
items: Trees: cap the depth, or set a minimum leaf size
Weighted sums: a penalty on large weights
Any model: fewer columns
The umbrella word: regularisation

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Wherever the assistant gives you one score, ask for two. [[1]] Training rows and held-out rows, side by side, in the same measure. [[2]] Each labelled with the rows it came from, and how many. A score that does not say where it was measured is a training score until shown otherwise. [[3]] For any model with a complexity setting, ask for both scores at several settings, from simple to flexible. For that table, the held-out rows come from inside the training months, and the test months stay closed. Next lesson shows how. [[4]] For a tree, ask for the number of leaves and the size of the smallest one.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Training score and held-out score, side by side
Each labelled with its rows and row count
Both scores at several settings, held-out rows from inside the training months
For a tree: number of leaves, smallest leaf (100 rows: about ±6 points for a rate near 12%, wider nearer 50%)

segments.narration: So a score with no rows named gets one reply from you: show me the other number. One problem is left. Somebody has to pick the depth, and picking the one that looks best on the test set spends the test set. That is next.

visual.text: The gap is the warning. The test score is the verdict.
visual.sub: Next: choosing the depth without spending the test set

takeaways: A training score cannot tell memorising from learning; only rows the model has never seen can.
A wide gap between training and test is a warning to look; the test score is the verdict.
Too simple fails too: aim for the best score on new rows, not the smallest gap.

quiz.concept: a training score is not evidence
quiz.q: The assistant reports a new churn model: 'AUC 0.99'. You ask which rows that was measured on. 'The training months.' What does 0.99 tell you about how the model will rank next month's advertisers?
options: It will rank them almost as well; a score that high leaves plenty of margin
Nothing yet; you need its score on the held-out months
It will rank them badly; a training score that high always means a useless model
It will score about 0.85, because that is what this data supports
quiz.why: A training score mixes what the model learned with what it memorised and cannot separate them, so it predicts nothing about new rows. 'Always useless' overshoots the other way: the model that averages 300 trees scores 0.98 in training and still 0.83 on new advertisers. Ask for the other number.

quiz.q: The assistant's report has this table for a decision tree. Depth 3: training AUC 0.787, test 0.767. Depth 12: training 0.955, test 0.582. Its summary reads: 'We recommend depth 12, which captures far more of the structure in the data (AUC 0.955).' What is wrong?
options: Depth 12 was scored on fewer rows than depth 3, so the two cannot be compared
Both depths are overfitted, since training beats test in both rows; reject both
The summary quotes the training score; on new advertisers depth 12 is far worse than depth 3
Depth 3 has almost no gap, so it is underfitting and deeper is the right direction
quiz.why: The headline figure is a training score; on held-out advertisers depth 12 scores 0.58 against 0.77, so it has memorised. A training score slightly above test, as at depth 3, is normal and no reason to reject, and a small gap alone does not prove underfitting or that deeper is better: the deeper option in this very table is the one that collapsed.

quiz.concept: the gap is a warning, not a verdict
quiz.q: Sales wants a lead-scoring model. The assistant tries two, scored on the same 5,000 held-out leads. Model A: training AUC 0.74, test 0.73. Model B: training 0.97, test 0.80. A colleague says B is obviously overfitted, so ship A. What is the right read?
options: Prefer B: it still ranks unseen leads better than A does
Ship A: its smaller gap means it will hold up better on new leads than B
Ship B: a training score of 0.97 shows it has learned far more about leads
Neither: with a gap that large, B's test score cannot be trusted either
quiz.why: Both test scores come from leads neither model saw, so 0.80 against 0.73 is an honest comparison and B wins it. B's gap says its training score is no evidence and a closer look is due; it does not make A better, and it does not contaminate a test score measured on held-out leads.

quiz.concept: making the model pay for complexity
quiz.q: The 25-level churn tree scores 1.0 on its training rows and 0.61 on the test months. The assistant offers four fixes. Which one addresses the cause?
options: Add the test months to the training data so the tree sees more examples, then re-score
Report accuracy instead of AUC, since the tree only answers yes or no anyway
Give the tree more columns, so it has more signal for the hard cases
Cap the depth or set a minimum leaf size, then report both scores again
quiz.why: The tree memorised because nothing stopped it carving leaves of a handful of advertisers; limiting depth or leaf size makes it pay for complexity. Folding the test months into training is the tempting one: more rows can help, but you would have no unseen rows left to show that it did.

review.concept: a training score is not evidence

variants.q: A model predicts which ad creatives will fatigue within two weeks. On the 8,000 creatives it was trained on, it is right 99 percent of the time. On 2,000 newer creatives it has never seen, it is right 64 percent of the time. What should you expect when it is put to use?
options: About 64 percent: only the unseen creatives measure what it learned
About 99 percent: it was built on four times as many creatives
About 82 percent: the midpoint of the two results is the fair summary
About 92 percent: the two results weighted by the number of creatives
variants.why: In use the model meets creatives it has not seen, so the unseen-creative figure is the forecast; the gap to 99 says much of the training result was memory. Averaging the two, by midpoint or by size, blends an honest number with a flattering one.

variants.q: Finance receives a model of each advertiser's spend next quarter. The summary says 'typical miss: 310 dollars'. The appendix shows a typical miss of 310 dollars on the advertisers used for training and 2,650 dollars on held-out advertisers. What should the summary have said?
options: Typical miss 310 dollars; the appendix figure is a worst case
Typical miss about 1,480 dollars, halfway between the two figures
Typical miss about 2,650 dollars; the model has largely memorised its training rows
Typical miss 310 dollars, since that is what the model achieved on its own data
variants.why: The held-out figure is the only one that describes advertisers the model has not seen, which is every advertiser it will be used on. A miss many times smaller on training rows is the signature of memorising, not a result to headline.

variants.q: A ticket-routing model was built from 600 labelled support tickets, and it routes all 600 of them correctly. A manager asks whether it is ready. What do you ask for first?
options: The 600 tickets ranked by difficulty, to see what it found hard
Its results on labelled tickets that were not among the 600
The same 600 tickets routed a second time, to confirm the result
A retrain on 6,000 tickets, so the perfect score is more precise
variants.why: A perfect result on the tickets a model was built from cannot distinguish learning from memorising; only tickets it has never seen can. Routing the same 600 again only repeats the training score. More training tickets might improve the model, but a perfect training score on 6,000 would be just as uninformative.

review.concept: the gap is a warning, the test score is the verdict

variants.q: Two invalid-traffic detectors are scored on the same held-out week. Detector X: training AUC 0.71, test 0.70. Detector Y: training 0.93, test 0.88. Which do you take forward, and why?
options: X: with almost no gap, its score is the more trustworthy of the two
X: Y is overfitted and will collapse on live traffic
Y: its training score of 0.93 is the highest figure in the comparison
Y: it ranks unseen traffic better, whatever its training score says
variants.why: Both test scores come from traffic neither detector saw, so they are equally trustworthy, and Y's is far higher. Y's gap means its training score is no evidence and it deserves a closer look; choosing Y because of the 0.93 would be the right pick for the wrong reason.

variants.q: An upsell model that uses a single column, account size, scores an AUC of 0.62 on its training rows and 0.62 on test rows. The analyst writes: 'No overfitting, so the model is sound.' What is the right read?
options: Not memorising, but possibly too simple: compare a more flexible model
Overfitted after all: a score as low as 0.62 shows it has memorised noise
Suspect: equal scores mean that test rows must have leaked into training
At its limit: with no gap left to close, more columns could only overfit
variants.why: Equal scores rule out memorising and nothing else; a model can be equally weak on both sets because it is too simple to hold the pattern. A low score is not the sign of overfitting; a gap is. More columns do not automatically overfit: the check is a more flexible model's score on the same test rows.

variants.q: Three versions of a model that predicts which trial accounts will convert are scored on the same held-out accounts. Simple: training 0.70, test 0.70. Medium: training 0.84, test 0.81. Flexible: training 1.00, test 0.66. Which do you take forward?
options: Simple: it is the only version with no gap at all
Flexible: a perfect training score shows the most capacity
Medium: it has the best score on accounts none of them saw
Simple or flexible: medium is neither the most honest nor the most powerful
variants.why: The choice is made on unseen accounts, and medium is best there; its small gap is the ordinary price of a model flexible enough to hold the pattern. Simple is too weak and flexible has memorised: the smallest gap and the highest training score are both the wrong thing to chase.

drill.q: A model scores perfectly on the rows it was trained on. Why is that not good news by itself?
drill.a: Because a flexible model can memorise its training rows, accidents included. Only its score on rows it has never seen tells you whether it learned a pattern.

drill.q: One model has a wide gap between its training score and its test score. Another has almost none. Which do you choose?
drill.a: Whichever scores better on the test rows. The gap is a warning to look closer, not the verdict, and a model with no gap can simply be too simple.

recall.prompt: A colleague shows you a tree that scores a perfect 1.0 on its training months. Explain in 30 seconds why that is not good news yet, and what you would ask to see.
recall.model_answer: A flexible model can memorise its training rows, accidents included, and a training score cannot tell memorising from learning. In the course data a 25-level tree scores 1.0 in training and about 0.61 on new advertisers, below a tree that asks one question. So I would ask for the score on held-out rows beside the training score. A wide gap is my warning to look closer; the test score is what I judge the model on.

lessons.ask_assistant: For every model you fit, report the score on the training rows and on held-out rows side by side, in [measure], each labelled with its rows and row count. For [model], also fit it at [several values of its complexity setting, from simplest to most flexible] and give me a table of the training score beside the cross-validated score, with folds made inside the training rows only (or scored on [a validation period I name]), plus [a size check, such as number of leaves and smallest leaf]. Keep the test rows out of that table: they are scored once, later, after a setting is fixed. Never quote a score without saying which rows it was measured on.
audit_checklist: Training and held-out scores side by side for every model, in the same measure, each labelled with its rows and row count
The table of scores by setting shows training beside cross-validated or validation-period scores, and has no test-row column
For a tree: the number of leaves and the size of the smallest leaf; a churn rate near 12% from about 100 advertisers is only good to about 6 points either way, and a rate nearer 50% to wider still
The headline number in the summary is a held-out score, named as such, and it matches the table
transfer: A creative-fatigue model fits last quarter's creatives perfectly: what does it score on creatives launched since?
An invalid-traffic rule was tuned in a spreadsheet until it flagged every case from last month: how many does it catch this month?
A spend forecast has a hand-made adjustment for every past dip and spike: how far off is it next month?

other_ways.approach: Collect more training rows
other_ways.when: When rows are cheap to get: with more examples, an accident in three accounts is harder to mistake for a pattern.

other_ways.approach: Switch to a less flexible kind of model
other_ways.when: When the pattern is mostly steady effects that each push one way: the weighted sum scores 0.849 in training and 0.845 on test here.

other_ways.approach: Average many deep trees instead of trusting one
other_ways.when: When one tree is too coarse while shallow and memorises once deep; lesson 4-3 covers it.

glossary.def: Fitting the accidents of the training rows along with the pattern, so the model scores well on rows it has seen and worse on new ones.
A model too simple to hold the pattern: it scores poorly on training rows and new rows alike.
The difference between a model's score on its training rows and on rows it has never seen; the tell of memorising.
Any way of making a model pay for complexity, such as capping a tree's depth or penalising large weights.
The pull between a model too simple to see the pattern (bias, underfitting) and one so flexible it learns the noise (variance, overfitting); the best setting scores best on new rows.

lessons.title: Validation without cheating
lessons.subtitle: How do you choose a model's settings without spending the test set?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can tell the assistant how to choose settings by cross-validation on training data, and spot folds that let the same advertiser, or the future, onto both sides.

predict.q: A table has six monthly rows for every advertiser. A flexible model is checked the usual way, by cross-validation with rows dealt into folds at random, and scores an AUC of 0.80. What does it score on advertisers it has never seen?
options: About 0.80: predicting that is what cross-validation is for
About 0.77: a little lower, as usual
About 0.63: much of the 0.80 was the model recognising advertisers
About 0.90: it does better once it has whole histories
predict.reveal: About 0.63. With the same advertiser on both sides of a fold, validation rewards memory. The lesson shows why, and the fix.

segments.narration: Last lesson's chart is still in your head, and the obvious instruction is forming. Depth 4 scored best on the test months, so use depth 4. Stop before you type it. Twelve depths were scored on the same 4,000 test advertisers, and you are about to keep the best. Part of that best is the tree. Part is luck on those rows. Pick the depth that scores best on the test set, and the test set has trained your model. The sealed envelope is open, and nothing honest is left to report. The same goes for any setting of any model, such as which columns feed a video-adoption model.

visual.title: Validation without cheating
visual.sub: Pick the depth that scores best on the test set, and the test set has trained your model

segments.narration: Choosing is also learning. [[1]] From its training rows, a model learns weights and splits. But a depth, a penalty, which columns go in: these are settings, and your assistant will call them hyperparameters. The model does not learn them. Somebody picks them, by trying several and keeping the best, and that picking needs rows of its own. [[2]] Those are validation rows: a mock exam, where you compare settings and choose. [[3]] The test rows are the final exam, opened once, after every choice is frozen.

segments.narration: A single validation slice costs you training rows and returns one noisy number. Cross-validation eases both. Cut the training data into five parts, called folds. [[1]] Train on four and check on the fifth. [[2]] Rotate. [[3]] Again. [[4]] And again. [[5]] Until every part has been the mock exam once. Then average the five. For the weighted sum on the training months, the scores run from about 0.82 to 0.87. Same model, same settings, a different fifth. That spread is the wobble from the noise lesson, for free. When two settings differ by much less than that, treat it as a tie, and let the simpler one win.

visual.title: Five-fold cross-validation: the weighted sum, training months only
visual.note: Mean 0.842, range 0.819 to 0.868. The sealed test months, opened afterwards: 0.845.

segments.narration: Now choose the depth that way. [[1]] Five folds at each of the twelve depths, inside the training months, with the test months still sealed. Depth 5 comes out on top, at about 0.77. Depth 4 is a hair behind: a tie, so either is defensible, as long as you decide now. Say the assistant keeps the top scorer, depth 5. Then open the envelope, once: depth 5 scores 0.76 on the test months. Mock exam and final exam nearly agree. [[2]] Now the temptation. The test months would have preferred depth 4, by less than a hundredth. You do not go back. Switch on that, and the test months have chosen your model.

right.label: The trap: best score on the test months

segments.narration: Cross-validation assumes that a row in the mock exam is new to the model. [[1]] In the main table that holds: each of its 12,000 advertisers appears once, and the three training months are much alike, so shuffled folds were safe there. Give a table a row per advertiser per month, and it stops holding. So the next result comes from a separate small simulation. [[2]] It has 1,500 advertisers. [[3]] Each has six monthly rows. [[4]] Within an advertiser, several columns hardly change from month to month. And because the label looks sixty days ahead, neighbouring months usually carry the same label. Deal those rows out at random, and an advertiser's March lands in training while its April sits in the mock exam.

segments.narration: Score a flexible model, one built from many trees, three ways. [[1]] Ordinary shuffled folds, with rows dealt at random, say about 0.80. [[2]] Folds that keep each advertiser's rows together say 0.63. [[3]] The truth, on 1,500 advertisers it has never met, is about the same. Nothing crashed, and the shuffled score was wrong. It is last lesson's memorising in a new place: the model recognises an advertiser by its near-constant columns and recalls how its other months turned out. [[4]] The simple weighted sum cannot do that. [[5]] Its shuffled and grouped scores match. [[6]] Both sit within two hundredths of the truth. And the cheat changes a decision. Shuffled folds say pick the flexible model, by a mile. On new advertisers, in this simulation, it is the one behind.

visual.title: Three ways to score, two models (AUC)
visual.note: Separate simulation. Flexible: many trees. Simple: logistic regression. Truth: 1,500 advertisers neither model has met.

segments.narration: [[1]] Leave the advertiser ID in as a column and it gets worse: 0.83 in shuffled validation, 0.61 on new advertisers. An ID is the perfect fingerprint. The fix has two halves, who and when. [[2]] Who: all of an advertiser's rows go on the same side of every fold. Your assistant will call these grouped folds. [[3]] When: never train on the future. Where months differ, or an advertiser's rows span them, the mock exam comes from later months than the training rows. [[4]] ID columns stay out of the features. [[5]] And the group is whatever repeats in your data: an advertiser, a creative, a device.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Every setting is chosen by cross-validation inside the training months. [[2]] The output says which case applies. One row per advertiser, from months that are alike: rotating folds will do. Several rows per advertiser, or months that differ: whole advertisers held out together, each check on later months than it trains on. With plenty of history, one later month set aside for choosing does the same job. [[3]] The output prints how many advertisers sit on both sides of a fold: zero. [[4]] It lists every fold score, not just the average. [[5]] And scoring the test months is its own last stage, triggered by you, with every scoring run listed beside the rows it used.

segments.narration: So when the assistant offers to tune anything, you ask which rows did the choosing, and whether anyone could sit on both sides of a fold. Next, the flexible models themselves, and two questions on one table that give them opposite verdicts.

visual.text: Choose on the mock exam. Report on the final exam. Open it once.
visual.sub: Folds keep each advertiser whole and, where months differ, check on later months

takeaways: Choosing settings is learning: do it by cross-validation on training rows, and open the test set once.
Folds must keep whatever repeats, such as an advertiser, on one side; where periods differ, each check must come later than the rows it trains on.
Fold scores wobble; a lead much smaller than the wobble is a tie, and ties go to the simpler setting.

quiz.concept: choosing by the test score spends the test set
quiz.q: The assistant's summary reads: 'I compared twelve tree depths between 1 and 25 and selected depth 4, which had the highest test AUC (0.769). Final model: depth 4, test AUC 0.769.' What is the problem with the final number?
options: The depth-4 tree was fitted on the test rows, so it must be refitted before it is scored
Only that it lacks an interval: with one added, 0.769 can stand as the final score
The test set chose the depth, so 0.769 is the best of twelve looks at the same rows
The depth should have been the one with the highest training AUC instead
quiz.why: Choosing by test score fits the choice to the test rows: the winner is partly the depth whose luck on those 4,000 advertisers was best, and nothing untouched remains to check it. The fitting step never saw those rows, which is why this slips through, but the choice did; an interval describes noise and does not undo that. Choose by cross-validation on the training months, then score the test set once: in the course data that picks depth 5, which scores 0.761.

quiz.concept: folds must keep related rows together
quiz.q: A creative-fatigue model is trained on 40,000 rows: one row per creative per week, from 3,000 creatives. The assistant reports a five-fold cross-validation AUC of 0.91. On creatives launched after the model was built, it scores 0.70. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Rows from the same creative sat on both sides of the folds, rewarding recognition
Five folds are too few for 40,000 rows; ten folds would have shown the 0.70 in advance
New creatives are simply harder to predict; the 0.91 was correct for the data it was measured on
The model is too simple; a more flexible one would have held up better on the new creatives
quiz.why: With about thirteen weekly rows per creative, shuffled folds put the same creative in training and in the mock exam, where a flexible model can recognise it and recall its outcome. The fix is folds that hold whole creatives out and check on later weeks. More folds change nothing: the same creatives are still on both sides.

quiz.q: The assistant tunes a flexible churn model by five-fold cross-validation. Two of its leading settings average 0.837 and 0.835, and the fold scores for each wobble by about 0.02. It writes: 'Configuration A is superior.' What is the right response?
options: Keep B instead: the lower of two close averages is the safer one to report
Score both on the test set and keep whichever does better there
Add more folds until one configuration pulls clearly ahead of the other
Call it a tie, keep the simpler of the two, and leave the test set closed
quiz.why: A lead of 0.002 is a tenth of the fold-to-fold wobble, so this evidence cannot separate the two; the tie goes to the simpler or cheaper setting. Using the test set as tie-breaker is the tempting move, and it is exactly the cheat this lesson is about: the test set would then have chosen your model.

quiz.q: An audit block from the assistant reads: 'Rows: 54,000 (9,000 advertisers, 6 monthly snapshots each). Features: 18, including advertiser_id. Validation: 5-fold, shuffle=True. CV AUC: 0.88.' What has to change before you believe 0.88?
options: Group the folds by advertiser and drop the ID column; the order of the months does not matter
Keep each advertiser's rows in one fold, check on later months, and drop the ID column
Drop the ID column and switch to ten folds, so that each check trains on more of the rows
Drop the ID column; once it has gone, shuffled folds are safe again for these rows
quiz.why: Six rows per advertiser with shuffled folds puts every advertiser on both sides, and the ID column hands the model a perfect way to recognise them. Dropping the ID alone is not enough: in the course's small simulation the flexible model without it still scored 0.80 in shuffled folds against about 0.63 on new advertisers, because near-constant columns identify an advertiser almost as well. More folds leave the same advertisers on both sides. And grouping without time order still trains on months later than the ones it is checked on, which never happens in use.

review.concept: choosing by the test score spends the test set

variants.q: An analyst builds 30 versions of a model that predicts which advertisers will accept a price increase, scores each on the same held-out accounts, and reports the best version's score: 0.81. What is the honest status of 0.81?
options: Optimistic: it is the luckiest of 30 looks at the same held-out accounts
Noisy but fair: no version trained on those accounts, so it errs up or down alike
Pessimistic: the best of 30 versions would score higher still on fresh accounts
Meaningless: once 30 versions have been scored on them, no score there says anything
variants.why: Thirty versions scored on the same accounts means the reported one is the luckiest of thirty looks, so 0.81 flatters it. No version was fitted to those accounts, which is why this feels safe; but the choice was fitted to them, so the error leans upward and the final figure needs accounts that played no part. The scores are still good for comparing versions, so they are not meaningless.

variants.q: A team tweaks a ticket-routing model eight times. After each tweak they re-score it on the same 300 test tickets and keep the change if the score went up. After the eighth tweak, what are those 300 tickets?
options: A stale test set: scoring the final model on them once more will restore it
A validation set: a fresh, untouched batch is needed for the final score
Useless: any tickets scored more than once have to be thrown away for good
A training set: the model has by now memorised all 300 of them
variants.why: Eight keep-or-discard decisions were made from those tickets, so they have helped shape the model and their score now runs high. They are still useful for choosing between versions, which is what a validation set is; the reported figure needs tickets that played no part, and scoring the same 300 again changes nothing.

variants.q: Your assistant offers to 'select the ten strongest columns for the churn model by trying combinations and keeping the set with the best score on the test months'. What do you tell it?
options: Let it select on the test months, then refit on the training months before reporting
Keep all the columns instead: choosing among columns is what causes overfitting
Select on the test months, then report the score from the training months
Select by cross-validation on the training months; score the test months once
variants.why: Which columns go in is a setting like any other, and choosing it by test score fits the choice to the test rows; refitting afterwards does not undo a choice those rows made. Cross-validation inside the training months does the same job and leaves the test months untouched for one honest score.

review.concept: folds must keep related rows together and never look ahead

variants.q: An invalid-traffic model is trained on click logs with about 200 clicks per device. Shuffled five-fold cross-validation gives an AUC of 0.97. What must be true of the folds before that figure says anything about devices the model has not seen?
options: Every fold must hold the same share of invalid clicks
All the clicks from one device must fall in the same fold
Every device must be represented in every one of the folds
The folds must be reshuffled several times and averaged
variants.why: With 200 clicks per device, shuffled folds put every device on both sides, and the model can score well just by recognising devices. Holding whole devices out is the only check that resembles meeting a new device; reshuffling or balancing the folds leaves the same devices on both sides.

variants.q: A model predicts each advertiser's spend next month from two years of monthly rows. The assistant validates with shuffled folds, so in some rounds the model trains on December rows and is checked on rows from the June before. What is wrong with that?
options: It trains on the future and is checked on the past, which never happens in use
The rounds are uneven: every month should appear in the checking part exactly once
June and December have different numbers of rows, so the folds are unbalanced
Two years of monthly rows is too little data to support five folds
variants.why: In use the model only ever predicts months later than everything it was trained on, so validation has to do the same: train on earlier months, check on later ones. Covering every month once does not help if the model has already seen what came after.

variants.q: A lead-scoring table has several rows per company, one for each contact who filled in a form. With shuffled folds a flexible model scores 0.86. With whole companies held out it scores 0.71. Which figure describes how it will do on companies it has not met?
options: 0.86, because shuffled folds are the standard method
About 0.79, the midpoint, as a fair compromise
0.71, because only there is every checked company new to the model
0.86, because holding out companies wastes training data
variants.why: Only the grouped folds check the model on companies it has never seen, which is how it will be used. The extra 0.15 under shuffled folds is the model recognising companies from their other contacts, and it disappears on new ones.

drill.q: Why can you not use the test set to choose a model's settings?
drill.a: Because choosing is a form of learning. Pick the best of several scores on the test rows and the choice is fitted to those rows, so the score flatters and nothing untouched is left to report.

drill.q: Your table has one row per advertiser per month. What must cross-validation do differently?
drill.a: Keep all of an advertiser's rows on the same side of every fold, and check on later months than it trains on. Otherwise a flexible model is rewarded for recognising advertisers it has already seen.

recall.prompt: Explain in 30 seconds how a model can score well in cross-validation and badly on new advertisers, and what you would ask the assistant to change.
recall.model_answer: If the same advertiser has rows on both sides of a fold, a flexible model can recognise it and recall its outcome, so validation rewards memory. In the course's small simulation that gave 0.80 in shuffled folds and about 0.63 on advertisers the model had never met. I would ask for folds that keep each advertiser's rows together and check on later months than they train on, with ID columns removed. Settings get chosen on those folds only, and the test set is scored once at the end.

lessons.ask_assistant: Choose every setting by cross-validation on the training rows only. Case one, one row per [unit] from [periods] that are alike: rotating shuffled folds are fine. Case two, several rows per [unit] or [periods] that differ: keep all rows of one [unit] in the same fold, make each fold check on later [periods] than it trains on, say how many such checks the data allows, and print how many [units] sit on both sides of any fold. Tell me which case applied and why. Remove ID columns. Report every fold score per candidate, with mean and range. Then stop: score [test period] only when I approve the frozen setting, and list every scoring run with the rows it used.
audit_checklist: How the folds were made (by advertiser, by time, or shuffled) and why that case applies, with the count of advertisers on both sides of any fold: 0
Every fold score for each candidate setting, with mean and range, not only the winner's mean
Test scoring is its own final stage that you trigger, and the output lists every scoring run with the rows it used: the test rows appear once
The feature list, with no ID column in it
transfer: Creative performance with one row per creative per day: are the same creatives on both sides of your validation?
Invalid-traffic detection with hundreds of clicks per device or publisher: what is the group to hold out together?
A support-ticket router tweaked again and again against one test batch: is that batch still a test set?

other_ways.approach: A later period held out for choosing
other_ways.when: When there is plenty of dated data: train on January and February and choose on March, or walk forward month by month when things drift, so every check looks ahead.

other_ways.approach: A fresh test set
other_ways.when: When the old one has been looked at too often to trust: a new month of data gives you a sealed envelope again.

other_ways.approach: A learning curve, before asking for more data
other_ways.when: When you wonder whether the rows left for training are enough: ask for the held-out score at growing training sizes, with the positives counted at each. Here the weighted sum reaches about 0.83 on 1,000 training rows and 0.845 on all 6,000, while 100 rows, with 11 churners, swing widely: count the churners, not the rows. The course scored that curve on its test months for illustration only.

glossary.def: A setting, such as a tree's depth, that somebody chooses before fitting; the model does not learn it from the rows.
Rows held out of training and used to compare settings or versions, so that the test set stays untouched.
Cutting the training data into parts called folds, training on all but one and checking on the one left out, in rotation.
Folds in which all rows from the same advertiser, or whatever else repeats, are kept on the same side.
The held-out score of one model trained on growing numbers of rows; it shows what more data would buy.

lessons.title: Forests and boosting
lessons.subtitle: When does a model built from many trees beat a simple weighted sum?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can ask for a simple model and a many-tree model on the same test rows, and decide between them by comparing their gap with the noise.

predict.q: A simple weighted-sum model and a far more flexible model built from a hundred or more small trees are run on two questions from the same advertiser table: who will churn, and who will start using video ads. Which model ranks better?
options: The flexible model, on both questions
The simple model, on both questions
One each
Neither: they tie on both questions
predict.reveal: One each: the simple model is ahead on churn by 0.009 AUC, the flexible one on video by 0.040. The lesson shows why you cannot tell in advance, and how to judge each gap.

segments.narration: Monday brings two requests. Retention wants the churn list. The video team wants a list of advertisers likely to start using the new video format in the next 60 days. Same table, same 17 columns, same two candidates: the weighted sum you already know, and a far more flexible model built from many trees. On one question the simple model finishes narrowly ahead. On the other it loses clearly. Nothing in the table tells you beforehand which is which. The same goes for any yes-or-no model, an invalid-traffic filter included: whether flexibility pays depends on the shape of the pattern, so you run both and measure.

visual.title: Forests and boosting
visual.sub: Two questions, one table, two different winners

segments.narration: One shallow tree is coarse: eight leaves, eight possible scores. One deep tree memorises. A forest escapes by numbers. [[1]] Give each tree its own random resample of the training advertisers, and let it consider only a random few columns at each split, so no two trees are alike. [[2]] Grow 300 of them, deep. Each overfits, but to different accidents. [[3]] Then average their scores. The accidents differ from tree to tree, so they mostly cancel. The pattern is shared, so it survives. On churn, that lifts the best single tree's 0.77 to about 0.83.

visual.title: A random forest: many deep trees, averaged

steps.label: Resample
steps.sub: each tree: its own random draw of rows, a random few columns per split

steps.label: Grow deep
steps.sub: 300 trees, each overfitting to different accidents

steps.label: Average
steps.sub: accidents cancel, the shared pattern stays

segments.narration: Boosting takes the opposite road: small trees, built one after another. [[1]] The first small tree gives a rough score. [[2]] Then the method looks at where that score is still wrong. [[3]] The next small tree is fitted to those misses, and a fraction of its correction is added in. [[4]] Repeat, a hundred rounds or more. The final score is the sum of many small corrections. It is powerful, and it has settings to choose: how deep each tree is, how many rounds, how big each step. The textbook name for both is an ensemble: many models, voting or correcting each other.

steps.label: Find the misses
steps.sub: where is the score still wrong?

steps.label: Next small tree
steps.sub: fitted to the misses, added in a small step (the learning rate)

segments.narration: So, churn. [[1]] Take boosting on default-looking settings, with trees four levels deep. It scores about 0.94 on its training rows and 0.83 on new advertisers. You know that signature: memorising. [[2]] Tuned by cross-validation on the training months, it prefers trees just two levels deep, and most of the gap closes. It lands at 0.836. [[3]] The forest is in the same neighbourhood. [[4]] And the weighted sum sits at 0.845. All that machinery finishes nine thousandths behind.

visual.title: Churn: training rows against new advertisers (AUC)
visual.note: Tuned: 16 combinations of settings compared by 5-fold cross-validation on the training months only.

segments.narration: Now the video question. [[1]] The single three-level tree was far behind on churn. [[2]] On video it matches the weighted sum. [[3]] The forest pulls ahead. [[4]] Tuned boosting reaches about 0.90 against 0.86, and this time cross-validation chose deeper trees. Why the reversal? In this simulation, adoption was built from thresholds and combinations: many creatives and a good click rate, a big spender who is also hitting goal. A weighted sum cannot say "and". Each column pushes at its own steady rate, whatever the others are doing. Trees say "and" for a living: a split inside a branch is exactly that. [[5]] Give the weighted sum three hand-built combination columns, and it reaches 0.88. That closes about half the gap.

visual.title: Two questions, same table, same models
visual.note: Top 200: churners or adopters among the 200 highest scores (a random 200 holds about 26 or 38). The churn tree is lesson 3-3's: depth 3, at least 100 advertisers per leaf; with no minimum, single trees peaked at 0.769. A combination that matters together is called an interaction.

segments.narration: Hold each gap against its own noise: an interval on the gap itself, measured on the same test rows, never one model's interval laid over the other's. [[1]] On churn the simple model leads by nine thousandths, and the interval on that lead only just clears zero. Probably real, and tiny. Now the team's units, the 200 highest scores. The simple model's list holds 136 churners and the boosted one 132. Nobody has put an interval on that difference of four, so call it unsettled. Either way, four names would not change the retention team's week. [[2]] On video the flexible model leads by about 0.04, and its interval sits far from zero. That one is settled. Its top 200 holds 185 adopters. The weighted sum's holds 153.

visual.title: Each gap against its own interval (95%)

left.label: Churn: logistic regression ahead by
left.sub: interval on the gap 0.002 to 0.015 · top 200: 136 against 132 churners, no interval on that difference of 4

right.label: Video: boosting ahead by
right.sub: interval on the gap 0.031 to 0.049 · top 200: 185 against 153 adopters

segments.narration: [[1]] The simple model took churn because of how this simulated world was built. Churn in it is close to a tidy weighted sum, each column nudging risk steadily one way. [[2]] Video was built the other way. Those are facts about the simulation, not about churn or video. On your data it could go either way. [[3]] A small neural network, a flexible model from module seven, starts its training from random numbers. A number called the random seed fixes those draws, so a rerun repeats exactly. Trained on churn six times, its test score ranged from about 0.81 to 0.835. [[4]] No better than the weighted sum, and a spread between its own runs wider than the whole churn gap. Training has luck in it too. The interval earlier covered only the luck of the test rows.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask for a simple model and a boosted one, scored on the same test rows. If the assistant hands you only the fancy one, send it back. [[2]] Boosted settings chosen by cross-validation on the training months, with the chosen depth reported, since that depth hints at the shape of the pattern. [[3]] Training and test scores for each. [[4]] The gap between them, with an interval. [[5]] And the gap in the decision's units: how many more churners in the list the team will work. Pay for complexity, which costs you readable weights, only when the gap is clear of the noise and big enough to matter.

segments.narration: So when a model built from many trees arrives, you ask for the simple one beside it on the same test rows, and pay for complexity only if the gap is real and worth something. Next, the video list again, and what three hand-built columns did to it.

visual.text: Run both. Compare the gap with the noise. Pay for complexity only when it buys something.

takeaways: A forest averages many deep trees; boosting adds up many small ones, each fitted to what is still wrong.
Flexible models pull ahead when the pattern is thresholds and combinations, and you cannot know that in advance.
Run both on the same rows, hold the gap against an interval on the gap itself, and pay for complexity only when it buys something.

quiz.concept: compare the gap with the noise
quiz.q: The assistant's churn report says: 'Logistic regression 0.845, tuned boosting 0.836. Logistic regression is the better model.' The interval on the difference runs from 0.002 to 0.015, and the two top-200 lists hold 136 and 132 churners. What is the fairest summary for the retention team?
options: The interval excludes zero, so the simple model is clearly stronger; the top-200 counts add nothing to that
Narrowly ahead on ranking; four churners in 200 would not change the calls, so take the readable model
Each model's own AUC interval is far wider than 0.009, so an interval on the gap that excludes zero must be a mistake
Boosting lost on this table, so it can be left out when the video team's list is built next week
quiz.why: The interval on the difference clears zero, so the lead is probably real on these test advertisers, and it is tiny: in the team's units, four churners in 200, a difference with no interval of its own and too small to change the calls. So complexity buys nothing here and the readable model is the sensible pick. Each model's own interval is the wrong ruler: both were scored on the same advertisers, so only an interval on the difference between them counts. And one table's loser can win the next question, which is why you run both again.

quiz.concept: always run the simple model too
quiz.q: For an invalid-traffic detector, the assistant reports a single model: 'Gradient boosting, test AUC 0.93, state of the art.' What do you ask for before accepting it?
options: A deeper boosted model, to see whether 0.93 can be pushed higher
Evidence that other teams use boosting for invalid traffic, since that makes it the safe choice
The same boosted model re-run with a different random seed
A simple model on the same test rows, with the gap and its interval
quiz.why: A score means little without the simpler alternative beside it: if a weighted sum scores 0.92, the complexity bought almost nothing, and if it scores 0.80 it bought a lot. 'Boosting is strongest' is the rule this lesson refuses, because which family wins depends on the shape of the pattern, and that has to be measured.

quiz.q: On a lead-scoring task the assistant reports: 'Boosting (depth 6, 500 rounds, default choices): training AUC 0.99, test 0.81. Logistic regression: training 0.79, test 0.80. Boosting wins.' What is the most useful next request?
options: Tune the boosted model by cross-validation, then compare again with an interval
Ship the boosted model as it is, since 0.81 is higher than 0.80 on the same test rows
Ship logistic regression, since boosting's gap proves it is the worse model
Raise the number of rounds until the boosted training score reaches 1.0
quiz.why: A training score of 0.99 against 0.81 says the boosted model is memorising on settings nobody chose, so 0.81 is not yet its best, and a lead of 0.01 with no interval is not a win. Rejecting it outright is the opposite mistake: once tuned it may pull clearly ahead or fall behind, and only the measurement says which.

quiz.concept: combinations a weighted sum cannot express
quiz.q: On the video question, logistic regression scores 0.861 and tuned boosting 0.901. A product manager needs a model she can explain to account managers. Which step is worth trying before accepting the less readable model?
options: Train logistic regression for longer, so that it can catch up with the boosted model
Remove columns from both models until the two of them score the same
Add hand-built combination columns to logistic regression, then re-measure
Average the two models' scores and report the result as 0.881
quiz.why: A weighted sum cannot represent 'this and that' unless the combination is handed to it as a column; three such flags lifted it to 0.882 here, closing about half the gap. Training for longer does not help, because the limit is the model's shape, not its effort.

review.concept: run both and compare the gap with the noise

variants.q: For predicting creative fatigue, a weighted-sum model scores 0.780 and a boosted model 0.786 on the same test creatives. The 95% interval on the difference runs from −0.010 to +0.022. What do you conclude?
options: Boosting is better: 0.786 is the higher of the two scores
A tie on this evidence, so the simpler model is the sensible pick
The weighted sum is better: simple models hold up better on new data
Neither is usable: a gap that small means both models are poor
variants.why: The interval spans zero, so these test rows cannot say which model is ahead, and the readable model costs less to run and explain. 'Simple models hold up better' is a rule this evidence supports no more than 'boosting is better'.
