variants.q: For an upsell list, a boosted model leads a weighted sum by 0.05 AUC, with an interval from 0.04 to 0.06, and puts 40 more buyers into the top 300. The weighted sum is easier to explain. What is the reasonable call?
options: The weighted sum: a simple model is always the safer choice when explaining matters
A tie: intervals are never precise enough to decide between models
Boosting: the gap is clear of the noise and large in the decision's units
Boosting: it is the stronger method on any table you give it
variants.why: The gap is far outside its noise and worth 40 buyers on the list the team works, so here complexity buys something. The last option picks the same model for a reason that is false: on another question the simple model can come out ahead, which is why you measure.

variants.q: A colleague says: 'On our churn table the simple model beat boosting, so on the new fraud project we can skip boosting and save the time.' What is the flaw?
options: He has the rule backwards: on a new project the flexible model is the safer one to keep
Fraud is too rare an outcome for boosting to work at all
Boosting should only be skipped on tables under 10,000 rows
Which family wins depends on the pattern in each problem, so measure again
variants.why: A simple model wins when the pattern is close to a weighted sum and loses when it is thresholds and combinations, and nothing in the churn result says which the fraud problem is. A rule about table size is no better: the two opposite results in this lesson came from the same table.

review.concept: a weighted sum cannot express combinations; trees can

variants.q: In a subscription business, customers cancel mostly when two things coincide: a price rise and a support complaint in the same month. Either one alone changes little. Which statement is right?
options: A weighted sum captures this as long as both columns are in the model
A weighted sum needs a combined column for this; tree models can find it unaided
No kind of model can capture this without a great deal more data
Only one shallow tree captures this; averaging many trees together blurs it away again
variants.why: A weighted sum gives each column one steady push, so 'only when both happen' is outside its shape unless you hand it a column that is yes exactly when both are true. Trees split on one column inside a branch of another, which is how they express 'and'.

variants.q: Cross-validation for a boosted lead-scoring model keeps choosing trees that are one level deep, so each tree asks a single question. What does that suggest about the pattern in the data?
options: Each column matters mostly on its own, not in combination with others
The boosted model is broken and should be rebuilt from scratch
The table has too few rows for boosting to work properly
Deeper trees would have won if they had been given more rounds
variants.why: A one-question tree has no branch to split inside, so it cannot express 'this and that'; if cross-validation prefers such trees, combinations are adding little. It is a clue, not proof, that a well-built simple model will be competitive, which you then measure.

variants.q: Clicks are usually invalid when the click rate is very high and time on site is near zero; either one alone is common in honest traffic. A weighted sum with both columns scores 0.74. Boosting scores 0.88, and the interval on the gap runs from 0.11 to 0.17. What best explains the gap?
options: Boosting has memorised the test rows, which inflates its score well beyond its real ability
The weighted sum was not trained for long enough to catch up
AUC is a measure that systematically favours tree-based models
The signal is a combination, which a weighted sum of the two columns cannot express
variants.why: The signal lives in the two columns together, and a weighted sum can only add a steady push from each. Memorising cannot explain a lead on rows neither model saw; that is what the test set protects you from.

drill.q: In a sentence each, how does a forest differ from boosting?
drill.a: A forest grows many deep trees on different random samples and averages them, so their individual mistakes cancel. Boosting grows small trees one after another, each fitted to what the earlier ones still get wrong.

drill.q: A colleague asks which is the better model, boosting or a simple weighted sum. What is the honest answer?
drill.a: It depends on the shape of the pattern, which you cannot know beforehand. Run both on the same test rows and compare the gap with the noise, and pay for the complex one only if the gap is real and big enough to matter.

recall.prompt: Your manager asks: 'Why didn't you just use boosting? Everyone says it is the best.' Answer in 30 seconds, using the two questions from this lesson.
recall.model_answer: We ran a simple weighted sum and tuned boosting on two questions from the same table. On churn the simple model was narrowly ahead, by about 0.009 with an interval on that gap that only just clears zero, and the two top-200 lists were four churners apart, too few to change what the team does, so the readable model was the better buy. On video adoption, which depends on combinations of columns, boosting was clearly ahead, by 0.04, far outside the noise. Which one wins depends on the shape of the pattern, and the churn result in particular is a property of how the simulation was built, so the only rule is to run both and compare the gap with the noise.

lessons.ask_assistant: Fit two models on the same training rows and score both on the same held-out rows: a simple one ([logistic or linear regression]) and a gradient-boosted one. Choose the boosted model's tree depth, number of rounds and step size (learning rate) by cross-validation on the training rows only; print every combination tried with its score. For each model print training score, test [metric], test row count and [outcome] cases in the top [list size]. Print the difference in test [metric] with a 95% interval from resampling the same test rows (a paired bootstrap), and the difference in top-list counts with its interval. If the gap is small, refit from [several] seeds and print the range.
audit_checklist: One table with the baseline, the simple model and the boosted model, each beside the number of test rows it was scored on; the counts match
Training score beside test score for each; a boosted model near 1.0 in training has probably not been tuned
The tuning table: every combination of settings tried, its cross-validation score on training rows, and the depth that won
An interval on the difference itself, not two separate intervals, and the same difference as a count in the top-K list
transfer: Lead scoring: does a boosted model put enough extra buyers in the sales team's top 100 to justify losing readable weights?
Invalid traffic: is the signal a combination, such as a high click rate together with almost no time on site, that a weighted sum would miss?
Spend prediction for finance: does a flexible model's smaller typical miss survive an interval on the difference?

other_ways.approach: Keep the weighted sum and hand it combination columns
other_ways.when: When readability matters and you can name the combinations: three such flags closed about half the video gap.

other_ways.approach: A single shallow tree
other_ways.when: When people must be able to read the rules aloud and a coarse ranking is enough: on video the depth-3 tree matched logistic regression (0.864 against 0.861).

other_ways.approach: A small neural network
other_ways.when: Not on this churn table: six runs ranged from 0.808 to 0.835, no better than the weighted sum and less stable. Its place in this course is text, in module 7.

glossary.def: Many deep trees, each grown on its own random resample of rows with a random few columns per split, with their scores averaged.
Many small trees built in sequence, each fitted to what the trees before it still get wrong, with their corrections added up.
The boosting setting for how large a step each new tree's correction is allowed to take.
A combination of columns that matters together, such as many creatives and a good click rate; trees can find one, a weighted sum has to be handed it.
A model made of many models whose scores are combined, by voting or averaging as in a forest, or by adding corrections as in boosting.
The number that fixes a method's random choices, so a rerun gives the same answer; changing it shows how much of a score is luck.

lessons.title: Features: where your knowledge goes in
lessons.subtitle: What moves a model more: the algorithm, or the columns you give it?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can brief a feature table built from dated events, put every column through the snapshot-date test, and measure what a group of columns is worth before paying for a fancier algorithm or more rows.

predict.q: A churn model is given just one group of columns at a time. Which group, used alone, gets closest to the score of all seventeen columns together?
options: Who they are: tenure, total spend, vertical, account manager
How they are set up: tracking, automated bidding, creatives
Performance against their own goal: CPA versus goal, click rate
What they did lately: spend trend, active days, logins
predict.reveal: What they did lately: those five columns alone score about 0.82, against about 0.85 for all seventeen. The lesson shows what that says about where a model's score comes from, and why it is a result about this data rather than a law.

segments.narration: The video team's list has a sequel. The plain weighted sum found 153 real adopters among its 200 highest scores. Boosting found 185. Then someone who knows the product handed the weighted sum three new columns, each a combination, such as many creatives together with a good click rate. Same algorithm, and its list now holds 171. Three columns of knowledge closed about half of the gap to the fancier algorithm. That pattern is general, for a yes-or-no model like this one or a number model like a spend forecast: what it is shown can matter more than which algorithm reads it. The churn table lets you check how much.

visual.title: Features: where your knowledge goes in
visual.sub: Video list, top 200: 153 adopters became 171 with three hand-built columns. Boosting: 185.

segments.narration: Before any work on columns, one question: would more rows help? Ask for a learning curve, the same model trained on growing samples of rows. The weighted sum reaches about 0.83 with 1,000 training rows. All 6,000 take it to 0.845. With 100 rows, only 11 of them churners, the score swings widely. So count the positives, not the rows. More rows would buy little here. Those figures belong to this simulated data. On yours, ask for the curve.

visual.title: Learning curve: the weighted sum on churn
visual.note: Main table, scored on the 4,000 test advertisers. 100 training rows hold 11 churners; 1,000 hold 111.

segments.narration: So, the columns. Keep the algorithm fixed, the plain weighted sum, and change only what it is shown. Same advertisers, same training months, same test months. [[1]] Start with what any account record holds, such as tenure and vertical. Who they are. On those five columns the model scores about 0.66. [[2]] Add how they are set up, conversion tracking and automated bidding among them. About 0.76. [[3]] Add performance against their own goal. About 0.79. [[4]] Then add what they have been doing lately, such as spend trend and active days. About 0.85, the number you have been looking at since module two.

visual.title: Same model, more columns: test AUC
visual.note: Who they are: tenure, spend, campaigns, vertical, account manager · Set up: creatives per campaign, creative age, tracking, auto-bidding, reviews · Vs goal: CPA vs goal, CTR · Recent: spend trend, active days, days since login, tickets, payment failures. Logistic regression each time; train Jan–Mar, test May–Jun.

segments.narration: [[1]] From the thinnest list of columns to the full one, the score moved by about 0.18. [[2]] From the weakest of the four algorithms, the single small tree, to the best, it moved by about 0.08. Between the two best, by about 0.01. And the learning curve had gone flat, so more rows promised little. All of that is a result about this simulated data, not a law. On the video list the better algorithm was worth about 0.04. So the habit is to measure each. And before you pay for a fancier algorithm, ask what the model is not being shown.

visual.title: What moved the churn score (test AUC)

right.label: Changing the algorithm
right.sub: weakest of four to best · only 0.009 between the two best

segments.narration: There is a second way to run the experiment: give the model one group at a time. [[1]] Who they are, about 0.66. [[2]] Setup, about 0.73. [[3]] Performance against goal, about 0.7. [[4]] Recent behaviour, about 0.82. Five columns, and nearly the whole result. Now think back to the first experiment. Recent behaviour went in last, so it only got credit for the final step, from 0.79 to 0.85. The groups overlap, and whichever goes in first collects the shared credit. So ask for both views before anyone calls a group of columns unimportant.

visual.title: Each group on its own: test AUC
visual.note: All 17 columns together: 0.845

segments.narration: Most of those seventeen columns come from a handful of recipes you already use on dashboards, and they travel to almost any table about customers. [[1]] How recent: days since the last login. [[2]] How often: active days in the last 28. [[3]] How much: spend over the window, on a log scale so a few giant accounts do not dominate. [[4]] The trend: the last four weeks divided by the four before. [[5]] The ratio to a goal: CPA divided by the advertiser's own target. Say a CPA is 40 dollars. Good or bad? You cannot tell until you divide by the goal. [[6]] The breadth: how many campaigns, how many creatives. A weighted sum only adds up what it is handed. Building these columns is your job, and it has a name: feature engineering.

visual.title: Recipes that travel
rows: What does it add up to?

segments.narration: This is your home turf, and it is where the danger gets in. Features are built in SQL from dated events, and the pattern never changes. Start from the snapshot table, one row per advertiser per snapshot date. Join the events to it with the date window inside the join condition: from 56 days before the snapshot up to, but not including, the snapshot day. Group back to one row per advertiser per snapshot. Every recipe is an aggregate inside that window: a SUM, a COUNT, a latest date, a ratio. The line that matters most is the upper bound on the date. Leave it off, or pull a column from a table that only holds today's state, and you have rebuilt the leak from module one.

visual.title: A point-in-time feature query
visual.code:
SELECT s.advertiser_id, s.snapshot_date,
  COALESCE(SUM(e.spend), 0) AS spend_8w,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_date >= s.snapshot_date - 28
                      THEN e.event_date END) AS active_days_28,
  SUM(CASE WHEN e.event_date >= s.snapshot_date - 28
           THEN e.spend ELSE 0 END) AS spend_last_4w
FROM snapshots s
LEFT JOIN spend_events e
  ON  e.advertiser_id = s.advertiser_id
  AND e.event_date >= s.snapshot_date - 56   -- window opens
  AND e.event_date <  s.snapshot_date        -- closes: no future
GROUP BY s.advertiser_id, s.snapshot_date;
visual.note: Window in ON, not WHERE: an advertiser with no events keeps a row of zeros. spend_trend = spend_last_4w ÷ NULLIF(spend_8w − spend_last_4w, 0), with a flag for no earlier spend. Date arithmetic varies by warehouse.

segments.narration: The brief and the audit. [[1]] Ask the assistant to build the feature table from dated events, one row per advertiser per snapshot. [[2]] Its output must show a feature list: every column, its source table and its date window. [[3]] Put each column through two questions. When is it known? And will it exist on the day we score? For a column kept only as today's value, like account tier, use its change history if one exists, start saving dated copies, or leave it out and say so. [[4]] Then the score with column groups added one at a time, and each alone, on the same test months. [[5]] When one new column moves the score a lot, it is your best idea this quarter or a leak. The feature list tells you which.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Features from dated events; one row per advertiser per snapshot
Feature list: column · source table · date window
Each column: known when? There on scoring day? Today's value only: change history, dated copies, or drop it
AUC by column group: added one by one, and alone
A big jump from one column: best idea, or leak?

segments.narration: So before you pay for a fancier algorithm, you ask what the model is not being shown, build it from dated events, and measure what it adds. Next, the question an account manager asks the moment she sees a list: why is this advertiser at the top?

visual.text: Before paying for a fancier algorithm, ask what the model is not being shown.
visual.sub: On this data: columns 0.18 thinnest to full · algorithms 0.08 weakest to best, 0.01 between the two best · more rows: the curve was flat

takeaways: On this data the columns moved the score by about 0.18, the algorithm by about 0.08 from weakest to best (0.01 between the two best), and extra rows by almost nothing.
Useful columns come from a few recipes: how recent, how often, how much, the trend, the ratio to a goal, the breadth.
Every feature must be computable on the snapshot date and exist on the day you score.

quiz.q: The churn model sits at an AUC of about 0.85. Your assistant proposes two more days tuning the boosted model. On this data the two best algorithms were about 0.01 apart. What do you ask for instead?
options: A deeper boosted model with more rounds, since extra depth is where the hidden signal usually sits
A larger test set, so that the small gap between the two algorithms becomes statistically clear
A list of what account managers watch that is not yet a column, and a test of adding it
The same two models on a shuffled split, to confirm which one is really ahead
quiz.why: Changing the columns moved this score by about 0.18, against about 0.08 across all four algorithms and about 0.01 between the two best, so the cheaper experiment is new information, measured the same way. More depth is the tempting move, but it only re-cuts the columns the model already has, and tuning here preferred shallow trees.

quiz.q: The assistant adds one column, account tier, joined from the accounts table, and the test AUC jumps from 0.85 to 0.93. Its feature list reads: source accounts table, value as of the export date. What is the right read?
options: Tier is a strong feature that the earlier columns missed; keep it and report the higher score to the team
A jump that large means the model is overfitting; ask for shallower trees and run it again
Tier has only a few categories, so the jump must be noise; rerun it with a different random seed
Tier was read after the outcome window and may encode who left; rebuild it as of the snapshot
quiz.why: A value read on the export date fails the time-travel test: if tiers are changed once an account goes quiet, the column carries the outcome. Calling it a great feature is the tempting read, but one column that moves the score this much is a leak until the feature list proves otherwise.

quiz.q: A model predicts which creatives will fatigue next week, meaning their click rate will fall. Its columns are format, image size and advertiser vertical, and it barely beats a coin. Which additions follow the recipes from this lesson?
options: Days since launch, impressions in the last 7 days, click rate now over click rate at launch
The creative's ID as a number, so that the model can learn the history of each creative separately
Next week's actual impressions for each creative, since heavy delivery is what produces fatigue
The same three columns again, fed to a boosted model in place of the weighted sum
quiz.why: How recent, how much and a ratio to the creative's own starting point are the recipes, and all three can be computed on the scoring date. Next week's impressions would predict best of all, which is the problem: the number does not exist when you score. An ID is never a feature.

quiz.q: A colleague reads the cumulative results: setup lifted the score from 0.66 to 0.76, recent behaviour only from 0.79 to 0.85. He concludes that setup is the more valuable group of columns. What do you tell him?
options: Agreed: the size of each step is the value of the group that was added at that step
Not from those steps: they depend on the order; alone, recent behaviour scores 0.82 and setup 0.73
Not from those steps: a group's value should be read from training scores, not test scores
Agreed, and by the same logic performance against goal is worth the least of the four groups
quiz.why: A cumulative step measures what a group adds to whatever went in before it, so when groups overlap the early ones collect the shared credit. On their own the order reverses: recent behaviour about 0.82, setup about 0.73. Reading step size as value is natural and wrong.

review.concept: before changing the algorithm, ask what the model is not being shown

variants.q: A lead-scoring model uses company size, industry and country. Logistic regression scores 0.62 and a tuned boosted model 0.63. Sales reps say the hot leads are the ones who came back to the pricing page this week. What is the most promising next step?
options: Tune the boosted model further, since it is already slightly ahead of the simpler one
Collect several thousand more leads described by the same three columns
Build visit columns, such as pricing-page visits in the last 7 days, and re-score
Lower the cut-off so that more leads are flagged as hot and passed to the sales reps
variants.why: Two algorithms 0.01 apart on the same thin columns says the limit is the information, and the reps have just named information the model lacks. More tuning re-cuts the same three columns; a lower cut-off changes who is flagged, not how well the model ranks.

variants.q: An upsell model predicting who will upgrade their plan has been tried with four algorithms; all land between 0.70 and 0.72. The assistant concludes that 0.72 is the ceiling for this problem. What is the better conclusion?
options: It is the ceiling for these columns; test new ones, such as usage against the plan limit
Correct: when four different algorithms agree this closely, the data has nothing more to give
Wrong: a fifth, more powerful algorithm such as a neural network is needed to break through
Wrong: score the models on their training rows to see where the true ceiling is
variants.why: Agreement between algorithms tells you about the columns they share, not about the problem. The ceiling moves when the model is shown something new, and usage as a ratio to the customer's own limit is a natural candidate to test.

variants.q: An invalid-traffic model receives each publisher's daily clicks and daily impressions as two raw columns and uses logistic regression. A fraud analyst says suspicious publishers show a click rate far above their category's norm. Why might the model be missing that?
options: It is likely a training problem: both raw columns are present, so the click rate is already available
Logistic regression cannot use more than one column describing the same publisher
Click counts leak the outcome, so the model was right to give them very little weight
A weighted sum cannot divide one column by another; the ratio must be built and handed to it
variants.why: A weighted sum adds columns; it cannot form a click rate, let alone a click rate relative to a category norm, unless someone builds that column. Assuming the raw ingredients are enough is the natural mistake, and it is why your knowledge of what suspicious looks like has to go in as a feature.

review.concept: a feature must be computable on the snapshot date and exist on scoring day

variants.q: The assistant's feature query sums spend from the events table, joined on advertiser, with one date condition: event date on or after 56 days before the snapshot. Row counts match the snapshot table. What is wrong?
options: A 56-day window is too short: a trend column needs at least a full quarter of spend history
There is no upper bound, so spend after the snapshot flows into the feature
The sum should be an average, so that a few very large accounts do not dominate the column
The join should also match on vertical, or rows will be duplicated
variants.why: Without a condition that the event date is before the snapshot, the sum runs on into the outcome window, so churners show low spend because they churned. Matching row counts only proves the grain is right; it says nothing about which dates were read.

variants.q: A model predicts each advertiser's spend for next month and is run on the 1st. One feature is last month's invoiced total, which billing finalises around the 10th. In the historical training table the column is complete for every month. What is the problem?
options: Invoices include credits and refunds, so the column measures something different from spend
Invoiced totals are in dollars and must be put on a log scale before the model can use them
On scoring day the column does not exist yet: the model learned from something it will not be given
The feature repeats information already carried by last month's spend
variants.why: A feature has to pass two tests: computable from data up to the snapshot, and actually available when you score. History looks complete only because you are reading it later; on the 1st the invoice is still ten days away.

variants.q: A lead-scoring model's strongest feature is the number of sales calls logged against the lead. Scores are produced the moment a lead arrives. Its test score is excellent. What is the right read?
options: Calls happen after scoring, and mostly to promising leads: the column knows the future
Calls are a sign of interest: exactly the kind of how-often behaviour feature the model should keep
The feature is fine, but should be divided by the lead's age in days to turn it into a rate
The score is excellent because the model has at last been given enough rows
variants.why: At the moment a lead arrives there are no calls, and the calls that follow go to leads already judged promising, so the count carries the outcome. It looks like a how-often feature, which is what makes it tempting, but it fails the question of when it is known.

drill.q: Your model's score has stalled, and someone suggests switching to a more powerful algorithm. What question should come first?
drill.a: Ask what the model is not being shown. In this course's churn data, changing the columns moved the score about twice as far as the whole range of algorithms did, and more rows promised little. New information is often the cheaper experiment, and you measure each rather than assume.

drill.q: What two things must be true of a column before it can be used as a feature?
drill.a: It must be computable on the snapshot date, using only data up to then. And it must actually exist on the day you score. If either fails, it is a leak, or a column the live model will never receive.

recall.prompt: A colleague wants to try a more complex algorithm on a model whose score has stalled. Explain what you would look at first, and what any new column has to pass.
recall.model_answer: I would look at the feature list before the algorithm: on the churn data, changing the columns moved AUC by about 0.18, against about 0.08 from the weakest algorithm to the best and about 0.01 between the two best, and the learning curve was flat long before all 6,000 rows, so the likelier gain is information the model has not been shown. I would build candidates from the standard recipes — how recent, how often, how much, the trend, the ratio to a goal, the breadth — and measure each group added to the model and on its own. Every new column must be computable from events dated before the snapshot and must exist on the day we score; a column that moves the score a lot is a leak until the feature list shows otherwise.

lessons.ask_assistant: Build the feature table in SQL from dated event tables: one row per [unit] per [snapshot date], every aggregate limited to the [window length] before the snapshot and strictly before it. Print a feature list: each column, its source table, its date window and whether it will exist on scoring day; flag any column read from a current-state table. Print rows and distinct [units] before and after each join. Then fit the same [simple model] with the column groups added one at a time and each group alone, and print [metric] for each on the same [test period]. Add a learning curve: [metric] for growing samples of training rows, with the count of [outcome] cases at each size.
audit_checklist: A feature list: every column with its source table, its date window and when its value is known; current-state sources are flagged, and no flagged column is among the big movers
Row count and distinct advertisers equal to the snapshot table, before and after the feature joins
Test AUC with column groups added cumulatively and each group alone, on the same test months
A learning curve: the score at growing numbers of training rows, with the count of positives at each size
transfer: Lead scoring: which leads will convert — days since the last visit, visits this week, pricing-page views as a share of all views.
Creative fatigue: which creatives will fade — days live, impressions per day, click rate now against click rate at launch.
Invalid traffic: which publishers look suspicious — click rate against the category norm, share of clicks at night, change against their own last month.

other_ways.approach: Let a flexible model find combinations of the raw columns on its own
other_ways.when: When you have plenty of rows and no clear idea which combinations matter. It still cannot use information that is not in the table.

other_ways.approach: Have the assistant generate many candidate aggregates and keep the ones that hold up in cross-validation
other_ways.when: When the event data is rich and you want breadth quickly. Every survivor still has to pass the time-travel test, and more candidates means more chance of a lucky one.

other_ways.approach: Bring in a new data source instead of re-cutting the same events
other_ways.when: When the recipes have been tried on the events you have and the score has stopped moving.

glossary.def: Building new columns from raw data so that the model is shown what you know matters.
A column computed only from events dated before the snapshot, so it could have existed on that day.
A quantity divided by the customer's own target, such as CPA over goal, which puts every customer on the same ruler.
The audit exhibit that names every column, its source table and its date window.
The test score of one model trained on growing numbers of rows; it shows what more data would buy.

lessons.title: Opening the black box
lessons.subtitle: What can you ask a model about its own answers, and what can it not tell you?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can ask for the three standard explanations of a model — what it leans on, how its answer moves, why this case — and state the limit of each in the same breath.

predict.q: One way to see what a model leans on: shuffle one column's values between advertisers and score it again. Shuffling the churn model's top column, spend trend, costs about 0.07 of AUC. What does shuffling all five recent-behaviour columns together cost?
options: About 0.07: the top column was carrying the whole group
About 0.10: a little more than the top column alone
About 0.18: more than the five single-column drops added up
About 0.35: the model falls back to a coin flip
predict.reveal: About 0.18, more than the five single-column drops add up to. Shuffled one at a time, overlapping columns cover for each other; the lesson shows what that does to the way you read an importance chart.

segments.narration: Monday morning the risk list goes out. By ten, an account manager is at your desk about one name on it. The advertiser's ID ends in 754, and the list says 73 percent. Her question is fair: why? Because the model said so is not something she can take into a call. This list comes from the weighted sum, but what follows works on any model, one that predicts who will hit their CPA goal as much as one that predicts who will leave. There are three questions to ask. What does it lean on overall? How does its answer move when one column changes? And why this advertiser? Each has a standard tool, and each tool has a limit that belongs in the same breath as the answer.

visual.title: Opening the black box
visual.sub: Advertiser 111754 is on the list at 73%. Why?

segments.narration: Question one: what does the model lean on? Take the test months, shuffle one column so that its values land on the wrong advertisers, and score again. If the score drops, the model was relying on that column. [[1]] Shuffle spend trend, and AUC falls by about 0.07. [[2]] Shuffle active days, about 0.03. [[3]] [[4]] [[5]] [[6]] [[7]] Then come five columns at about 0.01 each. The other ten cost almost nothing. This is called permutation importance, and it works on any model, because it never looks inside. But what it measures is narrow: how much this model's ranking depends on a column. Not how much that column matters to an advertiser.

visual.title: Shuffle one column: how far does AUC fall?
visual.note: Logistic regression, test months. The other 10 columns: 0.004 or less.

segments.narration: Now the catch. [[1]] Shuffle the five recent-behaviour columns together, as a group, and the score falls by about 0.18. [[2]] [[3]] [[4]] Every other group costs under 0.03. Why bother with groups? Because columns that carry overlapping information cover for each other. Shuffle one of a pair, and its neighbour is still there with much of the same signal, so the drop understates what the pair is worth. Which group wins here is a property of this simulated data. The catch is general. A bar near zero has two readings: the column may be useless, or it may be redundant, and the single-column test cannot tell you which.

visual.title: Shuffle a whole group together
visual.note: Logistic regression, test months. Columns shuffled together cannot cover for each other.

segments.narration: Question two: how does the answer move? Take CPA versus goal. For every advertiser who has one, set it to the same value, and average the model's predictions. Then raise the value and repeat. This exhibit uses the boosted model, not the weighted sum behind the list: a weighted sum can only draw a smooth slope, while boosting can bend. With CPA right at goal, the average predicted risk is about 5 percent. At one and a half times goal, about 11 percent. Most of that rise arrives between about 1.2 and 1.4 times goal. Read the curve as the model's behaviour, not as a promise about any advertiser. Nothing in it says that if her CPA came down, her risk would follow the curve back.

visual.title: As CPA vs goal rises, what does the model predict?
visual.xlabel: CPA vs goal (1 = exactly on goal)
visual.note: The model's behaviour, not a promise. Each point: set CPA vs goal to that value for every training advertiser who has one, then average the predictions. Some of those pairings are rare in real accounts, such as CPA far over goal with climbing spend.

segments.narration: Question three is hers: why this advertiser? Start from an advertiser who is average on every column. The model gives that one about 5 percent. Then measure how far she sits from average. [[1]] She was active on 5 of the last 28 days. [[2]] Her CPA is more than two and a half times her goal. [[3]] Her newest creative is 120 days old. [[4]] [[5]] Spend trend and click rate add two smaller pushes. Each push is the column's weight times her distance from average, in the scorecard points of module three, not percentage points. Add her pushes, about four points, to the average advertiser's score, then pass the total through the S-curve: 5 percent becomes 73. For complex models the same idea is called SHAP. Either way it is arithmetic, not a cause.

visual.title: Advertiser 111754: why 73%?
visual.note: Scorecard points add up before the S-curve; they are not percentage points. Average advertiser: 4.7%. Her pushes added to its score, then through the S-curve: 72.7%. Top five shown; averages from the training months. CPA vs goal is scaled after its empty values are filled, so its push does not reproduce exactly from the average shown.

segments.narration: [[1]] First, the useful half. A push tells you why the score is high, and that is what makes a list usable. A name and a percentage gets a shrug. A name with three reasons gets a call with a purpose. And the reasons are hers. Spend trend is the model's favourite column overall, yet it is only her fourth push, and your old rule of spend trend below 0.7 would have missed her. [[2]] Now the limit. A push says stale creatives raised her score. It does not say that fresh creatives would have kept her. She did leave, for the record. What would have changed that is a different question, and it belongs to the next module.

visual.title: What a push is, and is not

left.label: It tells you
left.sub: Stale creatives pushed her score up

right.label: It does not tell you
right.sub: Whether fresh creatives would have kept her

segments.narration: The brief and the audit. Ask the assistant for three exhibits, each naming its model and its rows. [[1]] Importance by shuffling, on test rows, for single columns and for groups. [[2]] A dependence curve for the columns the business asks about, captioned as the model's behaviour. [[3]] For every name on the list, the top three pushes, with the advertiser's value next to the average. Ask for those as per-row contributions, or SHAP values when the model is not a weighted sum. When a simple model scores close to the best, take the reasons from it. [[4]] Then check the verbs. If the output says a column drives the outcome, or that fixing it saves the account, send it back. The honest verbs are relies on, moves with, and pushed up.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Importance by shuffling: single columns and groups, test rows
Dependence curves, captioned as the model's behaviour
Top three pushes per name (ask for per-row contributions, or SHAP values): their value next to the average
Check the verbs: relies on · moves with · pushed up — never drives

segments.narration: So when someone asks why a name is on a list, you can give the model's reasons, and say in the same breath that they explain the score, not the customer. Next comes one more check before the list leaves your hands: who the model is wrong about.

visual.title: Three questions, three limits
rows: Shuffle a column, or a group
The model's behaviour, not a promise

takeaways: Shuffling shows what the model relies on; overlapping columns hide each other, so shuffle groups too.
A dependence curve is the model's behaviour, not a promise about any advertiser.
A push explains one score as arithmetic; it is not a cause.

quiz.concept: importance is reliance, and overlap hides columns
quiz.q: The importance chart for the churn model puts days since login at almost zero. A product manager concludes that login activity has nothing to do with churn and wants it off the account-health dashboard. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed: a bar near zero means the column carries no signal about churn, so the dashboard can lose it
Disagree: a bar near zero is the classic sign that the column is leaking the outcome
Agreed, provided the bar is also near zero when it is recomputed on the training months
Not yet: another column may carry the same signal; shuffle the related ones as a group
quiz.why: Importance measures how much this model relies on a column, and overlapping columns cover for each other, so a bar near zero can mean redundant rather than irrelevant. Reading it as no relationship with churn is the tempting step from the model to the world, and the chart cannot support it.

quiz.concept: a dependence curve is the model's behaviour
quiz.q: The assistant's report says: predicted churn rises from 5 percent to 11 percent as CPA versus goal goes from 1.0 to 1.5, so bringing advertisers back to goal will roughly halve their churn. Where is the flaw?
options: The curve came from the boosted model and should have been drawn from the weighted sum instead
The curve shows how the model's prediction moves, not what happens if an advertiser's CPA changes
A rise of six points between those values is inside the noise, so there is no pattern to act on
Dependence curves are only valid when they are computed on the training months
quiz.why: A dependence curve re-labels advertisers and averages the model's predictions. The model learned from advertisers who differ in many ways besides CPA, so the curve cannot promise what changing CPA would do. Which model drew it is a detail; the leap from moves with to will halve is the error.

quiz.concept: a push is arithmetic, not a cause
quiz.q: A lead-scoring model puts one lead at 81 percent. Its top pushes: six visits to the pricing page, a company of over 500 people, three opened emails. The sales director says: so if we get every lead to visit pricing six times, they will convert. What is the right read?
options: The pushes explain this lead's score; whether driving visits changes outcomes needs a test
He is right: the largest push identifies the lever with the largest effect on conversion
He is wrong, because pushes only mean something for a lead that is average on every column
He is right, but only for leads at companies of over 500 people, as the second push makes clear
quiz.why: A push is the model's arithmetic: weight times distance from average. Leads who visit pricing six times were already interested; steering uninterested leads there does not turn them into the same people. Treating the biggest push as the biggest lever is the mistake this tool invites.

quiz.concept: overall importance versus one case's reasons
quiz.q: Spend trend is the model's top column overall. An account manager gets an advertiser at 64 percent whose three reasons are payment failures, support tickets and low activity; spend trend is not among them. She suspects the reasons are broken. What do you tell her?
options: She is right: the model's top column overall should appear among every advertiser's reasons
She is right: reasons should be computed on the training months, where they are more stable
They are fine: they show where this advertiser is unusual, not what matters overall
The reasons are fine, but a score that lacks the top column behind it should not be acted on
quiz.why: Overall importance summarises the whole test set; one advertiser's pushes depend on her own values. If her spend trend is ordinary it contributes little, however heavily the model weighs that column in general. In the lesson's example, spend trend was only the fourth push for an advertiser at 73 percent.

review.concept: importance means reliance, and overlapping columns hide each other

variants.q: A model predicts creative fatigue. Two of its columns, days live and total impressions served, rise together. Shuffling days live costs 0.06 of AUC; shuffling total impressions costs 0.004. An analyst says impressions do not matter for fatigue. What is the right read?
options: Unproven: the two overlap, so shuffle them together before judging either
Correct: a drop of 0.004 is far too small for the column to matter to the model or to fatigue
Wrong: the much smaller drop shows that impressions is the column leaking the outcome
Correct, as long as the drop comes out the same on a second shuffle
variants.why: When two columns carry the same signal, the model can lean on one while the other looks idle. A single-column drop shows reliance, not relevance; shuffling the pair together, or testing the column on its own, tells you what the information is worth.

variants.q: In an invalid-traffic model, clicks per device is the top column by shuffling, at 0.05 of AUC. The team removes it and retrains, expecting a big loss. The score falls by only 0.004. What most likely happened?
options: The importance figure was computed wrongly the first time and should be discarded
The retrained model is overfitting to the remaining columns, which hides the real loss
A related column, such as clicks per IP address, took over the same signal
The column was leaking the outcome, so removing it could not hurt the score
variants.why: Importance says what one fitted model relied on. Take the column away, and a model refitted on the rest can lean on an overlapping neighbour instead. A calculation error is the tempting explanation, but both numbers can be right: they answer different questions.

variants.q: A renewal model has two columns that move together: seats purchased and plan price. Shuffled one at a time, each costs about 0.02 of AUC. Shuffled together, they cost 0.11. How do you report this?
options: Each is a minor column worth about 0.02, and neither deserves a place in the summary
The grouped figure must be an error, since it should equal 0.02 plus 0.02
Plan price is the cause of renewal, and the number of seats merely follows it
Account size, carried by the pair, is a major input; the single bars understate it
variants.why: Shuffling one column leaves the other standing in for it, so each single drop is small; shuffling both removes the shared signal. The drops are not supposed to add up, and nothing here says which of the two, if either, causes renewal.

review.concept: an explanation describes the model, not a cause

variants.q: A model predicts contract renewal. Its dependence curve for discount level climbs steadily: the bigger the discount, the higher the predicted renewal. Sales proposes larger discounts for everyone. What should you say?
options: The curve proves it: predicted renewal rises with the discount at every level on the chart
The curve is the model's behaviour; who got discounts before was not random, so test it
The curve is unreliable, because discount is measured in percent rather than in dollars
Give the larger discount only to the customers where the curve is at its steepest
variants.why: A dependence curve re-labels customers and averages predictions, so it inherits whatever decided who received a discount in the past. It describes the model; the proposal is a claim about cause, and that needs an experiment.

variants.q: A model flags support tickets likely to escalate. For one ticket, the largest push is that it contains the word refund. A team lead suggests that agents steer customers away from that word to reduce escalations. What is the right read?
options: Sensible: the push shows that the word itself raises the chance that a ticket will escalate
Sensible, but only if the word is also the top column in the model's importance chart
The word marks tickets that score high; dropping it changes the score, not the customer
The push must be wrong, because one word cannot carry that much weight in a model
variants.why: The push says the model's score is higher when that word is present. Customers who write it are already unhappy about money, and hiding the word leaves them exactly as unhappy. That is the gap between the model's arithmetic and a cause.

variants.q: An advertiser is on the risk list at 73 percent, and one of the reasons given is that her newest creative is 120 days old. The account manager asks: if she uploads new creatives tomorrow, what will her risk be? What is the honest answer?
options: The model's score would fall, but that is its arithmetic; it cannot tell you whether she stays
Her risk would fall by exactly the size of that push, so quote her the new percentage
Her score would stay where it is, because a push describes the past and cannot move
Her risk would fall to the level of an average advertiser, about 5 percent
variants.why: Re-scoring her with a fresh creative would lower the number, because the model's weight on that column has not changed. But the weight was learned from advertisers who differ in many other ways, so a lower score is not evidence that she would stay. Quoting the re-scored percentage as her new risk treats arithmetic as a cause.

drill.q: A column's importance comes out close to zero. Give the two possible explanations, and say how you would tell them apart.
drill.a: Either the column really carries no useful signal, or another column carries the same signal and covers for it. To tell them apart, shuffle the related columns together as a group, or test the column on its own.

drill.q: A model lists stale creatives as the top reason an advertiser is high risk. What does that reason tell you, and what does it not tell you?
drill.a: It tells you why the model's score is high: that value pushed the arithmetic up. It does not tell you that refreshing the creatives would keep the advertiser. That is a question about cause, and it needs different evidence.

recall.prompt: An account manager asks why a particular advertiser is on the risk list. Explain what you can tell her, and what you cannot.
recall.model_answer: I can show her the pushes: starting from an average advertiser, which of this advertiser's values moved the model's score up, and by how much — for example few active days, a CPA far over goal and stale creatives. That gives her a reason to open the call with. What I cannot tell her is that fixing those things would keep the account: a push is the model's arithmetic, weight times distance from average, not a cause. The same caution applies to the importance chart, where overlapping columns hide each other, and to a dependence curve, which is the model's behaviour and not a promise.

lessons.ask_assistant: For [model], produce three exhibits, and state on each the model and the rows used. One: permutation importance on [held-out rows] for each column and for each group of related columns ([groups]), as the drop in [metric]. Two: a partial dependence curve for [columns the business asks about]. Three: for each of the top [list size] rows, the three largest per-row contributions (coefficient times distance from the training mean for a linear model, SHAP values otherwise), with the row's value and the training mean beside each, plus the base value, so that base plus all contributions reproduces the row's score, after the S-curve if they are in log-odds. Caption every exhibit as a description of the model; no causal wording such as drives or impact.
audit_checklist: The importance table names its rows (held-out, with the row count) and shows single-column and grouped drops side by side
Each dependence curve names the model that drew it and is captioned as the model's behaviour

Per-row reasons show the row's value, the training average and the contribution; base value plus all contributions reproduces the printed score, after the S-curve when they are in log-odds and the score is a probability
A search of the text for drives, causes and impact finds none attached to a column
transfer: Lead scoring: why is this lead ranked first, and what does the model lean on across all leads?
Invalid traffic: explaining to a publisher which of their numbers got their traffic flagged.
A spend forecast for finance: which inputs the forecast relies on, and how its answer moves with each.

other_ways.approach: Use a model that explains itself: a shallow tree, or the weighted sum's own table of weights
other_ways.when: When the audience needs to follow the whole logic, and the simple model's score is close enough to the best.

other_ways.approach: Remove a column or a group, retrain, and compare the scores
other_ways.when: When the question is what the information is worth, rather than what this one fitted model happens to lean on.

other_ways.approach: Read the rows: pull twenty high-score and twenty low-score cases and look at them
other_ways.when: As a sanity check before trusting any explanation chart, and whenever a reason looks odd.

glossary.def: How far a model's score falls when one column's values are shuffled between rows.
The same test with a set of related columns shuffled together, so they cannot cover for each other.
The model's average prediction as one column is set to each value in turn; also called partial dependence.
One column's contribution to one prediction, in scorecard points: its weight times how far this case sits from average. Assistants call it a per-row contribution.
The name under which per-case pushes are computed for complex models.

lessons.title: Who is the model wrong about?
lessons.subtitle: What does one overall score hide, and what should the list be ranked by?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can ask for a model's results cut by business segment, read where the list falls short, and put what the list is ranked by in front of the business as a decision.

predict.q: The list of the 400 highest-risk advertisers catches about 42 percent of all churners. Among the largest third of accounts, what share of churners does the same list catch?
options: About 60 percent
About 42 percent, the same as overall
About 25 percent
Under 10 percent
predict.reveal: About 25 percent, against about 55 percent for small accounts. The lesson shows why, and why the model is not actually worse at ranking large accounts.

segments.narration: The list of the 400 highest-risk advertisers has been your best exhibit for weeks. More than half of them really churn. That is about four times what a random list would give you. Then someone on the commercial side sorts it by account size. 259 of the 400 are small accounts. Only 47 are large. Nothing is broken. The overall result was true, and it was hiding this. One number for everyone is an average, and an average can look healthy while one group inside it is poorly served. That is true of any model judged by one headline number, a list of leads likely to convert as much as this one. So before the list goes anywhere, cut the result open.

visual.title: Who is the model wrong about?
visual.sub: The list of 400 looks great. 259 of the 400 are small accounts.

segments.narration: Take the same list and cut it into three tiers by spend. [[1]] Among small accounts, 245 churned, and the list caught about 55 percent of them. [[2]] Among medium accounts it caught about a third. [[3]] Among large accounts, 117 churned, and the list caught about 25 percent. Recall, the share of churners you reach, is more than twice as high for small accounts as for large ones. Now weigh that against the money. Count what each churner was spending in the eight weeks before the snapshot, and large accounts are about two thirds of everything that walked out. The list is weakest exactly where a miss costs the most.

visual.title: The top-400 list, cut by account size
visual.note: Test months, tiers are thirds by spend. Spend lost = what the tier's churners spent in the 8 weeks before the snapshot; $1,373,066 in all.

segments.narration: So is the model worse at large accounts? No, and this is the part worth remembering. Score each tier separately, and the ranking is about equally good in all three, an AUC close to 0.84. Inside any tier, churners sit above stayers just as reliably. What differs is the level. Small accounts churn at about 18 percent and large ones at about 8, so small accounts carry higher scores across the board. One list, sorted by probability across everyone, fills up with small accounts before it ever reaches a risky large one. The ranking is sound inside each tier. The list is lopsided across them. That tilt is how this simulated world was built. Your own data may tilt another way, which is why you look.

visual.title: Equal ranking, unequal list
visual.note: Everyone: AUC 0.845, churn rate 13.2%, 400 places.

segments.narration: That raises a question nobody asked when the list was built: what should it be sorted by? [[1]] Sort by churn probability, as now, and the list holds about 42 percent of all churners, but only about a quarter of the spend that was lost. [[2]] Sort by probability times spend, the dollars you expect to lose, and the same slots hold fewer churners, about 29 percent, and 57 percent of the lost spend. The typical account on the first list spent under a thousand dollars in eight weeks. On the second, nearly five thousand. Same model, same scores, same number of slots. Only 137 names appear on both.

visual.title: Same model, same 400 slots, two ways to rank

left.label: Rank by churn probability
left.sub: 220 churners (41.7%) · 25.3% of lost spend · median account $744

right.label: Rank by probability × spend
right.sub: 151 churners (28.7%) · 57.0% of lost spend · median account $4,891

segments.narration: Neither list is the correct one. If the action is a cheap automated email, you want heads, and the first list reaches more of them. If it is an hour of a senior account manager's time, you probably want dollars. The model cannot make that choice. It belongs to whoever owns the retention budget. Your part is to put both lists side by side, so that the choice is made out loud and not by default. Sorting by probability was never neutral. It was a decision nobody noticed making.

visual.text: What you rank by is a decision. Make it out loud.
visual.sub: Heads or dollars: the model cannot choose for you.

segments.narration: The same cut works for any grouping the business cares about. [[1]] Overall, the list catches about 42 percent of churners. [[2]] [[3]] By size, you have seen the gap. [[4]] [[5]] By account manager there is another: about 45 percent for accounts without one, 28 for accounts with. [[6]] [[7]] By tenure there is hardly any gap at all. Then cut the percentages the same way. For large accounts the model predicts about 5 and a half percent, and about 8 and a half percent leave. The dollar ranking multiplies that low percentage by spend, so it still undercounts them. This is also how you check that a model is not quietly failing one group of clients. And remember that each slice is a smaller group, so its numbers wobble more.

visual.title: Share of churners the list catches, by segment
visual.note: Bars: share of churners caught. A separate check, predicted vs actual churn — small: 17.6% vs 18.3% · large: 5.5% vs 8.4% · new accounts: 12.6% vs 17.7% (caught as often as established accounts, but percentages 5 points low)

segments.narration: So, the brief and the audit. [[1]] Ask for every headline result again, cut by the segments the business cares about: size, account manager, tenure, vertical. For each slice the output must show four things. [[2]] The number of advertisers and of churners, so you can judge the wobble. [[3]] How many places on the list the slice got, and the share of its churners caught. [[4]] Predicted churn next to actual churn. [[5]] And the list built both ways, by probability and by probability times spend, with churners reached and dollars reached for each. If the business wants every tier covered, there is a third way: reserve places for each tier and take the riskiest accounts within it. A report with one overall number and no slices is not finished.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Every headline result by size, account manager, tenure, vertical
Per slice: advertisers and churners
Places on the list, and share of its churners caught
Predicted churn next to actual churn
The list ranked both ways: churners reached, dollars reached

segments.narration: So before a list leaves your hands, cut its results by the segments the business cares about, and get someone to choose what it is ranked by. The next module opens with the question stakeholders ask about a model's top column: if we change it, will churn go down?

visual.title: Before the list leaves your hands
items: One overall score is an average: cut it by segment
Equal ranking inside each tier can still give a lopsided list
Heads or dollars: what you rank by is a decision

takeaways: One overall score is an average: the same list caught about 55 percent of small churners and 25 percent of large ones.
Equal ranking inside each segment can still produce a lopsided list.
What you rank by, heads or dollars, is a decision to make on purpose.

quiz.concept: equal AUC by slice is not an equal list
quiz.q: The assistant's report says: AUC is 0.84 for small, 0.83 for medium and 0.85 for large accounts, so the model serves all sizes equally and the top-400 list needs no further checks by size. What is missing?
options: A separate model trained for each size tier, since one model cannot rank three sizes equally
Places on the list and churners caught per tier: one cut-off can still starve a tier
A significance test showing whether 0.85 for large accounts is truly higher than 0.83
The same three AUC figures recomputed on the training months, to confirm they are stable
quiz.why: AUC inside a tier says churners outrank stayers within that tier. The list applies one cut-off across tiers whose churn levels differ, so a low-churn tier can get few places and low recall despite an equal AUC: here 47 places and about 25 percent for large accounts. Equal AUC is reassuring, and is the tempting place to stop.

quiz.concept: what you rank by is a decision
quiz.q: The retention team has 400 call slots. Ranked by churn probability, the list reaches about 42 percent of churners and a quarter of the lost spend; ranked by probability times spend, about 29 percent and 57 percent. The head of sales asks which ranking is the right one. What do you say?
options: Probability: it is what the model was trained to predict, so it is the unbiased choice of the two
Probability times spend: it reaches more than twice the dollars, so it wins outright
Average the two rankings, so that the final list is not tilted towards either goal
Neither by itself: one reaches more accounts, the other more money; what is a call for?
quiz.why: The two lists serve different goals with the same model, so choosing between them is a business decision about the action and its cost. Using what the model predicts sounds neutral, but sorting by probability is itself a choice, one that here sends most slots to small accounts.

quiz.concept: an average hides the segment that matters
quiz.q: An invalid-traffic detector reports 80 percent recall overall. Cut by publisher size, it catches 86 percent of bad traffic on small publishers and 31 percent on the ten largest, which carry most of the spend. What is the right read?
options: The average hides that the detector is weakest where most of the money flows; report by tier
The overall figure is what counts; ten publishers is too small a group to conclude anything
The detector is unfair to small publishers and should be loosened for them
Recall of 80 percent is strong, so the figure for the large publishers must be a data error
quiz.why: The overall rate is dominated by the many small publishers, so it can look fine while the detector misses most of the bad traffic that costs money. A small group does mean a wobbly number, which is a reason to show the counts and look closer, not to ignore the slice that matters most.

quiz.concept: percentages by segment before multiplying by money
quiz.q: You rank by probability times spend. A check by size shows predicted against actual churn of 17.6 and 18.3 percent for small accounts, and 5.5 and 8.4 percent for large ones. What does this do to the dollar-ranked list?
options: It leaves the list as it was: a ranking depends only on the order of scores, not on their level
Large accounts are over-represented, because their probabilities are too high
Large accounts' expected loss is understated, so they still get too few places
The list is fine, but the model must now be retrained on large accounts alone
quiz.why: Multiplying by spend turns a probability into expected dollars, so a probability that runs low for large accounts shrinks their expected loss by the same proportion. That only the order matters is true when everyone is sorted by probability alone; it stops being true once percentages that are off by different amounts in different groups are multiplied by money.

review.concept: one overall score can hide the segment where the model fails

variants.q: A ticket classifier is 94 percent accurate overall. By category: billing 97 percent on 600 tickets, how-to questions 94 percent on 300, account lockouts 58 percent on 60. Lockouts are the urgent ones. What do you report?
options: 94 percent accuracy: the classifier is ready to be switched on for every category
The lockout figure rests on only 60 tickets, so it is too noisy to report
Strong on routine tickets, weak on the urgent ones; lockouts need a fix or a human
Accuracy recomputed after removing the lockout tickets from the test set
variants.why: The overall figure is carried by the large, easy categories and hides the one that matters most. Sixty tickets makes 58 percent a wobbly number, which is a reason to show the count beside it, not to drop the only slice where a miss is costly.

variants.q: A spend forecast is off by 3 percent across all markets combined. The three established markets are each within 2 percent; a market launched this year is off by 19 percent. Finance is using the forecast to set the new market's budget. What is the right read?
options: Good in total, poor for the decision it is being used for; show the error by market
An error of 3 percent is excellent, so the forecast is fit to use for every market
The new market's error will average out against the others, as the total already shows
The forecast is wrong everywhere and should be rebuilt from scratch before anyone uses it
variants.why: The total is dominated by the established markets, so its error says little about the new one, and the new one is the decision at hand. Errors do offset in a total, which is exactly why the total cannot be used to judge a single slice.

variants.q: A lead-scoring list of 200 contains 120 leads that convert, far better than chance. Cut by region, enterprise leads from one region are 40 percent of pipeline value and hold 9 of the 200 places. The model's AUC is nearly the same in every region. What should you ask for next?
options: An interval on each region's AUC, since nine places out of 200 must mean one of them is lower
A more complex model, since this one is clearly biased against leads from that region
A longer list, so that the region's number of places rises in proportion to its value
Places on the list and converters caught per region: equal ranking, unequal list
variants.why: AUC within a region measures the ordering inside it. One list across regions also depends on how common conversion is in each, so a valuable region with a low rate can get almost no places. A fancier model does not change that arithmetic.

review.concept: what you rank by, heads or dollars, is a decision

variants.q: An upsell model scores every account's chance of upgrading. Sales has 50 demo slots. Ranked by probability, the 50 are mostly tiny accounts; ranked by probability times upgrade value, they are larger accounts with lower odds. A manager asks you to send the correct list. What is the best response?
options: Send the probability list: it has the likeliest upgraders, which is what the model is for
Send the value-weighted list: revenue is always the goal of an upsell campaign
Send a random 50, since the two lists disagree and neither can be trusted
Send both, with upgrades and revenue expected from each, and ask what the demos are for
variants.why: The model supplies probabilities; whether to maximise upgrades or revenue is a choice about the goal and the cost of a slot. The lists disagreeing is not a flaw in the model. It is the decision showing itself.

variants.q: Investigators can review 30 publishers a week. Ranked by probability of fraud, the top 30 are mostly tiny publishers; ranked by probability times spend at stake, they hold fewer confirmed cases but far more money. Which statement is correct?
options: The probability ranking is correct, because it finds the most fraud for each review spent
Both are valid; the choice depends on whether the aim is cases closed or money protected
The money ranking is correct, because small publishers are never worth an investigator's time
The two should match; a difference means the model's percentages are wrong
variants.why: Same scores, different objectives. Most cases per review and most money per review are both defensible, so the ranking rule is a policy to be chosen. The two lists differ whenever size and risk are not the same thing.

variants.q: The team switches the churn list from ranking by probability to ranking by probability times spend. Next month's report says the model has got worse: churners on the list fell from 220 to 151. What is the right read?
options: The model did not change, the goal did: judge the new list by lost spend reached
Correct: fewer churners on the list means the model's ranking has degraded since last month
The model should be retrained, since a drop of that size is well beyond noise
The switch was a mistake, and the probability ranking should be restored
variants.why: The scores are identical; only the sort key changed, trading churners reached for dollars reached, here from about a quarter of the lost spend to 57 percent. Measuring the new list with the old yardstick makes a deliberate trade look like a failure.

drill.q: A model has a strong overall score. Why is that not enough before you hand its list to the business?
drill.a: Because one overall score is an average. It can hide a segment where the list catches far fewer cases, and that may be the segment that matters most in money. So you ask for the same results cut by the segments the business cares about.

drill.q: You can sort a risk list by probability, or by probability times spend. Which one is correct?
drill.a: Neither is correct in itself. Sorting by probability reaches more of the customers who leave. Sorting by probability times spend reaches more of the money. Which you want depends on the action and what it costs, so it is a decision someone should make on purpose.

recall.prompt: The churn list has a strong overall hit rate. Explain why you would still cut the results by account size before handing it over, and what the cut showed in this course's data.
recall.model_answer: An overall number is an average and can hide a group the list serves badly. Cut by size, the top-400 list caught about 55 percent of small churners but only about 25 percent of large ones, although large accounts were about two thirds of the spend lost. The model ranked equally well inside each tier; the list was lopsided because small accounts churn more and one list sorted by probability fills up with them. Ranking by probability times spend reaches fewer churners and more dollars, so what to rank by is a decision for the business, made with both lists side by side.

lessons.ask_assistant: Take [model]'s scores on [held-out rows] and the top [list size] list. Recompute every headline result by [segments the business cares about]: for each slice print the rows, the [outcome] cases, the places on the list, the share of its [outcome] cases caught, [ranking metric] within the slice, and predicted against actual [outcome] rate. Show that the slice counts add up to the totals. Then build the list a second way, ranked by probability times [value at stake], and print for both lists the [outcome] cases reached, the [value] reached and how many names they share. Do not recommend a ranking; lay out the trade.
audit_checklist: Every headline number repeated by segment, with the count of advertisers and churners in each; the segment counts add up to the totals
Per segment: places on the list, share of churners caught, and AUC within the segment
Predicted churn beside actual churn for each segment
The list built both ways, by probability and by probability × spend, with churners and dollars reached
transfer: Invalid traffic: does the detector catch as much on the largest publishers as on the long tail of small ones?
A spend forecast for finance: is the error for the newest market anything like the error for the total?
Lead scoring: which regions or deal sizes get almost no places on the list, and should it be ranked by chance of converting or by expected deal value?

other_ways.approach: Reserve places for each tier: take the riskiest accounts within each size tier
other_ways.when: When the business wants guaranteed coverage of every tier and a rule that is easy to explain.

other_ways.approach: Separate lists per segment, each worked by the team that owns it
other_ways.when: When segments get different actions, such as a call for large accounts and an email for small ones.

other_ways.approach: Correct the percentages per segment before multiplying by spend (recalibration)
other_ways.when: When you rank by expected dollars and the percentages are off by different amounts in different segments.

glossary.def: The same result recomputed for one group of customers only, such as large accounts.
The probability that a customer leaves times what they spend: the dollars you expect to lose.
What a list is sorted by; choosing it decides who gets the limited places.

lessons.title: Drivers are not causes
lessons.subtitle: What does a gap between two groups, or a model's weight, actually tell you?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can tell an association from an effect, and say what a gap between groups can and cannot support.

predict.q: Advertisers with conversion tracking churn about 11 points less than those without. Suppose you could run the world twice: once with tracking on for every advertiser, once with it off for all of them. How far apart would the two churn rates be?
options: About 11 points
About 6 points
About 2 points
They would be the same
predict.reveal: About 2 points, in this simulated world. The lesson shows where the other 9 come from, and why the table alone could never have told you.

segments.narration: It is the quarterly review, and a slide goes up. Advertisers with conversion tracking churn 11 points less. Recommendation: push tracking to every account. The arithmetic is fine. About 7 percent of advertisers with tracking churned, against about 18 percent of those without. But the slide measured a gap between two groups, then promised what will happen if you move an advertiser across it. The first is a GROUP BY. The second is a prediction about an action nobody has taken. This lesson is about the distance between them, in any gap between groups: if advertisers who use the video format spend more, that alone does not say what pushing video would do.

visual.title: Drivers are not causes
visual.sub: What a gap between groups can and cannot tell you

segments.narration: Here we can do something you can never do at work. This course's data is simulated, so we can run the world twice: once with tracking switched on for every advertiser, once with it switched off for all of them. Same advertisers, same everything else. What would have happened to the same advertisers otherwise has a name: the counterfactual. [[1]] The gap on the slide, call it the naive gap, was about 11 points. [[2]] The effect of actually switching tracking on is about 2 points. So tracking helps, a little. We know that true effect only because this world was built by hand. Real data gives you the first number and never the second.

right.label: True effect of switching it on
right.sub: 10.7% if everyone had it, 12.9% if nobody did (gap computed before rounding)

segments.narration: So where do the other 9 points come from? Some advertisers are simply more sophisticated. [[1]] Those advertisers are more likely to install tracking. [[2]] They are also less likely to churn, with tracking or without it. [[3]] And sophistication is not a column anywhere in the table. So the tracked group is stacked with advertisers who were going to stay anyway. [[4]] The naive gap mixes two things: what tracking does, and who chooses tracking. That second part is called selection bias. A hidden trait that pushes both the practice and the outcome is a common cause. The textbook word is confounder.

visual.title: One hidden trait, two results
items: Sophisticated advertisers install tracking more often
Sophisticated advertisers churn less, tracking or not
Sophistication is not a column in the table
Naive gap = what tracking does + who chooses tracking

segments.narration: The usual reply is: then control for it. Ask the assistant to compare like with like, holding tenure, spend, vertical and the rest fixed. That is what a regression weight does. [[1]] The naive gap was about 11 points. [[2]] Adjusted, it shrinks to about six and a half. [[3]] The truth is still about 2. Adjusting removed the part of the mirage the table can see. It cannot remove the part that comes from a trait nobody recorded. And nothing in the output warns you how far off it still is. Adjusted is a better description. It is still not the effect of acting.

visual.title: Tracking and churn: three numbers
visual.note: Adjusted for tenure, spend, campaigns, creatives, account manager and vertical.

segments.narration: Now the question your stakeholders love. What separates advertisers who hit their CPA goal from those who do not, and can we turn that into best practices? Take five candidates: automated bidding, four or more creatives, fresh creatives, an account manager, an optimisation review. Each has three numbers: the naive gap, the adjusted gap, and the true effect. Advertisers with fresh creatives hit their goal about 20 points more often, and freshness is truly worth about 13. So part of a gap can be real. Advertisers with an account manager hit their goal about 10 points more often. Here the true effect on hitting the goal is zero. That whole gap is who gets an account manager. Step through all five, and guess each true effect before you reveal it.

visual.name: practices
visual.title: Five practices: naive gap, adjusted gap, true effect
visual.note: Guess the true effect of each practice before you reveal it.

segments.narration: One of the five does something worse than shrink. [[1]] Accounts that had an optimisation review hit their goal about 25 points less often than the rest. As a best practice, that reads: stop doing reviews. [[2]] Adjust for tenure, spend, vertical and the other practices, and the gap does not move. [[3]] Rerun the world, and the review helps, by about 9 points. The gap has the wrong sign. Reviews are not handed out by lottery. They go to accounts already struggling, for reasons the table cannot see. So reviewed accounts look worse even though the review made them better. Here adjusting brought us no closer to the truth. It is never guaranteed to.

visual.title: Optimisation review and hitting the CPA goal
visual.note: Goal-hit rate: 46.9% with a review, 72.2% without.

segments.narration: Now connect this to your models. A column's weight in a regression is the same kind of number: a gap, adjusted for the other columns. Importance scores inherit that. [[1]] The churn model's weight for tracking takes a bit over 4 points off predicted churn. [[2]] The true effect is about 2. The weight is not a mistake. For prediction it is exactly right: tracking does tell you who is likely to stay. It does not tell you what happens if you install it. So choose your words. Tracking is associated with lower churn. Drives, causes and impact are words the table has not earned.
