visual.title: A model's weight is the same kind of number

right.label: True effect of tracking
right.sub: knowable only in a simulated world

segments.narration: Brief and audit. When you ask the assistant for drivers, every comparison must carry its evidence. [[1]] Group sizes and an interval beside every gap. [[2]] The adjusted gap, and what it was adjusted for. That list must hold nothing the practice itself changes: adjust for CPA when judging automated bidding, and you subtract the effect you are after. [[3]] One line per practice on who gets it or chooses it. The table cannot know that: ask the team that assigns the practice, and have the assistant print your line beside each gap. If it is the keen ones, or the ones in trouble, you know which way the number leans. [[4]] Then the wording: if the report says drives, impact or lift, and nobody tested the change, send it back.

visual.title: Brief and audit: a drivers report must show
items: Group sizes and an interval for every gap
The adjusted gap, and what it was adjusted for: nothing the practice itself changes
Who gets or chooses each practice: your line, from the team that assigns it
Wording: "is associated with", never "drives"

segments.narration: So when a slide turns a gap into a recommendation, you know what to send back: the gap is real, the promise untested. Testing it means making the change yourself, for a randomly chosen group of advertisers. That is an experiment, and it is the next lesson.

visual.text: A gap tells you what goes with an outcome. It does not tell you what happens if you change it.
visual.sub: Next: experiments

takeaways: A gap between groups says what goes with an outcome, not what happens if you change it.
Adjusting, like a model's weight, only removes differences the table records; the result can still be too big, empty or backwards.
Ask who gets or chooses the practice, and write "is associated with" until someone tests the change.

quiz.concept: a gap is not an effect
quiz.q: Advertisers running four or more creatives per campaign hit their CPA goal about 22 points more often than the rest, measured on thousands of advertisers with a tight interval. The onboarding lead wants to make four creatives mandatory and promise a 22-point lift. What is the right read?
options: Promise it: a gap on thousands of advertisers, with an interval this tight, is solid evidence.
The gap is real, but who chooses more creatives may explain much of it; the lift is unknown.
Hold off: a gap this large is probably noise, so wait to see whether it repeats next month.
Promise about half of it: true effects usually come out near half the size of the naive gap.
quiz.why: A tight interval says the gap between the groups is not noise; it says nothing about why the groups differ. Advertisers who run more creatives may be better run in other ways too, so forcing the practice could deliver far less. And 'about half' is not a rule either: in this course's world one gap was pure mirage and another had the wrong sign.

quiz.concept: who gets it can flip the sign
quiz.q: The assistant's 'drivers of CPA success' report says: 'Accounts that had an optimisation review hit their goal 25 points less often. The gap is unchanged after controlling for tenure, spend, vertical, number of campaigns and the other practices. Recommendation: scale reviews back.' What has the report missed?
options: It used a simple regression; a more flexible model would have adjusted more accurately.
A gap of 25 points is too large to be real, so a join must have duplicated rows upstream.
It controlled for too few columns; adding every column in the table would settle it.
It never asks who gets a review: if they go to struggling accounts, the gap is biased against reviews.
quiz.why: Reviews are given to accounts already in trouble, which pulls the reviewed group's rate down and can outweigh a real benefit, even flip the sign: in the simulation the review actually helps by about 9 points. Surviving the controls proves little, because adjusting only removes differences the table records, and neither a fancier model nor more columns can adjust for a reason that was never written down.

quiz.q: An upsell model predicts which customers will buy the premium tier, and it validates well on held-out customers. Its most important feature is logins in the last 30 days. A product manager proposes reminder emails to get everyone logging in more, 'since logins drive upgrades'. What is the right read?
options: Logins help predict who upgrades; that does not show pushing logins up makes anyone upgrade. Test it.
Sound plan: the model holds up on unseen customers, so its top feature is a proven lever.
Check the model's curve for logins: if predicted upgrades rise with logins, the emails will work.
Importance scores cannot be trusted at all, so logins should be dropped from the model.
quiz.why: Good validation proves the model predicts well, not that its inputs are causes: customers who already want the product log in more, so interest is a common cause of both. The model's curve for logins is only the model's behaviour restated, and dropping a useful predictor fixes nothing. To learn what the emails do, send them to a random group and compare.

quiz.q: You must write one playbook line about automated bidding. You have a naive gap of 19 points in goal attainment, 15 points after adjusting, and no test. Which line is honest?
options: Switching on automated bidding lifts goal attainment by 19 points, based on some 7,000 advertisers.
After controlling for account differences, automated bidding drives a 15-point improvement in goal attainment.
Advertisers on automated bidding hit goal 19 points more often (15 after adjusting); the effect is untested.
Automated bidding has no proven effect on goal attainment, so it should be left out of the playbook entirely.
quiz.why: The honest line reports what was seen at the strength it was seen: an association, raw and adjusted, with the limit stated. 'Drives' after controls is still a causal claim the table cannot support, because adjusting only handles recorded differences. Leaving it out overcorrects: an untested association is still worth reporting, and worth testing.

review.concept: a gap between groups mixes the effect with who is in each group

variants.q: Advertisers with an account manager hit their CPA goal about 10 points more often than self-serve advertisers. Sales proposes giving every account a manager 'to raise goal attainment by 10 points'. What should you ask first?
options: How accounts come to get a manager, and whether those accounts would hit their goal anyway.
Whether a 10-point gap is statistically significant, given the size of each group.
Whether a manager costs less per account than a 10-point lift in goal attainment is worth.
Whether the 10-point gap holds in every vertical, since an average can hide a reversal.
variants.why: Managers are assigned, not dealt at random, so the gap mixes what a manager does with which accounts get one; in this course's simulation the true effect on hitting the goal was zero. Significance, cost and a cut by vertical only matter once you know the gap is an effect at all.

variants.q: A retailer finds that customers who installed its mobile app spend 40 percent more per year than those who did not. Marketing wants to pay for app installs, expecting the same 40 percent from each new installer. What is the flaw?
options: The 40 percent is an average that big spenders pull up, so the forecast should use the median.
The 40 percent mixes seasons; it should be recomputed within each quarter before use.
Customers who chose the app were likely keener buyers already; the gap overstates an install.
App and in-store spending are recorded differently, so the two groups cannot be compared.
variants.why: Installing is a choice, and the customers who make it are likely the loyal ones: a common cause of both installing and spending. A median, or a cut by quarter, changes how the gap is summarised, not why the two groups differ, and people nudged into an install are not the same kind of customer as people who sought the app out.

variants.q: In a sales funnel, leads who attended a product webinar convert at 18 percent; leads who did not convert at 6 percent. The sales director wants every lead pushed into a webinar. Which reading is soundest?
options: Webinars triple conversion, so push every lead into one as early in the funnel as possible.
The gap is so large that, even discounted heavily, a webinar must at least double conversion.
Webinars clearly do nothing for conversion; the whole gap is which leads choose to attend.
Leads who sign up were already more interested: the gap shows who attends, not what it does.
variants.why: Interest drives both attending and buying, so the gap cannot be read as the webinar's effect, however large it is. But nor does it show the webinar is useless: a gap can overstate, be empty, or even have the wrong sign. You find out by inviting a random half.

review.concept: adjusting, and a model's weight, only handle what the table records

variants.q: Customers who were given a retention discount cancel more often than customers who were not, and the gap persists after the assistant controls for plan, region and tenure. A manager concludes that discounts cause cancellations. What is the better read?
options: With plan, region and tenure held fixed, other explanations are out: the discounts backfire.
Discounts go to customers who already looked likely to leave, which no control records.
Three controls are too few; with enough columns added, the discount's true effect will appear.
It must be noise or a data error, because a discount cannot plausibly make customers cancel.
variants.why: Help aimed at people in trouble makes the helped group look worse, and adjusting for plan, region and tenure cannot fix that, because the trigger (someone judged this customer to be wavering) was never recorded. More columns help only if the real reason is among them, which the table cannot tell you.

variants.q: A fraud model's strongest weight is 'publisher was manually audited': with the other columns held fixed, audited publishers get a much higher predicted rate of invalid traffic. A colleague says audits must be making traffic worse. What is the right read?
options: It helps prediction, but audits follow suspicion; it says nothing about what an audit does.
With the other columns held fixed, the weight isolates the audit's own effect on traffic quality.
The model must be broken or leaking: a quality audit cannot sensibly raise invalid traffic.
The column misleads the model and should be removed, even if the held-out score falls.
variants.why: A weight is a gap adjusted for the other columns, which makes it an association still. Audits go to publishers someone already suspected, and that suspicion is not a column, so 'held fixed' cannot separate the audit from the reason for it. The column remains a good predictor; it is just not evidence about the audit's effect.

variants.q: An analyst presents: 'Advertisers using the new bulk-upload tool spend 12 percent more, after controlling for 30 variables, so this is the tool's causal impact.' What is the weakest point in that claim?
options: Thirty controls is too many for one model, so the 12 percent is probably an artefact of overfitting.
A difference of 12 percent in spend is too small to be worth a causal claim in either direction.
A tree model would have adjusted for those 30 variables more flexibly than a regression can.
Controls remove only recorded differences; why advertisers adopt the tool may not be recorded.
variants.why: The number of controls is not the issue; what they cover is. If ambitious, growing advertisers are the ones who pick up a bulk tool, and ambition is not a column, the adjusted gap still carries it. Changing the model type changes how you adjust, not what you are able to adjust for.

drill.q: A dashboard shows that advertisers who use some feature do better than those who do not. Before anyone recommends the feature, what is the first question to ask?
drill.a: Ask who chooses that feature, or who is given it. If those advertisers differ in ways that also affect the outcome, the gap mixes the feature's effect with who uses it. It can be too big, empty, or even backwards.

drill.q: Why can adjusting for other columns not turn a gap between groups into a proven effect?
drill.a: Because you can only adjust for what is in the table. If the real common cause was never recorded, the adjusted number still carries it, and nothing in the output tells you how much.

recall.prompt: A stakeholder says: advertisers with conversion tracking churn 11 points less, so pushing tracking will cut churn by 11 points. Explain in 30 seconds why that does not follow.
recall.model_answer: The 11 points is a gap between two groups that differ in more than tracking: more sophisticated advertisers both install tracking and churn less anyway, so the gap mixes what tracking does with who chooses it. Adjusting for the columns we have shrinks the gap but cannot remove a cause that is not in the table. In our simulated world the real effect was about 2 points; with real data the only way to find out is to test the change. Until then the honest wording is 'associated with'.

lessons.ask_assistant: For each practice in [list of practices], compare [units] that have it with those that do not on [outcome] over [window]. Show both group sizes, both rates, the raw gap with a 95 percent interval, and the gap after adjusting for [columns fixed before the practice was adopted]; list exactly what you adjusted for, and adjust for nothing the practice itself could change. Beside each gap print, word for word, the line I supply on how [units] come to have that practice: [practice: chosen by them / assigned by us / triggered by poor performance]. Do not infer that from the data. Describe every result as an association; do not write 'drives', 'impact' or 'lift'.
audit_checklist: Group sizes and an interval beside every gap
The list of columns adjusted for, with nothing on it that the practice itself changes (CPA, spend trend): controlling for the route a practice works through removes the very effect you are measuring
Beside each gap, the line you supplied on who gets or chooses the practice, printed word for word, and no guess about assignment that the assistant inferred from the table
The wording says 'associated with'; 'drives', 'causes' and 'impact' appear only where a change was actually tested
transfer: Do video creatives really earn a higher CTR, or do the advertisers who can afford video differ in other ways?
Customers who use the mobile app spend more: would pushing the app raise spend?
Publishers on the premium list show fewer invalid clicks: is it the list, or who was picked for it?

other_ways.approach: Run a randomised experiment: give the change to a random group and compare
other_ways.when: Whenever you can control who gets the change or the encouragement; it balances even the causes nobody recorded, by design and without extra assumptions (next lesson).

other_ways.approach: Compare the change over time in a group that got a launch with a similar group that did not
other_ways.when: When the practice was rolled out to one group on a known date and an experiment is no longer possible (lesson 5-3).

other_ways.approach: Ask the people who assign the practice how they decide
other_ways.when: Always, and first: knowing that reviews go to struggling accounts tells you which way a gap is biased before any analysis.

glossary.def: Two things that tend to occur together in the data, whatever the reason.
The raw difference in an outcome between those who do something and those who do not, taken at face value.
A trait that influences both the practice and the outcome, so the gap between the groups differs from what the practice itself does.
Comparing like with like on the columns you have, usually with a regression; it cannot account for anything that was not recorded.
How much the outcome would change if you changed the practice and nothing else.
What would have happened to the same advertisers under the other choice; real data never shows it, so it can only be estimated, best by a randomised experiment.
The part of a gap that comes from who chose or was given the practice, not from what the practice does.

lessons.title: Experiments
lessons.subtitle: How do you find out what a practice really does?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can specify a randomised test of a practice, and read its result as an estimate with an interval.

predict.q: Today 60 percent of advertisers hit their CPA goal. You want an experiment that can reliably detect a lift to 62 percent. Roughly how many advertisers do you need in each group?
options: About 350
About 1,500
Over 9,000
Any size works if the split is random
predict.reveal: Over 9,000 in each group. The lesson shows why small effects need big groups, and what a too-small experiment looks like.

segments.narration: The playbook is due on Friday, and three practices are up for a place in it: automated bidding, more creatives per campaign, fresher creatives. What you hold is three gaps, raw and adjusted. Each could be too big, empty, or backwards, and the table cannot say which. So what can you responsibly write? Today, only that these practices are associated with hitting the goal. To write that one of them works, you need a comparison where the hidden trait is the same on both sides. There is one dependable way to get that, for a playbook practice or a new rule for routing support tickets alike: let chance decide who gets the change.

visual.title: Experiments
visual.sub: Let a coin decide who gets the change

segments.narration: [[1]] Flip a coin for each advertiser. [[2]] Heads get the change. Tails carry on as before: the control group. [[3]] Then compare the same outcome in both groups. The coin knows nothing about the advertisers. So the sophisticated ones land on both sides in about equal numbers. So does every other trait, including the ones nobody thought to record. You have not measured the common cause. You have made it irrelevant. The two groups now differ in one systematic way only: the change itself. So the gap in the outcome is the effect of the change, give or take noise. That is a randomised experiment.

steps.label: Randomise
steps.sub: a coin flip for each advertiser

steps.label: Treat
steps.sub: heads get the change; tails are the control group

steps.label: Compare
steps.sub: same outcome, same window, both groups

segments.narration: You cannot force an advertiser onto automated bidding. [[1]] What you can randomise is the encouragement: the coin decides who gets the prompt, the email or the call. [[2]] Then compare everyone who was encouraged with everyone who was not, whatever they went on to do. [[3]] Do not compare only the ones who took it up. They chose to: the trap from the last lesson. What you measure is the effect of the nudge, not of the practice itself. [[4]] So word it that way. With made-up numbers: advertisers prompted to switch hit their goal 3 points more often, give or take 2. About 40 percent of them switched. It is still the right number for your decision: the nudge is what you control.

visual.title: When you cannot force a practice
items: Randomise the encouragement: a prompt, an email, a call
Compare everyone encouraged with everyone not
Never compare only those who took it up
Write: "prompted advertisers hit goal X pts more often (interval); N% switched"

segments.narration: Two decisions belong before launch. First, write down the outcome and its window: share hitting their CPA goal over the next 8 weeks, say. Choose after looking, and you will pick whichever cut looks best. Second, size. Margins of error shrink slowly as groups grow, so small effects need big groups. Suppose 60 percent hit their goal today. [[1]] To reliably detect a lift of 10 points, you need about 350 advertisers in each group. [[2]] For a 5 point lift, about 1,470 in each. [[3]] For a 2 point lift, over 9,000. Count advertisers, not impressions: the coin is flipped once per advertiser. Reliably means four times in five. That chance of catching the lift is the test's statistical power. If you cannot reach the size, the test cannot answer the question.

visual.title: Advertisers needed in each group, starting from 60% hitting goal
visual.note: Sized to detect the lift 4 times in 5 (80% statistical power), with a 5% false-alarm rate. The unit is the advertiser, not the impression.

segments.narration: In a side simulation of this world, half of the 12,000 advertisers, chosen by coin flip, get a call from the success team, and we count who churns. [[1]] Being simulated, it comes with the truth: the call cuts churn by about 3 points. It also allows something impossible at work: the same experiment run 200 times, with fresh coin flips. [[2]] The measured effect ranged from just over 1 point to nearly four and a half. [[3]] Each run also reports an interval, and in 95 percent of runs it contained the truth. One experiment is one draw. The interval says how far that draw may sit from the truth.

stats.label: true effect of the call on churn
range of the measured effect over 200 runs
of runs whose interval contained the truth

segments.narration: Now read a single run as you would at work, with no truth column. [[1]] Take the run on all 12,000 advertisers. The measured effect is about 3 points. Its interval runs from about 2 points to about 4. [[2]] Now one month of advertisers, 2,000 of them. The estimate is almost the same, but the interval runs from almost nothing to over 5 points. The call probably helps. Whether it pays for a team, that run cannot say. Early on, every test is a small one, and small groups swing. Peek every morning and stop when the number looks good, and you have chosen your result. Fix the size first. Read it once.

visual.title: Same call, two sizes of experiment

right.label: One month: 2,000 advertisers
right.sub: 95% interval 0.2 to 5.4

segments.narration: Back to the playbook. For each claim, say which tier of evidence stands behind it. [[1]] Observed: advertisers who do this hit their goal more often. [[2]] Adjusted: the gap holds up when you compare like with like. Better, and still an association. [[3]] Tested: we randomised the encouragement and measured the lift, with its interval. Only the third earns the words works, lifts or causes. All three can appear in a playbook, as long as the wording matches the tier. Your three practices sit at tier two. Write them that way, and propose a test for the one that matters most.

visual.title: Evidence tiers: match the wording to the tier
items: Observed: "advertisers who do this hit goal more often"
Adjusted: "and the gap holds comparing like with like"
Tested: "randomised; the lift was X, interval Y to Z"

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask the assistant for the design before any analysis. [[1]] The plan, written before the results: outcome, window, group size, and the smallest lift that size can detect. [[2]] The counts assigned to each group, with a table showing the groups looked alike before the change: same typical spend, same share with tracking. If not, ask how they were really assigned. [[3]] The comparison is by assignment: everyone encouraged against everyone not. [[4]] And one estimate with its interval, read at the planned size. If the change cannot be withheld, propose a random holdout, or a rollout in random order: accounts still waiting are the control group.

visual.title: Brief and audit: an experiment must show
items: The plan, written first: outcome, window, group size
Counts per group, and that the groups were alike beforehand
Compared by assignment, not by who took it up
One estimate with its interval, at the planned size

segments.narration: So when the playbook needs the word works, you know which design earns it, sized before it starts. Sometimes the coin is not on offer: the change has already launched, to a whole group at once. What you can honestly say then is the next lesson.

visual.text: Randomise who gets the change, and the hidden common cause lands equally on both sides.
visual.sub: Next: when the change has already launched

takeaways: A coin flip spreads every trait, recorded or not, across both groups, so the remaining gap is the effect of the change.
Decide the outcome, the window and the group size before launch; small effects need big groups.
Read one estimate with its interval at the planned size, and word the claim by its tier: observed, adjusted or tested.

quiz.q: You randomise an in-product prompt recommending automated bidding: 3,000 advertisers see it, 3,000 do not. About 40 percent of those who saw it switched automated bidding on. The assistant reports: 'Advertisers who switched on had a goal-hit rate 14 points above the control group.' What is wrong with that comparison?
options: It is right for switchers; multiply the 14 points by the 40 percent uptake for the prompt's effect.
Switchers chose to switch, so they differ; compare everyone shown the prompt with everyone not.
With 3,000 per group and only 40 percent uptake, the test is too small to conclude anything.
The control group should be advertisers already on automated bidding, to isolate the practice.
quiz.why: The coin decided who saw the prompt, not who acted on it. The 40 percent who switched are the keen ones, so comparing them with the control group brings the hidden trait straight back and undoes the randomisation. The clean comparison is by assignment: all 3,000 shown against all 3,000 not shown, which measures the effect of the prompt. Scaling the 14 points by the uptake does not rescue it, because the 14 already contains the difference between keen advertisers and the rest.

quiz.concept: an estimate comes with an interval
quiz.q: An outreach experiment on one month of advertisers finds that the call cuts churn by 2.8 points, with an interval from 0.2 to 5.4. The success lead wants to hire four callers 'because calls cut churn by 2.8 points'. What is the best read?
options: The call probably helps, but by anywhere from near zero to over 5 points; plan for the low end.
The interval excludes zero, so 2.8 points is established and can go into the business case.
An interval this wide means the randomisation failed, so throw the result out and rerun.
An interval this wide means the experiment found nothing, so treat the call as having no effect.
quiz.why: An interval that only just clears zero tells you the direction, not the size. Hiring on 2.8 points treats one noisy draw as the truth, when the same call could be worth almost nothing or nearly twice as much. A wide interval is what a small experiment honestly looks like; it does not mean the randomisation failed or that nothing was found.

quiz.q: A team tests two ad headlines in an experiment planned to run three weeks. They check the dashboard every morning. On day four, headline B is ahead by 3 points and flagged as significant, so they stop the test and ship B. What is the problem?
options: Four days is fine; they only needed to confirm the gap on a second metric before shipping.
They should also have reported the segments where B won by most, to make the result more useful.
They needed a third headline in the test to act as a control for the other two.
Early gaps on small groups swing widely; stopping on the first good day picks a lucky moment.
quiz.why: Check every day and noise will sooner or later produce a 'significant' gap; stopping right then turns that luck into your result. The size and the stopping date are fixed in advance and the result is read once. Hunting for the segments where B won by most is the same mistake in another form: choosing what to report after looking. A second metric read at the same lucky moment inherits the same luck.

quiz.q: A support team wants to know whether a new onboarding call reduces tickets. A colleague suggests letting account managers pick which new customers get the call, 'because they know who needs it', and then comparing ticket counts. Which design tells you what the call does?
options: The managers' picks: aiming the call at customers who need it most gives the clearest effect.
The managers' picks, with the comparison adjusted for customer size and plan afterwards.
A coin flip: only chance makes the two groups alike in the traits nobody recorded.
Either one: with enough new customers, the question of who gets the call washes out.
quiz.why: Managers pick on judgement, which is exactly the kind of reason that never becomes a column, so their picks differ from the rest before any call is made. Adjusting handles only recorded differences, and more customers just makes a biased gap more precise. A coin cannot know who needs the call, which is why its two groups are comparable.

review.concept: randomising balances what you cannot see

variants.q: A new bid-recommendation panel is offered to all advertisers. Those who opt in spend 20 percent more afterwards than those who do not. Why would a randomised rollout have told you more?
options: Opt-in groups are usually too small for a stable estimate; a random rollout fixes the sizes.
Chance makes the two groups alike in every trait, ambition included; the gap is then the panel.
Randomly assigned groups have less noise, so the same effect shows up larger and clearer.
Opt-in data cannot be given a margin of error, so nobody could say if 20 percent is real.
variants.why: Advertisers who opt in are likely the ambitious, growing ones, so they would have spent more anyway. Random assignment does not make effects bigger or samples larger; it makes the groups comparable, which is exactly what letting advertisers choose destroys.

variants.q: Marketing emails a discount to its 'most engaged' customers and compares their purchases with everyone else's. To measure what the email itself does, what should change?
options: Send the email to many more customers, so the comparison rests on a bigger, steadier sample.
Compare the emailed customers with last year's most engaged customers over the same weeks.
Keep the comparison, but adjust it for customers' age, region and number of past purchases.
Hold back a random share of the engaged customers, and compare the emailed ones with them.
variants.why: Engaged customers buy more whether or not they are emailed, so comparing them with everyone else measures engagement. A random holdout inside the same group differs from the emailed customers only by the email. A bigger send, or a few adjustments, leaves the real problem, who was picked for the email, exactly where it was.

variants.q: A pricing team lets sales reps decide which prospects are offered a 10 percent discount, then finds that discounted prospects close less often. With 20,000 prospects, a colleague says the sample is big enough to trust the result. What is the right response?
options: Size does not fix who was chosen: reps may discount the very deals they already fear losing.
Agreed: with 20,000 prospects the margin of error is tiny, so 'discounts hurt sales' is safe.
The result must be a data error, because a discount cannot reduce the chance of closing a sale.
Split the 20,000 by region and deal size, and report the segments where the discount works.
variants.why: A large sample shrinks noise, not bias. If reps offer discounts on shaky deals, the discounted group was weaker from the start, and 20,000 rows only make that built-in gap more precise. Randomising who is offered the discount is what would make the two groups comparable.

review.concept: one experiment is an estimate with an interval: size it first, read it once

variants.q: A feature test with 150 users per group shows conversion of 10 percent in the control group and 12 percent with the feature; the difference is 'not significant'. The product manager concludes that the feature does nothing. What is the right read?
options: Correct: a randomised test found no significant difference, so the feature has no effect.
The feature works: 12 beats 10 percent, and a randomised test has no hidden causes to fear.
Too small a test to detect a lift that size: it neither confirms the feature nor rules it out.
The randomisation must have failed: a real 2-point lift would have come out as significant.
variants.why: With 150 users per group the margin of error is several points wide, so a real 2-point lift and no lift at all look the same. 'Not significant' in a small test means 'could not tell', not 'no effect'. Reading 12 against 10 as a win ignores the same noise.

variants.q: You want to test whether a prompt lifts goal attainment from 60 to 62 percent, and you can get 1,500 advertisers per group. The planning table says a 2-point lift needs over 9,000 per group. What should you do?
options: Run it anyway and report whatever comes out: any randomised test beats no test at all.
Run it, watch the gap daily, and stop as soon as the groups are 2 points apart.
Use the 1,500 advertisers who already adopted the practice in place of a random group.
Run longer to reach the size, or say up front it can only detect a much larger lift.
variants.why: At about 1,500 per group a test can reliably see a lift of around 5 points, not 2, so 'no difference' would mean nothing. Stopping when the gap first reaches 2 points picks a lucky moment, and using the advertisers who already adopted throws the randomisation away.

variants.q: An analyst checks a pricing experiment daily. After six days the new price is ahead, with an interval that just excludes zero; the plan said four weeks. A director asks to ship now. What is the best answer?
options: Ship now: the interval excludes zero, which was the test's criterion, and waiting only costs revenue.
Keep to the plan: a result picked on the first good-looking day is more likely to be luck.
Ship now, but only to the segments where the new price is clearly winning after six days.
Restart the test with a different outcome, one that shows a clearer gap between the two prices.
variants.why: An interval keeps its promise for one planned look, not for the best of many looks; peek daily and noise alone will produce 'significant' moments. Shipping to the winning segments, or switching the outcome after looking, is the same error: choosing the result.

drill.q: Why does flipping a coin for who gets a change let you read the difference in outcomes as the effect of that change?
drill.a: Because the coin knows nothing about the advertisers, every trait, recorded or not, ends up spread about equally over both groups. The only systematic difference left is the change itself, so the gap is its effect, give or take noise.

drill.q: You randomised an offer, and only some of the people who got the offer took it up. Which two groups do you compare?
drill.a: Everyone who was offered against everyone who was not, whatever they did next. Comparing only those who took it up brings back the problem of people choosing for themselves.

recall.prompt: A stakeholder asks why you cannot just compare advertisers who use a practice with those who do not, instead of running an experiment. Explain in 30 seconds.
recall.model_answer: Advertisers who adopt a practice chose to, so they differ from the rest in ways nobody recorded, and the gap mixes the practice with those differences. A coin knows nothing about the advertisers, so every trait lands about equally on both sides and the only systematic difference left is the change. The remaining gap is its effect, give or take noise, which is why you size the test in advance, compare by assignment, and report the estimate with its interval.

lessons.ask_assistant: Design first; do not analyse anything yet. We want to test whether [change or encouragement] raises [outcome] over [window]. Propose the unit to randomise ([advertiser / account / user]), the group size needed to detect a lift of [smallest lift worth acting on] from today's [baseline rate], and your assumptions. If the change cannot be withheld, propose a random holdout or a rollout in random order instead. When results arrive, compare by assignment (everyone assigned against everyone not, whatever they did next) and report: counts per group, a table showing the groups were alike beforehand, the share who took the change up, the estimate with its 95 percent interval, and every date on which results were computed.
audit_checklist: A plan dated before launch: outcome, window, group size, and the smallest lift that size can detect
Counts assigned to each group, and a before-the-change table showing the two groups were alike
The result table compares everyone assigned with everyone not assigned, its counts match the assigned counts, and the share who took the practice up is a separate line
One estimate with its interval, on the planned group sizes, beside a list of every date the results were computed: one date, no early stop
transfer: Does a new bid-recommendation prompt raise spend, or do growing advertisers simply click it more?
Does a reminder email before renewal reduce cancellations?
Does a warning notice sent to publishers reduce invalid traffic?

other_ways.approach: A random holdout: everyone gets the change except a small random group
other_ways.when: When the change is expected to help and nobody wants to withhold it widely; the comparison stays clean, with a wider interval.

other_ways.approach: A rollout in random order: every account gets the change eventually, and the order is drawn by lot
other_ways.when: When the change must reach everyone and has to be staged anyway; accounts still waiting act as the control group.

other_ways.approach: Compare the launch group with a similar untreated group over time
other_ways.when: When the change already launched without a coin flip; weaker evidence, and the subject of the next lesson.

glossary.def: A comparison in which chance alone decides who gets the change, so the groups are alike in everything else on average.
The randomly chosen advertisers who do not get the change, kept as the yardstick.
Randomising who is nudged towards a practice when the practice itself cannot be forced; everyone nudged is compared with everyone not.
The number of randomised units in each group (here advertisers, not impressions); the smaller the lift you need to detect, the larger it must be.
The chance that a test detects a lift of the size it was planned for, if that lift is real; tests are usually sized for four times in five (80 percent).
How strong the support for a claim is: observed (a gap), adjusted (a gap comparing like with like) or tested (a randomised experiment).

lessons.title: When you cannot experiment
lessons.subtitle: A change launched without a coin flip. What can you still say about its effect?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can estimate a launch's effect against a comparison group, and check the one assumption that estimate rests on.

predict.q: A setup flow launched for ecommerce advertisers only. Their goal-hit rate went from 60.5% to 69.5%. Over the same weeks the other verticals, which never got it, went from 66.8% to 71.1%. What is the best estimate of the flow's effect?
options: About 9 points
About minus 1.6 points
About 4.7 points
It cannot be estimated without an experiment
predict.reveal: About 4.7 points: ecommerce's rise minus the rise everyone had anyway. The lesson shows the one assumption that answer rests on.

segments.narration: Product launched a guided creative setup flow for ecommerce advertisers in week 13. Twelve weeks on, the slide is ready. The share of ecommerce advertisers hitting their CPA goal rose from about 60 percent to nearly 70. Nine points. Success? Nobody flipped a coin here. The flow went to every ecommerce advertiser at once, so there is no experiment to read. The question is what you can honestly say with what you have. This example is a separate small simulation built for this lesson, so once again we will know the true answer.

visual.title: When you cannot experiment
visual.sub: A launch, a comparison group, and one assumption to check

segments.narration: Answer one is the slide's answer: before against after, in ecommerce alone. Plus 9 points. The trouble is that the weeks after launch differ from the weeks before in more than the flow. It was a good season. The other verticals never got the flow, and their rate climbed too, from about 67 percent to about 71. So some of ecommerce's 9 points would have arrived anyway. A before and after comparison credits the launch with everything that changed over those weeks. The season, a price change, a holiday. All of it lands on the one thing you happened to be watching. The same holds for any launch, an invalid-traffic filter as much as a setup flow: you need the change in a similar group that went without.

visual.title: Share hitting CPA goal, week by week
visual.note: Ecommerce: 60.5% before launch, 69.5% after. Other verticals: 66.8%, then 71.1%.

segments.narration: So bring in the other verticals. Answer two: compare the two groups after the launch. [[1]] Ecommerce, with the flow, sits just under 70 percent. [[2]] The others, without it, sit at about 71. Ecommerce is lower by 1.6 points. Now the flow looks harmful. And the trouble is the one from two lessons ago: the groups were never alike. Before the launch, ecommerce was at about 60 percent and the others at about 67. Ecommerce started well behind, for reasons that have nothing to do with the flow. Comparing the groups after launch blames the flow for that old gap.

visual.title: After launch: ecommerce against the rest

right.label: Other verticals (no flow)
right.sub: before launch: 66.8%

segments.narration: Notice that each wrong answer fixes the other's flaw. Before against after compares ecommerce with itself, so the starting level drops out, but the season stays in. Ecommerce against the others uses the same weeks, so the season drops out, but the starting level stays in. So combine them. [[1]] Take the change in the group that got the flow: up 9 points. [[2]] Take the change over the same weeks in the group that did not, the comparison group. That stands in for what the season would have done to ecommerce anyway. [[3]] Subtract. What is left is about 4.7 points. [[4]] The interval runs from about 3 points to about 6. The effect built into this simulation is 4. The method is called difference-in-differences.

visual.title: The change minus the change
lines: Ecommerce: 60.5% → 69.5%, up 9.0 pts
Other verticals, same weeks: 66.8% → 71.1%
95% interval 3.2 to 6.2 · true effect 4.0
visual.note: Difference-in-differences

segments.narration: That answer rests on one assumption. Without the launch, the two groups would have moved in parallel. Not at the same level. In parallel, so the gap between them would have stayed put. You can never observe that, because the launch happened. What you can check is the weeks before it. Was the gap steady then? [[1]] Here, over the twelve weeks before launch, the gap drifted by about a tenth of a point a week. [[2]] The margin of error on that is larger than the drift itself. [[3]] So there is no sign the groups were pulling apart or closing up. That is not proof they would have stayed together. It is the evidence available, and you should always ask for it.

visual.title: Were the two groups moving together before launch?

stats.label: drift of the gap between the groups, weeks 1 to 12
margin of error on that drift
not distinguishable from zero

segments.narration: Here is what it looks like when the assumption fails. Same launch, same true effect of 4 points, in a second simulated world where the other verticals were barely improving. Ecommerce was already catching up before anything launched. [[1]] In the first world the arithmetic gave about 4.7. [[2]] In this one, the same arithmetic gives about 8. Twice the truth, and nothing in the calculation complains. It has credited the launch with improvement that was already under way. The warning sits in the weeks before launch, and it is faint. The gap was closing by about a third of a point a week, with a margin almost as large. Take a borderline flag like that seriously: a small weekly drift adds up over every week of the comparison.

visual.title: Same arithmetic, same true effect of 4.0 pts

right.label: Already closing the gap before launch
right.sub: pre-launch drift 0.33 ± 0.31 pts a week

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask the assistant for the change in both groups, and make the output show four things. [[1]] The weekly series for both groups. [[2]] The four averages, each group before and after, with the estimate and its interval. [[3]] The check on the weeks before launch: how fast the gap was drifting, with its margin. [[4]] And anything else that hit one group only around the launch date. You supply that list, because the data cannot know about a price change. [[5]] Then word it honestly: goal attainment rose 4.7 points more than in the comparison group, assuming the two would have moved together. Stronger than an adjusted gap, weaker than an experiment. If another rollout wave is coming, ask for it in random order.

visual.title: Brief and audit: a launch estimate must show
items: Weekly series for both groups, all weeks
Four averages with group sizes; the estimate with its interval
Pre-launch check: drift of the gap, with its margin
Other changes at launch: listed by you; breaks in size or mix reported by the assistant
Wording: "rose 4.7 pts more than the comparison group; assumes they would have moved together"

segments.narration: So the next time a launch slide shows a before and an after, you will ask for two things: the comparison group, and the weeks before launch. Next, a different question about actions: knowing that something works on average does not tell you who it works on.

visual.title: Did the flow work? Three answers
rows: credits the launch with the season
blames the launch for an old gap
needs the groups to move in parallel
visual.note: True effect in this simulation: 4.0 pts. Interval on the third answer: 3.2 to 6.2.

takeaways: Before-and-after credits a launch with everything else that changed over the same weeks.
Subtract the change, over the same weeks, in a similar group that did not get the launch.
That works only if the two groups were moving in parallel, so check the weeks before launch.

quiz.q: A bid-suggestion feature launched for finance advertisers only. Their goal-hit rate averaged 62 percent in the ten weeks before and 68 percent in the ten weeks after. The product manager writes: 'the feature lifted goal attainment by 6 points.' What do you need before accepting that?
options: Before and after rates for verticals that did not get the feature, to see what moved anyway.
A longer 'after' period, twenty weeks rather than ten, so the 68 percent is more stable.
An interval on the 6 points: if it excludes zero, the rise is not noise and the claim stands.
Proof that the same advertisers are in both periods, so that they act as their own control.
quiz.why: Comparing a group with itself removes differences between groups, but not everything else that changed over those weeks: the season, the market, other launches. Only the change in a group that did not get the feature shows how much of the 6 points would have happened anyway. An interval or a longer window makes the 6 points more precise, not more attributable to the feature.

quiz.q: The assistant reports: 'Difference-in-differences: the launch raised goal attainment by 7.9 points. Pre-launch check: the launch group, which started lower, was gaining on the comparison group by 0.33 points a week, plus or minus 0.31.' It concludes that the launch was worth about 8 points. What should you flag?
options: Without a randomised experiment an estimate like this is worthless and should not be reported.
The gap was probably closing before launch already, so some of the 8 points was coming anyway.
Only the missing interval on the 7.9: the drift is tiny next to 8 points, so the check passed.
The estimate should be replaced by the simple before-and-after difference in the launch group.
quiz.why: The method assumes the gap between the groups would have stayed steady without the launch. Here the pre-launch drift only just clears zero: a borderline flag, not a pass, and it points the dangerous way. A third of a point a week sounds small, but it accumulates over every week of the comparison, and the arithmetic hands all of it to the launch. That makes the estimate probably too high rather than worthless, and plain before-and-after would ignore the comparison group altogether.

quiz.q: A subscription service raised its price in one country on March 1 and nowhere else. Weekly cancellations there went from 2.0 to 2.6 percent. In two neighbouring countries with no price change they went from 1.8 to 2.1 percent over the same weeks. What is the best estimate of the price rise's effect, and what should be checked?
options: Plus 0.6 points: the rise where the price changed; check that the sample is large enough.
Plus 0.5 points: the gap between the countries afterwards; check that the weeks are the same.
Plus 0.3 points: its rise minus the neighbours' rise; check that they moved together before March.
No estimate is possible: no two countries are alike, so only a randomised price test would do.
quiz.why: Cancellations rose everywhere, so 0.3 of the 0.6 points would have happened anyway; subtracting the neighbours' change removes it. The after-only gap of 0.5 mixes in the fact that this country already cancelled more. Countries differing in level is fine: what matters is that they were moving in parallel beforehand, which is the check.

quiz.q: A support inbox adds an automatic first reply for billing tickets in week 8, and billing resolution time falls. You need a comparison group to judge the change. Which is the best choice?
options: The billing tickets from the same weeks that did not trigger the automatic reply.
Whichever category without the reply had the closest resolution time to billing in week 7.
Billing tickets from the same weeks one year earlier, when there was no automatic reply.
A category without the reply whose resolution time had been moving in step with billing.
quiz.why: A comparison group earns its place by moving in parallel with the group that got the change, before the change, not by sitting at the same level in one week. Billing tickets that did not trigger the reply differ in kind from those that did, so the two groups were never alike, and last year's tickets cannot show what this season did.

review.concept: subtract the change that would have happened anyway

variants.q: An onboarding checklist launched for self-serve accounts only. Their 30-day activation rate went from 40 to 52 percent. Managed accounts, which did not get it, went from 55 to 60 percent over the same period. What is the best estimate of the checklist's effect?
options: About 12 points
About minus 8 points
About 5 points
About 7 points
variants.why: Self-serve rose 12 points, but managed accounts rose 5 without the checklist, so about 5 of the 12 would have happened anyway: 12 minus 5 leaves 7. Twelve credits the checklist with the whole period; minus 8 just compares the two groups afterwards and blames the checklist for self-serve having started lower.

variants.q: A push-notification feature shipped on Android only. Weekly sessions per user went from 5.0 to 5.9 on Android, and from 6.0 to 6.5 on iPhone over the same weeks. A slide says 'notifications added 0.9 sessions per user'. What should it say?
options: About 0.4 sessions: Android's rise minus the rise iPhone had without the feature.
About 0.9 sessions, as written: Android is compared with itself, so nothing else can explain it.
Notifications reduced sessions, because Android with the feature is still below iPhone without it.
About 0.5 sessions: the rise that was seen on iPhone over the same weeks.
variants.why: iPhone rose 0.5 without the feature, which is the best available guess at what Android would have done anyway; 0.9 minus 0.5 leaves 0.4. Comparing Android with itself removes the difference between platforms, but not whatever lifted both platforms over those weeks.

variants.q: After a checkout redesign for returning customers, their average order value was 10 percent higher in the following month than in the month before. Which single extra number does most to make the claim 'the redesign raised order value' credible?
options: The average order value of the same returning customers in each of the six months before.
The number of returning customers behind each monthly average, and an interval on the 10 percent.
The change in order value over the same two months for customers who did not get the redesign.
The share of returning customers who said in a survey that they liked the new checkout better.
variants.why: A rise after a launch only means something next to the rise that happened without it. Sample sizes and an interval tell you whether the 10 percent is noisy, not whether the redesign caused it, and more history for the same group is still before-and-after: it cannot show what that particular month did to everybody.

review.concept: the comparison only works if the groups would have moved in parallel

variants.q: A feature launched for gaming advertisers, with health advertisers as the comparison group. In the ten weeks before launch, gaming's spend was growing 3 percent a week and health's 1 percent a week. Change-minus-change says the feature added 15 percent. How should you read that?
options: As the feature's effect: subtracting the comparison group's change removes any trend in spend.
As too low: gaming's faster growth before launch hides part of what the feature added.
As overstated: gaming was already pulling ahead, and that head start is credited to the feature.
As invalid: verticals of different sizes and spend levels cannot be each other's comparison.
variants.why: The subtraction removes only the trend the two groups share. Gaming was already growing faster, so the gap would have widened with no feature at all, and the arithmetic counts that widening as effect. Different sizes or levels are not a problem; different trends before launch are.

variants.q: A delivery fee changes in one region, the treated region, and you are choosing a comparison region. Region A had the same order rate as the treated region last month, but the two have been drifting apart all year. Region B's order rate is far higher, but its gap to the treated region has been steady all year. Which do you pick?
options: Region A, because it matches the treated region's current level most closely.
Region B, because a steady gap means the two were moving in parallel.
Neither: a comparison region must match on level as well as trend.
The average of both regions, so that their flaws cancel out.
variants.why: The method subtracts changes, so a constant difference in level cancels out; what it cannot survive is a gap that was already moving. Region A's matching level last month is one point on a drifting path: it would have kept drifting, and that drift would be read as the fee's effect.

variants.q: A new invalid-traffic filter was switched on for one traffic source in week 20. In the same week, that source's largest publisher was suspended for unrelated reasons. Invalid clicks on the source then fell much more than on the other sources, which had tracked it closely until then. What can you conclude about the filter?
options: The filter caused the whole extra drop, since the sources tracked each other before week 20.
No conclusion is possible: without a randomised experiment a launch cannot be evaluated.
The filter did nothing: the suspension of the largest publisher explains the whole extra drop.
The extra drop is the filter and the suspension together; the comparison cannot split them.
variants.why: Moving together beforehand supports the claim that the sources would have stayed in step, but only if nothing else changed for one of them. The suspension broke that, so the extra drop belongs to both events and the arithmetic cannot split it. Giving all of it to either one is a guess.

drill.q: A feature launched for one group of advertisers and their results improved afterwards. Why is the before and after difference not the effect of the feature?
drill.a: Because other things changed over the same weeks, such as the season. You need the change in a similar group that did not get the feature, and you subtract it from the change in the group that did.

drill.q: When you use a comparison group to judge a launch, what has to be true of the two groups, and how do you check it?
drill.a: They must have been moving in parallel, so that without the launch the gap between them would have stayed steady. You check the weeks before launch. If the gap was already drifting, the estimate is contaminated.

recall.prompt: A feature launched for one group and their numbers rose. Explain how you would estimate its effect without an experiment, and what would make you distrust the answer.
recall.model_answer: Before-and-after alone credits the launch with everything else that changed, and comparing the two groups afterwards blames it for where they started. So take the change in the launch group and subtract the change over the same weeks in a similar group that did not get it. That only works if the two would have moved in parallel, so check that the gap between them was steady in the weeks before launch. If it was already drifting, or something else hit one group at launch, the estimate is contaminated.

lessons.ask_assistant: [Change] launched for [treated group] on [launch date] and for nobody else. Estimate its effect on [outcome] as a difference-in-differences: the treated group's change from before to after, minus the change in [comparison group] over the same periods. Show the [weekly] rate for both groups across all periods, the four averages (each group, before and after) with counts, the estimate with a 95 percent interval, and how fast the gap between the groups was drifting before launch, with its margin. Other changes around the launch that I know of: [list, or 'none known']. Print that list back, and report any break at launch in either group's size or mix that the data shows; do not guess at causes.
audit_checklist: The weekly series for both groups, before and after launch, not just two averages
The four averages (each group, before and after) with group sizes, and the estimate with its interval
The pre-launch check: how fast the gap was drifting per week, with its margin, and whether that is distinguishable from zero (a borderline result is a warning, not a pass)
The other changes around launch that you listed, printed back, and each group's size and mix on either side of the launch date, so a break would show
transfer: Did the price rise in one region cause the fall in renewals there?
Did the new fraud filter on one traffic source cut invalid clicks, or was all traffic getting cleaner?
Did moving a set of accounts to a new account-management team raise their spend?

other_ways.approach: A randomised experiment or a random holdout
other_ways.when: Whenever you still control who gets the change, for example the next rollout wave; a coin needs no assumption about parallel movement.

other_ways.approach: A staggered launch: groups get the change on different dates
other_ways.when: When a rollout happens in waves; each wave gives another comparison against groups still waiting, so a single coincidence is less likely to fool you.

other_ways.approach: Forecast the launch group from its own history and compare what happened with the forecast
other_ways.when: When no untreated group exists at all; the answer is only as good as the forecast, which module 6 covers.

glossary.def: The outcome after a change minus the outcome before it, in the same group; it credits the change with everything else that happened over that time.
A group that did not get the change, used to show what would have happened anyway.
The change in the group that got the launch, minus the change over the same period in a comparison group.
The assumption that, without the change, the two groups would have moved in step, so the gap between them would have stayed constant.
Testing whether the gap between the two groups was already drifting in the weeks before the change; a borderline result is a warning, not a pass.

lessons.title: Uplift: who changes because you acted
lessons.subtitle: Are the accounts most likely to leave the ones most worth calling?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can explain why a risk list is not a call list, and say what data and what evidence an uplift ranking needs before you trust it.

predict.q: A success team calls the 400 advertisers with the highest churn risk. Roughly what share of those 400 would have left whether or not anyone called?
options: About 5 percent
About 20 percent
About 45 percent
About 90 percent
predict.reveal: About 45 percent: nearly half the list was beyond saving, and the lesson shows why most likely to leave and most worth calling are different rankings.

segments.narration: The success team has time for 400 calls this month, so they do the obvious thing. They sort advertisers by churn risk and call the top 400. Two months later plenty of those accounts are still spending, and the slide says the calls worked. In the simulated outreach programme from the experiments lesson, nearly half of that list was going to leave whatever anyone said. About as many again were going to stay without any call. So which accounts did the calls actually change? Ask that of any list built from a score. The leads most likely to convert are not necessarily the ones a sales call tips.

visual.title: Uplift: who changes because you acted
visual.sub: Most likely to leave is not the same as most worth calling

segments.narration: Take one account and one call. Only four things can be true. [[1]] It leaves unless you call. That is the persuadable account, the only kind where a call earns anything. [[2]] It leaves either way: a lost cause. [[3]] It stays either way: a sure thing. [[4]] Or it leaves because you called, a sleeping dog: here, a small healthy self-serve account that did not want the interruption. Only about 3 percent of advertisers here are persuadable. About 10 percent are lost causes, and about 87 percent are sure things. Sleeping dogs are under 1 percent. We can sort advertisers this way only because the programme is simulated: for every advertiser we know what happens with the call and without it. Real life shows you one of the two, never both.

visual.title: One account, one call: four kinds
visual.note: Knowable only in a simulation: both outcomes are known for every advertiser.

segments.narration: Now ask who the risk list actually calls. [[1]] About 45 percent of the 400 leave either way. Many of them top a risk list because they have already gone quiet. [[2]] Another 47 percent would have stayed with no call at all. [[3]] That leaves about 8 percent the call could save. And this is why the sentence, we called them and many stayed, proves nothing. Many stay on any list. You met the cure in the experiments lesson: a control group, comparable advertisers who were not called.

stats.label: leave either way
would stay with no call
persuadable

segments.narration: So change the question. Risk asks who is likely to leave. Uplift asks whose chance of leaving drops if we call. That is a difference between two futures, and no advertiser ever shows you both. A randomised outreach gets round that. [[1]] A coin flip decides who is called, so the two groups are alike, on average, in everything else. [[2]] Fit one churn model on the called group. [[3]] Fit a second on the not called group. [[4]] Then score every advertiser with both. The gap between the two predictions is the predicted uplift, and you sort by that.

steps.label: Coin flip
steps.sub: decides who gets the call (here: all 12,000 advertisers)

steps.label: Model A
steps.sub: churn risk, learned from the called

steps.label: Model B
steps.sub: churn risk, learned from the not-called

steps.label: Uplift = B − A
steps.sub: score everyone with both, sort by the gap

segments.narration: Here is what each way of picking 400 buys. Only a simulation can count this: it needs both futures for every advertiser. The counts are net, the accounts a call saves minus the few it pushes out. [[1]] Pick 400 at random and the calls prevent about 13 churns. [[2]] Call the 400 highest risks and they prevent 32. [[3]] Call the 400 with the highest predicted uplift and they prevent 44. [[4]] Someone who knew every advertiser's true kind would prevent 136. So uplift beats risk here, and it is still far from perfect. How big the gain is will differ from one business to the next. You measure it, with the check in the brief.

visual.title: Churns prevented by 400 calls
visual.note: Net of the accounts a call pushes out. Countable only because both outcomes are known for every simulated advertiser.

segments.narration: Why does it do better? Because of who each list reaches. [[1]] On the risk list, 45 percent leave either way and 8 percent are persuadable. [[2]] On the uplift list, 19 percent leave either way and 11 percent are persuadable. Its accounts are also busier: about 18 active days against 13. The two models learned to walk past accounts that have gone quiet. Still, 11 percent is modest. Uplift is a difference between two predictions, so it carries the error of both and is noisier than risk. And it can only be learned where the action was assigned at random. If account managers chose whom to call, the gap mixes the call's effect with their choice.

left.label: Top 400 by risk
left.sub: 44.8% leave either way · 12.9 active days of 28

right.label: Top 400 by uplift
right.sub: 19% leave either way · 17.9 active days of 28

segments.narration: One more contender, with a caveat. [[4]] Take a hand rule: call accounts that are still active and have a fixable problem, such as stale creatives or CPA somewhat over goal, highest risk first. That prevents 73, more than either list. Do not read that as rules beating models. The rule matches how this simulation was written: the call was programmed to help exactly those accounts. So 73 is a best case. In real life you would not know your rule was right. What carries over: a rule that encodes how you think the action works is a fair candidate, and it is tested the way a model is, on randomised data.

visual.title: Churns prevented by 400 calls, with a hand rule
visual.note: The rule matches how the simulation was written: a best case for a hand rule, not proof that rules beat models.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. First ask whether the outreach was assigned at random. If not, the stop-gap is the risk list minus accounts already gone quiet, with a random slice left uncalled for next time. If it was, ask for the two models and check four things. [[1]] How many were called and not called, and a table showing the groups looked alike beforehand. [[2]] The overall effect of the call, with its interval. [[3]] The check you can run at work, on held-out advertisers: inside the top of each list, churn among the called against the not called. [[4]] And an interval on every gap. Split 400 names in two and it is several points wide, enough to swallow the whole effect, so pool several rounds before ranking one list above another.

visual.title: What the output must show
items: Called and not-called: how many, and a table showing the groups were alike beforehand
The overall effect of the call, with its interval (here 2.9 pts, 1.8 to 3.9)
Held-out rows: called vs not-called churn inside each list's top (uplift, risk, random)
Group sizes and an interval on every gap: expect several points either way

segments.narration: So before the next call list goes out, you will ask which accounts a call can still change, and for the randomised comparison that shows it. Next: how far down a list to go, which turns out to be a question about money.

visual.text: Most likely to leave is not most worth calling.
visual.sub: Risk ranks who leaves. Uplift ranks who changes because you acted.

takeaways: A risk list is mostly accounts that leave either way and accounts that stay either way; a call pays only on the few it changes.
Uplift ranks by the predicted change from acting, and can only be learned where the action was assigned at random.
Rule or model, a targeting policy is judged the same way: called against not-called inside its own list.

quiz.q: The success team called the 400 highest-risk advertisers. Sixty days on, about half are still spending, and the team lead reports that the calls saved roughly 200 accounts. What is the right read?
options: Fair: the model said they would churn, so every account still spending was saved by a call
The model is broken: half of its highest risks did not churn, which a good model would not allow
Unknown: many on a risk list stay with no call, so it takes a comparable group that was not called
Fair, but only for accounts scored above 0.5; the lower scores should not be counted as saves
quiz.why: On a risk list a large share would have stayed anyway, so still spending is not the same as saved; only a comparable not-called group shows what the calls changed. Half of a high-risk list staying does not mean a broken model either: a score is a probability, not a promise.

quiz.q: You ask the assistant for an uplift list. Its output says: 'Trained on last quarter's outreach log: the advertisers the account managers chose to call, about a quarter of the log, against the rest. Two models fitted; top 400 by predicted uplift attached.' What is the flaw?
options: Managers chose whom to call, so the gap between the models mixes the call with their choice
The two groups are very different sizes, so models fitted on them cannot be compared fairly
It fitted two simple models, and uplift only shows up with a flexible model such as boosting
One quarter of outreach is too little to rank 400 advertisers; the log needs another quarter
quiz.why: Uplift can only be learned where the action was assigned at random; if managers picked, called and not-called accounts differ in ways the table cannot see, and the gap between the models inherits that. Unequal group sizes are fine as long as the assignment was random.

quiz.q: The assistant compares two lists of 400 on held-out advertisers and writes: 'The uplift list contains far fewer eventual churners than the risk list, so the risk list is the better call list.' What is the right read?
options: Agreed: a list with more churners on it gives the success team more accounts it could rescue
Agreed, provided the difference in churners between the two lists is outside its interval
Neither list can be judged until the team has actually called both and waited 60 days
Wrong yardstick: the test is churn among called against not-called inside each list
quiz.why: Counting churners on a list measures risk, and the risk list wins that by construction, yet much of what it catches leaves either way; an uplift list is meant to skip churners nobody can save. The fair test is the churn gap between called and not-called advertisers inside the top of each list, and the randomised data already contains it, so no new calls are needed.

quiz.q: A product team emails an upgrade offer to the 5,000 users a model scores as most likely to upgrade. 30 percent of them upgrade, against 4 percent across all users. What does that show?
options: That the email lifts upgrades by 26 points for the users who receive it
That the model ranks well; the email's effect needs a random un-emailed slice
That the offer should go to the lowest-scoring users instead, who have the most room to move
That the model is leaking: an upgrade rate of 30 percent is too high to be real
quiz.why: High scorers were likely to upgrade anyway, so 30 against 4 mostly reflects who was chosen, not what the email did; a held-back random slice of the same users separates the two. Switching to the lowest scorers is a guess as well: who responds is something you measure.

review.concept: most likely is not most changeable

variants.q: A retention team can make 150 calls. The 150 highest churn scores are mostly accounts with no activity for three weeks. What is the strongest argument against simply calling those 150?
options: The model must be overfitted if its top scores all turn out to be inactive accounts
Many have in effect already left, so calls earn more where the outcome can still move
Inactive accounts are cheap to lose, so they can be left out of retention work altogether
150 is too short a list for any model to rank reliably, so the order means little
variants.why: Risk ranks who is likely to leave, not whom a call can still change, and accounts already gone quiet are often beyond saving. That is not a fault in the model, which answered the question it was asked, and it is not a reason to write those accounts off without measuring.

variants.q: A retailer sends a 15 percent discount code to the customers a model scores as most likely to buy this month. Sales to that group are high, but margin falls. What most likely happened?
options: Most would have bought at full price, so the discount changed few decisions
The model's scores were too low, so the code went to the wrong customers
Discounts never change the behaviour of customers who are already likely to buy
The group was too small for the discount to show any effect on sales
variants.why: The likeliest buyers are mostly people who buy either way, so the discount paid for purchases that were coming anyway and gave margin away. That is not a law that discounts never work on them: whether it changes behaviour is something only a random hold-back can show.

variants.q: Sales reps call the leads with the highest conversion scores. A random hold-back shows those leads convert at about 60 percent whether called or not, while mid-scoring leads convert at 25 percent when called and 12 percent when not. Where should the calls go?
options: To the highest scorers: 60 percent is the best conversion rate on offer
To nobody: the hold-back shows that calls do not work
To the lowest scorers, who have the most room to improve
To the mid-scoring leads, where calling changes the outcome most
variants.why: The call adds nothing at the top and about 13 points in the middle, and it is the change that pays for a call, not the conversion rate. The lowest scorers were not measured here, so sending calls there would be a guess.

review.concept: uplift needs a randomised comparison

variants.q: A slide says: 'We called 300 at-risk advertisers and 70 percent of them are still active. Outreach works.' What one thing would make that claim checkable?
options: The churn scores of the 300, to confirm that they really were at high risk
The same figure for last quarter's at-risk advertisers, as a point of comparison
The rate for similar at-risk advertisers, chosen at random, who were not called
A longer list, so that the 70 percent comes with a narrower interval
variants.why: Without a comparable not-called group nobody can say how many of the 70 percent would have stayed anyway. Last quarter's accounts differ in season and mix, and a tighter interval around 70 percent still does not say what the calls changed.

variants.q: An assistant builds an uplift model for 'refresh your creatives' nudges from a campaign in which marketing hand-picked the recipients it thought were most engaged. What is the problem?
options: A nudge is too small an action for an uplift model to detect reliably
The nudged and un-nudged groups differed before any nudge was sent
Uplift models need at least a year of history before they can be fitted
The outcome should have been churn rather than creative refreshes
variants.why: Uplift is the gap between what happens with and without the action for comparable accounts; when marketing picks the recipients, the gap reflects their choice as much as the nudge. The cure is to assign the nudge at random, not to collect more history.

variants.q: A subscription app uses a past randomised campaign to compare two ways of picking 500 users for a win-back offer. In the top 500 by predicted uplift, cancellation was 12 percent with the offer and 22 percent without. In the top 500 by cancellation risk it was 51 percent with and 55 percent without. Which list should get the offer?
options: The uplift list: the offer moves cancellation by about 10 points there, against about 4
The risk list: it contains far more users who cancel, so there is more to win back
The risk list: at 51 percent there is far more room for improvement than at 12 percent
Neither: both lists still show cancellations with the offer, so it does not work
variants.why: The offer is paid back by the gap between with and without, and that gap is larger on the uplift list. The risk list holds more cancellers, but most of them cancel either way. With groups this size both gaps still need an interval before anyone commits.

drill.q: Why is the list of accounts most likely to churn not automatically the best list to call?
drill.a: Because many of them will leave whatever you do, and many others would have stayed anyway. A call only pays where it changes the outcome, and that is a different ranking.

drill.q: What kind of data do you need before you can estimate who is changed by an action, and why?
drill.a: Data where the action was assigned at random, so the people who got it and the people who did not are alike. Otherwise the difference between them mixes the action's effect with whoever was chosen.

recall.prompt: Your manager asks why the success team should not simply call the highest-risk accounts. Explain it back in 30 seconds.
recall.model_answer: High risk means likely to leave, not likely to be changed by a call: in the simulated outreach nearly half of the top 400 by risk left whatever happened and nearly half would have stayed anyway. What we want is the accounts whose outcome moves if we call, which is uplift. We can only estimate that from a randomised outreach, by comparing called with not-called accounts, and any list, from a model or a rule, should be tested the same way.

lessons.ask_assistant: We ran [action] with [units] assigned to it at random; the assignment is in [assignment column]. Fit one [outcome] model on the treated group and one on the untreated group, using only features known at [decision date], and rank held-out [units] by predicted [outcome] without the action minus predicted [outcome] with it. For the top [list size] by that uplift, the top [list size] by plain risk and a random [list size], show [outcome] among treated versus untreated inside each list, with group sizes and 95 percent intervals. Start the output with the size of each group, a table showing the two groups were alike before the action, and the overall effect with its interval.
audit_checklist: The size of the called and not-called groups, with a table showing they were alike before the calls: a coin flip leaves them alike, hand-picking does not
The overall effect of the call, with its interval
On held-out advertisers: called versus not-called churn inside the top of the uplift list, the risk list and a random list
The group size and an interval beside every one of those gaps
transfer: Which customers should get a discount code: the likeliest buyers, or the ones a discount would tip?
Which leads should sales call first, when the hottest leads often buy without a call?
Which advertisers should get a 'refresh your creatives' nudge, when the most engaged would refresh anyway?
