other_ways.approach: A hand rule that encodes how you believe the action works (still active, with a fixable problem), tested on the same randomised data
other_ways.when: You have a clear view of the mechanism and too little randomised data to fit two models

other_ways.approach: Read the experiment by a few segments chosen in advance and send the action where the measured effect is largest
other_ways.when: The segments are few and large, and you want something simpler and less noisy than a score per advertiser

other_ways.approach: Keep the risk list but leave out accounts that have already gone quiet
other_ways.when: No randomised data exists yet; treat it as a stop-gap and randomise the next round of outreach

glossary.def: The change in an advertiser's chance of an outcome caused by acting on them: the chance without the action minus the chance with it.
An account that leaves if you do nothing and stays if you act: the only kind where the action earns its cost.
An account that leaves whether or not you act.
An account that would have stayed but leaves because you acted.
Fit one model on those who got the action and one on those who did not, then rank by the gap between the two predictions.

lessons.title: From score to action
lessons.subtitle: How far down the list should the team go?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can turn a cost, a value and a success rate into a cut-off on each advertiser's own probability, and say what must be checked and measured before anyone acts on it.

predict.q: Toy numbers: a call costs $30, a saved advertiser is worth $1,500, and a call saves one churner in five. Of the 4,000 scored advertisers, how many are worth calling?
options: 141: those scored above 0.5
About 400: the top tenth
About 1,300
predict.reveal: About 1,300: every advertiser whose own churn probability is above 10 percent, and the lesson shows where that 10 percent comes from.

segments.narration: The scored list is on the success team's desk, and somebody has to decide where it stops. The assistant's script already did: it flagged everyone scored above 0.5, which gives 141 names. Nobody chose that number. It is a default, and nothing about your costs or your team is in it. A call costs something. A saved advertiser is worth something. And a call does not always work. Put those three together and the cut-off becomes a decision you can defend. The same arithmetic draws the line under any score that triggers an action, such as which advertisers likely to miss their CPA goal get a review.

visual.title: From score to action
visual.sub: The cut-off comes from costs and capacity, not from a default

segments.narration: Start with one advertiser and some toy numbers. They are hypothetical and round, here only to show the method, so swap in your own. Say a call costs 30 dollars and a saved advertiser is worth 1,500. And say a call saves one churner in five. [[1]] The expected value of a call is the advertiser's probability of churning, times the chance the call works, times the value saved, minus the cost. Expected means on average, over many calls like it. [[2]] With these numbers each churner you reach is worth 300 dollars on average, and each call costs 30. [[3]] So a call pays for itself when the probability is 30 over 300. That is 10 percent.

visual.title: What one call is worth (hypothetical dollars)
lines: expected value = probability × chance it works × value saved − cost
= probability × 0.2 × $1,500 − $30 = probability × $300 − $30
break-even probability = $30 ÷ ($1,500 × 0.2) = 0.10
visual.note: Round numbers to show the method. Replace them with your own.

segments.narration: Now the part that is easy to get wrong. That 10 percent is a test for one advertiser, using their own probability. It is not a target for the list's precision, its overall hit rate. Walk down the ranked list. Each name has a lower probability than the one before. You keep calling while the next name is above 10 percent, and you stop when it is not. The word for this is marginal: judge the next one, not the average so far. Everyone above the line is expected to return more than the call costs. Everyone below it is expected to lose money, however good the list looks as a whole.

visual.title: Walking down the ranked list
columns: Probability at the bottom of the list
visual.note: Hypothetical dollars: $30 a call, $1,500 a save, one churner in five saved.

segments.narration: Here is the mistaken version, because you will meet it. Break-even is 10 percent, so keep extending the list while its hit rate stays above 10 percent. [[1]] Call all 4,000 and about 13 percent of them are churners. That is above break-even, so by this reading you call everyone, and it earns about 38,000 dollars. [[2]] The rule about the next advertiser stops near 1,300 names and earns about 85,000. A strong top of the list holds the average up, while thousands of calls further down are each expected to lose money.

left.label: Average: the list's hit rate is above 10%

right.label: Marginal: the next advertiser's own probability is above 10%
right.sub: call 1,311

segments.narration: As the list grows, net value climbs steeply, flattens, peaks at around 1,300 names, and then falls. The default of 141 names is worth about 27,000 dollars. The rule's list is worth roughly three times that. If the team can only make 400 calls, capacity decides instead, and you can read off what a second caller would add. The toy value is the same for every advertiser. Real accounts differ, as you saw when you ranked by probability times spend. So drag the list size to your own team's capacity, then switch the ranking to expected dollars and see who moves up.

visual.name: ranklist
visual.title: How far down the list?
visual.note: Drag the list size and watch churners reached and net value. Then rank by expected dollars instead of probability.

segments.narration: This multiplies a probability by money, so it leans on two things. [[1]] The percentages must be right, not just the ranking. Here they run a little low: advertisers scored at about 7 percent churned at nearly 10. So names just under the line were at break-even, and going on to 1,600 earns about the same. Here that cost almost nothing. Do not count on it. [[2]] One in five is a guess, and a kind one: on the risk list, the last lesson's calls saved fewer than that, and not equally everywhere. [[3]] The pattern is general: the chance something happens, times what it is worth. For spend, the chance an advertiser stays times their spend if they stay matches the best model from the regression lesson.

visual.title: What the arithmetic leans on
items: Percentages that are right, not just the ranking · rule's list $84,570, best in hindsight $85,170
A success rate that is a guess, and not the same for everyone
The general pattern: chance it happens × what it is worth (spend: chance of staying × spend if they stay)

segments.narration: A cut-off gives you a list, not an action. [[1]] Attach the reasons to each name, the pushes you met when we opened the black box. [[2]] Different reasons need different plays. An account with CPA far over goal needs an optimisation conversation. One with payment failures needs someone from billing. [[3]] Then, before anyone dials, set aside a random slice of the list and do not call it. [[4]] After the 60 days, compare churn among the called with churn in that slice. That gap, with its interval, is the only honest measure of whether the calls work. A small slice gives a wide interval, so size it like an experiment, or pool several months, before it replaces the guessed one in five.

visual.title: From a list to an action you can measure

steps.label: Reasons
steps.sub: why each name is on the list

steps.label: Random holdout
steps.sub: a slice of the list nobody calls

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Give the assistant your three numbers, cost, value and success rate, and ask for the net value at every list size, not one recommended cut-off. What must the output show? [[1]] The assumptions in dollars, and the break-even probability they imply. [[2]] A predicted against actual table around the cut-off, so you know 10 percent means 10 percent. [[3]] The net value curve, with the default cut-off and your team's capacity marked. [[4]] And the holdout: how many names were held back, a table showing they resemble the called names, and later the gap with its interval.

visual.title: What the output must show
items: The assumptions in dollars, and the break-even probability they imply
Predicted vs actual around the cut-off
Net value by list size, with the default cut-off and team capacity marked
The holdout: how many names, shown to match the called names; later, the gap with its interval

segments.narration: So the next time a script hands you a list cut at 0.5, you can replace the default with your own costs and capacity, and say how the action will be measured. Next: what happens after you ship, when the world moves.

visual.text: Stop where the next advertiser's own probability no longer pays for the call.
visual.sub: cost ÷ (value × success rate), capped by capacity, then measured

takeaways: The cut-off is the cost of acting divided by what a successful action is worth, not the default 0.5.
It applies to each advertiser's own probability: judge the next name on the list, never the list's average hit rate.
The arithmetic needs trustworthy percentages and a measured success rate, so check calibration and hold back a random slice.

quiz.q: You give the assistant a cost of $30 per call, a value of $1,500 per saved advertiser and a save rate of one in five. It replies: 'Break-even precision is 10 percent. The full scored list of 4,000 has a precision of 13 percent, so contacting all 4,000 is profitable. Recommended list size: 4,000.' What is the flaw?
options: Only capacity: calling all 4,000 is right in principle, but the team cannot make that many calls
It tested the list's average hit rate; the 10 percent is for each advertiser's own probability
Break-even should be 50 percent, the standard cut-off for a model that predicts yes or no
It should have used recall: keep contacting until 10 percent of the churners are reached
quiz.why: The 10 percent is a test for the next advertiser's own probability; the list's average stays above it because the top of the list carries the bottom. Calling all 4,000 does end up positive, about $38,000, but the 1,311 names above the line earn about $85,000, because every call below the line is expected to cost more than it returns. So 4,000 is the wrong answer before capacity even comes into it.

quiz.q: Break-even is a churn probability of 10 percent. The model ranks well, but a predicted-versus-actual table shows that advertisers it scores at around 8 percent actually churn about 12 percent of the time. What happens if you cut the list at a score of 0.10?
options: You stop too early: some advertisers scored under 0.10 are really above break-even
You get the right list: the model ranks well, and a good ranking is all a cut-off needs
You call too many: the model is overstating risk, so the list is longer than it should be
The cut-off no longer matters; a model with wrong percentages has to be rebuilt first
quiz.why: A cut-off in percent is only as good as the percentages: here the scores run low, so advertisers worth calling sit just under the line. A good ranking is enough when you take a fixed top K, but not when you compare a probability with a number derived from money.

quiz.q: The team called every advertiser above the cut-off. Sixty days later churn among them is 25 percent. The model's average prediction for the same advertisers was 31 percent, and the team lead reports 'six points of churn saved'. What is the right read?
options: Correct: the model's prediction is what would have happened without the calls
The calls failed: 25 percent is still far above the churn rate of advertisers overall
Unproven: compare instead with the advertisers below the cut-off, who were not called
Unproven: only a random slice of the same list, left uncalled, can show that
quiz.why: A model's average prediction can be several points off with no calls at all, so it cannot stand in for the missing comparison, and advertisers below the cut-off are a different, lower-risk group. A random held-back slice of the same list is alike in everything except the call.

quiz.q: An invalid-traffic team reviews suspicious publisher batches by hand. A review costs $40. Catching a truly invalid batch avoids a $2,000 refund, and a review of an invalid batch catches it half the time. A model gives each batch a probability of being invalid. Which batches are worth a review?
options: Batches scored above 0.5, where invalid is more likely than not
Batches down the ranking for as long as the reviewed list's hit rate stays above 4 percent
Each batch whose own probability is above 4 percent, as far as the team's time allows
Only batches scored above 0.96, so that almost no review is wasted
quiz.why: Break-even is the cost divided by value times success rate: 40 over 1,000, or 4 percent, applied to each batch's own probability and capped by capacity. The 0.5 default ignores the money, and a list's hit rate stays above 4 percent long after the individual reviews at the bottom have stopped paying.

review.concept: the cut-off comes from costs

variants.q: A call to an at-risk advertiser costs $40, a saved advertiser is worth $1,000, and calls save about one churner in five. From which churn probability is a call worth making?
options: Above 4 percent
Above 20 percent
Above 50 percent
Above 80 percent
variants.why: A churner reached is worth 1,000 times one in five, so $200 on average, and a $40 call pays when the probability is above 40 over 200: 20 percent. Four percent forgets that most calls fail, and 50 percent is only the default nobody chose.

variants.q: A product demo by a sales engineer costs $300. An upgrade is worth $6,000, and a demo closes one interested customer in four. A model scores each customer's probability of being interested, and the assistant suggests demoing customers scored above 0.5. What is the better cut-off?
options: Keep 0.5: below it a customer is more likely uninterested than interested, so a demo is wasted
About 0.05: the demo costs $300, a twentieth of the $6,000 an upgrade is worth
Whichever cut-off gives the highest accuracy on the test set, since that means fewest mistakes
About 0.20: the $300 cost against the $1,500 a demo returns on average when there is interest
variants.why: An interested customer returns 6,000 times one in four, so $1,500 per demo on average, and a $300 demo pays above a probability of 0.20. The 0.5 default and best accuracy both ignore that a missed upgrade costs far more than a wasted demo; 0.05 forgets that three demos in four do not close.

variants.q: A finance team can phone accounts with overdue invoices. A call costs $10 of staff time. When an account really was going to default, a call recovers the invoice, worth $400 on average, about half the time. A model gives each account a probability of defaulting. Which statement is right?
options: Phone every account with a default probability above 5 percent, as far as staff time allows
Phone only accounts above 50 percent; below that a call is more likely wasted than not
Phone accounts above 2.5 percent, since the $10 call is a fortieth of the $400 invoice
The cut-off cannot be set until the model's AUC is known, since it depends on the ranking
variants.why: Each real defaulter reached returns 400 times one half, $200 on average, so a $10 call pays above 10 over 200, or 5 percent. A call that is probably wasted can still be worth making when a miss is expensive, and AUC describes the ranking, not where to cut.

review.concept: marginal, not average

variants.q: Break-even for a call is a churn probability of 15 percent. The top 1,000 advertisers on the ranked list have an overall hit rate of 35 percent. The 1,000th advertiser has a predicted probability of 9 percent. Should the list be extended to 1,500?
options: Yes: at 35 percent the list is far above break-even, so there is plenty of room to grow
Yes, and keep going until the list's overall hit rate has fallen to 15 percent
No: each name past that point is below 15 percent; the list should have stopped sooner
It depends on the model's AUC: with a strong ranking the extra 500 will still pay
variants.why: The test is each next advertiser's own probability, and at 9 percent the 1,000th is already under break-even. The list's 35 percent is held up by the names at the top; adding more names lowers it only slowly while every added call loses money.

variants.q: A sales team calls leads in score order. The assistant reports: 'Across the first 2,000 leads called, revenue per call is $55 against a cost of $20, so keep going.' What should you ask for before agreeing?
options: The revenue per call across every lead in the database, for a fuller average
The expected revenue of the next leads on the list, not the average so far
The model's accuracy at a 0.5 cut-off, to confirm the scores can be trusted
The total revenue to date, to check that the $55 figure was computed correctly
variants.why: An average over the first 2,000 says the calls so far paid, not that the next one will; the decision to continue rests on what the next lead is expected to bring against the $20 cost. An average over even more leads blurs that further.

variants.q: A team reviews flagged ad creatives for policy problems, most suspicious first, and every review costs the same. A review pays for itself when the chance of finding a problem is above 5 percent. After 500 reviews the day's hit rate is 30 percent, but the last 100 reviews found only two problems. What is the right call?
options: Carry on: 30 percent is six times break-even, so the queue is clearly worth reviewing
Carry on until the day's overall hit rate has dropped all the way to 5 percent
Stop only when a run of reviews finds nothing at all, since any find beats zero
Stop about here: the latest reviews are finding only about 2 percent, below break-even
variants.why: Whether to do the next review depends on what the next reviews are likely to find, and the most recent 100 are the best guide: about 2 percent, under break-even, whatever the day's average says. The day's 30 percent is history from the top of the queue.

drill.q: A model gives each account a probability of leaving. How do you decide the cut-off for who gets contacted?
drill.a: Work out what a contact costs and what it is worth on average when the account really is leaving. Contact every account whose own probability is above the cost divided by that worth, up to what the team can handle.

drill.q: Why is it a mistake to keep extending a contact list for as long as its overall hit rate stays above break-even?
drill.a: Because the average is held up by the strong names at the top. The test applies to the next account's own probability, and at the bottom of the list each extra contact loses money.

recall.prompt: A colleague says the 0.5 cut-off is what the model recommends. Explain in 30 seconds how the cut-off should really be chosen.
recall.model_answer: 0.5 is a default, not a recommendation. A contact is worth making when the advertiser's own probability is above the cost divided by the value saved times the chance the contact works; with the lesson's hypothetical numbers that is 10 percent, about 1,300 advertisers instead of 141. It is a test for each next advertiser, not for the list's average hit rate, and it is capped by the team's capacity. Because it multiplies a probability by dollars, the percentages have to be checked, and a random slice of the list is held back to measure whether the action works.

lessons.ask_assistant: Using the [outcome] scores on [evaluation period], compute the net value of acting on the top N [units] for every N, assuming [cost per action], [value of a success] and [share of cases where the action works]. State the break-even probability these imply and apply it to each [unit]'s own probability, not to the list's average hit rate. Show predicted versus actual around the break-even, and mark the default cut-off and our capacity of [capacity] on the curve. Then draw a random holdout of [size] that nobody acts on: show how it was drawn, its average score beside the rest, and the size needed to detect a gap of [smallest gap worth acting on].
audit_checklist: The three assumptions in dollars, and the break-even probability they imply
Predicted versus actual churn for the score bands around the cut-off
Net value by list size, with the default 0.5 cut-off and the team's capacity marked
The holdout: how many names, how it was drawn, and its average score beside the called names'; once outcomes arrive, the called-versus-holdout gap with its interval
transfer: Which flagged traffic batches are worth a manual review, given what a review costs and what a caught batch saves?
Which leads deserve a sales call, given the cost of a call and the value of a closed deal?
Which overdue invoices are worth a phone call instead of an automated reminder?

other_ways.approach: Take the top K the team can handle and skip the economics
other_ways.when: Capacity is far below the break-even point, so every name on the list clears it anyway

other_ways.approach: Rank by expected dollars: probability times the account's own value
other_ways.when: Accounts differ widely in value, and losing one large account matters more than losing several small ones

other_ways.approach: Replace probability times a fixed success rate with a predicted uplift for each advertiser
other_ways.when: You have randomised outreach data showing that the action works on some accounts and not on others

glossary.def: What an action is worth on average: the chance it pays off times what it pays, minus what it costs.
The probability at which an action's expected value is zero: its cost divided by the value saved times the chance the action works.
About the next case on its own, as opposed to the average of all the cases so far.
Predict the chance something happens and its size if it does, then multiply: for spend, the chance of staying times the spend if they stay.
A randomly chosen slice of the list that is deliberately not acted on, so the effect of the action can be measured.

lessons.title: Keeping a model honest
lessons.subtitle: How do you know a shipped model is still right?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can set up and read a monitoring check for a live model: predicted against actual by segment with margins, early signals while the labels are pending, and an untouched holdout.

predict.q: For gaming advertisers in June the model predicted 14 percent churn and 31 percent left. How much did the model's overall ranking score, AUC, fall between May and June?
options: By about 0.02: barely at all
By about 0.10
By about 0.25
It collapsed to 0.5, a coin flip
predict.reveal: By about 0.02, from 0.855 to 0.835: a headline score can sit almost still while one segment goes badly wrong, and the lesson shows where to look instead.

segments.narration: Your churn model has been live for a few months, and the monthly check looks calm. The ranking score, AUC, slipped by about 0.02 between the May and June advertisers. Both months sit inside the interval you saw around that score in the noise lesson, so nobody calls a meeting. Then the outcomes for one vertical land on your desk. For gaming advertisers in June the model predicted 14 percent churn. 31 percent left. The headline barely moved while the model was badly wrong about a whole segment. This lesson is about how you catch that, and how soon you can.

visual.title: Keeping a model honest
visual.sub: The world moves after you ship. Where do you look?

segments.narration: So where should you have been looking? Not at the ranking score. It asks one thing: do churners get higher scores than stayers? Inside gaming they still did, about as well as anywhere else. What broke was the level. [[1]] For gaming in June the model said about 14 percent, and the truth was about 31. [[2]] For everyone else put together it said about 11 percent, and 11 percent left. So the check that matters after launch is predicted against actual, cut by segment. It is the calibration table from module 2, sliced the way module 4 taught you to slice. And it is the check for any model left running: a lead score or a spend forecast can keep its headline number while one segment goes wrong.

right.label: Everyone else · 1,728 advertisers
right.sub: actual ± 1.5 points

segments.narration: In this simulated world something shifts for gaming advertisers in June, and no column records it. Nothing in their inputs gave it away: the model's prediction for gaming was about 15 percent in May and about 14 in June. A world that moves away from what the model learned is called drift, and it comes in two kinds. [[1]] Sometimes the inputs move: a new mix of advertisers, a column that goes empty. You can see that the same day. [[2]] Here the relationship between the inputs and the outcome moved. A model is a frozen summary of how things related in its training months, so it cannot know. Drift can also be slow. Churn creeps up a little every month here, one reason the percentages ran low in the calibration lesson.

visual.title: Two ways the world moves
items: The inputs move: a new mix of advertisers, a column goes empty. Visible the same day
The relationship moves: same inputs, different outcome. Visible only when outcomes arrive

segments.narration: Could you have seen it coming? [[5]] Take May. Gaming churn was about 23 percent, against a prediction of 15. But with only about 220 gaming advertisers, the measured rate carries a margin of about five and a half points. The prediction sits just outside it. Part of that miss is not about gaming: the model ran about 2 points low for everyone in May. And with six verticals checked every month, a miss like this can turn up by chance. So May is a warning: note it, look for a cause, watch the next month. In this simulation the change was written in for June only. [[6]] June is different. 31 percent against 14, with the same margin. That is far outside it. It is not noise.

visual.title: Gaming churn by month (actual)
visual.note: May: predicted 14.9%, actual 22.6% ± 5.6 (217 advertisers). June: predicted 13.5%, actual 30.5% ± 5.5 (272).

segments.narration: There is a harder problem underneath. Churn takes 60 days to show. So on the day you score the June advertisers you cannot check June at all, and the comparison you just saw arrives two months late. While you wait, watch what you can see today. [[1]] The inputs: the share of missing values and the average of each column, by segment. [[2]] The scores: what share of advertisers the model flags. [[3]] And when the labels land, predicted against actual. Be honest about the early signals, though. They catch a broken pipeline or a changing mix of advertisers. Here they would have stayed silent, because the inputs never moved.

visual.title: What to watch, and when
items: Today · inputs: missing values and averages per column, by segment
Today · scores: the share of advertisers flagged
After 60 days · predicted vs actual, by segment, with margins

segments.narration: A second trap arrives the moment the model is used. The success team calls the list, and some of those advertisers stay because of the call. In the data they look like mistakes: scored high, did not churn. Judge the model on them and it seems to cry wolf. Retrain on them and the next model learns that the accounts you rescued were never at risk. This is what the random holdout from the last lesson is for. [[1]] The called accounts show the model and the calls mixed together. [[2]] The untouched slice shows the model alone.

visual.title: Where to judge the model once the team acts

left.label: Accounts the team called
left.sub: saved accounts look like false alarms

right.label: Random untouched holdout
right.sub: the fair predicted vs actual

segments.narration: Brief and audit. Ask the assistant for a monthly monitoring table, not a single score. What must it show? [[1]] Predicted and actual rates for every segment the business cares about, each with its group size and its margin. [[2]] Which month's advertisers each row describes, so nobody reads a two month old result as today's. [[3]] Input and score checks for the newest month. [[4]] And the retraining rule, written down. Retrain on a schedule, and whenever a check trips. If a segment has clearly shifted and there are too few labels since to retrain on, correct that segment's percentages meanwhile, or fall back to a simple rule for it. Keep the old model running until the new one beats it on the same test rows.

visual.title: What the monitoring table must show
items: Predicted vs actual by segment, with group size and margin
Which month each row describes: labels lag 60 days
Input and score checks for the newest month
Retraining rule: on schedule or a tripped check; the old model stays until the new one wins on the same test rows

segments.narration: So when someone asks whether the model still works, you will not answer with one score: you will show a dated table of predicted against actual, by segment. That closes module 5. The next module is about time itself, starting with a forecast of daily spend.

visual.text: A steady headline score can hide a segment that has gone badly wrong.
visual.sub: Predicted vs actual · by segment · with margins · on accounts nobody touched

takeaways: A steady headline score can hide a segment whose predictions have gone badly wrong, so compare predicted with actual by segment.
Size every gap against its margin: a narrow miss on a small group is a warning, a gap far outside the margin is a shift.
Labels arrive late and actions contaminate them, so watch inputs and scores meanwhile and keep an untouched holdout.

quiz.q: The assistant's monthly monitoring note reads: 'AUC 0.855 in May, 0.835 in June. Ranking quality is stable. No action needed.' What is missing before you can agree?
options: The AUC to more decimal places, to see whether the fall from May to June is real
Accuracy for each month, as a second opinion on what the AUC is saying
Predicted against actual churn for each segment, with group sizes and margins
The same AUC figures for the training months, to see how far the score has moved
quiz.why: AUC measures ordering across everyone, so one segment's level can be far off while it holds: in June gaming was predicted at about 14 percent and came in at about 31. The fall of 0.02 is indeed within noise, which is exactly why it tells you so little about whether the model is fine.

quiz.q: It is the May check. Gaming churn came in at 22.6 percent against a predicted 14.9, on 217 advertisers, with a margin of plus or minus 5.6 points. The gaming lead wants the model retrained today. What is the best response?
options: Treat it as a warning: look for a cause, and see whether June repeats it before retraining
Retrain today: a gap outside its margin is proof that the model is broken for gaming
Ignore it: 217 advertisers are too few to conclude anything at all about a segment
Merge gaming with the other verticals, where predicted and actual agree, and re-check
quiz.why: One miss just outside its margin, on one small group among six checked every month, in a month when predictions ran a little low for everyone, is not proof of a shift: it earns attention, not a rebuild. Ignoring it is the opposite mistake: June's gap, 30.5 against 13.5 with a similar margin, was far too large to be noise.

quiz.concept: acting on the list changes the labels
quiz.q: At launch, 74 percent of advertisers scored above 0.5 went on to churn. Since then the success team has called everyone above 0.5, and the latest report says: 'Only 48 percent of them churned. The model has degraded; retrain on the latest months.' What is the right read?
options: Agreed: precision has dropped sharply, so retrain on the freshest data available
The calls changed the outcomes; judge the model on a random slice nobody called
Raise the cut-off until precision on the called list is back at 74 percent
Precision is the wrong measure here; check whether the AUC has fallen as well
quiz.why: Advertisers the calls saved show up as high scores that did not churn, so the model looks worst exactly where the team succeeded. Retraining on them would teach the next model that rescued accounts were safe; an untouched random slice is the only fair test.

quiz.q: An invalid-traffic model's labels come from refund disputes, which take about 45 days to settle. On Monday the share of traffic it flags jumps from 3 percent to 11 percent, and one input column, device type, has been 40 percent empty since Friday's tag release. What do you do first?
options: Wait for the disputes to settle, then compare predicted with actual as usual
Retrain the model on the most recent week of data so that it adapts to the change
Raise the cut-off until the flagged share is back at its usual 3 percent
Treat it as an input fault now: trace the empty column back to the release
quiz.why: The labels are six weeks away, but a jump in the flagged share alongside a column gone empty is an early signal you can act on today. Retraining on broken inputs or moving the cut-off would only hide the fault.

review.concept: predicted versus actual, by segment, with margins

variants.q: A churn model's overall ranking score has not moved in three months. For one vertical of 300 advertisers it predicted 12 percent churn and 29 percent left, with a margin of plus or minus 5 points. What is the right read?
options: The overall score is the summary that matters after launch, and it has not moved
It is noise: 300 advertisers is a small group, and small groups jump around
The level is wrong for that vertical; the overall score could not show it
The whole model has failed, and its scores should be withdrawn for every vertical
variants.why: A gap of 17 points against a margin of 5 is far outside chance, and an overall ranking score averages across everyone and ignores level. It is a problem for that segment; the others should be checked the same way, not written off unseen.

variants.q: A lead-scoring model predicted 10 percent conversion for partner-referral leads last month; 16 percent converted. There were 90 such leads, giving a margin of about plus or minus 8 points. Every other source matched its prediction. What is the sensible reading?
options: Within the margin: note it and look again next month before changing anything
The model under-predicts referrals: add 6 points to their scores from now on
Retrain the model now, since one source is clearly off its prediction
Drop referral leads from the monitoring; the group is too small to bother with
variants.why: With 90 leads a measured 16 percent is compatible with a true 10, so the gap is a prompt to watch, not a finding. Patching the scores or retraining chases noise, and dropping the segment throws away the check that would catch a real shift later.

variants.q: After a price change to one plan, an upsell model's predictions for that plan's 1,200 customers average 20 percent; 9 percent actually upgrade, plus or minus 2 points. For other plans predicted and actual agree, and the affected plan's input columns look unchanged. What has most likely happened?
options: A data pipeline fault: one of the input columns must have broken
Ordinary month-to-month noise of the kind any group of customers shows
The model was overfitted from the start, and it has only now shown
The link between the inputs and upgrading changed for that plan
variants.why: The gap is many times its margin and confined to the plan whose price changed, while the inputs look normal: the same kind of customer now behaves differently, and a frozen model cannot know that. A pipeline fault would show in the inputs, and overfitting would have shown on the test set before launch.

review.concept: labels arrive late

variants.q: Churn is defined as no spend in the 60 days after the snapshot. The model has just scored this month's advertisers. What can you check today?
options: This month's predicted against actual churn, cut by vertical and by size tier
This month's inputs and share flagged; predicted against actual for an older month
Only that the scoring job ran: every check on the model must wait for the 60 days
This month's precision and recall at the cut-off the success team is working with
variants.why: This month's outcomes do not exist yet, so anything that needs labels has to wait two months. What exists today is the inputs, the scores, and the labels of an older month, and those are worth checking now.

variants.q: A model predicts whether a new lead will convert within 90 days. A manager asks for a weekly chart of the model's accuracy on that week's leads. What is the honest answer?
options: Fine: accuracy can be computed as soon as the week's leads have been scored
Use the leads that have already converted this week as an early estimate of it
Not yet: chart inputs and scores now, accuracy for leads from 90 days ago
Shorten the conversion window to one week, so that the chart can be built now
variants.why: Until the 90 days are up a lead that has not converted is not yet a no, so early accuracy is wrong in a predictable direction, and counting only quick converters has the same flaw. Shortening the window to fit the chart changes the question the business asked.

variants.q: For two months the input averages, missing-value rates and share flagged of a model that screens for invalid traffic all look normal. When the confirmed outcomes finally arrive, predicted and actual differ sharply for one group of publishers. What does that combination tell you?
options: The monitoring was broken: a real problem always shows up in the inputs first
The outcomes must be mislabelled, since nothing else about the data changed
The model was never accurate, and the test before launch must have been wrong
The inputs held steady, but the way they lead to the outcome changed for that group
variants.why: Input and score checks catch a broken pipeline or a changing mix, but they are blind to a change in how the same inputs lead to outcomes. That kind of shift shows only when the labels land, which is why both kinds of check are needed.

drill.q: A model's overall score has not moved since launch. Why is that not enough to say it is still working?
drill.a: Because an overall score can hide one segment that has gone badly wrong. Compare predicted with actual outcomes segment by segment, with the group sizes and margins.

drill.q: Your labels take two months to arrive. What can you watch in the meantime, and what will it miss?
drill.a: The inputs and the share of accounts the model flags. They catch a broken pipeline or a changing mix, but not a change in how the inputs relate to the outcome. Only the labels show that.

recall.prompt: The model has been live for three months and its overall score is unchanged. Explain in 30 seconds what you would check before saying it is still working.
recall.model_answer: I would compare predicted with actual outcomes segment by segment, with group sizes and margins, because an overall ranking score can hold steady while one segment's level is far off: in the course's June data gaming was predicted at 14 percent and came in at 31. I would remember that the newest labels are 60 days old, so for the latest month I can only check the inputs and the share flagged. And I would judge the model on the random holdout nobody acted on, since accounts the team saved otherwise look like false alarms.

lessons.ask_assistant: Build a monitoring table for [model], one block per [period]. For each [period] whose [outcome window] has closed, show predicted and actual [outcome] rates overall and by [segments the business cares about], with the number of [units] and a 95 percent margin on each actual rate; where [the action] has been taken, use only the untouched holdout and label those rows. For the newest [period], which has no labels yet, show the missing-value rate and mean of every input column and the share of [units] above [working cut-off], next to the same figures for the training period. Flag every segment whose predicted rate falls outside the margin, and state which [period] each row describes.
audit_checklist: Predicted and actual rates by segment, each with its group size and margin
The month behind every row, so a two-month-old result is not read as current
Input and score checks for the newest month, beside the training-month values
A label on every row saying where its actuals come from (the untouched holdout, or accounts the team acted on), with that row's count
transfer: Is the lead-scoring model still right for leads from a channel that launched after it was trained?
Is the invalid-traffic detector still catching fraud after a publisher changed its page layout?
Is the spend prediction still right for one group of advertisers after their pricing changed?

other_ways.approach: Retrain on a fixed schedule with the newest labelled months, without waiting for a check to trip
other_ways.when: The world drifts slowly and steadily and retraining is cheap; still compare old and new on the same test rows

other_ways.approach: Recalibrate the percentages for the affected segment and leave the ranking alone
other_ways.when: The ranking still holds inside the segment and only the level has moved

other_ways.approach: Fall back to a simple rule or a manual review for the affected segment
other_ways.when: A segment has clearly shifted and there are not yet enough labels from after the shift to retrain on

glossary.def: A change after launch in the inputs a model sees, or in how those inputs relate to the outcome, that makes a frozen model's predictions go stale.
The wait between scoring a case and knowing its outcome; for churn here, 60 days.
Regular checks on a live model: its inputs, its scores, and its predictions against what actually happened.
A random slice of the list that nobody acts on, kept so the model can still be judged fairly once the team starts acting.

lessons.title: Forecasting: start with the calendar
lessons.subtitle: What does a forecast have to know to beat 'same as last week'?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can direct a forecast in the right order: naive baselines first, then a model that names the trend, the weekly and yearly rhythm and the known event dates, and you can check what it found against what you already know.

predict.q: Copying the same weekday from last week forward misses daily platform spend by about 6 percent on this series. A model that is told the trend, the weekday, the time of year and the holiday dates removes how much of that error?
options: Almost none: the rest is noise
About a fifth of it
More than half of it
Nearly all of it
predict.reveal: More than half: about 6 percent falls to under 3. The lesson shows which ingredient buys what, and why this is a best case.

segments.narration: It is the last week of the month and finance wants a number: platform spend, day by day, for the next four weeks. The quickest answer in the building is, same as last week. That is not a silly answer. It is a baseline, the forecasting cousin of predicting that everyone stays. So what does a forecast have to know to beat it, and by how much? Our series is simulated daily spend for a whole platform, 851 days of it, so we know exactly what went into it.

visual.title: Forecasting: start with the calendar
visual.sub: Trend, rhythm and the dates you already know

segments.narration: Pull the series apart and you find four ingredients and a leftover. [[1]] A trend: growth of about 15 percent a year. [[2]] A weekly rhythm: weekends run roughly 20 percent below weekdays. [[3]] A yearly rhythm: spend sags through spring and summer, then climbs to a peak in late November. [[4]] Known events: Black Friday week, Christmas, New Year's Day. [[5]] The leftover is noise, the wobble no method can forecast. None of this is machine learning yet. It is the calendar, and you could find most of it with a GROUP BY on weekday, month and year. The idea is general: any daily count, say next month's support tickets for staffing, is forecast from its trend, its rhythm and its known dates.

visual.title: What is in 851 days of platform spend
items: Trend: about +15% a year
Week: weekends about 20% below weekdays
Year: low in March, peak in late November
Known events: Black Friday week, Christmas, New Year's Day
Noise: whatever is left

segments.narration: Start with three naive forecasts. Each predicts the next 28 days from the first of a month, twelve months running. The score is the average daily miss, as a percentage of that day's actual spend. [[1]] Carry the last day's value forward and you are off by about 14 percent a day: the last day you saw may be a Friday, and tomorrow is a Saturday. [[2]] Use the same weekday from last week instead, and the miss falls to about 6 percent. More than half the error was the weekly rhythm. [[3]] Average the last four of each weekday and it improves a little more. Its worst month is far milder too: one unusual week is no longer copied forward alone.

visual.title: Naive forecasts: average daily error (MAPE), 28 days ahead
visual.note: Worst of the twelve months: 27.3%, 23.6% and 9.8%.

segments.narration: Now give a model those ingredients by name. [[1]] It is the weighted sum from module three, fitted on the log of spend: a trend, an effect for each weekday, a smooth curve for the time of year, and a flag for each known event. [[2]] It trains only on days before the forecast date, then predicts the next 28. [[3]] Its average daily miss is under 3 percent, about half that of the best naive method, and its worst month is barely worse than its average. A boosted tree model given the same calendar columns manages about 5 percent, level with the four week average.

visual.title: A model that names the calendar
lines: log(spend) = trend + weekday + time of year + event dates
trained only on days before the forecast date
average daily error 2.8%  ·  best naive method 5.7%
visual.note: Worst month 3.5%. Boosted trees on the same calendar columns: 5.4%.

segments.narration: The model is readable, which a copied week is not. [[1]] It found growth of about 15 percent a year, the rate that was built into the series. [[3]] Saturdays and Sundays around a fifth below Mondays. [[4]] Black Friday week about 22 percent up. [[6]] Christmas and New Year's Day down by a fifth to a quarter. Because it works on the log scale, these effects multiply, as they did in the spend model from module three. Each of those is something you can check against a dashboard you already own, and argue about with finance.

visual.title: What the model found
visual.note: Fitted on log spend, so the effects multiply.

segments.narration: Now take one ingredient away: fit the same model without the event dates. [[1]] With them, the average miss was 2.8 percent and the worst month 3.5. [[2]] Without them the average barely moves, to 3.3 percent. But the worst month climbs to 6.3, close to double. An average can hide a holiday; the worst month cannot. Nothing in the rhythm of the data tells a model that one particular week in late November is special. Somebody has to say so. The calendar is where your domain knowledge goes in, the way features were in module four.

visual.title: Same model, with and without the event dates

right.label: Not told
right.sub: worst month · average 3.3%

segments.narration: Before you quote 2.8 percent, look at where it came from. This series has a version with seven planted incidents, kept for a later lesson. These scores use the version without them, so forecast error is not mixed up with outage days. And this world is stable by construction, with a model of the same form as the equation that generated it. It was even handed the holiday dates. That is a best case, and a real series, with breaks nobody planned, will score worse. What carries over is the order of work, not the number. Now try it: one forecast, made on the first of March. Switch between the methods and see where each parts from what happened.

visual.name: forecast
visual.title: One 28-day forecast, method by method
visual.note: A forecast made on 1 March 2026 against what happened. First figure: this forecast's daily miss. Second: the average over all twelve.

segments.narration: The brief. Ask the assistant to work in this order, and make the output prove each step. [[1]] Baselines first: same weekday last week, and the average of the last four. [[2]] Then the model, with event dates that you supply and it lists back. [[3]] Every method scored on the same forecast dates, each trained only on earlier days. [[4]] The worst month beside the average. [[5]] And the fitted effects in percent: growth per year, the weekend dip, each event. If the weekend dip it reports is not the one on your dashboard, stop there. And for a small decision a few weeks out, a four week average in a spreadsheet, adjusted by hand for known events, will do.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Baselines first: same weekday last week, average of the last four
The model, with your event dates listed back
Same forecast dates for every method, trained on earlier days only
Worst month beside the average
Fitted effects in percent: trend, weekdays, events

segments.narration: Next time finance asks for a number, you know the order of work, and most of the ingredients are already on your dashboards and calendar. Next lesson: testing a forecast from a past date forward, and giving a range, not one number.

visual.text: Most of a forecast is calendar: trend, rhythm and the dates you already know.
visual.sub: Baselines first. Then name the ingredients.

takeaways: Ask for naive baselines first: the same weekday last week, and the average of the last four.
Most of a forecast is trend, weekly and yearly rhythm, and known event dates; a model that names them can be read and checked.
Event dates are knowledge only you can supply, and a score from a stable simulated series is a best case.

quiz.q: An analyst forecasts the next four weeks of platform spend by carrying the last day's value forward, and reports an average daily miss of 14 percent. A colleague concludes that the series is simply too noisy to forecast. What is the better read?
options: The colleague is right: a miss of 14 percent is noise, and no method can remove noise from a series
Most of that miss is the weekly rhythm: score 'same weekday last week' before blaming noise
The series needs a more flexible model with many more columns before the noise can be cut through
A longer average is the fix: forecast each day as the mean of the last 30 days
quiz.why: One day's value says nothing about which weekday is being forecast: on this series, copying the same weekday from last week cut the miss from about 14 to about 6 percent with no model at all. A 30-day mean still predicts the same value for a Saturday as for a Wednesday, so the rhythm that caused the miss is still unaccounted for.

quiz.concept: known events and the worst month
quiz.q: The assistant's report says: 'Calendar model: average daily error 3.3 percent over twelve monthly forecasts, against 6.4 percent for the baseline.' The features listed are trend, weekday and time of year. What do you ask for before this goes to finance?
options: The worst month, and a rerun with the known event dates added: an average can hide a holiday
The same average over twenty-four monthly forecasts instead of twelve, to make 3.3 percent steadier
The same test with a more complex model, to see whether the error can be pushed lower still
The error restated in dollars, because finance cannot act on a percentage
quiz.why: The feature list has no event dates, and that gap does not show in an average: on this series leaving them out moved the average only from 2.8 to 3.3 percent but nearly doubled the worst month. A more complex model, or a steadier average, chases the same number while the hole in the feature list stays open.

quiz.q: The support lead needs daily ticket volumes for next month's staffing. In the history, Mondays run far above Fridays, volume drifts up month after month, and it jumps whenever a product release ships. The assistant proposes forecasting every day as the average of the last 30 days. What is missing?
options: A longer window: a 90-day average would smooth out the release jumps and give staffing a steadier level
History: several more years of data are needed before any of these patterns can be trusted
The three things already known to be in the series: the weekday pattern, the drift, the releases
Power: a pattern this complex needs a neural network, not an average
quiz.why: The weekday pattern, the drift and the release calendar are the ingredients a forecast should name; a flat average predicts the same volume for a Monday as for a Friday and knows nothing about the next release. More history, a longer average or a bigger model does not help while those ingredients are still left out.

quiz.q: On the simulated series the regression missed by under 3 percent a day. A stakeholder asks what accuracy to expect from the same approach on the real platform next quarter. What is the honest answer?
options: About the same, under 3 percent: the method is identical, so its accuracy carries over
Better than 3 percent, provided the real model is given more columns than the simulated one had
Better than 3 percent, because the real platform has many more years of history to learn from
Worse, by an amount nobody knows yet: rehearse on your own history and quote that number
quiz.why: The simulated series never changes its behaviour and the model has the same form as the equation behind it, so under 3 percent is a best case, not a prediction of your accuracy. The method carries over; the number has to be measured on your own data.

review.concept: naive baselines come first

variants.q: A new model for daily platform spend reports an average miss of 5.5 percent on its test forecasts. What do you need to see before deciding whether that is good?
options: Whether 5.5 percent is under the 10 percent that is generally taken to mean a good forecast
What 'same weekday last week' and a four-week weekday average score on the same dates
How many columns the model was given, since more columns mean a better forecast
Whether the model is a regression or is built from trees
variants.why: A forecast error means nothing without the cheap alternatives beside it: on the course series a four-week weekday average already scores 5.7 percent, so 5.5 would be almost no gain. There is no universal percentage that makes a forecast good.

variants.q: A client's e-commerce team forecasts daily orders with a model that misses by 9 percent on average. Orders run much higher at weekends. Which comparison tells you whether the model earns its keep?
options: Its error on the period it was trained on, where the model has the most data to work with
Last year's total orders divided by 365, used as the forecast for every day
A second, more complex model's error on the same days, to see which one wins
The same weekday last week, scored on the same days as the model
variants.why: With a strong weekly rhythm the fair bar is a baseline that already knows the weekday; if copying last week scores 9 percent too, the model adds nothing. Error on the training period flatters any model and is not a comparison at all.

variants.q: A team shows a forecast of weekly new-advertiser sign-ups and says its error is 12 percent. Sign-ups have grown steadily all year. What is the natural naive forecast to demand beside it?
options: Last week's figure carried forward, perhaps with the recent weekly growth added
The average of every week since the platform launched, which uses the most data
A random draw from the range the series has covered in the past
The team's own target for weekly sign-ups, since that is what the forecast serves
variants.why: For a weekly series the cheap forecast is 'same as last week', possibly nudged by recent growth; a model has to beat that to be worth running. An all-time average ignores the growth, lands far too low, and would make almost any model look brilliant.

review.concept: known event dates are domain knowledge

variants.q: A spend forecast is accurate most of the year, yet every year it misses badly in the week of a large shopping event. The model has a trend, weekday effects and smooth yearly terms. What is the best fix?
options: Add a flag for the event's dates, taken from the business calendar
Add several more years of history and let the model discover the event by itself
Switch to a more flexible algorithm that can bend around the event
Drop that week from the evaluation as an outlier
variants.why: Smooth yearly terms cannot single out one particular week, so the model has to be told the dates; then it can learn the size of the effect. Dropping the week from the evaluation hides the miss in exactly the week the business cares about most.

variants.q: A sports advertiser's daily spend surges on days with a big televised match. Match days are announced weeks ahead but fall on no fixed weekday. Your forecast of that account's spend misses every one of them. What should you ask the assistant to do?
options: Smooth the history so that the match-day surges no longer distort the average
Add the match dates, past and announced, as an input to the forecast
Train only on weeks that had no match, to keep the pattern clean
Strengthen the weekly rhythm terms until they absorb the surges
variants.why: Match dates are known in advance to anyone who looks, but they are invisible in the weekday and the month: given as an input, past matches teach the size of the surge and announced ones place it. Smoothing or excluding those days teaches the model that match days do not exist.

variants.q: An education client's lead volume drops sharply during school holidays, whose dates shift each year and differ by region. A forecast built on weekday and month of year keeps missing them. Why, and what fixes it?
options: The model is memorising; remove the month term and the problem goes away
Lead volume is simply too noisy to forecast during school holidays
Month of year cannot follow dates that move; supply the holiday calendar for each region
Daily data is the problem; forecast yearly totals, which do not depend on holiday timing
variants.why: A month term assumes the same pattern on the same dates every year, which moving holidays break; the actual holiday dates are knowledge the model can only get from you. Aggregating to yearly totals removes the miss by removing the forecast anyone needed.

drill.q: Before any forecasting model is built, which simple forecasts should you ask for, and why?
drill.a: The same weekday last week, and the average of the last few of that weekday. They are the bar: a model that cannot beat them is not worth having.

drill.q: A forecast has the trend and the weekly rhythm right, but its worst month is twice as bad as its average month. What is probably missing?
drill.a: The known events: holidays, promotions, launches. The rhythm of the data cannot tell a model those dates are special, so you have to supply them.

recall.prompt: Explain to a colleague why 'same as last week' is a respectable forecast, and what a model has to be told to beat it.
recall.model_answer: Copying the same weekday from last week already handles the weekly rhythm, which is most of the day-to-day movement, so it is the baseline any model must beat. To do better, a model has to name what else is in the series: the trend, the time-of-year rhythm, and the dates of known events such as holidays. Those event dates are domain knowledge the data cannot supply by itself. On the simulated series this roughly halved the error, which is a best case because that series is stable and built like the model.

lessons.ask_assistant: Forecast [series] for each [day or week] of the next [horizon]. Start with two naive baselines: the same [weekday] one [week] back, and the average of the last [four] of them. Then fit a regression on the log of [series] with a trend, [weekday] effects, time-of-year terms and a flag for each event date in this list: [event dates]. Score every method on the same forecasts: [horizon] ahead from each of the last [twelve] [month starts], each trained only on data before its forecast date. Show, per method, the average error and the worst [month]; list the event dates you used and each forecast's last training date; and report the fitted effects in percent.
audit_checklist: Baselines and model are scored side by side on the same forecast dates
Each forecast shows its last training day, and that day is before the days it predicts
The worst month is reported next to the average
The event dates used are listed, and the fitted trend and weekend effects match your dashboards
transfer: How many support tickets will arrive each day next month, so the team can be staffed?
How many new advertisers will sign up each week next quarter?
How much traffic will a client's landing page get each day over the holiday season?

other_ways.approach: Forecast the big pieces separately and add them up
other_ways.when: When a few verticals or large clients move the total and you know something about their plans.

other_ways.approach: A boosted-tree model on calendar columns
other_ways.when: When rhythms interact in ways a fixed formula cannot express. Judge it against the same baselines: on this series it scored 5.4%, level with the four-week average.

other_ways.approach: A run-rate from the last four weeks, adjusted by hand for known events
other_ways.when: When the horizon is short, the decision is small and a spreadsheet is all the question deserves.

glossary.def: The slow, persistent rise or fall of a series underneath its ups and downs.
A pattern that repeats on a calendar cycle, such as the weekend dip or the yearly peak in late November.
A forecast that needs no model, such as the same weekday last week; it is the baseline a model must beat.
A dated occasion, such as a holiday or a promotion, whose effect a model can only learn if it is told the dates.
Mean absolute percentage error: the average daily miss as a percentage of that day's actual value.

lessons.title: Backtesting and uncertainty
lessons.subtitle: How do you test a forecast honestly, and how sure should you sound?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can insist that a forecast is tested from past dates forward, hand it over with a range for the number asked for and a plain statement of what that range does not cover, and tell the model about a change in level instead of waiting for it to adjust.

predict.q: A boosted-tree forecasting model misses daily spend by about 3 percent when it is tested on randomly held-out days. What happens when it is tested on the four weeks after its training data ends?
options: About the same: 3 percent
Slightly better: about 2 percent
Clearly worse: about 5 percent
It falls apart: over 20 percent
predict.reveal: Clearly worse, about 5 percent: random hold-outs let it fill in gaps between days it already knows. The lesson shows the honest test.

segments.narration: The assistant has a forecast ready for finance: boosted trees fed the calendar. Average miss, about 3 percent. It was tested with ordinary cross-validation: hold out a random fifth of the days, train on the rest, rotate. Before you forward it, ask what that test resembled. A held out Wednesday sits between a Tuesday and a Thursday the model has already seen. Finance is not asking you to fill in a missing Wednesday. They are asking about next month, where there are no neighbours to lean on.

visual.title: Backtesting and uncertainty
visual.sub: Test a forecast the way it will be used

segments.narration: [[1]] That 3 percent came from random hold outs. [[2]] Now judge the same model the way it will be used: train up to a date, forecast the next 28 days, score only those. The miss is about 5 percent. The first test let the model fill gaps between days it knew; the second made it reach past the end of its data. It is module four's trap in time: there, one advertiser sat on both sides of a fold. And it is general: any forecast is tested from a past date forward, and a forecast of weekly lead volume for sales needs exactly this test. A footnote: last lesson's plain regression, the trend model for short, scored the same both ways, which you only learn by running the honest test.

visual.title: The same model, judged two ways

left.label: Random days held out
left.sub: it trained on the days around them

right.label: The 28 days after training ends
right.sub: the job it will really do

segments.narration: The honest test is called backtesting, and it is a rehearsal. [[1]] Pick a past date and pretend it is today. [[2]] Train on nothing after it. [[3]] Forecast the next 28 days. [[4]] Score that against what happened. [[5]] Then move on a month and repeat. Last lesson's scores came from twelve of these, because one rehearsal can be lucky. The trend model's monthly miss ranged from about 2 percent to about 3 and a half. One month alone shows nothing of that spread.

Now the range, from the trend model's own track record. [[1]] Take its daily misses from the first six backtests. Find the band that held on four days in five. It runs from about 4 and a half percent below the forecast to about 4 percent above. [[2]] Check that band on the six backtests it was not built from. It held 78 percent of the time, against a promised 80. A range is a promise about how often you will be right, so test it on rehearsals it was not built from, like any model.

visual.title: A range from the model's own track record

stats.label: daily band, −4.5% to +3.8%: held 4 days in 5 on the first six backtests
of days inside it on the next six backtests (promised 80%)

segments.narration: Two limits go on the page with it. [[1]] First, a range built from past misses covers only the kinds of days it has already seen. Put the planted incidents back into the series, and the same band holds only 71 percent of the time. [[2]] Second, it is a range for one day. Over a four week total the daily misses partly cancel: the total was typically off by about 1 percent. So when finance wants a total, build its range the same way, from the rehearsals' totals. The daily band, stretched over a month, would be far too wide.

visual.title: Two limits to state with the range

stats.label: of days inside the same band once incident days are back in the series
typical miss of a 28-day total: a total needs its own range, built from totals

segments.narration: Now a change no range was built for. From the first of November everything steps up by 12 percent and stays there, and no method is told. In November both miss badly: neither had seen it. The four week average has a short memory. By December the old level has left its window, and its error is exactly what it would have been with no step. The trend model fits its whole history, so it keeps blending the new level with the old. It is still about 8 percent off in December and January, more than twice its normal miss, and it takes four months to get back within a point of normal.

visual.title: A 12% step up on 1 November that nobody announced
visual.note: 4-week average: 18.6% in November against a normal 8.9%, then exactly its normal error from December. Trend model in April: 4.4% against a normal 1.9%. Same simulated series, incidents removed: a best case.

segments.narration: So should you switch to the quick method after a shift? Not on this series: over an ordinary year it misses by about twice as much as the trend model. Tell the better model what you know instead. [[1]] Name the break date. You usually can: a pricing change, a large client arriving, a tracking fix. [[2]] Have the assistant add a step from that date, a column that is zero before it and one after, like the holiday flags of last lesson. [[3]] Then run the backtest again, and check that the months after the break are back to normal. And the sign of a break nobody named is a run of misses all on the same side.

visual.title: After a change in level: tell the model

steps.label: Name the break date
steps.sub: pricing change, big client, tracking fix

steps.label: Add a step
steps.sub: a column: 0 before the date, 1 after

steps.label: Re-run the backtest
steps.sub: months after the break back to normal?

segments.narration: The brief. Ask for a test from past dates forward. [[1]] The output shows the forecast dates, each with its last training day. [[2]] The miss by month and by week ahead, beside the naive methods. [[3]] A range for the number asked for, a day or a total, and how often it held on rehearsals it was not built from. [[4]] If you name a break date, a step from that date, and the backtest run again. If you cannot, train on recent history only, and check it the same way. [[5]] And one thing no backtest can supply: a forecast cannot see what has never happened. If a pricing change is coming, give finance scenarios: the forecast as it stands, and one with the change put in by hand.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Forecast dates, each with its last training day
Error by month and by week ahead, beside the naive methods
A range for the number asked for, a day or a total, and how often it held on backtests it was not built from
A break date you name: a step from that date, and the backtest again
Scenarios for changes you know are coming

segments.narration: So the 3 percent that opened this lesson would not leave your desk now: you would send it back for a rehearsal from past dates, and a range. A forecast is also a statement of what was expected: next lesson uses that to decide whether yesterday's drop was unusual.

visual.text: Test from a past date forward, many times. Then give a range, and say what it does not cover.
visual.sub: A forecast cannot see what has never happened.

takeaways: Test a forecast from a past date forward, many times; random hold-outs flatter a flexible model.
Give a range built from past errors for the number you were asked for, a day or a total, and say how often it held; it covers only the kinds of days it has seen.
After a change in level a long-memory model adjusts slowly: name the break date, add a step from it, and re-run the backtest.

quiz.q: The assistant's report on a spend forecast reads: 'Boosted trees on calendar features. 5-fold cross-validation, shuffled, on 851 days. Average error 3.2 percent.' What is the flaw in the evidence?
options: Five folds are too few for 851 days: ten folds would make the score reliable enough to quote
Each tested day sits between days the model trained on; ask for forecasts from past dates forward
The metric is the flaw: a percentage error hides dollar misses, so ask for the average miss in dollars
Boosted trees need far more than 851 days, so the reported score is, if anything, too pessimistic
quiz.why: A forecast is used beyond the end of its data, and shuffled folds never test that: here the same model went from about 3 percent on shuffled days to about 5 percent on the 28 days after training ended. More folds would repeat the same mistake more often.

quiz.concept: a range and what it covers
quiz.q: Finance wants a daily spend forecast for next month to set pacing limits, and asks for 'just the numbers'. Your backtests show that actual daily spend fell within roughly 4 percent of the forecast on four days out of five. What do you send?
options: The daily numbers alone, as requested: a range would only confuse whoever reads them
The daily numbers lowered by 4 percent, so that any surprise is a pleasant one for finance
Only the range for each day, with no central figure, so that nobody anchors on a number
The numbers with that range, how often it held in backtests, and what it does not cover
quiz.why: The range is part of the forecast: it tells finance how much weight each number can bear, and the backtest hit rate is the evidence for it. Quietly shaving the forecast swaps an honest estimate for a biased one and still says nothing about how wrong it could be.

quiz.q: A support team forecasts daily ticket volume with a model fitted on three years of history. In March an acquisition doubles the customer base overnight. In June the forecast is still too low every single day. What is the best reading?
options: A model fitted on its whole history is slow to accept a new level, so one-sided misses are expected
The model has stopped working altogether and should be replaced with a more complex one right away
It is a seasonal effect: support always runs high in early summer, so add more time-of-year terms
Ticket volume has become unpredictable since the acquisition, so forecasting should pause for a while
quiz.why: A long memory keeps blending the new level with years of the old one, so the misses all point the same way for months: on the course series a 12 percent step in November left the trend model well above its normal error through February, and off again in April. The practical fix is to tell the model about the break: add a step from the acquisition date and re-run the backtest, or train only on the months since. A more complex model with the same long memory has the same problem, and a miss that always points one way is the opposite of unpredictable.

quiz.concept: a daily band is not a range for a total
quiz.q: The assistant's report gives next month's total spend with 'an 80 percent range of plus or minus 4 percent, from backtest errors'. The method note says the band was cut from the model's daily percentage errors. What do you send back?
options: Scale the band up for the month: a total adds a month of daily errors, so its range must be far wider
Widen the band until it holds on every backtest day, since finance cannot plan on four days in five
That band is for one day; build the total's range from the 28-day totals of the backtests instead
Rebuild the band from the most recent month's daily errors only, so it reflects the latest behaviour
quiz.why: Daily misses partly cancel when the days are added up, so a band cut from daily errors is the wrong width for a total: on the course series the daily band was about plus or minus 4 percent, while the 28-day total typically missed by about 1 percent. A range for a total has to come from rehearsed totals; scaling, widening or re-cutting the daily band keeps the wrong ingredient.

review.concept: test a forecast forward in time

variants.q: Two test designs for a daily spend forecast: design A holds out 20 percent of days at random; design B forecasts the 28 days after each of twelve past month starts, using only earlier data. A flexible model scores better under A. Which score do you report, and why?
options: A, because it tests the model on more days and so gives a steadier number
B, because only B makes the model predict beyond its data, as it will in use
The average of A and B, since each design captures something the other misses
A, because random sampling is the unbiased way to choose a test set
variants.why: A forecast is only ever used past the end of its training data, and design B is the one that rehearses that. Under design A every tested day has trained neighbours on both sides, so a flexible model scores well by filling gaps.

variants.q: A retail client's analyst checks a weekly demand forecast by hiding 30 of the last 150 weeks at random and reports 4 percent error. The forecast will be used to order stock eight weeks ahead. What should replace that test?
options: The same test with 60 hidden weeks instead of 30, so that the error is measured on more weeks
Training on all 150 weeks and reporting the error on those same weeks
Forecasts of the following eight weeks from several past dates, each using only earlier weeks
The same 30 hidden weeks scored with a stricter metric, so that the large misses count for more
variants.why: The order decision needs eight weeks ahead with nothing known after the forecast date, so the test must do the same from several past dates. Hiding random weeks, however many, lets the model lean on the weeks either side.

variants.q: A dashboard vendor says its forecast 'explains 97 percent of the variation in your historical daily revenue'. What does that leave unanswered?
options: Whether 97 percent clears the level that is usually accepted for a forecast of daily revenue
How it performs on days after its training data ends, the only place a forecast is used
Whether the fit would reach 99 percent with more history
Which algorithm the vendor used to reach that figure
variants.why: Fitting history well is the training-score problem from module four in a new costume; a forecast has to be scored on dates after the data it learned from. A better fit to the past is not evidence about the future.

review.concept: a range covers only what it has seen

variants.q: Your spend forecast comes with a range built from last year's backtest errors. Next month the platform's first ever price change takes effect. How should the forecast be presented?
options: As usual: a range built from a year of errors already allows for surprises like this one
With the range doubled, which is the cautious choice before any change of this kind
With the usual range for ordinary days, plus explicit scenarios for the price change
Not at all: a forecast made before a price change is not worth sending
variants.why: A range built from past errors describes the kinds of days in those errors, and a first-ever price change is not one of them. Doubling the range is a guess with no evidence behind it; a named scenario says what you are assuming and can be argued with.

variants.q: A support staffing forecast has a range that held on about four days in five in backtests. In a week with a major outage, actual tickets land outside the range on five days out of seven. What does that show?
options: The range was miscalculated and should be thrown away before anyone relies on it again
The range was built from ordinary days and never described outage weeks
The backtests must have been run incorrectly, since four days in five did not hold
The forecast model has memorised its training data
variants.why: On the course series the same band went from holding 78 percent of the time to 71 percent once incident days were included: a range covers what it has seen. That is a limit to state up front, not an error in the arithmetic.

variants.q: A client's e-commerce team has a daily demand forecast whose range held well all year. They are planning their first ever site-wide flash sale and ask whether the upper end of the range is a safe stock level for that day. What do you tell them?
options: No: the range reflects days like those in its history, and a first flash sale is not one of them
Yes: the upper end of a range that held all year is a conservative figure by construction
Yes, provided the range is recomputed on the most recent three months only
No: ranges are never reliable for single days, only for monthly totals
variants.why: The range was cut from errors on ordinary days, so it says nothing about a kind of day that has never happened; the sale needs its own scenario, built from what the team expects the sale to do. Recomputing the range on recent months changes nothing, because those months contain no flash sale either.

drill.q: Why is testing a flexible forecasting model on randomly held-out days too kind to it?
