drill.a: Because each held-out day sits between days the model trained on, so it can fill in the gap. The real job is to predict beyond the end of the data, so test from a past date forward.

drill.q: A forecast comes with a range built from its own past errors. What kind of day does that range not cover?
drill.a: Any kind it has not seen: an outage, a sudden change in level, something new. For those you need scenarios, not a slightly wider band.

recall.prompt: Explain how you would check a forecast before giving it to finance, and what you would hand over with it.
recall.model_answer: I would backtest it: stand at several past dates, train only on earlier days, forecast forward and compare with what happened, next to the naive methods. Random hold-outs are not enough, because the model can fill in between days it has seen. I would hand over the forecast with a range built from those backtest errors for the number asked for, a day or a total, and say how often the range held on backtests it was not built from. And I would say what it cannot cover: changes that have never happened before, which need scenarios.

lessons.ask_assistant: Backtest this forecast of [series]: from each of the last [twelve] [month starts], train only on data before that date and forecast the next [horizon]. For each backtest print the forecast date and the last training date. Report the average percentage error by [month] and by [week ahead], for the model and for two naive methods. Build an [80] percent range for [the number I need: one day, or the total over the horizon] from backtest errors of that same kind, using the earlier backtests, and report how often it held on the later ones. If I name a break date, add a step from that date and re-run the backtest: [break date, or none].
audit_checklist: Every backtest lists its forecast date and its last training day, and the training day is always earlier
Errors are shown by month and by week ahead, beside the naive methods
The range names what it covers, a day or a total, was built from errors of that same kind, and shows how often it held on backtests it was not built from
If you named a break date: the fitted size of the step is printed, and the error by month is shown before and after adding it
transfer: How many support agents are needed each day next month, and how wrong could that be?
How much stock should a client order for the next eight weeks?
Will this quarter's revenue target be met, and with what margin of doubt?

other_ways.approach: Train only on a recent window of history
other_ways.when: When you suspect the level or the rhythm has changed and cannot name a clean break date; check it with the same backtest.

other_ways.approach: A separate range for each week ahead
other_ways.when: When error grows with distance: copying last week forward missed by 5.1% in week one and 8.5% in week four, while the trend model stayed near 3%. Check each band on later backtests: with few of them the hit rates are noisy, here from 67% to 91%.

other_ways.approach: A tree model, with the trend taken out first
other_ways.when: When rhythms interact in ways a formula cannot express. A tree can only output values it has seen: asked for the raw level a year ahead, boosted trees ran about 9% low here; with the trend removed first, about 4% high.

glossary.def: A rehearsal of forecasting: pretend a past date is today, train only on earlier data, forecast forward and compare with what happened.
A band around the forecast inside which actual values are expected to fall a stated share of the time.
A lasting step up or down in a series, as opposed to a one-day spike.
A column that is 0 before a named date and 1 from it on, which lets a model learn a new level instead of blending it with the old one.
A forecast made under a named assumption about a change the history cannot show, such as a price change.

lessons.title: Anomalies: is this unusual?
lessons.subtitle: How do you tell a real incident from an ordinary day?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can specify an alert as an expectation plus a band, and insist that it is tested on planted incidents with alert days, incidents caught and false alarms counted separately.

predict.q: An alert fires whenever daily platform spend moves more than 15 percent from the day before. Over nine months it fired on 89 days. On which days did most of those alerts land?
options: Days with a real incident
Saturdays and Mondays
Public holidays
Evenly across the week
predict.reveal: Saturdays and Mondays: more than four in five of them. The lesson shows why, and what to compare with instead of yesterday.

segments.narration: Somebody once set an alert on the platform spend dashboard: tell me when spend moves more than 15 percent since yesterday. Run it over nine months of the daily series, the version with its incidents left in. Seven were planted there, so we know exactly where they are: an outage, a slow leak, a few spikes. The alert fired on 89 days. On 6 of them an incident was under way. On the other 83 it cried wolf. An alert like that stops being read, so it is also ignored on the day it is right.

visual.title: Anomalies: is this unusual?
visual.sub: First say what was expected

segments.narration: [[1]] Look at when it fired. [[2]] More than four in five of those alerts were Saturdays and Mondays. Spend falls into the weekend and climbs back out by more than 15 percent, week after week. The rule has no idea what a weekend is. [[3]] The one incident it missed is the instructive one: a spike on a Saturday, 30 percent above a normal Saturday. That looks like an ordinary weekday. Compared with yesterday, nothing happened. So the rule fails in both directions for one reason. Yesterday is the wrong thing to compare with. Unusual means far from what was expected. So first, say what was expected. It holds for any alert or outlier list: ask which publishers have a suspicious click rate, and the first question is, suspicious compared with what.

stats.label: alert days in 270
of them on a Saturday or a Monday
incident missed: a +30% spike on a Saturday

segments.narration: Second attempt. [[1]] Expect today to look like the same weekday over the last six weeks, and take the middle value. [[2]] Measure how far today is from that, in percent. Call it the surprise. [[3]] Alert only when the surprise is beyond three times its own normal wobble. Now a Saturday is judged against Saturdays. Alert days drop from 89 to 17. It still catches six of the seven incidents. And its false alarms now mean something: seven of the nine fall on known holidays. A holiday really is odd for its weekday; the detector just lacks the calendar. Have it skip the known holiday dates and nine false alarms become two.

visual.title: A better expectation: the same weekday
lines: expected = middle value of the same weekday, last 6 weeks
surprise = today ÷ expected − 1
alert when the surprise is beyond 3 × its normal wobble (its typical size in recent weeks)
visual.note: Result: 17 alert days · 6 of 7 incidents · 9 false-alarm days, 7 on known holidays (2 left if holidays are skipped).

segments.narration: [[1]] So far: a rule that compares with yesterday, [[2]] and one that compares with the same weekday. [[3]] The third takes its expectation from the forecast of the last two lessons, which already knows the weekday, the season, the trend and the holidays. Same band. Ten alert days, all seven incidents caught, no false alarms. Keep two counts apart here. Those incidents lasted 13 days in all, and 10 of those days were flagged. An incident counts as caught when any one of its days raises an alert. This detector also caught what the weekday one missed: a slow leak, spend running 12 percent below normal for five days. But it spoke up on the third day, not the first.

visual.title: Three detectors, the same nine months
visual.note: Seven planted incidents, 13 days in all; caught = any of its days flagged. The yesterday rule 'caught' the slow leak only on its last day, a Saturday.

segments.narration: Why can the forecast see a leak that the weekday comparison could not? [[1]] On an ordinary day, spend sits about 5 percent away from its same weekday level. [[2]] It sits under 2 and a half percent away from the forecast. A 12 percent drop hides inside the first and only just clears the second. Two of its five days were flagged, and a slightly wider band would have missed it. The sharper the expectation, the smaller the problem you can see. Now the caveat. This forecast has the same form as the equation that generated the series, in a world that never changes. No false alarms is a best case. On a real series, expect more.

visual.title: Typical gap from the expectation on an ordinary day

right.label: From the forecast
right.sub: a 12% leak just clears the band

segments.narration: Where to set the band is module two's cut-off decision, unchanged. Take the weekday detector. [[1]] Set the band at two and it catches every incident, at the price of 23 false alarm days. [[2]] Three was the setting we used. [[3]] Set it at five and the false alarms vanish. So do three of the seven incidents. Precision one way, recall the other. Which to favour is a business call: what does a missed outage cost, against a wasted morning?

visual.title: The weekday detector at three band settings
visual.note: A wider band: fewer false alarms, more missed incidents.

segments.narration: How do we know any of these counts? Only because the incidents were planted. On your own series, usually nobody has labelled the outages, so do the same: take a stretch of history, inject drops and spikes of known size and length, and count what the detector finds. Now try it. Switch between the three detectors, move the band, and watch three counts: alert days, incidents caught and false alarms. Then find the slow leak in late January, and see which settings catch it.

visual.name: anomalies
visual.title: Three detectors, one band, seven planted incidents
visual.note: Switch detector and move the band width. Watch alert days, incidents caught and false-alarm days. The slow leak starts on 20 January.

segments.narration: The brief. Ask the assistant for an alert, and make the output state five things. [[1]] What each day is compared with. If the answer is yesterday, send it back. [[2]] The band, and the reason for that setting. [[3]] A test on planted incidents of several sizes and lengths, including a slow one. [[4]] Three counts kept apart: alert days, incidents caught, false alarm days. Precision alone hides the misses; incidents caught alone hides the noise. [[5]] And the dates of the false alarms. Here they were mostly holidays, which told us what the detector did not know.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Compared with what? Not just yesterday
The band, and why that setting
Tested on planted incidents, including a slow one
Three counts: alert days, incidents caught, false-alarm days
The dates of the false alarms

segments.narration: So when an alert or an outlier list reaches you, series or table rows alike, ask what was expected, how far this is from it, where the cut-off sits, and how it was tested. Next, the last lesson on time: not whether an advertiser will leave, but when.

visual.title: The recipe, for a series or for rows

takeaways: Unusual means far from expected: compare with the same weekday or a forecast, never just with yesterday.
The alert band is a cut-off: wider means fewer false alarms and more missed incidents.
Test a detector on planted incidents, counting alert days, incidents caught and false alarms separately.

quiz.q: The conversions dashboard has an alert: 'conversions down more than 20 percent versus yesterday'. It fires most Saturdays and nobody reads it any more. Which change fixes the cause without hiding one-day incidents?
options: Raise the trigger to 40 percent, so that an ordinary Saturday no longer fires
Mute the alert at weekends, when the drop is expected and nobody is watching
Compare each day with what is expected for that weekday, and alert on the gap
Alert on the seven-day average instead, which smooths the weekend away
quiz.why: The alert fires because yesterday is the wrong comparison for a metric with a weekly rhythm; judging a Saturday against Saturdays removes the cause. Raising the trigger or muting weekends quietens the alert by also silencing real incidents, and a seven-day average spreads a one-day incident over seven days until it is too small to see.

quiz.q: The assistant reports on a new spend alert: 'Tested on nine months of history: 5 alert days, every one of them during a real incident. Precision 100 percent.' What must the output also show before you call it a good detector?
options: The precision of the same alert on a second metric, to confirm that 100 percent is no fluke
How many incidents occurred in those nine months, and how many of them it caught
The alert threshold expressed in dollars of spend instead of as a percentage
The same test repeated on at least five years of history, to make the precision stable
quiz.why: A detector that rarely alerts can be perfectly precise while missing most incidents: on the course series the weekday detector at its widest band raised 5 alert days, none of them false, and caught only four of seven. Precision counts the alerts that were right; you also need the incidents that got no alert.

quiz.q: The traffic-quality team wants to flag publishers with suspicious clicks. Nobody has labelled past fraud. In your data, click rate runs several times higher on some placement types than on others. The assistant proposes flagging the top 1 percent of publishers by click rate. What is the first gap?
options: No definition of normal: 'high' must be judged against what is expected for that placement type
The cut-off: flagging the top 5 percent instead of the top 1 percent would be the safer choice
Labels: without known fraud cases no detector can be built, tested or trusted at all
The method: a ranking is too simple, so a more advanced algorithm is needed to find fraud
quiz.why: Ranking by raw click rate mostly finds the placement types that always run high, just as the yesterday rule mostly found Saturdays. Say what is expected for each kind of publisher first; and missing labels are handled by planting known cases, not by giving up.

quiz.q: The spend alert has been live for a month. The on-call analyst is tired of false alarms and asks you to widen the band until there are none. What do you bring to that conversation?
options: Agreement: a detector that raises no false alarms at all is exactly what the team wants
A refusal: a band of three is the statistical standard and should not be changed
A proposal to narrow the band instead, since more alerts are always the safer side
A table of band settings: false-alarm days beside planted incidents missed
quiz.why: Widening the band buys fewer false alarms at the price of more missed incidents, so the right setting depends on what each mistake costs; the table puts both on the page. No setting is a standard: three happened to suit one simulated series.

review.concept: say what was expected before calling something unusual

variants.q: Spend for one vertical is 18 percent lower on a Sunday than on the Saturday before, and an alert calls it an anomaly. What do you check first?
options: Whether the 18 percent drop is above the trigger that the alert was set to fire at
What that vertical's recent Sundays looked like compared with their Saturdays
Whether the vertical's account managers or large clients changed that week
Spend on the same date one year earlier, which is the only fair comparison
variants.why: A day is unusual only against what was expected for it, and for a Sunday that is what recent Sundays looked like. A drop from Saturday to Sunday, taken alone, measures the weekly rhythm, which is how the yesterday rule ended up firing on Saturdays and Mondays.

variants.q: An advertiser's CPA is 40 dollars against a platform average of 15, and a report lists it as an anomaly. The advertiser is in finance, where your data shows CPAs running several times higher than in gaming. What is the right read?
options: It is an anomaly: 40 dollars is far from the platform average, whatever the vertical
It cannot be judged at all without first training a model on every advertiser
Judge it against what is normal for finance advertisers; there it may be ordinary
Remove finance advertisers from the report, since they distort the comparison
variants.why: The platform average is the wrong expectation for a vertical that always runs high, just as yesterday is the wrong expectation for a Saturday. Define normal for the kind of row you are looking at, then measure the distance from that.

variants.q: A publisher's click volume triples every Tuesday morning, when its weekly newsletter goes out, and the traffic-quality alert fires every Tuesday. What is the alert really telling you?
options: That the publisher is sending invalid traffic once a week and should be suspended
That the detector does not know about the newsletter; for a Tuesday this is normal
That the alert's trigger is set too low and should be raised until it stops firing
That click counts from this publisher are too erratic to be worth monitoring
variants.why: The volume is far from an average morning but not far from what a newsletter Tuesday normally looks like, so the surprise comes from the detector's ignorance of the schedule. It is the holiday false alarm again: compare Tuesdays with Tuesdays. Raising the trigger would also hide a real problem on every other day.

review.concept: an alert cut-off trades false alarms for misses

variants.q: A spend alert's band is widened from three to five times the normal wobble, and false-alarm days fall from 9 to 0. What else must you look at before celebrating?
options: Whether precision at the wider band has now reached 100 percent
How many of the known incidents it still catches at the wider band
Whether the total number of alert days also fell, as it should have
Whether a band of five also works for the platform's other metrics
variants.why: A wider band removes false alarms and catches together: on the course series the same change took the weekday detector from six of seven incidents caught to four. Fewer alert days is guaranteed by a wider band and tells you nothing about misses.

variants.q: A click-fraud filter has been tuned so that it never blocks a legitimate publisher, and the team reports this as success. Which number is missing?
options: The share of known or planted fraudulent publishers that it lets through
The average click rate of the publishers that the filter does block
The total number of publishers on the platform, to put the result in proportion
The time the filter takes to run on a full day of traffic
variants.why: Never blocking a legitimate publisher is perfect precision, which a filter that blocks almost nobody achieves easily. The other half of the trade is recall: how much real fraud passes untouched.

variants.q: A payments team has tuned its alert on failed card charges so that it catches every one of last year's known outages. It now fires on roughly one day in three. What is the right way to describe that setting?
options: Ideal: an alert that misses none of the known outages cannot be improved on, so leave it there
Broken: an alert that fires on one day in three must contain a bug and needs debugging
One end of a trade: every outage caught, paid for in false alarms; pick the point by cost
Too sensitive by definition: a useful alert should fire less than once a month
variants.why: Catching everything and firing rarely pull against each other, exactly like recall and precision, and this setting sits at the catch-everything end. Whether that is right depends on what a missed outage costs against a wasted investigation, not on a rule about how often an alert may fire.

drill.q: An alert fires whenever a daily number moves more than a fixed percentage from the day before. Why is that a poor alert for a metric with a weekly rhythm, and what should it compare with instead?
drill.a: Every weekend looks like a big move, so it fires constantly, and a real problem at a weekend can look normal. Compare each day with what is expected for that weekday, or with a forecast.

drill.q: Nobody has labelled past incidents. How do you find out what an anomaly detector would miss?
drill.a: Plant incidents of known size and length in a copy of the history, then count how many it catches and how many false alarms it raises.

recall.prompt: Explain what a good anomaly alert needs, and how you would show that one works.
recall.model_answer: An alert needs an expectation and a band. Say what the value should have been, such as the same weekday in recent weeks or a forecast that knows the calendar, and flag days that are further from it than the normal wobble explains. The band is a cut-off, so widening it trades false alarms for missed incidents. To show it works, plant incidents of known size in the history and report alert days, incidents caught and false alarms separately.

lessons.ask_assistant: Build an anomaly alert for [metric] by [day]. Compare each [day] with an expectation that knows the calendar: [the median of the same weekday over the last few weeks, or a forecast]. Alert when the gap exceeds [k] times its typical size over recent weeks, and say how you measured that typical size. Test it by injecting incidents of several sizes and lengths, including a slow multi-day one, into a copy of the history, and list them. For [three] band settings report alert days, incidents caught, incident days flagged and false-alarm days, and list the dates of the false alarms.
audit_checklist: A table of sample days shows actual, expected and the gap; the expectation is not simply yesterday's value, and the output says how the normal variation behind the band was measured
Alert days, incidents caught and false-alarm days are reported separately, for more than one band setting
The planted incidents are listed with their size and length, including a slow one
The false-alarm dates are listed, so you can see whether they are holidays or other known events
transfer: Is this advertiser's click-through rate suspiciously high for its vertical and placement mix?
Did the conversion rate on a client's landing page really break yesterday?
Which of this month's invoices are unusual enough to check by hand?

other_ways.approach: Average the surprise over several days
other_ways.when: In principle, for slow drifts too small to stand out on one day. Test it first: on this series a seven-day average caught only two of the seven incidents.

other_ways.approach: Alert on the parts as well as the total
other_ways.when: When a problem in one vertical or one large account is too small to move the platform total.

other_ways.approach: A fixed business limit
other_ways.when: When what matters is a hard line, such as spend above a credit limit, and not whether the day is statistically unusual.

glossary.def: A value far from what was expected for that moment, given what is known about the calendar.
What a detector assumes the value should have been: yesterday, the same weekday in recent weeks, or a forecast.

How far from the expectation a value may fall before an alert fires, measured against the normal wobble: the typical size of the surprise over recent weeks. An assistant may report it as a number of standard deviations or a z-score threshold.
A made-up problem of known size and date, injected into history to test what a detector catches.
An incident with at least one of its days flagged; not the same as flagging every bad day.

lessons.title: When, not whether: time to event
lessons.subtitle: How long do advertisers last, when half of them have not left yet?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can spot an average lifetime that ignores customers who are still active, ask for a survival curve instead, and say when a fixed-window yes/no label is safe to use.

predict.q: A table holds 6,000 advertisers who joined over the last two years. About half have churned, and those who churned lasted 21 weeks on average. After how many weeks have half of all advertisers left?
options: About 10 weeks
About 21 weeks
About 43 weeks
Unknowable until everyone has churned
predict.reveal: About 43 weeks, double the naive figure: the average left out everyone who is still active. The lesson shows how to count them.

segments.narration: You already build cohort retention tables, and you leave the unfinished cells blank. Hold that thought. A product manager asks how long advertisers last, and the assistant averages the weeks between joining and leaving, for everyone who has churned. About 21 weeks. Computed properly, from the same table, the halfway point is 43 weeks: only then have half of all advertisers left. Double. The SQL was fine. What was wrong is who the query left out. One note: this is a separate simulation, 6,000 advertisers who joined over the last two years, so the true answer is known.

visual.title: When, not whether
visual.sub: How long advertisers last, counted properly

segments.narration: Here is who is missing. A little over half of the 6,000 have churned. The 21 weeks is their average. The other 48 percent are still active. They have no end date, so the query dropped them. But they are not missing data. Say an advertiser joined 60 weeks ago and is still spending. That is a lifetime of at least 60 weeks. The word for that is censored. We know a floor, not the final figure. So an average of the leavers is an average of the quick leavers. The advertisers who last longest are still here. Any how long question has this trap: ask how long a creative lasts before it fades, and the long lived ones are still running.

left.label: Average lifetime of those who churned

right.label: Week by which half of everyone has left
right.sub: all 6,000 advertisers counted

segments.narration: The fix is to ask a small question many times, instead of one question about a whole lifetime. [[1]] For each week of tenure: who was still active at the start of it, and still being watched? [[2]] Of those, what share left during that week? An advertiser who joined ten weeks ago counts in the first ten of these questions, then steps out. Nobody is thrown away, and nobody's outcome is guessed. [[3]] Multiply the shares who stayed, week after week, [[4]] and you get the share still active after any number of weeks. That is your cohort table pooled across join months, which assumes recent joiners behave like earlier ones. Its name is the Kaplan–Meier curve. From here on, the survival curve.

visual.title: A small question, asked every week

steps.label: Each week of tenure
steps.sub: who is still active and still being watched?

steps.label: Multiply
steps.sub: the shares who stayed, week after week

steps.label: Survival curve
steps.sub: share still active after each week

segments.narration: After 13 weeks, three quarters of advertisers are still active. After a year, about 45 percent. And the curve crosses one half at 43 weeks. That is the typical lifetime: the week by which half have gone. Because this is a simulation, we can hold the estimate against the truth: they agree to within a point out to a year and a half. Two years out, it drifts. The curve says 26 percent where the truth is 28, because few advertisers have been watched that long. The far end of a survival curve rests on the fewest people. Try it now: pick a week and read off who is left, then split the curve by account manager.

visual.name: survival
visual.title: Share of advertisers still active
visual.note: Move the week slider: 13 weeks, one year, and where the curve crosses one half. Then split by account manager.

segments.narration: The curve also answers something an average never can: when is the danger? Take the advertisers still active at the start of each 13 week block, and ask what share leave during it. [[1]] In the first block, a quarter. [[2]] In the second, about 18 percent. [[4]] Then it eases, [[6]] and after the first year it settles near one in eight per quarter. Risk falls with tenure. That changes the retention conversation: the expensive weeks are the first thirteen. In this simulation that falling risk was built in. On your own data it is something to measure, not to assume.

visual.title: Of those still active at the start of each quarter, the share who leave during it

segments.narration: You do not always need the curve. A yes or no label in a fixed window is a fine target for a model: here, churned within 26 weeks of joining. But it only works for advertisers you have watched for at least 26 weeks. [[1]] Here that is about 4,700 of the 6,000. The newest fifth is set aside, because their window has not closed. Among the rest, about 39 percent churned inside the window, which agrees with the curve. [[2]] Count everyone instead, and you get 36 percent. Too low, and wrong in a predictable direction: every not yet has been counted as a no.

left.label: Only advertisers watched 26 weeks or more

right.label: Counting all 6,000
right.sub: every 'not yet' counted as 'no'

segments.narration: So which framing, when? It follows the decision, as in module one. [[1]] If the team needs a list of who to call this quarter, a yes or no in a fixed window is the right target, built from advertisers whose window has closed. [[2]] If the question is how long advertisers last, [[3]] or in which weeks they are most at risk, that is the survival curve. [[4]] And when most of your customers are recent, only the curve can use them all.

visual.title: Which framing for which question
rows: Who should we call this quarter?
Yes/no in a fixed window, closed windows only
Survival curve: risk by block of tenure

segments.narration: The brief. Ask for a survival curve, never an average lifetime, and five things in the output. [[1]] How many advertisers went in, and how many are still active. [[2]] How many are still being watched at each point on the curve. [[3]] The median lifetime, the halfway point, read from the curve. [[4]] And whenever it reports a rate like churned within 26 weeks, how many advertisers it left out because their window had not closed. If that number is zero, be suspicious. [[5]] And the curve by join period: your cohort table again, which shows whether recent joiners behave like earlier ones. For any other split, a gap between curves is a gap between groups, not proof of cause.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Advertisers in, and how many are still active
Number still being watched at each point of the curve
Median lifetime, read from the curve
For any fixed-window rate: how many were left out because their window had not closed
The curve by join period: your cohort table again

segments.narration: So the next time a lifetime or a time to convert appears on a slide, ask who has not finished yet, and how they were counted. Next module: what you can learn when there is no answer column at all.

visual.text: Not yet is not no.
visual.sub: Count every customer for as long as you watched them.

takeaways: Customers who are still active are censored, not missing: you know they lasted at least this long.
Averaging only those who left counts the quick leavers; a survival curve uses everyone for as long as they were watched.
A fixed-window yes/no label is valid only for customers whose window has fully closed.

quiz.q: The assistant's report states: 'Average advertiser lifetime: 21 weeks, based on 3,099 churned advertisers.' The source table has 6,000 advertisers. What is the right response?
options: Ask for a margin of error around the 21 weeks, because 3,099 advertisers are only a sample of 6,000
Ask for the median of those 3,099 instead of the mean, since lifetimes are skewed
Ask it to add the active advertisers, counting their tenure so far as their full lifetime
Ask for a survival curve over all 6,000: the 2,901 left out are mostly the long-lasting ones
quiz.why: The figure describes only advertisers who have already left, and those are disproportionately the quick leavers; the curve over everyone put the halfway point at 43 weeks. A median of the same 3,099 has the same blind spot, a margin of error only puts an interval around it, and treating tenure so far as a finished lifetime understates every advertiser who is still going.

quiz.concept: a window that has not closed
quiz.q: A new self-serve tier launched 10 weeks ago. A dashboard tile reads 'churned within 26 weeks: 8 percent' for the new tier, against 39 percent for older advertisers. A stakeholder calls the launch a retention win. What is wrong?
options: Nobody in the new tier has been watched for 26 weeks, so the tile counts 'not yet' as 'no'
The window is too short to separate the tiers: 'churned within 52 weeks' would show the gap more clearly
The new tier is a much smaller group, so its rate needs a margin of error before any comparison
The two groups joined in different seasons, so the rates need a seasonal adjustment
quiz.why: Nobody in the new tier has had 26 weeks in which to churn, so the 8 percent can only count those who left within 10 weeks and is bound to be too low, whatever the tier is really like. Compare the two groups at 10 weeks on survival curves instead; a margin of error would only put an interval around a number that measures the wrong thing.

quiz.q: To plan creative refreshes, the assistant measures how many days a creative runs before its click rate falls to half its launch level. It averages the creatives that have already reached that point: 9 days. Half of the creatives launched this quarter have not reached it yet. What does 9 days tell you?
options: That the typical creative lasts about 9 days before it needs replacing, so plan refreshes weekly
That no figure can be trusted yet: lifetimes cannot be analysed until every creative has faded
The average of the fastest faders only; counting those still running, the typical life is longer
An overestimate, because the creatives still running are the ones about to fade
quiz.why: The creatives still running are censored: each has already lasted as long as it has run and will last longer, so leaving them out pulls the answer down. You do not have to wait for all of them to fade; a survival curve uses each creative for as long as it has been observed.

quiz.q: The retention team asks two things: which current advertisers to call this month, and in which weeks of an advertiser's life the risk of leaving is highest. Which pairing fits?
options: A survival curve for the call list; an average lifetime of churned advertisers for the timing
A fixed-window yes/no model for the call list; risk by tenure block for the timing
A fixed-window yes/no model for the call list, and the same model for the timing
An average lifetime of churned advertisers for the list and for the timing
quiz.why: A call list needs a score for each advertiser over a fixed period ahead, which the yes/no model gives; the overall survival curve has one value per week of tenure, the same for everyone, so it cannot rank individuals. When risk peaks is a question about tenure, which the curve answers block by block: here it fell from a quarter in the first 13 weeks to about one in eight per quarter later.

review.concept: still active means censored, not missing

variants.q: A support dashboard shows 'average resolution time: 2.1 days', computed from closed tickets. A fifth of this month's tickets are still open, some of them for more than two weeks. What is the right read?
options: About right: closed tickets are the only ones with a known resolution time, so 2.1 days stands
Too low: open tickets are mostly the slow ones, and each has already lasted its age so far
Too high: the open tickets are about to close quickly and will pull the average down
Unknowable: nothing can be said about resolution time until every ticket has closed
variants.why: Closed tickets are the ones that closed fast enough to be closed already; the slow ones are mostly still open, and each already counts for at least its age. Ignoring them as 'no data' is the same mistake as averaging only churned advertisers, and a survival curve shows you do not have to wait for all of them.

variants.q: A growth analyst reports that new advertisers take 12 days on average to launch a first campaign, measured on those who have launched one. Forty percent of sign-ups from the last two months have not launched yet. What does the 12 days leave out?
options: The sign-ups who launched on their very first day, who drag the average down and need trimming
The seasonal pattern in sign-ups over those two months, which shifts the average
A margin of error around the 12 days, which would make the figure safe to quote
Everyone still waiting, who will take longer than they have waited so far, or never launch
variants.why: Sign-ups who have not launched are censored: each has already waited some days and will take longer, so the typical time is above 12 days. A margin of error would be an interval around a number that only describes the fast starters.

variants.q: An agency client reports: 'Account managers who left stayed 14 months on average.' Most account managers hired in the last three years are still employed. How should the 14 months be used?
options: As the expected tenure of a new hire, since it is the only tenure figure that is complete
As an upper limit on how long account managers stay with the agency
Not as typical tenure: it describes only those who left soon enough to have left already
As the median tenure, since mean and median are close for durations like these
variants.why: The people still employed are the long-tenure ones and are missing from the average, so 14 months understates how long a typical hire stays. It errs on the low side, so it is no upper limit either; a survival curve over all hires gives the usable answer.

review.concept: a fixed-window label needs a closed window

variants.q: You want the share of advertisers who churn within 26 weeks of joining. Your table includes advertisers who joined between 4 and 104 weeks ago. Which advertisers go into the calculation?
options: All of them: more rows give a steadier rate, and the recent joiners are customers too
Only those who joined at least 26 weeks ago
Only those who have already churned, since their outcome is known
Only those who joined in the last 26 weeks, since they are the most relevant
variants.why: An advertiser who joined 10 weeks ago cannot yet be a 'no' for a 26-week window; including them counts every 'not yet' as a stay. On the course data that pulled the rate down from about 39 percent to 36.

variants.q: A lead-scoring model is trained on the label 'converted within 30 days'. The training table includes leads created up to yesterday, and any lead not yet converted is labelled 0. What is the effect?
options: Leads from busy weeks are over-represented, so the table needs reweighting by the week of creation
The model will overstate the chance of conversion for every lead it scores
The label needs shortening to 'converted within 1 day' so that every lead has an answer
Recent leads that will still convert are labelled failures; drop leads younger than 30 days
variants.why: A lead created last week has not had its 30 days, so a 0 on it means 'not yet', not 'no'. Training on those rows teaches the model that whatever is true of recent leads predicts failure, and makes the conversion rate look lower than it is.

variants.q: A finance report shows the '90-day refund rate' by order month. The two most recent months show much lower rates than the older ones, and the assistant concludes that product quality has improved. What is the more likely explanation?
options: Orders from the last two months have not yet had 90 days in which to be refunded
Customers have become more satisfied with the product since the last release
The refund policy was tightened two months ago, which mechanically lowers the rate
Ordinary month-to-month noise in refunds, which a margin of error would cover
variants.why: A 90-day rate for an order placed 40 days ago is unfinished by construction, so recent months will always look better than they are. Check the mechanical explanation before the flattering one: recompute using only orders that are at least 90 days old.

drill.q: Why does averaging the lifetimes of customers who have already left understate how long customers last?
drill.a: Because it leaves out everyone who is still active, and those are the ones lasting longest. You end up averaging the quick leavers.

drill.q: You want the share of customers who churn within six months of joining. Which customers may you count?
drill.a: Only those who joined at least six months ago, so the window has fully closed. Counting newer customers treats not yet as no, and the rate comes out too low.

recall.prompt: Explain why 'average lifetime of churned customers' is misleading, and what to ask for instead.
recall.model_answer: It averages only customers who have already left and drops everyone still active, who are exactly the long-lasting ones; they are censored, meaning we know they lasted at least this long. A survival curve fixes that by asking, week by week, what share of those still active and still being watched left, so every customer counts for as long as they were observed. From it you read the median lifetime and when the risk is highest. A fixed-window yes/no label is also fine, but only for customers whose window has fully closed.

lessons.ask_assistant: Estimate how long [customers] last with a survival curve (Kaplan–Meier), not an average over those who have already [left]. Treat everyone still [active] as censored at their tenure so far. Report how many went in, how many are still [active], the share still [active] at [four or five tenure points] with the number still being watched at each, and the median lifetime. Add the risk of [leaving] per [block of tenure], and the curve split by [join period]. For any '[event] within [N weeks]' rate, use only those who started at least [N weeks] ago and print how many you left out.
audit_checklist: The counts add up: everyone in = already churned + still active, and the curve's first point starts from everyone
Each point on the curve shows how many advertisers were still being watched
The median lifetime is the week where the plotted curve crosses one half, and curves by join period show whether recent joiners differ
Any fixed-window churn rate prints how many advertisers were left out because their window had not closed
transfer: How long does a creative run before its click-through rate fades to half its launch level?
How long do support tickets take to resolve, when some are still open?
How many days until a new sign-up launches a first campaign, when many have not yet?

other_ways.approach: A fixed-window yes/no model
other_ways.when: When the decision is a list for a fixed period ahead, and enough customers have a fully closed window.

other_ways.approach: A cohort retention table
other_ways.when: When you want the same picture in dashboard form, or suspect that join months behave differently: the share of each join month still active after each month, with unfinished cells left blank.

other_ways.approach: A model of time to churn that uses features
other_ways.when: When you need to know which advertisers leave sooner, not only the overall curve; the same rule about censoring applies.

glossary.def: Observed only up to now: we know the customer lasted at least this long, not how long in the end.

The share of customers still active after each week of tenure: a cohort retention table pooled across join months, estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method so that every customer counts for as long as they were watched.
The tenure by which half of customers have left, read where the survival curve crosses one half.
Framing a question as how long until something happens, instead of whether it happens within a fixed window.

lessons.title: Clustering: segments without labels
lessons.subtitle: The algorithm returned four tidy segments. How do you know they mean anything?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can commission a clustering and run the checks that show whether its segments are a finding or an artefact of the method.

predict.q: The assistant runs k-means and gets four advertiser segments. You ask for the identical analysis again, changing only the random starting point. What comes back?
options: Exactly the same four segments: the data has not changed
The same four segments, listed in a different order
Possibly a noticeably different set of segments
An error: clustering needs an answer column to learn from
predict.reveal: Possibly quite different: on this course's table, six re-runs agreed with the first anywhere from 0.76 down to 0.17, where 1 means identical. The lesson shows why, and what to check.

segments.narration: The request lands on a Tuesday: segment our advertisers. You hand it to the assistant, and twenty minutes later four tidy segments are on your screen. Churn runs from under 5 percent in the best to 35 percent in the worst. Someone is already drafting names. Champions. Strugglers. Before those names reach a slide, one awkward fact. Clustering always hands back groups. Ask for four and you get four, whether or not four kinds of advertiser exist. That holds for any rows grouped without an answer column: ask what kinds of publisher send you traffic, and groups come back just the same. Whether they mean anything is yours to check.

visual.title: Clustering: segments without labels
visual.sub: Four tidy segments, churn from 4.5% to 35.1%. Are they real?

segments.narration: The assistant ran k-means. Think of it as a GROUP BY where nobody supplied the groups. [[1]] You choose k, the number of groups. Here, four. [[2]] The method drops four centres into the data at random. [[3]] Each advertiser joins its nearest centre. [[4]] Each centre moves to the middle of its advertisers. [[5]] Assign again, move again, until nothing changes. That is the whole algorithm. Notice what never appeared: an answer column. Churn was not shown to it. It only made the groups compact.

visual.title: k-means: a GROUP BY that invents its own groups

steps.label: Assign
steps.sub: each row to its nearest centre

steps.label: Move
steps.sub: each centre to the middle of its rows

segments.narration: Nearest centre. That word needs a ruler. Distance adds up the differences between two advertisers, column by column. Spend runs in the thousands of dollars. Active days, campaigns and creatives are small numbers. So on raw columns, distance is almost entirely a difference in spend. Here is a test of the ruler alone: predict churn from the 25 most similar past advertisers. [[1]] On raw columns that scores an AUC of about 0.63. [[2]] Put every column on a common scale first, as you did for the weighted sum, and it scores about 0.80. Only the ruler changed.

visual.title: Grading the ruler, not building groups: predict churn from the 25 most similar advertisers (AUC)

right.label: Columns on a common scale
right.sub: every column gets a say · churn is only the referee here

segments.narration: The assistant did use a common scale, on eight behaviour columns. The best segment holds over a third of advertisers and loses under 5 percent of them. The worst holds about one in ten and loses 35 percent. It looks like a discovery. Now read across the columns instead of down the churn. In the first segment, everyone uses auto-bidding. In the second, nobody does, and everybody has conversion tracking. In the third, nobody has tracking. Only the fourth is something new: creatives last refreshed about 80 days ago. Three of your four segments are, near enough, two yes-or-no columns you already had.

visual.title: The four segments k-means returned
visual.note: k = 4, eight behaviour columns on a common scale. Churn was never shown to the method. Which columns dominate is a quirk of this simulated table.

segments.narration: [[1]] First check. Write the plain GROUP BY yourself: tracking, yes or no, by auto-bidding, yes or no. Score how closely the two groupings agree, where zero means unrelated and one means identical. The score is 0.7: a lot of overlap for a method meant to find something new. On a common scale a yes-or-no column is two piles with a wide gap between them, and k-means loves a gap. [[2]] Second check. The centres start at random, so run the same clustering from six different starting points and compare each with the first. The same method on the same data should score close to one. The best re-run scored 0.76 and the worst 0.17: nearly a different segmentation.

stats.label: agreement with a plain GROUP BY on tracking × auto-bidding: high for a method meant to find something new
agreement with its own first run, across six random starts: the same segments coming back would score close to 1

segments.narration: [[1]] A third check. Drop those two columns and cluster on the six that remain. [[2]] The new segments are close to unrelated to the old ones: agreement 0.17. Yet churn spreads just as widely, from 4 percent to 32. Two unrelated ways of cutting the same advertisers, and both seem to explain churn. Why? In this simulated world good habits and low churn travel together, so almost any grouping on behaviour sorts advertisers by churn. A GROUP BY on spend tier and account manager, no algorithm at all, spreads churn from 5 percent to 19. That is the baseline. Only one profile shows up both times and beats it: the stale creatives, at 35 and 32 percent churn.

visual.title: Cluster again without the two yes/no columns

right.label: Without them
right.sub: agreement with the first segments: 0.17

segments.narration: And the number four? You chose it. K-means reports an error: how far advertisers sit from their centres. Add a segment and the error falls. It always does, because more centres are always closer. A natural number of groups would show as a sharp bend. From two segments to eight the error simply keeps sliding. Nothing in the data says four. So when does clustering earn its place? When there are many columns and no obvious cut. And when a segment holds up: it returns from a different random start and in a second month of data, and it separates an outcome it never saw better than your GROUP BY does.

visual.title: More segments always fit better: nothing says stop at four
visual.note: A natural number of groups would show as a sharp bend. The curve keeps sliding.

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask the assistant to list the columns it clustered on and how they were scaled, with no outcome column among them. [[2]] Ask for a profile of every segment: its size and the average of each column, so a segment that is one column in disguise shows itself. [[3]] Ask for runs from several random starts, with an agreement score between them. [[4]] Ask for the error at each k from two to eight. [[5]] And ask for the plain GROUP BY you would have written, beside the segments, on the same outcome. When you already hold the outcome the segments should differ on, ask for a shallow decision tree on it instead: each leaf is a segment with a rate.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Show: columns used, how scaled, no outcome column among them
Show: a profile per segment (size, average of every column)
Show: agreement between runs from several random starts
Show: the error for k = 2 to 8
Show: a plain GROUP BY beside the segments, same outcome

segments.narration: So the next time someone asks for segments, order the checks in the same breath as the clustering, and name nothing until a segment has come back twice. Next, distance does something less obvious: it measures how close two pieces of text are in meaning.

visual.title: Keep this
items: Clustering always returns groups, real or not
Distance needs a common scale, or the biggest unit wins
Believe a segment that survives a re-run and beats a plain GROUP BY

takeaways: Clustering returns as many groups as you ask for, every time; tidy segments are not evidence that the groups exist.
Similarity depends on the ruler: put columns on a common scale, or the column with the biggest units decides everything.
Trust a segment only after it survives a re-run from another random start and separates an unseen outcome better than a plain GROUP BY.

quiz.q: The assistant clusters advertisers on eight columns left in their raw units. The four segments differ sharply on spend, from a group of very small accounts up to a group of very large ones, and hardly at all on any other column. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Spend is what truly separates kinds of advertiser, and the method has simply discovered that.
Raw dollars swamp the other columns in the distance, so this is only a spend tier.
Four segments are too few; with more of them, the other columns would start to show up.
K-means cannot handle money columns, so spend should be removed from the inputs.
quiz.why: Distance adds up differences column by column, so a column in thousands of dollars drowns columns measured in single digits and the result is a GROUP BY on spend tier. That is a property of the units, not a discovery about advertisers, which is why the first option is tempting and wrong. More segments would only cut spend finer; the fix is a common scale, not dropping the column.

quiz.concept: a churn spread is not proof
quiz.q: The assistant's report reads: 'K-means, k = 4, eight standardised behaviour columns, one run with random seed 42. Churn was not used. Segment churn ranges from 4.5 to 35.1 percent, which confirms the segments are real.' What is missing before you can accept the last sentence?
options: A significance test on the spread, to show that 4.5 against 35.1 percent is not chance.
The churn column among the inputs, so that the segments are built to explain churn.
A larger k: four segments cannot describe twelve thousand different advertisers.
Re-runs from other random starts, and a plain GROUP BY's churn spread beside it.
quiz.why: One run with a fixed seed hides whether the segments come back, and a churn spread proves little on its own: on this table an unrelated clustering and a plain GROUP BY on spend tier and account manager also spread churn widely. A significance test is the tempting request, but the spread is not in doubt: any grouping on behaviour will sort churn when good habits and low churn travel together, so a spread that is clearly not chance still does not show that these four groups exist. Feeding churn in would simply bake the answer into the groups.

quiz.concept: clusters differ on their own inputs by construction
quiz.q: A sales-operations analyst clusters 8,000 inbound leads into five personas using twenty form and browsing columns. The deck's evidence that the personas are real: 'the five groups differ significantly on 17 of the 20 columns.' What is the right response?
options: That is circular. Do the personas return next month and differ on conversion?
Ask how large the seventeen differences are: big gaps on most columns would settle it.
Drop the three columns that do not separate the personas and run the clustering again.
Increase the number of personas until all twenty columns differ between the groups.
quiz.why: Groups built by pulling leads apart on those twenty columns must differ on them, so the test would pass for any clustering of any data. Evidence comes from outside the inputs: the same personas reappearing on fresh leads, and differing on an outcome the method never saw. Counting significant differences, or measuring how big they are, feels rigorous, which is what makes the second option the usual mistake.

quiz.concept: the data does not choose k
quiz.q: To settle the number of segments, the assistant runs k-means for every k from 2 to 8 and writes: 'The error is lowest at k = 8, so eight segments is the best choice.' The error falls by a similar amount at each step. What is the right read?
options: Take the middle of the range, k = 5: it balances a low error against simple segments.
Keep increasing k beyond eight until the error finally stops falling altogether.
The error always falls as k grows; with no sharp bend, the number is your call to make and to check.
Choose two segments, because the first step is where the method learned the most.
quiz.why: More centres are always closer to the rows, so the error keeps falling until every advertiser is its own segment: lowest error simply means most segments. A natural number of groups would show as a sharp bend, and a smooth slide means the data is not choosing, so the middle of the range is as arbitrary as either end. Pick the number the team can act on, then check those segments hold up.

review.concept: clustering always returns groups: check they hold up

variants.q: An analyst clusters 3,000 publisher sites into six groups by traffic pattern and labels one small group 'suspicious'. A re-run with a different random seed splits that group, and half its sites land in a large ordinary one. The fraud team wants to block the original list today. What is the right call?
options: Fix the random seed and run it again: once the group is reproducible, the list can be blocked.
Hold off: the group is unstable, so test it against sites already known to be invalid.
Run it a third time and block the sites that two of the three runs agree on.
Average the two runs' group numbers for each site and block the highest values.
variants.why: A group that dissolves when only the random start changes is a product of the start, not yet of the sites. Fixing the seed makes the result repeatable without making it true, and a vote between runs still never asks whether the group means anything. Treat the cluster as a lead and check it against an outcome the method never saw, such as confirmed invalid traffic.

variants.q: A retailer's analyst presents three customer segments from a clustering on twelve columns. A colleague notices that grouping by two existing flags, loyalty card and online-only, reproduces the segments almost exactly. What should the team take from that?
options: Add columns to the clustering until its segments stop matching the two flags.
The two flags should be removed, because they are contaminating the clustering.
The clustering has failed, and the twelve columns should be collected again.
The segments are those two flags, so use the plain GROUP BY instead.
variants.why: When a clustering mostly matches a GROUP BY you could have written, it has rediscovered columns you already had, and the GROUP BY is easier to explain and does not move between runs. The match is not a second confirmation either: both groupings come from the same two flags, and adding columns until the match disappears would only hide that. Dropping the flags is worth trying as a check, but not because they 'contaminate' anything.

variants.q: Four advertiser segments have been named and an account plan is being built around them for the year. Before sign-off you may ask the assistant for one more piece of evidence. Which is most useful?
options: The same clustering on a later month from other random starts, with churn beside a plain GROUP BY.
A chart showing how different the four segments are on each of the columns used to build them.
The same clustering with ten segments, to see whether finer groups look even tidier.
A longer description of each segment, so the names are easier for the sales team to remember.
variants.why: A year-long plan needs segments that come back on new data and from a different start, and that separate an outcome better than the obvious GROUP BY. Segments always look different on the columns that built them, so that chart would pass for any clustering. More segments and better names add polish, not evidence.

review.concept: distance needs a common scale

variants.q: To find advertisers 'like this one', the assistant measures distance on raw columns: monthly impressions in the millions, click rate around 0.3, and number of campaigns between 1 and 20. The ten nearest matches to a gaming advertiser come from every vertical but have almost identical impressions. Why?
options: Gaming advertisers are too few, so the method had to borrow matches from other verticals.
Ten neighbours are too few; with fifty, the other columns would begin to count.
Impressions are in millions, so they decide the distance on their own.
Nearest-neighbour matching only works within one vertical at a time.
variants.why: A difference of a million impressions dwarfs any possible difference in click rate or campaign count, so 'nearest' means 'nearest in impressions'. More neighbours would just be more advertisers with similar impressions, and the number of gaming advertisers has nothing to do with it. Put the columns on a common scale and every column gets a say.

variants.q: A retail chain clusters 400 stores on annual revenue in dollars, a satisfaction score from 1 to 5, and staff count. The result is three groups: small, medium and large. The operations lead concludes that satisfaction plays no part in what kind of store it is. What does the result actually show?
options: That satisfaction varies too little between stores to separate one kind from another.
That revenue in dollars dominated the distance, so satisfaction never got a say.
That a score from 1 to 5 has too few distinct values to be useful in a clustering.
That survey columns are too noisy for clustering and should be left out of it.
variants.why: With revenue in the hundreds of thousands and satisfaction between 1 and 5, raw distance is a revenue difference and nothing else. The method did not weigh the columns; the units did, so the result says nothing about how much satisfaction varies or how noisy it is. Rescale the columns and run it again before concluding anything about satisfaction.

variants.q: The assistant clusters video creatives on length in seconds and completion rate as a fraction between 0 and 1. A colleague re-runs it with length converted to minutes and gets completely different groups. What does that tell you?
options: The first run was wrong, and minutes are the correct unit for video length.
Clustering is too unreliable to use on creatives of different lengths.
The second run was wrong, and seconds are the correct unit for video length.
The groups depend on an arbitrary unit: neither run had a sensible ruler.
variants.why: If changing seconds to minutes changes the answer, the grouping reflects the unit, not the creatives: in seconds, length drowned completion rate, and in minutes it no longer does. Neither unit is the right one. Put both columns on a common scale so the result no longer depends on how a column happens to be recorded.

drill.q: A clustering comes back with five neat customer segments. Why is that, on its own, not evidence that five kinds of customer exist?
drill.a: Because the method returns as many groups as you ask for, every time, whatever the data looks like. Believe them only if they come back from a different random start and on fresh data, and beat a plain GROUP BY on an outcome they never saw.

drill.q: Why do columns need a common scale before you measure how similar two rows are?
drill.a: Because distance adds up differences across columns, so a column in thousands of dollars drowns columns measured in single digits. Without a common scale you are grouping by the biggest unit, not by behaviour.

recall.prompt: A stakeholder loves the four named segments and wants to build the account plan around them. Explain what you would check first, and why.
recall.model_answer: Clustering returned four groups because I asked for four, so first I check they are not an artefact of the method. I compare them with a plain GROUP BY, since here they mostly matched two yes-or-no columns, and I re-run from other random starts to see whether the same segments come back. Then I check that they separate an outcome they never saw, such as churn, better than the GROUP BY I could have written. Only what survives those checks goes into the plan.

lessons.ask_assistant: Cluster [the rows: one per what] with k-means on [the columns I list], each put on a common scale, with no outcome column among the inputs. Show the error for [a range of k], and for [the k I pick] a profile table: each segment's size, the average of every input column, and [an outcome the method never saw]. Re-run from [several] different random seeds and report an agreement score (adjusted Rand index) between each run and the first. Repeat on [a second period] and say which segments return. Beside the segments, show the same outcome for a plain GROUP BY on [two or three columns I already use]. Do not name the segments.
audit_checklist: The input columns and how each was scaled are listed, and no outcome column is among them.
A profile table per segment shows its size and the average of every input, so a segment that is one column in disguise is visible.
An agreement score is printed for each re-run from a different random start (the same segments coming back score close to 1), not one run with a fixed seed.
The same unseen outcome is shown for the segments and for a plain GROUP BY side by side, with the error for each k tried.
transfer: What kinds of publisher sites send us traffic? Groups will come back either way; check they survive a re-run before anyone acts on a 'suspicious' one.
What personas are in our inbound leads? A persona should reappear in next month's leads and differ on conversion.
Which creatives are alike? Length in seconds and click rate need a common scale before 'alike' means anything.

other_ways.approach: A plain GROUP BY on two or three business columns you already trust
other_ways.when: When an obvious cut exists: it is stable, easy to explain, and the baseline any clustering has to beat.

other_ways.approach: A shallow decision tree on the outcome you care about
other_ways.when: When you have an answer column and want segments built to differ on it: each leaf is a segment with a rate.

other_ways.approach: Other clustering methods: hierarchical clustering, DBSCAN, Gaussian mixtures
other_ways.when: When you do not want to fix the number of groups in advance or expect groups of uneven shape; the same checks apply.

glossary.def: Grouping rows by how similar they are, with no answer column to learn from.
A clustering method: place k centres, assign each row to its nearest centre, move each centre to the middle of its rows, and repeat.
The rows closest to a given row under some measure of distance.
The random first placement of the centres; different starts can end in different segments.
A number comparing two groupings of the same rows: 1 means identical, 0 means unrelated. Re-runs of one method on the same rows should score close to 1.

lessons.title: Embeddings: meaning as coordinates
lessons.subtitle: How can a model tell that two tickets with hardly a word in common are about the same thing?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can explain what an embedding is, use nearness to search, group or classify text, and say what must be checked before the result is trusted.

predict.q: Support tickets fall into six categories, so blind guessing scores about 17 percent. You label just twelve tickets, two per category, turn every ticket into an embedding and train a simple model. Roughly how accurate is it on tickets it has not seen?
options: About 17 percent: twelve examples teach it nothing
About 30 percent
About 54 percent
About 90 percent
predict.reveal: About 54 percent on average, and anywhere from 45 to 62 depending on which twelve you happened to label. The lesson shows where that head start comes from.

segments.narration: Two tickets reach the support inbox. The first says the browser extension reports the base tag as installed, yet the conversions column shows a dash after 300 clicks. The second says they pasted the tracking code into their store theme, placed a test order, and no conversion appeared. Any account manager reads those as one problem: a pixel that is installed and counting nothing. A keyword search for the word tag finds the first and misses the second. Beyond small words, they share almost nothing. You need to match on meaning, not spelling. That need is general: place any text by what it means, and you can find the live ad headlines repeating a claim policy already rejected, whatever their wording.

visual.title: Embeddings: meaning as coordinates
visual.sub: Two tickets, hardly a word in common, one broken pixel

segments.narration: The tool for that is an embedding. [[1]] You hand a ticket's text to an embedding model. [[2]] That model is a neural network: a stack of the weighted sums you met in module three, with a bend between the layers so the stack can learn curves. Trained on enormous amounts of text, it works out its own features. [[3]] What comes back is a list of numbers, 256 for each ticket. [[4]] So a thousand tickets become a table with 256 numeric columns. No single column means anything you could name. Position carries the meaning. Think of the numbers as coordinates: tickets that mean similar things land close together.

steps.label: Embedding model
steps.sub: a neural network trained on text

segments.narration: [[1]] Near means similar. Check it. Take the first ticket, the one with the dash in the conversions column, and pull the three tickets closest to it. Closeness is a similarity score that tops out at one. [[2]] The nearest: a pixel helper shows a green checkmark, yet the dashboard shows zero results. [[3]] Next, the test order. [[4]] Then conversions that appear in another analytics tool but not on the platform. Three customers, three vocabularies, one broken pixel. This ticket's similarity to others in its category averages about 0.81. To tickets in other categories, about 0.72. So the scale does not start near zero: tickets about other things still score high. Read the gap between scores, not the level.

visual.title: One ticket and its three nearest neighbours
rows: My browser extension says the base tag is installed correctly, so why does the conversions column still just show a dash after 300 clicks?
Pixel helper extension shows green checkmark on our thank-you page but your dashboard still shows 0 results after $800 spent. Is the traffic even real?
Pasted the tracking code in theme liquid file on our store. Did a test order with real credit card, no conversion in campaign dashboard…
Conversions showing … but zero in your platform. Pixel helper extension says tag is loaded and event fired on the order confirmation page.
visual.note: Average similarity to this ticket: same category 0.809, other categories 0.716. Even other topics score high: read the gap, not the level.

segments.narration: Nobody can picture 256 directions, so the map squashes them down to two. Squashing many columns into a few is called dimensionality reduction, and the classic method is PCA. Every dot is a ticket, and dots that sit close together are tickets the model considers similar. The squashing loses a lot, so expect neighbourhoods with blurred edges, not islands. And nobody told the embedding model about our six categories. Whatever grouping appears comes from the text alone. Take a minute with the map. Find where one category gathers, then find a border where two of them run into each other.

visual.name: ticket_map
visual.title: Tickets as dots: near means similar
visual.note: 256 numbers squashed to 2 for drawing. Find where a category gathers, and a border where two blur.

segments.narration: Once text is numbers, everything from earlier in the course applies. Run k-means on the embeddings, ask for six groups, and never show it a category. Each cluster turns out to be dominated by a different category, and about three quarters of its tickets belong to it. Topics fall out of the text with no labels at all: a decent first read of an unsorted inbox. Now last lesson's honesty. We asked for six because we knew there were six. On a real inbox you would not know. And roughly one ticket in four sits in the wrong pile.

visual.title: k-means on the embeddings: six clusters, no labels used
visual.note: Overall, 76.3% of tickets sit with their cluster's main category. Six was our choice, not the data's.

segments.narration: The second move is the one you will use most. Label a handful of tickets by hand and train plain logistic regression on the 256 columns. With two labelled tickets per category, twelve in all, it sorts unseen tickets with about 54 percent accuracy. Blind guessing gets 17. The figure wobbles with which twelve you picked, from about 45 to 62 percent. With 600 labelled tickets it reaches about 75. Now see what the embedding bought. Feed the same model plain word counts, and it needs all 600 tickets to match what the embedding managed with twelve. Most of the learning was done before you arrived.

visual.title: Accuracy on unseen tickets, by how many you labelled
visual.note: Averages over 20 random draws. Guessing scores 16.7%. With 12 labels the embedding route ranged from 44.7% to 62.0%.

segments.narration: Now the limits, plainly. [[1]] An embedding captures topic far better than fine distinctions. That nearest neighbour was filed under performance: same pixel, but the customer's real question was whether the traffic is genuine. Trained on all 600 labels, the model gets about 94 percent of ordinary test tickets right. On tickets that tangle two issues, about 65. [[2]] These tickets are synthetic, written to order by language models. A real inbox is messier. [[3]] The labelled tickets came from one writer and the test tickets from another, with far more tangled ones. That handicaps the trained model, and it is realistic: what arrives later rarely matches what you trained on. [[4]] And embedding a ticket means sending its text to a model. Know where it goes.

visual.title: What an embedding cannot do, and what these numbers cannot say
items: Topic, not fine distinctions: 94.0% on ordinary tickets, 65.3% on tangled ones
Synthetic tickets, written to order by language models
Trained on one writer, tested on another with more tangled tickets
Embedding a ticket means sending its text to a model

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Before anything is embedded, ask which model, what it will cost, and where the text goes. A hosted model receives every ticket. One that runs on your own machines does not. Client text needs an approved destination first. [[2]] Ask for a nearest-neighbour check: five tickets you choose, each with its closest matches. [[3]] If it trains a model, the rules from module two still hold: labelled test tickets the model never saw, with blind guessing beside it. [[4]] Ask for accuracy at several training sizes, repeated on different random draws. [[5]] And ask for ordinary and tangled tickets separately. When what you want has a fixed spelling, an error code or a product name, a plain keyword search is still the right tool.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Before embedding: which model, hosted or in-house, the cost, where the text goes
Show: nearest neighbours for five tickets you chose
Show: accuracy on unseen labelled tickets, beside guessing
Show: accuracy by training size, with the range over repeats
Show: ordinary and tangled tickets separately

segments.narration: So when a question turns on what a text means and not on how it is spelled, have it embedded, and read the nearest neighbours yourself before you trust anything built on top. Next: if a model already knows this much about language, why train anything at all?

visual.title: Keep this
items: An embedding: text as coordinates, similar meanings close together
Then text is a table: search it, cluster it, train on a few labels
Strong on topic, weak on fine distinctions: test it like any model

takeaways: An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers placed so that similar meanings sit close together, whatever words were used.
Once text is numbers it is just another table: search by nearness, cluster it, or train a simple model on a few labelled rows.
Embeddings catch topic far better than fine distinctions, so the usual rules apply: unseen labelled examples, a baseline, and a look at the hard cases.

quiz.q: An account manager searches last month's tickets for the word 'pixel', finds 40, and reports that tracking problems are rare. You suspect an undercount. What is the best next step?
options: Add synonyms such as 'tag', 'snippet' and 'tracking code' to the search until the count stops rising.
Embed the tickets, pull those nearest to known tracking tickets, read a sample.
Report the 40 with a margin of error, since one month of tickets is only a sample.
Cluster all the tickets into two groups and report the size of the smaller group.
quiz.why: Customers describe the same broken pixel in many vocabularies, and nearness between embeddings finds them by meaning; reading a sample confirms that near really is similar. A synonym list only finds the words you thought of, which is why it feels sufficient and is not. A margin of error covers sampling luck, not the tickets a keyword cannot see: the 40 is exact about spelling, not about the problem.

quiz.concept: text is a table: the same rules apply
quiz.q: The assistant reports: 'Embedded 1,050 tickets, 256 columns each. Trained logistic regression on all 1,050 labelled tickets. Accuracy: 99 percent.' What is the flaw?
options: The embedding already contains each ticket's category, so the features leak the label.
Accuracy is the wrong measure whenever there are more than two categories.
The model was scored on the tickets it trained on, so the figure shows memory.
A table with 256 columns is too wide for logistic regression to be fitted at all.
quiz.why: With 256 columns a model can fit its own training rows almost perfectly, so only labelled tickets it never saw can tell you how it sorts new ones. Text does not change that rule. The leak answer is tempting, but an embedding is computed from the ticket's words alone and never sees the label.

quiz.q: The ad review team has 30 headlines that were rejected last quarter for misleading health claims. The wording varies a lot. They want a shortlist of live headlines that deserve a second look. What do you ask the assistant for?
options: A keyword filter built from the words that appear in the 30 rejected headlines.
A neural network trained from scratch, using the 30 rejected headlines as its examples.
K-means with two clusters on the live headlines, treating the smaller cluster as risky.
Embeddings for all headlines, then the live ones nearest the 30, sampled by hand.
quiz.why: The claim can be made in endless wordings, so the shortlist has to be built on meaning: embed everything and rank live headlines by nearness to the known bad ones, then check a sample by hand. A keyword filter catches only wordings already seen. Thirty examples are far too few to train a network from nothing, and two clusters have no reason to line up with 'risky'.

quiz.q: Two tickets have a similarity of 0.90. One asks for a refund of a double charge. The other says: 'Charged twice, but I do NOT want a refund, just correct the invoice.' A colleague wants each new ticket routed to the queue of its nearest labelled neighbour, with separate queues for refunds and invoice corrections. What is the right read?
options: Risky: both are billing tickets, and the split turns on a detail. Test it on labelled examples first.
Route by nearest neighbour and expect one ticket in ten misfiled: 0.90 is a 90 percent match.
Raise the similarity needed for a match from 0.90 to 0.95, then route as the colleague plans.
