Unworkable: embeddings can be used for search but never for routing tickets.
quiz.why: Embeddings place same-topic tickets close together, and both of these are about a double charge; whether they also separate 'refund' from 'correct the invoice' is exactly the kind of fine distinction where they were weakest in this lesson, so measure it on labelled tickets from both queues. A similarity score measures closeness between coordinates, not a probability of a match, and raising a cut-off without a test is a guess.

review.concept: near in an embedding means similar in meaning, not shared words

variants.q: A product team has 5,000 free-text answers to 'why did you cancel?'. A word count shows 'price' in 12 percent of them, and a manager concludes that 12 percent left over cost. What would embeddings add?
options: A sentiment score per answer, showing how strongly each customer felt about the price.
Answers like 'could not justify the bill' sit near the 'price' ones and get counted.
A fix for plurals, so that answers containing the word 'prices' are also counted.
A trained classifier, though only once all 5,000 answers have been labelled by hand.
variants.why: People give the same reason in different words: 'too expensive', 'cheaper elsewhere', 'could not justify the bill'. Embeddings place those near the answers that say 'price', so you can count the theme instead of one spelling of it. Handling plurals helps a little, but still only finds words you thought to look for. Nearness says what an answer is about, not how strongly it was felt, and finding neighbours needs no labels at all.

variants.q: Support wants to merge duplicate questions in the help centre. Two of them read 'How do I change the card on file?' and 'Update payment method?'. Which approach will find pairs like this one?
options: Lower-case the questions, strip punctuation, and look for exact matches.
Count the words each pair shares and list the pairs with the highest overlap.
Sort the questions alphabetically so that duplicates end up next to each other.
Embed every question and list the closest pairs for a person to confirm.
variants.why: These two questions mean the same thing and share no content words, so any method that compares spelling scores them as unrelated. Embeddings compare meaning, which puts them close together. A person should still confirm the pairs, because close does not always mean duplicate.

variants.q: Another team searches its support inbox for 'login' and gets 60 tickets. A search for the tickets nearest to five known login tickets returns 140, including 'cant get in since I changed phone' and 'the two step code never arrives'. Their manager says the extra 80 must be errors, since none of them contains the word. What is the right response?
options: Read a sample of the 80: the same problem in other words is the point.
Drop the 80: a ticket that never mentions the word login cannot be about logging in.
Keep only the tickets that appear in both searches, to be on the safe side.
Discard the keyword search entirely, because embeddings are always more accurate.
variants.why: A missing keyword is not evidence that a ticket is about something else; customers rarely use the support team's vocabulary. Whether the 80 belong is settled by reading a sample of them, not by checking for a word. Keeping only the overlap throws away exactly the tickets the keyword could not find.

review.concept: embedded text is just another table: the same rules of evidence apply

variants.q: Sales reps write free-text notes after each call. You want every note tagged 'budget', 'timing', 'competitor' or 'no need'. You have 40 hand-tagged notes and 20,000 untagged ones. What is a sensible first plan?
options: Wait until about 5,000 notes are tagged by hand; text needs far more examples than a table.
Cluster the notes into four groups and treat the four clusters as the four tags.
Embed the notes, train a simple model on part of the 40, score it on the rest.
Train a simple model on all 40 tagged notes and report its accuracy on those 40.
variants.why: In this lesson a simple model on embeddings got a long way with a few dozen labels, and holding some of them back is the only way to see how far yours gets. Waiting for thousands of labels assumes the answer before measuring it. Four clusters need not match your four tags, and scoring on the training notes shows memory, not skill.

variants.q: A vendor says: 'Our embeddings understand language, so the review classifier needs no evaluation. Here are ten app reviews it sorted correctly.' Your team has 300 reviews already tagged by hand into five themes. What do you do?
options: Run ten reviews of your own through it, and accept it if all ten are sorted correctly.
Ask the vendor for twenty more examples of reviews it sorted correctly.
Check first that the embedding has enough dimensions to separate five themes.
Score it on your 300 tagged reviews, beside the commonest theme's share.
variants.why: Ten examples are a demo, not a score, whether the seller picks them or you do. Your 300 hand-tagged reviews are labelled rows the classifier has not seen, which is what any model is judged on, and the commonest theme is the baseline it has to beat. However the columns were made, the rules of evidence are the ones from module two.

variants.q: The assistant embeds support tickets, trains on 60 labelled ones, and reports 67 percent accuracy on 450 unseen labelled tickets in six equally common categories. A stakeholder says 67 percent sounds poor. Which comparison should come first?
options: With 100 percent, the score that a perfect classifier would get on these tickets.
With blind guessing, which scores about 17 percent on six equal categories.
With the churn model's AUC of about 0.85 from earlier in the course.
With its own accuracy on the 60 tickets it was trained on.
variants.why: A score means something only beside its baseline: with six equally common categories guessing gets about one in six, so 67 percent from 60 labels is a large step; after that, ask what more labels would add. An AUC and an accuracy are different measures on different problems and cannot be set side by side. Accuracy on the training tickets only shows what the model memorised.

drill.q: In a sentence or two, what is an embedding?
drill.a: A list of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text, placed so that texts with similar meanings get similar numbers. Once you have it, text behaves like any other table of numeric columns.

drill.q: Why can an embedding search find a support ticket that a keyword search misses?
drill.a: Because customers describe the same problem in different words. A keyword matches spelling. An embedding places texts by meaning, so two tickets about the same problem sit close together even with no words in common.

recall.prompt: Explain to a colleague what an embedding is, what you can do once you have one, and one thing it is bad at.
recall.model_answer: An embedding is a list of numbers a neural network produces for a piece of text, arranged so that similar meanings land close together even when the words differ. Once every ticket has one, text is an ordinary table: I can find the nearest tickets to an example, cluster them into topics, or train a simple model on a few labelled rows. It is good at topic and weak at fine distinctions, such as which of two tangled issues is the main one, so I would still score it on labelled tickets it has not seen.

lessons.ask_assistant: Before sending anything, tell me which embedding model you would use, whether it is hosted or runs on [our own machines], where [the text] would go and what [that many texts] will cost; wait for my go-ahead. Then embed [the text column] and report the number of columns per text. Show [the items I name], each with its [N] nearest neighbours and similarity scores. Train logistic regression on the embeddings using [a few] labelled examples per [category], score it on labelled examples it never saw, and report accuracy at several training sizes with the range over repeated random draws, beside [guessing or the commonest category]. Split the final accuracy by [easy and hard cases].
audit_checklist: The embedding model is named before any text is sent: hosted or run in-house, where the text goes, the quoted cost, and the number of columns per text.
Nearest neighbours are printed, with similarity scores, for items you chose, so you can read whether near means similar.
The counts of labelled examples used for training and for testing are printed, with none in both, and the guessing baseline sits beside the accuracy.
Accuracy is shown at several training sizes with the range over repeated draws, and the final figure is split by easy and hard cases.
transfer: Which live ad headlines resemble ones that were rejected before, whatever words they use?
What themes run through thousands of open-text survey answers nobody has had time to read?
Which questions in the help centre are duplicates of each other in different words?

other_ways.approach: A keyword rule or a LIKE search
other_ways.when: When the thing you want has a fixed spelling: an error code, a product name, an invoice number.

other_ways.approach: Word counts with a simple model
other_ways.when: When you have many labelled examples, the text must stay in-house, and you want to read which words carry the weight.

other_ways.approach: Ask a language model directly, with instructions and no training
other_ways.when: When you have no labelled examples to train on; the next lesson scores it against this one.

glossary.def: A list of numbers a model produces for a piece of text, arranged so that similar meanings get nearby numbers.

A neural network, trained on large amounts of text, that turns a piece of text into its embedding. It is either hosted, so the text is sent to a vendor, or run on your own machines. A text is embedded once, and the result can be stored and reused.

Squashing many columns into a few that keep as much of their structure as possible, for example 256 embedding numbers down to 2 so they can be drawn. The classic method is principal component analysis (PCA).
A model built from stacked layers of weighted sums with a bend between the layers, which learns its own features from data.

A number for how close two embeddings are; it tops out at 1 for texts the model places at the same point. The usual one for embeddings is cosine similarity. Its level depends on the model, so compare scores with each other, not with a fixed bar.

lessons.title: Language models as classifiers
lessons.subtitle: If a model can label text from instructions alone, how do you find out how good it is?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can put a language model on the same scoreboard as any other classifier and say which differences on that scoreboard are real.

predict.q: 450 unseen support tickets, six categories. A simple model trained on 600 labelled tickets, using embeddings, sorts them. So does a cheap language model given only the category names and a line about each. Which scores higher?
options: The trained model, clearly: it has learned from 600 examples
The cheap language model, by about 6 points
The cheap language model, by more than 20 points
Neither: the two finish level
predict.reveal: The cheap language model: 81 percent against 75. The lesson shows why that 6-point gap is real, why it could be as small as 1 point, and why it comes with an asterisk.

segments.narration: The head of support has a few hundred tickets and one question: what are advertisers writing in about? Six categories: billing, tracking setup, ad review, performance, account access, feature requests. There are at least five ways to sort them. At one end, an afternoon spent writing keyword rules. At the other, a paragraph of instructions handed to a language model that has never seen a labelled ticket. The assistant will build any of them in minutes. Your job is to make all five sit the same exam. The rule is general: a model that needed no training still needs a test, whether it sorts tickets or tags leads as ready to buy.

visual.title: Language models as classifiers
visual.sub: Five ways to sort 450 tickets, one exam

segments.narration: Here is the ladder. [[1]] Rung one: keyword rules. If the ticket says invoice, call it billing. [[2]] Rung two: a bag-of-words model. Count the words and short phrases in each ticket, one column each, and let logistic regression learn the weights from 600 labelled tickets. [[3]] Rung three: last lesson's embeddings, with the same logistic regression and the same 600 tickets. [[4]] Rung four: a cheap language model, given only the six category names and a line describing each. No examples, no training: what is called zero-shot. [[5]] Rung five: a stronger language model, same instructions. All five face the same 450 unseen test tickets, where blind guessing scores about 17 percent.

visual.title: Five rungs, one exam: 450 unseen tickets

steps.label: Bag-of-words model
steps.sub: word counts + logistic regression, 600 labelled tickets

segments.narration: The marks, from the bottom rung up. [[1]] Keyword rules: 29 percent. On 103 tickets no keyword matched, so they gave no answer at all. [[2]] The bag-of-words model: 54. [[3]] Embeddings with a simple model: 75. [[4]] The cheap language model, with no training: 81. [[5]] The stronger one: 96. Each mark comes from a sample of tickets, so each carries an interval. The cheap language model could plausibly sit anywhere from 77 to 84 percent. The embedding model, from 71 to 79. Those ranges overlap. So is the cheap language model really ahead, or just lucky with these tickets?

visual.title: Accuracy on the same 450 unseen tickets
visual.note: In brackets: the 95% interval. Blind guessing among six equal categories scores 16.7%.

segments.narration: Overlapping intervals do not mean a tie: that test is too blunt, and here both models sat the same exam. Module two had the sharper test: compare them ticket by ticket and put an interval on the gap itself. [[1]] Bag-of-words over keyword rules: 25 points, clearly real. [[2]] Embeddings over bag-of-words: 21 points, clearly real. [[3]] The cheap language model over embeddings: 6 points. Its interval runs from about 1 point to 11, so real, and possibly small. [[4]] The stronger model over the cheap one: 15 points, clearly real. The narrow step is the one from training on labels to using none.

visual.title: Is each step real? Gaps measured on the same 450 tickets
visual.note: An interval that included 0 would be a tie. None does.

segments.narration: Now cut the result by difficulty. A third of the test tickets are ordinary: one clear problem. The rest are deliberately tangled: two issues in one message, or vague about what is wrong. On ordinary tickets the embedding model scores 94 percent and the cheap language model 92. Level, near enough. On tangled tickets the trained models fall hard: embeddings to 65 percent, bag-of-words to 40. The cheap language model holds at 75, and the stronger one barely notices. The cheap model's whole lead comes from the tangled tickets. A headline says which method wins. The cut says where.

visual.title: Accuracy on ordinary and on tangled tickets
visual.note: 300 of the 450 test tickets are deliberately tangled: two issues in one message, or vague wording.

segments.narration: Four limits before anyone quotes 96 percent. [[1]] The tickets are synthetic, written to order by language models, so the answer key is simply what was requested. Real labels are disputed: two people often disagree about the main issue, and that caps what any score can mean. [[2]] The sorting models come from the same family as the writing models, so their scores flatter them. [[3]] The trained methods carry a handicap: they learned from one writer's tickets, a quarter of them tangled, and were tested on another's, two thirds tangled. That is realistic, but it puts an asterisk on that narrow step. [[4]] And the keyword rules were written once and never tuned. Expect lower scores on a real inbox.

visual.title: Four honest limits
items: Synthetic tickets with a known answer key; real labels are disputed
Writers and sorters are one model family: language-model scores are optimistic
Trained methods: one writer's tickets to learn from, another's in the test, with more tangled ones
The keyword rules were written once and never tuned

segments.narration: So which rung? A trade, not a ranking. The trained rungs cost labelled examples up front. The language models need none, but you pay per ticket and wait longer for each answer. Mind where the text goes: only keyword rules and the bag-of-words model keep it in-house by default. A language model or an embedding model receives every ticket, unless it runs on your own machines. One cheap safeguard: run two models and compare. [[1]] They give the same label on about four tickets in five, [[2]] and those agreed labels are right 97 percent of the time. [[3]] They disagree on 82 tickets, nearly nine in ten of them tangled. A ready-made queue for a person. A flag, not a guarantee: two models can be wrong together.

visual.title: Two language models, the same 450 tickets

stats.label: of tickets: both give the same label
of those agreed labels are right
tickets where they disagree; 87.8% of them tangled

segments.narration: Brief and audit. [[1]] Ask for a test set labelled by people, blind to any model's answer. Your assistant is a language model too, and it does not mark its own work. Nothing is trained or tuned on those tickets. [[2]] Ask for every method on the same tickets, with blind guessing beside them and an interval on each score. [[3]] Ask for precision and recall per category. The cheap model's 81 percent hides that it catches only 60 percent of feature requests. [[4]] Ask for ordinary and tangled tickets separately. [[5]] Before any text is sent, ask for the exact instructions, the model and version, and where the text goes. If two categories keep getting confused, add a few labelled examples to the instructions, which is called few-shot, and score again on fresh tickets.

visual.title: Brief and audit
items: Show: a test set labelled by people, unseen, with nothing tuned on it
Show: every method on the same tickets, with guessing and intervals
Show: precision and recall for each category
Show: ordinary and tangled tickets separately
Before sending: the exact instructions, the model and version, where text goes

segments.narration: So the next time someone demos a language model on your text, ask what it scored on tickets people labelled, and against what, before you look at a single example. Next, the last skill: writing the numbers up so the report survives a hard question.

visual.title: Keep this
items: A language model can classify from instructions alone
Same exam as any model: unseen labels, baseline, intervals, hard cases
Synthetic data flatters it: measure on your own text

takeaways: A language model can label text from instructions alone, with no training examples, and on these tickets it beat every trained method.
It is scored like any other model: labelled examples it has not seen, a baseline, an interval, results per category and on the hard cases.
These tickets are synthetic and were written by the same family of models that sorted them, so expect lower scores on a real inbox and measure before you believe.

quiz.q: On the 450 test tickets the embedding model scores 74.9 percent, interval 70.7 to 78.7, and the cheap language model 80.9, interval 77.0 to 84.3. A colleague says: 'The intervals overlap, so it is a tie.' The comparison on the same tickets gives a gap of 6.0 points with an interval of 1.1 to 10.9. What is the right read?
options: A tie: whenever two intervals overlap, there is no difference between the methods.
The language model really is ahead, though perhaps by as little as one point.
The language model is six points better, and the interval adds nothing to that.
No conclusion is possible until the test set is several times larger than 450.
quiz.why: Both methods answered the same tickets, so the right test is the interval on the difference, and it excludes zero: the step is real. Overlap between two separate intervals is too blunt a test, which is why the tie is tempting. But the low end is about one point, so 'six points better' claims more than the data shows.

quiz.concept: instructions tuned on the test tickets
quiz.q: The assistant reports: 'Classification by a language model from instructions alone: 94 percent accuracy. Method: I wrote the instructions, checked the output on 50 labelled tickets, reworded the instructions where it went wrong, and repeated until those 50 tickets scored 94 percent.' What is the flaw?
options: Fifty tickets are too few for an accuracy figure to be calculated at all.
A language model cannot be scored with accuracy, only by reading its answers.
The instructions were tuned on the same 50 tickets used to score them.
Instructions should never be reworded once a language model has started on a task.
quiz.why: Rewording instructions until a set of tickets scores well is choosing settings on the test set: those tickets have now trained the instructions, and the 94 percent is flattering. Rewording is fine, but the final score must come from labelled tickets that were kept aside. Fifty is a small sample with a wide interval, which is a real weakness but not the one that pushes the number up.

quiz.concept: a demo is not a score
quiz.q: Marketing wants the free-text message on every inbound lead tagged 'ready to buy', 'researching' or 'not a fit'. In a vendor demo a language model tags eight of eight sample messages correctly. Past data says about 70 percent of leads are 'researching'. What do you ask for before agreeing?
options: Results on a few hundred hand-tagged leads, per tag, beside that 70 percent.
Eight more sample messages, so that the demo covers sixteen leads instead of eight.
The model's own stated confidence in each of the eight answers it gave.
Only the instructions it was given: a model nobody trained cannot have memorised anything.
quiz.why: Eight examples picked by the seller are a demo; a score needs labelled leads the model has not seen, and since tagging everything 'researching' is already 70 percent accurate, it needs precision and recall per tag as well. The last option is the tempting one: nothing was trained, so nothing can be overfitted, and reading the instructions feels like enough. But untested is untested, whether or not there was training.

quiz.concept: disputed labels limit what a score can mean
quiz.q: One of the stronger model's 'misses': a customer writes that their ad was rejected, and that the appeal link then reports a problem with their profile. The answer key says account access; the model said ad review. You show the ticket to two support leads and they split. What does that tell you about the 96 percent?
options: The true figure is lower than 96 percent, because the model failed on a simple ticket.
The answer key should be changed to the model's label wherever the two differ.
Tangled tickets should be taken out of the test set so that the score is cleaner.
Some 'errors' are disputes: where people split on a label, a higher score means little.
quiz.why: When careful people file the same ticket two ways, the label itself is uncertain, and disputed labels put a ceiling below 100 percent on what any score can measure. Rewriting the key to match the model makes the score circular, and removing the tangled tickets makes the test stop resembling the inbox. Both are tempting ways to tidy a number that is honestly untidy.

review.concept: a model that needed no training still needs a test

variants.q: A language model flags ad headlines that break policy. On 200 hand-checked headlines, 20 of which really broke policy, it is reported as 91 percent accurate. What should you ask next?
options: For an interval on the 91 percent: if its low end clears 85, the result is strong.
For a larger sample, because 200 headlines cannot give a reliable accuracy.
How many of the 20 it caught and how many flags were right: flagging nothing scores 90 percent.
For the model's instructions, because the wording matters more than the score.
variants.why: Only 20 of 200 headlines break policy, so a model that flags nothing is already 90 percent accurate and 91 says almost nothing. Recall on the 20 and precision of the flags are the numbers that describe it; an interval on the accuracy would only measure a nearly empty number more precisely. A language model is not exempt from the baseline just because nobody trained it.

variants.q: Finance uses a language model to sort 5,000 invoice dispute notes into four reasons. The analyst reads ten of the results, finds them all sensible, and proposes publishing the breakdown. What is the better plan?
options: Publish with a caveat that the breakdown comes from a model and may contain errors.
Label a few hundred random notes by hand, blind to the model, then score it.
Ask the model to sort the notes a second time and publish if the two runs agree.
Read another ten results, and publish if those also look sensible.
variants.why: Ten results that look sensible to someone who has already seen the model's answer are not a test. A random sample labelled blind gives an accuracy with an interval, and shows which reasons get confused. Running the same model twice checks that it is consistent, not that it is right, and a caveat tells readers that errors exist without telling them how many.

variants.q: The team's ticket classifier, a language model with fixed instructions, was scored on a labelled test set last quarter. The vendor now offers a newer version of the model and says it is better. What should happen before the switch?
options: Ask the vendor for the new version's benchmark scores, and switch if they are higher.
Switch, then compare this month's category shares with last month's to check for a change.
Keep the old version permanently, since it is the one that was tested.
Run the same labelled test set through the new version and compare the two.
variants.why: A different model is a different classifier, and the old score does not carry over. The same labelled tickets, compared with the old version one by one, show whether the change is real and where it differs. Category shares can move because the inbox changed, so they cannot tell you whether the model got better, and the vendor's benchmark was not run on your tickets.

review.concept: disagreement shows where the label is uncertain

variants.q: Two reviewers independently label 500 ad creatives as compliant or not, and agree on 88 percent of them. A model agrees with the first reviewer on 86 percent. The product lead will not launch until the model reaches 95 percent. What is the right response?
options: The reviewers only agree 88 percent of the time, so settle the label first.
Keep improving the model: 95 percent is a reasonable bar for a compliance task.
Score the model against the second reviewer instead, and use whichever figure is higher.
Drop the 12 percent of creatives where the reviewers disagree, then measure again.
variants.why: If two trained people agree only 88 percent of the time, a model at 86 percent is about as consistent with a reviewer as another reviewer is, and 95 is beyond what the labels can support. The useful work is sharpening the definition and settling the disputed cases. Dropping them would produce a clean score on a test that no longer looks like the real queue.

variants.q: You run two different language models over the messages on 10,000 leads, and they give the same tag on 85 percent. The team can afford to check 1,500 leads by hand. Which ones?
options: A random 1,500 from the 10,000, so that the check is unbiased.
The 1,500 longest messages, since long messages are harder to tag.
Mostly the leads where the two disagree, plus a small random sample of the rest.
A random 1,500 of the leads where the two agree, to confirm that agreement is safe.
variants.why: The 1,500 disagreements are where the tag is most likely to be wrong or genuinely ambiguous, so that is where a person adds most. A small random sample of the agreed tags tells you how often the two are wrong together. A purely random check would spend most of the effort on leads where both models were already right, and a check of the agreed leads alone would spend all of it there.

variants.q: On the course's support tickets the two language models gave the same label about four times in five, and the agreed label was right 97 percent of the time. A teammate concludes that agreed labels never need checking. What is the right response?
options: Agreed labels are safe to skip once the two models come from two different vendors.
Three in a hundred agreed labels were still wrong, so sample them now and then.
Agreed labels need the same full review as the rest: agreement carries no information.
Agreed labels are safe on short tickets, so review only the long ones the two agree on.
variants.why: Agreement raises confidence without making it certainty: 97 percent right means 3 percent wrong together, and here both models came from one family, so shared mistakes should not surprise anyone. Different vendors would make shared mistakes rarer, not impossible, and nothing here says the wrong ones are the long ones. Agreement is still informative, since most of the disagreements were tangled tickets, so the sensible routine is a person on the disagreements and an occasional sample of the rest.

drill.q: A language model sorts support tickets from instructions alone, with no training. How do you find out how good it is?
drill.a: The same way as for any model. Score it on labelled tickets it has not seen, next to a baseline such as guessing, with an interval, and broken down by category and by easy versus hard tickets.

drill.q: Two models label the same tickets and disagree on some of them. What is that disagreement good for?
drill.a: It is a cheap flag for human review. The tickets where two models disagree tend to be the hard, ambiguous ones, so send those to a person. Agreement is not proof, though: two models can be wrong together.

recall.prompt: A vendor says their language model classifies your tickets at 96 percent with no training needed. What do you ask before you believe it?
recall.model_answer: I ask what it was scored on: labelled tickets it had not seen, how many, and who decided the right answers. I want a baseline and an interval beside the score, precision and recall per category, and the result on messy multi-issue tickets shown separately. I also ask whether the test tickets resemble my inbox, because scores on tidy or synthetic text run high, and whether the instructions were tuned on the same tickets that were used for scoring.

lessons.ask_assistant: Classify [the text] into [our categories, one line describing each] with an approved language model given instructions only (zero-shot). Before sending any text, show me the exact instructions, the model name and version, and where the text will go, and wait for my go-ahead. Score it on [the test set people labelled, which no method has seen], beside [the simpler methods] and [guessing or the commonest category], each with a 95 percent interval, plus an interval on the gap between neighbouring methods on the same items. Report precision and recall per category, and accuracy on [easy and hard cases] separately. Never adjust the instructions after seeing test items; list every version you tried and on which items.
audit_checklist: The test set is described: how many items, who labelled them (people, blind to every model's answer), and a list of every version of the instructions with the items it was tried on, none of them test items.
One table holds every method on the same items: the number scored, the guessing baseline, an interval on each score and on each gap between neighbours.
Precision and recall are shown per category, and accuracy for easy and hard cases separately.
The exact instructions, the model name and version, and where the text goes are printed, and were shown before any text was sent.
transfer: Does this ad headline make a claim our policy forbids?
Which inbound leads sound ready to buy, judging by the message they typed?
What reason does each answer to the cancellation survey give?

other_ways.approach: Put a few labelled examples inside the language model's instructions
other_ways.when: When instructions alone confuse two categories; score it again on tickets that were not used as examples. A bigger step, fine-tuning, retrains the model itself on your labelled tickets and needs the same unseen test.

other_ways.approach: Embeddings with a simple trained model
other_ways.when: When you have labelled examples and a high volume of text. The text stays in the building only if the embedding model runs on your own machines; a hosted one receives every text, exactly as a language model does.

other_ways.approach: A language model for the bulk, and people for the tickets where two models disagree
other_ways.when: When mistakes are costly and a human review queue already exists.

glossary.def: A model fed counts of the words and short phrases in each text, ignoring their order.
Asking a language model to label text from instructions alone, with no training examples.
The same, with a handful of labelled examples added to the instructions; score it on tickets that were not among the examples.
Training a language model further on your own labelled examples, so the model itself changes; a bigger step than adding examples to the instructions, and it needs the same unseen test.
Comparing two methods on the same test items, with an interval on the gap between them.
How often two people give the same item the same label; when people often disagree, the answer key itself is uncertain, which caps what any model's score can meaningfully show below 100 percent.

lessons.title: The report you can stand behind
lessons.subtitle: What must a report show before you put your name on it?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can check a model report for six things (bound numbers, sizes and intervals, a baseline, wording that fits the evidence, segment results, first-page limits) and rewrite a sentence that fails.

predict.q: You catch a bug. Your assistant reruns the analysis and regenerates the HTML report. Where is a wrong number most likely to survive?
options: In the charts, because they are redrawn from scratch
In the sentences, where numbers typed around the first run stay put
In the appendix tables, which are the hardest part to rebuild
Nowhere: a rerun refreshes every number in the report
predict.reveal: In the sentences: a typed number stays put while the chart beside it moves, and the lesson shows how to make that impossible and what else a report has to carry.

segments.narration: Two reports on one yes-or-no model, the churn model you know. Same data, same test advertisers, both drafted by an assistant. The first is handsome: a gradient header, a bold headline, a confident summary. The second is plainer, and half a page longer. On Thursday one of them goes in front of the head of account management, and she will do what good stakeholders do: ask a question. Compared with what? How sure are you? So should we push tracking? The handsome report has nothing to say back. The plain one has already answered. The difference is not style. It is a short list of things you can check, and the same list fits any report: a spend forecast for finance, an invalid-traffic review.

visual.title: The report you can stand behind
visual.sub: Two reports, one model. Only one survives a question.

segments.narration: Start with the headline sentence. [[1]] The handsome report says the model identifies at-risk advertisers with high accuracy. Nothing in that can be checked. And accuracy is a strange boast, when predicting that nobody leaves is already about 87 percent accurate. [[2]] The plain report says this. Of the 200 advertisers the model ranked highest, 136 really churned. A random 200 would hold about 26. The interval on that count runs from 123 to 150, which is roughly how far it moves with the luck of who landed in the test months. And it names the rows: 4,000 advertisers from May and June that the model never saw. A count, a baseline beside it, an interval, and the rows. Every part can be checked.

left.label: Cannot be checked
left.sub: “The model identifies at-risk advertisers with high accuracy.”

right.label: Survives a question
right.sub: random 200: about 26 · 95% interval 123 to 150 · 4,000 unseen advertisers, May–June

segments.narration: Now the failure you will meet most often. Remember the leaked column that produced a perfect list: all 200 of the top 200 churned. Suppose you catch it after the report is drafted. The assistant reruns, and the chart now shows 136. The paragraph under the chart still celebrates 200. Nothing crashed. That sentence was typed once, around the first result, and only the chart was regenerated. The cure is mechanical. Every number in the prose is inserted by the script, from the same results file that feeds the charts. Nothing is typed. Then a rerun moves the sentence and the chart together, and the assistant can list every number in the text beside its source.

visual.title: Typed numbers go stale. Bound numbers cannot.
visual.code:
# Typed: survives the rerun, wrongly
summary = "All 200 of the top 200 churned."

# Bound: read from the checked results
r = results["top_200"]
summary = (f"Of the top {r['k']}, "
           f"{r['churners']} churned.")
visual.note: After the leak is fixed the results file says 136. Only the bound sentence follows it.

segments.narration: Next, the verbs. The handsome report says conversion tracking reduces churn by 11 points. Reduces is a claim about changing something, and evidence comes in four tiers. [[1]] Observed: two groups differed. That earns churned less, or is associated with. [[2]] Adjusted: the gap survives holding fixed background columns like tenure and vertical. Say it remains after adjusting. [[3]] Compared: the change in a group that got something, minus the change in a similar group without it. Module five's launch earns rose about 5 points more than the comparison group, assuming the two would have moved together. [[4]] Tested: a coin decided who got the change. Only this tier earns reduces. Tracking's true effect in this simulated world is about 2 points. On real data you cannot look it up, so the verb must carry the tier.

visual.title: The verb must match the evidence
rows: Two groups compared: 7.2% vs 18.4% churn, gap 11.2 pts
Background columns held fixed: gap 6.5 pts
Change in the launch group minus change in a similar untreated group: +4.7 pts, interval 3.2 to 6.2
“rose 4.7 points more than the comparison group”; assumes the two would have moved together
A coin decided who got the change
visual.note: Row 3 is the module 5 launch; the other rows are conversion tracking, whose true effect in this simulated world is 2.3 pts. Knowable only because it is simulated.

segments.narration: The assistant drafts the prose as well, and its default register is confident. Hand it a bar chart and it writes a story. [[1]] Something like: gaming churn rose sharply in April, pointing to growing dissatisfaction in the vertical. Read that the way you would read its code. Sharply, against what? Dissatisfaction, measured where? [[2]] Underneath: 14 percent in March and 19 in April. Each month is about 250 advertisers. The interval on that difference runs from about minus 2 to plus 11 points. Zero is inside it. The dissatisfaction explains a rise that may not exist. Every comparison carries its group sizes and its interval, and the sentence may not say more than they do.

visual.title: Read the prose like the code

left.label: The assistant's sentence
left.sub: “Gaming churn rose sharply in April, pointing to growing dissatisfaction.”

right.label: What the numbers support
right.sub: 14.2% of 253 advertisers, then 19.1% of 246: within noise

segments.narration: Last, the first page. Two things go there. [[1]] One is a provenance line: when the data was pulled, which rows were in, which model version. Here: 6,000 advertisers from January to March to train, April left out, 4,000 from May and June to test. The other is a short paragraph on what the reader should not conclude. [[2]] This model ranks risk. It does not say why advertisers leave, or that a call would keep them. [[3]] Its percentages run low. [[4]] And it does not serve every size equally. The working list catches about 55 percent of small churners and about 25 percent of large ones, though large accounts are two thirds of the dollars lost. Limits in an appendix are limits nobody read.

visual.title: First page, before any chart
items: Provenance: pull date · train Jan–Mar 6,000 · April out · test May–Jun 4,000 · model version
Ranks risk. Not why they leave, nor who a call would keep
Percentages run low: predicted 10.9%, actual 13.2%
Top 400 catch 55% of small churners, 25% of large (two thirds of lost spend)

segments.narration: Brief and audit. The report is stage four, built only from checked numbers. Ask for six things, and look for each in the output. [[1]] Every number in the text read from the results file, with a list of where each came from. [[2]] Group sizes and an interval beside every comparison. [[3]] The baseline next to the model, at the same list size. [[4]] Each finding labelled observed, adjusted, compared or tested, with verbs to match. [[5]] Results by segment. [[6]] A first page with the provenance line and what not to conclude. Then read every sentence and ask which number on the page supports it. If none does, the sentence goes. A fresh assistant session, handed only the draft and told to list every unsupported sentence, makes a cheap second reader.

visual.title: Brief and audit: six things a report must show
rows: Where did that number come from?
Group sizes and an interval by each comparison
Compared with what? Rule 246 of 711, model 321
Wording that matches the evidence tier

segments.narration: So before your name goes on a report, run the six checks, and send back any sentence that claims more than its evidence. One lesson is left: the whole course folded into a path you can walk with a question you have never seen.

visual.title: The report you can stand behind
items: Every number traces back to a computed result
Every claim uses the words its evidence has earned
The limits are on the first page

takeaways: Every number in the text is read from a computed result and carries its baseline, group size, interval and rows.
The verb matches the evidence tier: observed, adjusted, compared with an untreated group, or tested. Only a tested claim says reduces or drives.
Provenance and what not to conclude go on the first page; read the assistant's prose as critically as its code.

quiz.concept: the provenance line shows which rows a result was measured on
quiz.q: The assistant sends a new draft of the churn report. The headline looks better than last week's, and the provenance line reads: 'Model trained on January to March. Headline result scored on all 12,000 advertisers, January to June.' What is the right read?
options: Too coarse: six months are pooled, so the headline should be split month by month
Stale: a model trained on January to March is too old to be scored on June rows
Not a test result: the headline now includes the model's own training rows
Too uncertain: it needs an interval before it can be compared with last week's
quiz.why: A result counts only on rows the model never saw, and half of those 12,000 are the rows it learned from, so the headline flatters it. An interval or a month-by-month cut would not repair that: a tight interval around a number measured on training rows is still the wrong number, and scoring later months is exactly what a test should do. The provenance line is what let you see it.

quiz.q: The assistant's draft says: 'Optimisation reviews hurt performance: reviewed accounts hit their CPA goal 25 points less often. Recommend scaling reviews back.' The numbers are computed correctly. Which rewrite can you stand behind?
options: 'Optimisation reviews may hurt performance: reviewed accounts hit goal 25 points less often.'
'After adjusting for size, tenure and vertical, reviews lower the goal-hit rate by 25 points.'
'Reviews cause a 25-point drop in goal-hit rate (1,798 reviewed accounts against 5,218 not reviewed).'
'Reviewed accounts hit goal 25 points less often. Observed only: reviews go to struggling accounts.'
quiz.why: This is an observed gap, and reviews are given to accounts already in trouble, so it cannot show what a review does; in this simulated world the review actually helps by about 9 points. Adding 'may' keeps the causal verb and only sounds careful, and adjusting for the visible columns neither moves this gap nor turns it into a tested effect.

quiz.concept: numbers bound to results, never typed
quiz.q: A creative-fatigue report drafted by an assistant says: 'Video creatives lose half their CTR 40 percent faster than static ones.' A join that double-counted impressions has since been fixed, and the chart under that sentence, regenerated, now shows a much smaller gap. The report goes out tomorrow. What do you ask for?
options: Every number in the text read from the results by the script, then a full reread
That one sentence corrected by hand, so that it matches the regenerated chart
The earlier chart restored, so that the text and the chart agree with each other
A footnote under the chart, saying that figures quoted in the text are approximate
quiz.why: The sentence was typed around an earlier run, so nothing ties it to the results, and if one number went stale after the join was fixed, others probably did too. Correcting it by hand repairs today's symptom and sets the same trap for the next rerun; the request is for bound numbers, checked row counts, and a reread of every sentence.

quiz.concept: one overall claim hides the segments
quiz.q: The assistant's segment section reads: 'Performance is consistent across account sizes: the ranking score is 0.840 for small accounts, 0.825 for medium and 0.851 for large.' The success team will work the 400 highest scores. What must be added before you sign that sentence?
options: An interval on each of the three scores, to confirm that the sizes really are tied
For each size: the share of churners on the list, and the dollars they carry
The overall ranking score, so that readers can see the three segments agree with it
The same three scores on the training months, to rule out memorising
quiz.why: A ranking score is measured inside each segment; it says nothing about how one list of 400 is shared out between them. Here that list catches about 55 percent of small churners and about 25 percent of large ones, while large accounts are two thirds of the spend lost. 'Consistent' is true of the score and false of the thing the team will use, and intervals on the three scores would only confirm a tie that is beside the point.

review.concept: the verb must match the evidence tier

variants.q: A guided bid-setup panel went live for every finance advertiser in March; no other vertical got it. Finance's goal-hit rate rose 7 points from the eight weeks before to the eight weeks after. Over the same weeks the other verticals rose 3 points, and the two had moved in step before the launch. Which sentence belongs in the report?
options: The panel raised finance's goal-hit rate by 7 points: the rate before launch against the rate after.
The panel is associated with a higher goal-hit rate in finance; no more can be said without an experiment.
Finance rose 4 points more than verticals without the panel, assuming both would have moved together.
The panel causes a 4-point lift in goal-hit rate, which the comparison with the other verticals has proved.
variants.why: The change in the group that got the panel, minus the change in a similar group that did not, is stronger evidence than an adjusted gap and weaker than an experiment, so the sentence reports the difference between the two changes and names the assumption it rests on. Seven points credits the panel with what the season did for everyone. 'Causes' and 'proved' claim a coin flip that never happened, and retreating to 'associated with' throws away what the comparison group bought.

variants.q: A pricing team offered a lower minimum budget to a randomly chosen half of new advertisers. First-month activation was 4 points higher in that half, with an interval from 1 to 7 points. The assistant writes: 'A lower minimum budget is associated with higher activation.' What is the right edit?
options: Keep it and add 'a test is needed': cautious wording is the safe choice for any finding
Strengthen it: the lower minimum raised activation by about 4 points (1 to 7)
Weaken it: with an interval that wide, the difference may well be due to chance
Rewrite it around the two activation rates to more decimals, and drop the interval
variants.why: A coin decided who got the lower minimum, so hidden differences between advertisers are balanced across the two halves: this is the tested tier, and the causal verb has been earned, as long as it travels with its interval. Hedging a tested result throws away what the experiment bought, and the interval already excludes zero. The test has been run, so asking for one is not caution.

variants.q: After adjusting for the background columns in the table, advertisers on automated bidding churn about 4 points less than the rest. No experiment was run. Which sentence matches the evidence?
options: After adjusting for the background columns in the table, a gap of about 4 points remains
Automated bidding lowers churn by 4 points, controlling for confounders
Automated bidding has no real effect, because the raw gap shrank when adjusted
Automated bidding is the main driver of retention among the practices
variants.why: Adjusting removes only the differences the table can see; a trait that sits in no column can still be behind the gap, so the claim stays one tier below tested. 'Controlling for confounders' sounds rigorous, but it promises that all of them were controlled, which no table can guarantee.

review.concept: a sentence that can be checked: count, baseline, interval, rows

variants.q: An assistant's report on a ticket-routing model says: 'The language model classifies tickets with excellent accuracy.' Which replacement could survive a question?
options: 'It reaches 96.0 percent accuracy across all six categories, well ahead of every other method tried.'
'I read 40 of its labels myself and found only one or two that I would have changed.'
'Of 450 unseen test tickets it got 432 right (interval 93.8 to 97.5 percent); keyword rules got 131.'
'The language model is highly accurate in most categories, and its few errors are on tangled tickets.'
variants.why: A count on named rows, an interval and a baseline on the same tickets can each be checked; adjectives cannot. A decimal place looks precise but adds no evidence: a bare percentage still hides how many tickets, which tickets, and how far ahead of what. Forty labels read by hand is a count, but too few to carry an interval worth having, and with nothing beside it.

variants.q: A report for finance says: 'The model forecasts daily platform spend very accurately.' Which version can you stand behind?
options: 'The model follows the last two years of daily spend almost exactly, weekends and holidays included.'
'Twelve forecasts from past dates forward missed by about 3 percent a day; same weekday last week, 6.'
'Across the full history the model's error averages about 3 percent, far better than any naive method.'
'The model includes trend, weekday and holiday effects, which is why its forecasts can be relied on.'
variants.why: It says how the error was measured, from past dates forward and twelve times over, and puts the naive method's number beside it, so a reader can check both the test and the size of the gain. Following history closely, or a low error across the full history, is a score on days the model has already seen, and 'far better than any naive method' names no bar.

variants.q: An invalid-traffic report says: 'The new detector catches bad traffic far better than the old threshold.' Which rewrite is the strongest?
options: 'The new detector flagged 60 publishers last month, against 35 for the old threshold: 71 percent more.'
'The new detector's scores separate normal and suspicious publishers far more sharply than before.'
'Three analysts reviewed 20 of the new detector's flags and judged every one of them convincing.'
'Of 50 planted incidents the detector caught 44 and the threshold 29, with 9 and 31 false alerts.'
variants.why: Planted incidents have a known answer, so catches and false alerts can be counted for both methods on the same cases: a count, a baseline and the rows. Flagging more publishers is not evidence of catching more bad traffic; without known cases it may simply be more false alarms.

drill.q: A report says that a practice reduces churn. Which four tiers of evidence do you check that verb against, and which one earns it?
drill.a: Observed, adjusted, compared with a similar untreated group, and tested. Only tested, where a coin decided who got the change, earns reduces or drives. Observed is associated with, adjusted remains after adjusting, and compared rose more than the comparison group, assuming the two would have moved together.

drill.q: After a rerun, the chart in a report changed but the sentence under it did not. What went wrong, and what do you ask for so it cannot happen again?
drill.a: The number in the sentence was typed instead of read from the results. Ask for every number in the text to be inserted by the script from the same results file as the charts, with a list of where each one came from.

recall.prompt: A colleague is about to send out a model report that an assistant drafted. In thirty seconds, tell them what to check before it goes.
recall.model_answer: Check that every number in the text is read from the computed results, not typed, and that each comparison shows its group sizes, an interval and the baseline, on rows the model never saw. Check the verbs: an observed gap is associated with, an adjusted gap remains after adjusting, a change set against an untreated group rose more than the comparison group, and only a tested effect reduces or drives. Make sure results are shown by segment, and that the first page carries a provenance line and a plain statement of what the reader should not conclude. Then read the prose as critically as the code: any sentence no number supports comes out.

lessons.ask_assistant: For every report you draft for me: build it only from [the results file we checked in earlier stages]. Insert every number in the text from that file by code, and append a table matching each number in the prose to its source. Beside every comparison print both group sizes and a 95 percent interval. Put [the baseline] next to the model on the same unseen rows at the same list size, and break headline results out by [segments]. Tag each finding observed, adjusted, compared with an untreated group, or tested; use causal verbs only for tested ones. Open with a provenance line ([pull date, rows in and out, model version]) and what the report does not show.
audit_checklist: A source table at the end: every number in the prose matched to the computed result it was read from, with none missing
Both group sizes and an interval beside every comparison, and the baseline beside every model result, on the same unseen rows and at the same list size
Every finding tagged observed, adjusted, compared with an untreated group, or tested; no causal verb on an untested one, and each compared one states its assumption
A first page that opens with the provenance line (pull date, rows in and out, model version) and what not to conclude, with headline results broken out by segment
transfer: A creative-fatigue analysis: 'video fatigues faster' needs the number of creatives in each group, an interval, and a verb that fits an observed gap.
A spend forecast for finance: the error measured from past dates forward, the naive method's error beside it, and a range on the first page instead of a single figure.
An invalid-traffic review of publishers: the count of confirmed or planted cases each method caught, its false alerts, and how many clicks each publisher's rate rests on.

other_ways.approach: A one-page decision memo instead of a full report
other_ways.when: When the reader has one decision to make. It holds fewer numbers, and every one of them still needs its source, baseline, interval and tier.

other_ways.approach: A live dashboard fed by the results tables
other_ways.when: When the numbers must stay current without a rerun. Binding comes free, but the evidence tier and the limits have to be written onto the page as fixed text.

other_ways.approach: A second reader briefed to attack the draft: a colleague, or a fresh assistant session
other_ways.when: When the report feeds an expensive decision. Ask for a list of every sentence that no number on the page supports.

glossary.def: A number in the text that the script inserts from the computed results, so it cannot disagree with the chart beside it.
Prose that still quotes an earlier run's number after the analysis was rerun.

How a claim was established: observed (two groups differ), adjusted (they still differ with background columns held fixed, never ones the practice itself changes), compared (the change in a group that got something minus the change in a similar untreated group) or tested (a coin decided). It decides which verbs the sentence may use.
One line saying when the data was pulled, which rows were in and out, and which model version produced the results.

lessons.title: Choosing an approach: the playbook
lessons.subtitle: A question you have never seen arrives. What do you do in the first ten minutes?
lessons.goal: After this lesson you can take an unfamiliar question through nine questions, from the decision it feeds to how the result will be watched, and say whether it needs a model, a rule or a report.

predict.q: The design team can replace twenty creatives a week and asks which new ones will burn out fastest. Past creatives have a known ending. Which framing serves that decision best?
options: What the median creative lifetime is across all past launches
Which groups of similar creatives exist, found by clustering
Whether each creative fatigues within two weeks, yes or no
What the average CTR across all creatives will be next month
predict.reveal: The yes or no in a fixed window: a weekly list of twenty needs one score per creative to rank by, and a median lifetime describes the whole pool without ranking any creative in it. The lesson walks nine such choices through three problems no lesson worked through.

segments.narration: Monday morning. The head of creative strategy writes: can we predict which new creatives will burn out fastest? No lesson worked that problem through. Your assistant could put a model on your screen in ten minutes. Spend those ten minutes another way. Nine questions come before any code, and they are the same nine whatever the topic. To prove it, take two more requests from the same week. Supply wants publishers with suspicious traffic flagged. Support wants a forecast of next month's ticket volume. Three questions no lesson worked through. One path.

visual.title: Choosing an approach: the playbook
visual.sub: Nine questions for a problem you have never seen

segments.narration: Three questions frame the problem. [[1]] What decision does it feed? Say the design team can replace twenty creatives a week. The output is a ranked list of twenty. [[2]] What kind of problem is it? Past creatives have a known ending, so there is an answer column. Fatigued within two weeks, yes or no, is classification. Days until fatigue is time to event, with running creatives censored. For a weekly list, the yes or no is the simpler route. [[3]] What is one row, the target and the timeline? One creative, three days after launch. Fatigued means CTR down by half, if the room agrees. Features come only from those three days. Last week's launches have no label yet.

visual.title: Frame it: the first three questions

steps.label: 1 · What decision?
steps.sub: who acts, and on how many

steps.label: 2 · What kind of problem?
steps.sub: answer column? category, number, time, or a change?

steps.label: 3 · Row, target, timeline?
steps.sub: what is known when; has the outcome had time?

segments.narration: The same questions sort the other two requests, and question four gives each a bar to beat. [[1]] Creatives: classification, against the rule the team already uses on day three: the twenty whose CTR has fallen most since launch. [[2]] Suspicious publishers: nobody recorded which ones were bad, so there is no answer column. That makes it anomaly detection. Define normal, measure distance from it, choose a cut-off. The baseline is the threshold someone already eyeballs. [[3]] Ticket volume: time is the main axis, so it is forecasting, and the baseline is the same weekday last week. So before any model exists, each problem has a cheap method on the board.

visual.title: Question 4: every problem gets a bar to beat
rows: The team's day-three rule: the twenty steepest CTR drops

segments.narration: Question five: how will we know it worked, and on which rows? The decision picks the measure. [[1]] A list of twenty is judged by how many of the twenty fatigued, next to the rule's twenty. [[2]] A publisher flag trades precision against recall, because a wrongly suspended partner and a missed fraud cost different money. [[3]] A staffing forecast is judged in tickets, with a range. The rows are ones the method never saw, split the way it will be used: later creatives, planted incidents, forecasts from past dates forward. Question six: simplest model first. Something more flexible stays only if its gain is bigger than the noise. Otherwise the cheaper method wins.

visual.title: Question 5: the decision picks the measure
rows: Fatigued in the top twenty, model vs rule
Recall on planted incidents; precision from hand-checked flags
Error in tickets, with a range
visual.note: Question 6: simplest model first. Complexity stays only if its gain is bigger than the noise.

segments.narration: The last three are about trust. [[1]] Who does it fail? Cut every result by segment. A fatigue model can score well overall and still miss every video creative. [[2]] Is this a prediction, or a claim about cause? Which creatives will fatigue is a prediction. Whether shorter headlines slow fatigue is a question about changing something. No model weight answers that. A test does. [[3]] How will it be used and watched? Name who acts and what they do. Leave a random slice untouched, so the action can be measured. Then track predicted against actual by segment, knowing the labels arrive late.

visual.title: Trust it: the last three questions

steps.label: 8 · Prediction or cause?
steps.sub: a weight is not an effect; a test is

segments.narration: Sometimes the path ends early, and that is a result, not a failure. [[1]] A rule or a report already answers it. If the team's rule clears the bar, or a plain GROUP BY shows where the tickets pile up, ship that. [[2]] There are too few examples. A handful of confirmed bad publishers cannot teach a model a pattern that repeats. Use a rule, review by hand, and start recording outcomes. [[3]] Nobody will act on the output. Ask who does what differently on Tuesday. If the answer is nobody, stop.

visual.title: When not to use ML
items: A rule or a report already answers it
Too few examples to learn from
Nobody will act on the output

segments.narration: Three duties come with using it. [[1]] A column can stand in for something you should not decide on. If the publisher flag leans on country, it has stopped judging traffic and started judging where someone is based. The check is one you know: cut the results by segment, this time by the groups that could be treated unfairly. [[2]] Client data stays in tools approved for it. That covers rows pasted into an assistant, and ticket text sent to an outside model. [[3]] A model in use changes the data it learns from next. Replace every flagged creative and you never see which ones would have fatigued. Keep the untouched slice.

visual.title: Using it responsibly
items: Columns that stand in for something you should not decide on
Client data stays in approved tools
A model in use changes the data it learns from

segments.narration: Brief and audit, one last time. Do not ask for a model yet. Ask for a one-page plan before any code, and check the page for five things. [[1]] The decision, and who acts on it. [[2]] The kind of problem, with one other framing it considered. [[3]] One row, the target and the timeline, a sentence each. [[4]] The baseline, the measure and the held-out rows, fixed in advance, with a stop condition: the result at which the rule is enough. [[5]] How it will be trusted: the segments to cut by, prediction or cause, the slice left untouched. Often the best first request is smaller still: the baseline and the scoreboard, no model, so you learn what the cheap method scores. Then stages, gates, and evidence in the output, as always.

visual.title: Brief and audit: the one-page plan
items: The decision, and who acts on it
The kind of problem, plus one other framing
One row, the target, the timeline
Baseline, measure, held-out rows, stop condition: fixed in advance
Trust: segments to cut by, prediction or cause, untouched slice

segments.narration: You will forget some of the numbers, so keep the nine questions and the habit of asking what the output shows, and use them on the unframed question already in your inbox. When you want more, the names to look for are recommendation, deeper causal methods and deep learning.

visual.title: The course on one page
visual.note: Where next, by name: recommendation · deeper causal methods · deep learning

takeaways: Nine questions fit any problem: frame it, score it, then decide whether to trust it.
The question picks the kind of problem, the decision picks the measure, and the cheapest method that clears the bar wins.
Stop when a rule or a report is enough; mind stand-in columns, client data, and models that reshape their own data.

quiz.concept: the question picks the kind of problem
quiz.q: Supply asks you to flag publishers with suspicious traffic. Nobody has ever recorded which publishers turned out to be bad. The assistant proposes: 'I will train a classifier to predict fraud and report its accuracy.' What is the right read?
options: Ask for precision and recall too: flagging is yes or no, so classification fits
Better: cluster the publishers and treat the smallest cluster as the fraud
No answer column: define normal, set a cut-off, check planted cases and hand-review flags
Have a language model label each publisher, then train the classifier on its labels
quiz.why: A classifier needs past cases with a known answer, and there are none, so this is a question about what is unusual: say what normal looks like, measure distance from it, and choose the cut-off as a trade between precision and recall: planted incidents show what it catches, and a person reviewing a sample of flagged publishers shows how many flags are false alarms. Better measures cannot rescue a classifier with nothing to learn from. Clustering always returns groups, and nothing makes the smallest one fraud; a language model's guesses are not known outcomes either.

quiz.q: The assistant's one-page plan for a lead-scoring model reads: 'Decision: sales calls the 50 best new leads each week. Row: one lead on the day it arrives. Target: paying customer within 90 days. Train: leads up to June. Test: leads from October on, whose 90 days have passed. Baseline: the current rule, company size above 200. Measure: accuracy on the test leads.' Which line has to change?
options: The test: recent leads are few, so a random split of all the leads is safer
The measure: count customers in the top 50, model against rule, on the same leads
The baseline: a hand rule is too weak, so compare with a second model instead
The target: 90 days is a long wait, so use whether the lead replied to an email
quiz.why: The decision is a list of 50, so the proof is how many of a top 50 became customers, next to the rule's 50; accuracy mostly rewards saying no to everyone when few leads convert. The time-ordered test with its gap and the hand-rule baseline are exactly right, and swapping the target for a quicker stand-in would change the question being answered.

quiz.concept: the cheapest method that clears the bar wins
quiz.q: Support operations ask for 'an ML forecast' of next month's ticket volume, for staffing. In twelve backtests from past dates, the average of the last four same weekdays stayed inside the error the staffing plan can absorb. A model with calendar effects did slightly better on average, but it won only about half the backtests and the interval on the difference between the two crossed zero. What do you recommend?
options: Use the four-week average, show the comparison, and re-test when the pattern shifts
Use the model: a lower average error is a lower error, however small the difference
Try a more flexible model: a gain that small means the first one was too simple
Average the two forecasts, so that neither method's mistakes can dominate the plan
quiz.why: The simple method already clears the bar the decision sets, and the model's edge is inside the noise, which makes it a tie; a tie goes to the cheaper method. Reaching for more flexibility treats 'use ML' as the goal, when the goal was a staffing plan that holds.

quiz.concept: a model in use changes the data it learns from
quiz.q: A creative-fatigue model has been live for two months, and every creative it flags is replaced early. The assistant's monitoring note says: 'Precision has collapsed: almost none of the flagged creatives went on to fatigue. Recommend retraining on the last two months.' What is the right read?
options: Retrain, but on the last six months, so that two odd months cannot dominate the model
Raise the cut-off, so that only the most certain creatives are flagged from now on
The model was overfitted from the start; replace it with a simpler one and re-test
Replaced creatives could not fatigue; judge the model on the untouched random slice
quiz.why: Acting on the list removed the outcome: a creative replaced early never gets the chance to fatigue, so 'did not fatigue' is no evidence that the flag was wrong. Retraining on those rows, two months of them or six, would teach the model that its own flags mean safe. The untouched random slice is the one place where prediction and outcome can still be compared.

review.concept: the question picks the kind of problem

variants.q: The pricing team asks: 'What happens to activation if we lower the minimum budget?' The assistant offers to train a model that predicts activation from account columns, including each advertiser's current minimum. What kind of problem is this?
options: Classification: activation is yes or no, and the weight on the minimum is the answer
A question about a change: it needs a randomised test, not a model's weight
Regression: predict the activation rate at each budget level and pick the best
Clustering: group advertisers by their minimum and compare activation by group
variants.why: 'What happens if we change it' is a question about cause. A predictive model's weight only describes which advertisers had low minimums and activated, and those advertisers may differ in ways no column records. Randomising who gets the lower minimum is the design that removes that hidden difference.

variants.q: Product asks: 'How long does a newly launched campaign typically keep running?' Half of the campaigns launched in the past year are still live. The assistant averages the run time of the campaigns that have ended. What is the right framing?
options: Regression: predict run time from the campaigns that have already ended
Classification: label each campaign as ended or live, and report the share
Forecasting: project the monthly count of live campaigns forward in time
Time to event: a campaign still live counts as running at least this long
variants.why: Campaigns that have not ended yet are censored: dropping them, whether to average or to fit a regression, keeps only the short ones and understates the typical run. A survival curve uses every campaign for as long as it was watched, while an ended-or-live label ignores how long each one has had in which to end.

variants.q: The research team has four thousand free-text answers from an advertiser survey and asks: 'What are people telling us?' There is no category column. What is a sound first framing?
options: Classification: train a model to predict the category of each answer
Anomaly detection: flag the answers that look least like all the others
No answer column: embed the answers, cluster them, read samples per group
Forecasting: project how many answers the next survey is likely to collect
variants.why: With no labels there is nothing for a classifier to learn from. Embeddings turn the answers into a table, clustering proposes themes, and reading examples from each group is how you check the groups mean something, because clustering always returns groups. Unusual answers and future counts are different questions.

review.concept: the cheapest method that clears the bar wins

variants.q: For an upsell list, a boosted model finds 3 more adopters in its top 200 than a simple weighted-sum model. The interval on that difference runs from 9 fewer to 15 more. The boosted model needs tuning and is harder to explain. Which do you ship?
options: The boosted model: it found more adopters on the test rows, and that is the measure
The boosted model, once more tuning has made the gap on the test rows clearer
Neither: two models landing this close together means the test itself is broken
The simple model: the gap is inside the noise, which makes the comparison a tie
variants.why: An interval that includes zero means the two models cannot be told apart on this test, and a tie goes to the one that is cheaper to run and to explain. Tuning until the gap looks bigger on the same test rows just fits the test.

variants.q: An analyst has 14 publishers confirmed as fraudulent and several thousand that nobody has reviewed. The assistant offers to train a boosted classifier on the 14. What is the better plan?
options: Train it: a flexible model makes the most of a small number of cases
Copy the 14 cases many times to balance the classes, and then train
A simple rule plus manual review, while confirmed outcomes are recorded
Train on the 14, then check the model by scoring those same 14 cases
variants.why: Fourteen positives are too few to learn a pattern that repeats on new publishers: a flexible model will memorise their quirks, and copying rows adds no information. A rule with human review does the job now and produces the labelled cases a model would need later.

variants.q: A sales director asks for 'a machine-learning model of which verticals are furthest from their CPA goals'. The table holds CPA versus goal and vertical for every tracked advertiser. What do you build?
options: A report: goal-hit rate by vertical, with group sizes and intervals
A decision tree, so that the verticals are split in order of importance
A clustering of advertisers, to rediscover the verticals from behaviour
A boosted model, reporting its importance score for the vertical column
variants.why: The question is about what is happening now, in groups you can already name, so a GROUP BY with sizes and intervals answers it completely: the lowest rung of the ladder. A model would add prediction machinery to a question that asks for none.

drill.q: A question you have never worked on lands on your desk. Before any code is written, what do you pin down first?
drill.a: The decision it feeds, the kind of problem, and what one row is, with its target and timeline. Then the baseline, and how you will know it worked and on which rows.

drill.q: Name three situations in which you should not reach for machine learning.
drill.a: When a rule or a report already answers the question, when there are too few examples of the outcome to learn from, and when nobody will act on the output.

recall.prompt: A colleague has been handed a question they have never modelled before. In thirty seconds, walk them through the path.
recall.model_answer: Start with the decision the answer feeds, then name the kind of problem and pin down one row, the target and the timeline. Set a baseline and decide how you will know it worked, on which unseen rows, before anything is built. Try the simplest model first and keep complexity only if its gain is bigger than the noise; then ask who it fails, whether you are predicting or claiming a cause, and how it will be used and watched. If a rule or a report clears the bar, stop there.

lessons.ask_assistant: Before any code, draft a one-page plan for [the question as asked]. State the decision it feeds and who acts, on [how many cases, how often]. Name the kind of problem, one other framing you considered, and whether it predicts or claims a cause. Define one row, the target with its [outcome window], and when each feature is known. Fix the simplest baseline ([today's rule or report]), the measure that matches the decision, and exactly which rows are held out. Say which [segments] results will be cut by and which random slice stays untouched. End with the result at which we stop at the baseline, and any column standing in for [something we must not decide on].
audit_checklist: Frame: the decision with who acts and on how many cases; the kind of problem with one other framing considered; one row, the target and the timeline, a sentence each
Score: the baseline, the measure tied to the decision and the exact held-out rows are written in the plan before any model is fitted, and every later result repeats them unchanged
Trust: the segments every result will be cut by, a line saying prediction or claim about cause, and the random slice nobody acts on
Stop: the result, as a number, at which the baseline rule or report is enough, with any column that could stand in for something we must not decide on
transfer: Which leads should sales call first? A ranked list for a fixed number of calls, judged against the rule sales uses today, on leads whose outcome window has passed.
Should the minimum bid for a new placement go up? A question about changing something: the path ends in a randomised test, not in a predictive model.
How much will each client spend next quarter? A number per client, where run-rate is the bar to beat and the error measure depends on what a miss costs finance.

other_ways.approach: Start from a solved neighbour: adapt the plan of a past project whose row, target and decision look most like this one
other_ways.when: When the new question is an old one in different clothes. Still answer the nine questions, because the timeline and the cost of a miss rarely carry over unchanged.

other_ways.approach: Baseline and test only: build the rule and the scoreboard, and no model yet
other_ways.when: When you doubt the question is worth a model. A week later you know what the cheap method scores, and whether there is a gap for a model to close.
