A column that is 0 before a named date and 1 from it on, which lets a model learn a new level instead of blending it with the old one.
The result, agreed in advance, at which the baseline rule or report is good enough and no model gets built.
Learning from past rows that have an answer column, the label: classification and regression are both supervised.

The share of customers still active after each week of tenure: a cohort retention table pooled across join months, estimated by the Kaplan–Meier method so that every customer counts for as long as they were watched.
Rows held back from training and used only to judge the model; also called a hold-out.
The nine questions asked of any new problem, in order: frame it, score it, then decide whether to trust it.
Training on earlier periods and testing on later ones, to rehearse how the model will be used.
Framing a question as how long until something happens, instead of whether it happens within a fixed window.
The check for every column: could this exact value have been computed on the snapshot date, using only data up to then?
The K highest-scoring rows: a list sized by what the team can handle, judged against what a random list of that size would hold.
Predicted total divided by actual total, minus one: the measure that matters when predictions are summed.
The difference between a model's score on its training rows and on rows it has never seen; the tell of memorising.
A scikit-learn helper that divides rows into training and test sets, at random unless told otherwise.
Adjusting a model until its outputs line up with the known labels of past rows.
The slow, persistent rise or fall of a series underneath its ups and downs.
A Python block that catches an error and lets the script carry on, which can hide a failed step.
Fit one model on those who got the action and one on those who did not, then rank by the gap between the two predictions.
Predict the chance something happens and its size if it does, then multiply: for spend, the chance of staying times the spend if they stay.
The typical value is the middle one, half above and half below; with a few very large values, the average sits above it.
A model too simple to hold the pattern: it scores poorly on training rows and new rows alike.
Finding structure in rows with no answer column, such as clustering and anomaly detection. Reinforcement learning, learning by trial and reward, is a third family this course does not cover.
A random slice of the list that nobody acts on, kept so the model can still be judged fairly once the team starts acting.
A random part of the list that nobody acts on, kept so that the action and the model can still be measured.
The change in an advertiser's chance of an outcome caused by acting on them: the chance without the action minus the chance with it.
Rows held out of training and used to compare settings or versions, so that the test set stays untouched.
How much the prediction changes per unit of a column, with the other columns held fixed; also called a coefficient.
How many points one step of a column adds to or takes off the total, with the other columns held fixed.
Asking a language model to label text from instructions alone, with no training examples.

items.q: In one sentence, what is the difference between a rule you write by hand and a machine learning model?
items.a: They are the same kind of thing. In a model, the columns, the cut-offs and the weights are chosen by checking against past cases with known outcomes, instead of being chosen by you.

items.q: A model reproduces almost every known outcome in the table it was trained on. Why is that not good news yet?
items.a: Because matching the past is easy. The test that counts is how the frozen model does on rows it has never seen.

items.q: What are the four triage questions for working out which kind of problem you are facing?
items.a: Is there an answer column for past cases. Is the answer a category or a number. Is time the main axis. And do I want to predict it, or change it.

items.q: There is a ladder of four ways to answer a business question, from simplest to most complex. Name the rungs, and the rule for climbing.
items.a: A report, a rule, a simple model, a complex model. Climb a rung only when the one below has been tried and is not good enough for the decision.

items.q: What three things does a label definition have to pin down before anyone builds a model?
items.a: What exactly counts as the outcome. Who, meaning what one row is and which rows are eligible. And when, meaning a snapshot date, with features from before it and the outcome from a fixed window after it.

items.q: Churn means no spend at all in the sixty days after a snapshot. An advertiser has not spent in the three weeks since theirs. Why can you not label them yet?
items.a: Because their outcome window has not closed. They may be gone for good or only pausing, and nobody can tell which until the sixty days are up. Call them churned and the rate runs too high. Call them stayed and it runs too low.

items.q: What is leakage, and why does a model with a leak fail once it goes live?
items.a: Leakage is a feature recorded after the moment of prediction, so it carries the answer. The model looks brilliant on past data, but on scoring day that future value does not exist yet.

items.q: What is the time-travel test for a feature?
items.a: Ask whether you could have computed that exact value on the snapshot date, using only data up to that date. If not, or if you are not sure, the column stays out.

items.q: Why not ask an AI assistant for the model and the report in a single prompt?
items.a: Because everything arrives at once, and an early mistake is buried under everything built on it. Working in stages gives you one small output to check before the next step starts.

items.q: What goes into the audit block that every output should end with?
items.a: Row counts after every step and the date range. From stage two, the label rate. From stage three, the list of features with where each came from and the latest date it used, and the baseline next to the model.

items.q: Someone tells you a model is ninety percent accurate. Which two questions do you ask before reacting?
items.a: Measured on which rows: ones the model never saw, from a later period? And compared with what: what does the simplest baseline score on those same rows?

items.q: Why leave a gap month between the training months and the test months?
items.a: Because the label takes sixty days to appear. On the day you score a new month, the month just before it has no finished answers yet, so training on it would use information you would not have.

items.q: Why can a model that is ninety-five percent accurate be useless?
items.a: Because accuracy counts every row the same. If only five cases in a hundred are positive, answering no to everything is already ninety-five percent accurate and finds nothing. Always compare accuracy with the do-nothing guess.

items.q: What is the difference between precision and recall?
items.a: Precision starts from the flagged list: of those flagged, how many were right. Recall starts from the real cases: of all the real ones, how many were flagged. Same numerator, different denominator.

items.q: A model gives every customer a score between zero and one. Who decides where the cut-off goes, and how?
items.a: You do, not the model. Usually by capacity: sort by score and take as many as the team can handle. The halfway line is only a default in the code.

items.q: What does an AUC of zero point eight five mean in plain words, and what does it not tell you?
items.a: Pick one churner and one stayer at random: eighty-five times in a hundred, the churner has the higher score. It measures ranking only. It does not tell you how good the top of the list is, or whether the scores are right as percentages.

items.q: A model ranks customers well. Does that mean you can trust its percentages?
items.a: No. Ranking only needs the order to be right. Every score could be too low or too high and the order would be the same. Check the percentages separately, by comparing predicted with actual in score buckets on rows the model never saw.

items.q: When does it matter that a model's percentages are right, and when does it not?
items.a: It matters whenever the score is used as a number: multiplied by money, or compared with a cut-off stated in percent. It does not matter when you only sort and take the top of the list.

items.q: Two models have the same average miss, but one has a much higher root mean squared error. What does that tell you about it?
items.a: It makes a few very large misses. Squaring makes big misses count far more, so its root mean squared error climbs while its average miss stays the same.

items.q: Per-customer predictions are going to be added up into a revenue forecast. Besides the average miss, which number do you ask for, and why?
items.a: Predicted total against actual total. The average miss ignores direction, so misses that all lean low can look small for each customer and still leave the total far short.

items.q: Two random groups of advertisers, treated exactly the same, show different churn rates. Why, and what does group size have to do with it?
items.a: Every rate measured on a sample wobbles by chance, and small groups wobble most. To halve the wobble you need about four times as many advertisers.

items.q: Someone shows you a jump in a metric for one small segment. What two things do you ask for before looking for a cause?
items.a: How many advertisers are in the segment, and an interval around the jump. If zero is inside the interval, the data cannot tell the jump from chance.

items.q: What is a linear regression, and how are its weights chosen?
items.a: A weighted sum: a base amount, plus each column multiplied by its own weight. The weights are the ones that make the squared misses on the training rows as small as possible.

items.q: A model fitted on the log of spend is turned back into dollars and added up into a revenue total. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
items.a: A log model predicts the typical account, and a few very large accounts pull the average above the typical, so the total runs low. Correct the predictions to averages before adding them up, and check the predicted total against the actual one.

items.q: A logistic regression gives one column a large weight. What do you need to know before you can say what that weight means?
items.a: Its unit, meaning one standard deviation or yes versus no, and what it does to the predicted probability in points. Even then it describes an association, not what happens if you change the column.

items.q: Someone tells you a column has an odds ratio of one half, so it halves the chance of churn. What is wrong with that?
items.a: Odds are not probabilities. Halving the odds moves the probability by an amount that depends on where the advertiser started, so ask for the shift in probability points.

items.q: Someone shows you a decision tree. How do you read what it predicts for one advertiser?
items.a: Start at the top and answer each yes or no question for that advertiser until you reach a leaf. The leaf's rate, the share of training advertisers there who churned, is the prediction.

items.q: What does a small decision tree give up in exchange for being readable?
items.a: Fine-grained scores. Everyone in a leaf gets the same score, so a tree with a few leaves cannot order the advertisers inside a leaf, and that can cost it on ranking.

items.q: A report's headline rate is far from the number on your dashboard, and nothing crashed. What do you ask the assistant for first?
items.a: A table of row counts, distinct advertisers and the label rate after every step, to see where rows were dropped, multiplied or deleted.

items.q: Why is it dangerous to drop every row that has a missing value?
items.a: Because a value is usually missing for a reason. The rows you lose can be one particular kind of customer, so the result describes a different population, and a model trained on it has never seen the people you dropped.

items.q: Name the six parts of a modelling script, in order.
items.a: Load the table, choose the features and the label, split into training and test rows, prepare the columns, fit on the training rows, and score on the test rows.

items.q: A script reports a single, very high score. What is the first thing you check, and where?
items.a: Which rows the score was computed on. Go to the scoring line near the end and see whether it uses the test rows or the same rows the model was fitted on.

items.q: A model scores perfectly on the rows it was trained on. Why is that not good news by itself?
items.a: Because a flexible model can memorise its training rows, accidents included. Only its score on rows it has never seen tells you whether it learned a pattern.

items.q: One model has a wide gap between its training score and its test score. Another has almost none. Which do you choose?
items.a: Whichever scores better on the test rows. The gap is a warning to look closer, not the verdict, and a model with no gap can simply be too simple.

items.q: Why can you not use the test set to choose a model's settings?
items.a: Because choosing is a form of learning. Pick the best of several scores on the test rows and the choice is fitted to those rows, so the score flatters and nothing untouched is left to report.

items.q: Your table has one row per advertiser per month. What must cross-validation do differently?
items.a: Keep all of an advertiser's rows on the same side of every fold, and check on later months than it trains on. Otherwise a flexible model is rewarded for recognising advertisers it has already seen.

items.q: In a sentence each, how does a forest differ from boosting?
items.a: A forest grows many deep trees on different random samples and averages them, so their individual mistakes cancel. Boosting grows small trees one after another, each fitted to what the earlier ones still get wrong.

items.q: A colleague asks which is the better model, boosting or a simple weighted sum. What is the honest answer?
items.a: It depends on the shape of the pattern, which you cannot know beforehand. Run both on the same test rows and compare the gap with the noise, and pay for the complex one only if the gap is real and big enough to matter.

items.q: Your model's score has stalled, and someone suggests switching to a more powerful algorithm. What question should come first?
items.a: Ask what the model is not being shown. In this course's churn data, changing the columns moved the score about twice as far as the whole range of algorithms did, and more rows promised little. New information is often the cheaper experiment, and you measure each rather than assume.

items.q: What two things must be true of a column before it can be used as a feature?
items.a: It must be computable on the snapshot date, using only data up to then. And it must actually exist on the day you score. If either fails, it is a leak, or a column the live model will never receive.

items.q: A column's importance comes out close to zero. Give the two possible explanations, and say how you would tell them apart.
items.a: Either the column really carries no useful signal, or another column carries the same signal and covers for it. To tell them apart, shuffle the related columns together as a group, or test the column on its own.

items.q: A model lists stale creatives as the top reason an advertiser is high risk. What does that reason tell you, and what does it not tell you?
items.a: It tells you why the model's score is high: that value pushed the arithmetic up. It does not tell you that refreshing the creatives would keep the advertiser. That is a question about cause, and it needs different evidence.

items.q: A model has a strong overall score. Why is that not enough before you hand its list to the business?
items.a: Because one overall score is an average. It can hide a segment where the list catches far fewer cases, and that may be the segment that matters most in money. So you ask for the same results cut by the segments the business cares about.

items.q: You can sort a risk list by probability, or by probability times spend. Which one is correct?
items.a: Neither is correct in itself. Sorting by probability reaches more of the customers who leave. Sorting by probability times spend reaches more of the money. Which you want depends on the action and what it costs, so it is a decision someone should make on purpose.

items.q: A dashboard shows that advertisers who use some feature do better than those who do not. Before anyone recommends the feature, what is the first question to ask?
items.a: Ask who chooses that feature, or who is given it. If those advertisers differ in ways that also affect the outcome, the gap mixes the feature's effect with who uses it. It can be too big, empty, or even backwards.

items.q: Why can adjusting for other columns not turn a gap between groups into a proven effect?
items.a: Because you can only adjust for what is in the table. If the real common cause was never recorded, the adjusted number still carries it, and nothing in the output tells you how much.

items.q: Why does flipping a coin for who gets a change let you read the difference in outcomes as the effect of that change?
items.a: Because the coin knows nothing about the advertisers, every trait, recorded or not, ends up spread about equally over both groups. The only systematic difference left is the change itself, so the gap is its effect, give or take noise.

items.q: You randomised an offer, and only some of the people who got the offer took it up. Which two groups do you compare?
items.a: Everyone who was offered against everyone who was not, whatever they did next. Comparing only those who took it up brings back the problem of people choosing for themselves.

items.q: A feature launched for one group of advertisers and their results improved afterwards. Why is the before and after difference not the effect of the feature?
items.a: Because other things changed over the same weeks, such as the season. You need the change in a similar group that did not get the feature, and you subtract it from the change in the group that did.

items.q: When you use a comparison group to judge a launch, what has to be true of the two groups, and how do you check it?
items.a: They must have been moving in parallel, so that without the launch the gap between them would have stayed steady. You check the weeks before launch. If the gap was already drifting, the estimate is contaminated.

items.q: Why is the list of accounts most likely to churn not automatically the best list to call?
items.a: Because many of them will leave whatever you do, and many others would have stayed anyway. A call only pays where it changes the outcome, and that is a different ranking.

items.q: What kind of data do you need before you can estimate who is changed by an action, and why?
items.a: Data where the action was assigned at random, so the people who got it and the people who did not are alike. Otherwise the difference between them mixes the action's effect with whoever was chosen.

items.q: A model gives each account a probability of leaving. How do you decide the cut-off for who gets contacted?
items.a: Work out what a contact costs and what it is worth on average when the account really is leaving. Contact every account whose own probability is above the cost divided by that worth, up to what the team can handle.

items.q: Why is it a mistake to keep extending a contact list for as long as its overall hit rate stays above break-even?
items.a: Because the average is held up by the strong names at the top. The test applies to the next account's own probability, and at the bottom of the list each extra contact loses money.

items.q: A model's overall score has not moved since launch. Why is that not enough to say it is still working?
items.a: Because an overall score can hide one segment that has gone badly wrong. Compare predicted with actual outcomes segment by segment, with the group sizes and margins.

items.q: Your labels take two months to arrive. What can you watch in the meantime, and what will it miss?
items.a: The inputs and the share of accounts the model flags. They catch a broken pipeline or a changing mix, but not a change in how the inputs relate to the outcome. Only the labels show that.

items.q: Before any forecasting model is built, which simple forecasts should you ask for, and why?
items.a: The same weekday last week, and the average of the last few of that weekday. They are the bar: a model that cannot beat them is not worth having.

items.q: A forecast has the trend and the weekly rhythm right, but its worst month is twice as bad as its average month. What is probably missing?
items.a: The known events: holidays, promotions, launches. The rhythm of the data cannot tell a model those dates are special, so you have to supply them.

items.q: Why is testing a flexible forecasting model on randomly held-out days too kind to it?
items.a: Because each held-out day sits between days the model trained on, so it can fill in the gap. The real job is to predict beyond the end of the data, so test from a past date forward.

items.q: A forecast comes with a range built from its own past errors. What kind of day does that range not cover?
items.a: Any kind it has not seen: an outage, a sudden change in level, something new. For those you need scenarios, not a slightly wider band.

items.q: An alert fires whenever a daily number moves more than a fixed percentage from the day before. Why is that a poor alert for a metric with a weekly rhythm, and what should it compare with instead?
items.a: Every weekend looks like a big move, so it fires constantly, and a real problem at a weekend can look normal. Compare each day with what is expected for that weekday, or with a forecast.

items.q: Nobody has labelled past incidents. How do you find out what an anomaly detector would miss?
items.a: Plant incidents of known size and length in a copy of the history, then count how many it catches and how many false alarms it raises.

items.q: Why does averaging the lifetimes of customers who have already left understate how long customers last?
items.a: Because it leaves out everyone who is still active, and those are the ones lasting longest. You end up averaging the quick leavers.

items.q: You want the share of customers who churn within six months of joining. Which customers may you count?
items.a: Only those who joined at least six months ago, so the window has fully closed. Counting newer customers treats not yet as no, and the rate comes out too low.

items.q: A clustering comes back with five neat customer segments. Why is that, on its own, not evidence that five kinds of customer exist?
items.a: Because the method returns as many groups as you ask for, every time, whatever the data looks like. Believe them only if they come back from a different random start and on fresh data, and beat a plain GROUP BY on an outcome they never saw.

items.q: Why do columns need a common scale before you measure how similar two rows are?
items.a: Because distance adds up differences across columns, so a column in thousands of dollars drowns columns measured in single digits. Without a common scale you are grouping by the biggest unit, not by behaviour.

items.q: In a sentence or two, what is an embedding?
items.a: A list of numbers that a model produces for a piece of text, placed so that texts with similar meanings get similar numbers. Once you have it, text behaves like any other table of numeric columns.

items.q: Why can an embedding search find a support ticket that a keyword search misses?
items.a: Because customers describe the same problem in different words. A keyword matches spelling. An embedding places texts by meaning, so two tickets about the same problem sit close together even with no words in common.

items.q: A language model sorts support tickets from instructions alone, with no training. How do you find out how good it is?
items.a: The same way as for any model. Score it on labelled tickets it has not seen, next to a baseline such as guessing, with an interval, and broken down by category and by easy versus hard tickets.

items.q: Two models label the same tickets and disagree on some of them. What is that disagreement good for?
items.a: It is a cheap flag for human review. The tickets where two models disagree tend to be the hard, ambiguous ones, so send those to a person. Agreement is not proof, though: two models can be wrong together.

items.q: A report says that a practice reduces churn. Which four tiers of evidence do you check that verb against, and which one earns it?
items.a: Observed, adjusted, compared with a similar untreated group, and tested. Only tested, where a coin decided who got the change, earns reduces or drives. Observed is associated with, adjusted remains after adjusting, and compared rose more than the comparison group, assuming the two would have moved together.

items.q: After a rerun, the chart in a report changed but the sentence under it did not. What went wrong, and what do you ask for so it cannot happen again?
items.a: The number in the sentence was typed instead of read from the results. Ask for every number in the text to be inserted by the script from the same results file as the charts, with a list of where each one came from.

items.q: A question you have never worked on lands on your desk. Before any code is written, what do you pin down first?
items.a: The decision it feeds, the kind of problem, and what one row is, with its target and timeline. Then the baseline, and how you will know it worked and on which rows.

items.q: Name three situations in which you should not reach for machine learning.
items.a: When a rule or a report already answers the question, when there are too few examples of the outcome to learn from, and when nobody will act on the output.
